units.title: Short fiction I
units.description: Observe details, build warranted inferences, and explain how a story works.

units.title: Poetry I
units.description: Read a speaker’s situation through language, images, and the movement of a poem.

units.title: Longer fiction & drama I
units.description: Connect character, conflict, and structure to an interpretation beyond plot summary.

units.title: Short fiction II
units.description: Examine relationships, narrative perspective, and the distance between telling and knowing.

units.title: Poetry II
units.description: Hear and see how syntax, lineation, sound, and figurative patterns shape meaning.

units.title: Longer fiction & drama II
units.description: Trace layered structures, theatrical choices, and the pressures of a social world.

units.title: Short fiction III
units.description: Test ambiguity, omission, symbolic patterns, and the ethical limits of interpretation.

units.title: Poetry III
units.description: Interpret the tensions among form, voice, address, and competing meanings.

units.title: Longer fiction & drama III
units.description: Build and revise a sustained whole-work interpretation that accounts for complication.

lessons.definition: Close reading is a repeated movement between particular words and a developing account of the text. Begin with what is present: a repetition, a qualification, an image, an interruption, or a change in emphasis. Then ask what that choice does in its immediate situation. A detail becomes evidence when you explain its relation to a claim; underlining many devices is not yet interpretation.
lessons.importance: Your first response is useful, but it is provisional. A passage that initially sounds affectionate may also reveal control. Close reading lets you explain this tension without replacing the text with a general opinion about marriage, illness, or society. It also gives you a way to reject an attractive MCQ answer: test its whole claim against the words, including the words it overlooks.
steps: Read once for the literal situation: who writes, where she is, and who makes decisions. Put a question mark beside information the narrator does not establish.
On a second reading, connect the repeated questions about what one can do with the later descriptions of schedules and direction. Explain the relationship rather than merely naming repetition.
Write a sentence that holds two details together. Then reread a detail that could complicate it: the narrator calls John loving even as she describes his restrictions.

worked.observation: The narrator calls John “very careful and loving” and immediately says he “hardly lets me stir without special direction.”
worked.inference: Care and restriction are intertwined in her account.
worked.commentary: The adjoining clauses make affection difficult to separate from supervision. Her later feeling of ingratitude suggests that the language of care also shapes how she judges her own resistance.
worked.qualification: This describes the tension in her account; it does not establish that every affectionate gesture is calculated deception.

lessons.pitfall: Do not turn close reading into a hunt for a predetermined moral. A claim should remain answerable to details that resist it. Nor does a first-person report give direct access to the husband’s private intentions.

practice.task: Explain what changes when “before him, at least” interrupts the narrator’s claim that she controls herself. Use the surrounding two sentences.
practice.response: The qualification separates outward compliance from inward feeling. Because she attributes the demand for self-control to John and then calls the effort tiring, the phrase makes restraint appear performed under supervision rather than freely achieved calm.

terms: Observation: a verifiable feature of the words.
Inference: a conclusion drawn from details.
Commentary: an explanation of the connection between evidence and interpretation.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s “The Yellow Wallpaper” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how Gilman uses literary elements and techniques to portray the narrator’s complex response to the care she receives.

lessons.definition: An observation reports what the text states or presents. An inference explains something the text implies without directly asserting it. Neither is automatically more valuable: an interpretation needs accurate observations and warranted inferences. Distinguish a character’s assertion from a fact established by the narrator, and distinguish the narrator’s words from an uncomplicated statement of the author’s beliefs.
lessons.importance: AP-style reading questions often offer an inference that is possible in the world but unsupported in the passage. Your task is narrower: choose the account best justified by these particular details. Degrees of certainty matter. “Suggests a desire to direct the conversation” requires less evidence than “proves a lifelong hatred.” A useful inference also explains more than a paraphrase does.
steps: List three things explicitly stated about the newcomer. Beside each, identify who supplies the information and whether that speaker has met him.
Separate Mrs. Bennet’s intention from Bingley’s supposed intention. Follow Mr. Bennet’s question about Bingley’s “design” to see why the distinction matters.
Test an inference against both the dialogue and the closing description. If one of these contradicts it, narrow the inference rather than ignoring the difficulty.

worked.observation: Mrs. Bennet calls the wealthy unmarried newcomer “a fine thing for our girls” before reporting any knowledge of his wishes.
worked.inference: She interprets his arrival primarily as a marriage opportunity for her daughters.
worked.commentary: The possessive family language directs her attention away from the newcomer’s individuality. Mr. Bennet’s question about his “design” exposes the gap between her hopes and his unestablished intentions.
worked.qualification: This does not show which daughter Bingley would prefer or whether he intends to marry at all.

lessons.pitfall: A plausible historical custom is not automatically a fact of this scene. Use supplied context to understand words and institutions, then ground the answer in the passage. Avoid treating irony as a license to reverse every statement.

practice.task: Sort these claims: Bingley is unmarried; he has chosen a Bennet daughter; Mrs. Bennet wants an introduction. Explain which is unsupported.
practice.response: The dialogue reports that Bingley is unmarried and explicitly shows Mrs. Bennet urging a visit. Nothing establishes his preference for a daughter. Her hope that he may fall in love is evidence of her intention, not of his.

terms: Explicit: directly stated.
Implied: supported without direct assertion.
Warrant: the reasoning that permits a conclusion from evidence.

frq.prompt: Read the opening chapter of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice. Write an essay analyzing how Austen uses literary elements and techniques to reveal the differences between the Bennets’ stated concerns and the priorities suggested by their conversation.

lessons.definition: Textual evidence is a selected detail used to support an interpretation: wording, a narrated action, a pattern, a structural contrast, or a significant absence established by context. A quotation is one way to present evidence, not evidence’s entire definition. Choose the smallest amount of text that preserves the relevant meaning, and explain why its particular language matters.
lessons.importance: A passage can support more than one interpretation, but it does not support every interpretation equally. A strong paragraph usually needs evidence of both the pattern it claims and any consequential complication. Quoting a whole paragraph does not compensate for a missing connection. In a whole-work essay, accurately described scenes can supply evidence even when exact quotations are unavailable.
steps: Make a narrow claim before collecting quotations: for example, that the narrator privately resists judgments she outwardly follows. Underline the words in the claim that each quotation must help establish.
Find evidence from two different moments. Distinguish statements of private disagreement from descriptions of public conduct.
Introduce the relevant situation, quote only the decisive phrase, and follow it with an explanation. Check whether removing the quotation would leave the same unsupported generalization.

worked.observation: She writes “Personally, I disagree with their ideas,” yet reports taking prescribed remedies and controlling herself “before him, at least.”
worked.inference: Her compliance does not erase her disagreement.
worked.commentary: The explicit assertion of a personal judgment contrasts with the account of supervised behavior. The interrupting qualification makes the division between inward and outward responses visible in the sentence itself.
worked.qualification: Her admission that writing exhausts her complicates a claim that she rejects every concern about her health.

lessons.pitfall: Do not quote a speaker’s claim as though it were independently verified. “He does not believe I am sick” establishes the narrator’s account of his view; a claim about his concealed motive would need further support.

practice.task: Choose one detail supporting the narrator’s attraction to the house and one complicating that attraction. Explain their relation in three sentences.
practice.response: The “delicious garden” establishes pleasure in the surroundings, while the broken greenhouses disturb the image of well-kept abundance. Together they suggest a setting that invites imaginative enjoyment while retaining signs of neglect. The second detail qualifies rather than cancels the first.

terms: Evidence: a relevant textual detail.
Context: the situation needed to interpret a detail accurately.
Sufficiency: enough varied evidence to justify the scope of the claim.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from “The Yellow Wallpaper.” Write an essay analyzing how Gilman uses the narrator’s descriptions of the house to develop her complex response to her situation.

lessons.definition: Characterization is the construction of a person through selected details. These may include an explicit description, an action, speech, bodily responses, objects, or another character’s judgment. Ask who supplies each detail and what that perspective can know. The resulting character may combine apparently incompatible qualities: a threatening figure can also be frightened, hungry, and exposed.
lessons.importance: A list of adjectives stops where analysis should begin. Explain how the text produces an impression, changes it, or lets impressions coexist. In fiction, the order of revelation matters: meeting a voice before seeing a body can create fear that later visual detail complicates. A character’s function in a relationship can matter as much as a stable trait.
steps: Track the stranger’s introduction in order: voice, threat, visible body, movements, and response to food. Note what each stage adds.
Separate Pip’s evaluative labels from the concrete details that permit a reader to interpret the stranger differently.
Describe Pip through his language and conduct as well. Explain how the contrast in physical power shapes the encounter without making either figure simple.

worked.observation: The stranger threatens Pip, but his clothes are damaged, his teeth chatter, and he eats the bread “ravenously.”
worked.inference: The figure who terrifies Pip is also materially vulnerable.
worked.commentary: The accumulating bodily injuries interrupt a purely monstrous portrait. His ability to seize the child gives him immediate power, while hunger and exposure reveal limits to that power.
worked.qualification: Vulnerability does not cancel the violence of the threat; the passage sustains both aspects.

lessons.pitfall: An action may reveal a situation rather than a permanent personality. Pip’s frightened obedience during a threat does not prove that he is always passive. Avoid diagnosing a fictional person when the task asks how details construct an impression.

practice.task: Explain what Pip’s repeated “sir” contributes that the narrator’s statement “in terror” does not establish by itself.
practice.response: The repeated address performs deference in the dialogue. It lets the reader hear the child trying to appease an aggressor, so fear appears as a social and verbal response rather than only a reported emotion.

terms: Direct characterization: an explicit description or evaluation.
Indirect characterization: an impression built through conduct or detail.
Foil: a contrast that makes a quality more visible.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Charles Dickens’s Great Expectations. Write an essay analyzing how Dickens uses literary elements and techniques to develop the complex portrayal of the stranger Pip encounters.

lessons.definition: Motivation connects a character’s desires, fears, beliefs, and pressures to a choice. Characters need not fully understand their own motives, and a narrator may present conflicting impulses instead of a single explanation. Keep the difference between an immediate desire, a longer-term need, and an external constraint visible. A contradiction may be the center of the portrayal rather than a problem to eliminate.
lessons.importance: Explaining motivation requires more than supplying a general human reason for an action. Ask what this text emphasizes and how it frames uncertainty. A desire for freedom may coexist with fear of isolation; a pleasurable experience may be disturbing because it changes a person’s sense of self. Precise language preserves these relationships.
steps: State the visible action before explaining it: Edna declines an invitation and then follows. Do not replace that sequence with an invented plan.
Read the light metaphor as a double claim. Identify what awareness makes possible and what it makes difficult.
Connect the inward movement to the sea’s language. Explain how invitation, solitude, and embrace complicate one another.

worked.observation: The narrator calls Edna’s impulses contradictory and describes a light that both shows and forbids the way.
worked.inference: Her developing self-awareness attracts her while unsettling the terms on which she has lived.
worked.commentary: The paradox refuses to make awakening a straightforward arrival at certainty. The sea’s invitations extend this attraction into imagery that joins sensuous closeness with inward solitude.
worked.qualification: The excerpt presents a beginning, not a completed decision about how she will live.

lessons.pitfall: Do not substitute knowledge of the novel’s ending for the uncertainty experienced here. A later outcome may illuminate a pattern, but an analysis of this moment must preserve its partial, emerging character.

practice.task: Explain why “followed in obedience” is complicated when Edna follows an impulse of her own.
practice.response: The phrasing makes a self-originating impulse feel like a force acting upon her. It complicates a simple equation of personal desire with deliberate control: she responds to an attraction she cannot yet explain.

terms: Motive: a pressure or desire contributing to action.
Agency: a capacity to choose and act.
Ambivalence: simultaneous, conflicting responses.

frq.prompt: Read the selection from chapter VI of Kate Chopin’s The Awakening. Write an essay analyzing how Chopin uses literary elements and techniques to portray Edna’s emerging self-awareness as a complex experience.

lessons.definition: Setting includes physical place, time, weather, objects, and social arrangements. A description is selective: it directs attention to some features and leaves others out. Ask how the selection shapes a character’s possibilities and a reader’s expectations. A room may offer shelter while marking exclusion; the same landscape may appear inviting to one observer and hostile to another.
lessons.importance: “The setting creates mood” is a starting point that needs particulars. Identify whose response the setting mediates, which sensory details produce it, and how that response relates to conflict. Distinguish the physical space from figurative spaces imagined through reading, memory, or comparison. Their interaction can be more revealing than either alone.
steps: Sketch the drawing-room, breakfast-room, window, curtain, and outdoors from the passage. Label who occupies or controls each boundary.
Track the cold and isolated landscapes in Jane’s book alongside the weather outside. Note how a chosen imaginative space differs from enforced social exclusion.
Explain the double function of a barrier: the glass protects but does not fully separate; the curtain conceals while enclosing.

worked.observation: Jane sits behind a curtain beside glass that is “protecting, but not separating” her from the weather.
worked.inference: Her retreat offers partial shelter without removing her emotional relation to the bleak world outside.
worked.commentary: The distinction prevents the window-seat from functioning as an uncomplicated refuge. The book’s solitary landscapes extend this combination of protection and imagined exposure.
worked.qualification: Jane calls herself happy there, so an account of pure imprisonment would ignore the refuge she actively creates.

lessons.pitfall: Avoid universal symbol dictionaries: red curtains do not always mean passion or danger. Start with their literal function in this scene and then argue for any additional significance through repeated or contrasting details.

practice.task: Compare the family around the fire with Jane behind the curtain. What does their placement establish beyond the rooms’ layout?
practice.response: The grouped family occupies shared warmth, while Jane must fashion a separate refuge. Spatial arrangement makes unequal belonging visible. Her pleasure in reading complicates this exclusion by giving her a limited space of chosen attention.

terms: Setting: the physical and social circumstances of a text.
Atmosphere: the felt quality produced by selected details.
Spatial contrast: a meaningful difference between places or positions.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre. Write an essay analyzing how Brontë uses setting and other literary elements to portray Jane’s complex experience of withdrawal from the Reed family.

lessons.definition: Conflict is a consequential tension between desires, values, people, or conditions. External conflict involves pressures between a character and another person or force; internal conflict involves competing impulses within a character. These categories can overlap. Trace what each side wants, how each side attempts to achieve it, and what becomes difficult to reconcile.
lessons.importance: Conflict is not limited to an argument shouted aloud. A pleasant exchange can stage unequal control; joking language can soften or conceal a disagreement. In drama, movement, props, and pauses join dialogue in making pressure visible. Ask what the apparent resolution actually changes and what it leaves intact.
steps: Identify the immediate disagreement about spending and borrowing. Separate Nora’s expectation of future income from Torvald’s concern with when it arrives.
Track the pet names, gestures, and money as parts of the conflict. Decide how each affects the terms on which disagreement can occur.
Examine the movement from objection to gift. Does receiving money resolve the underlying difference about authority or only alter the mood?

worked.observation: Nora moves toward the stove after accepting Torvald’s refusal; he follows, calls her his skylark, and offers money.
worked.inference: The exchange restores affection without establishing equal power over financial decisions.
worked.commentary: Movement first makes withdrawal visible, and the gift draws her attention back. The pet name connects the restoration of warmth with the dependent role in which he addresses her.
worked.qualification: Nora’s enthusiastic counting and generous purchases also show activity and desire; dependence does not make her inert.

lessons.pitfall: Naming “person versus person” is not sufficient. Specify the contested value and the mechanism of pressure. Do not import later revelations into the opening as knowledge both characters already openly share.

practice.task: Explain how the hidden macaroons establish conflict before the characters debate borrowing.
practice.response: Nora listens at Torvald’s door and later hides the packet and wipes her mouth. These visible precautions suggest conduct she prefers him not to see. The audience therefore encounters a gap between private action and the cheerful shared conversation.

terms: External conflict: competing pressures between a character and others or conditions.
Internal conflict: competing impulses within a character.
Subtext: an implication beneath explicit speech.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Henrik Ibsen’s A Doll’s House, translated by R. Farquharson Sharp. Write an essay analyzing how Ibsen uses dramatic elements and techniques to develop tension beneath Nora and Torvald’s affectionate exchange.

lessons.definition: The author composes the work; the narrator is a constructed voice that tells it; a character participates in its represented world. One figure can be both narrator and character, but that figure is not thereby the author. In drama, much information comes through staged action and speech rather than a narrating voice. In poetry, use “speaker” unless a different term is justified.
lessons.importance: Keeping these roles distinct prevents an interpretation from confusing a fictional confession with biography or an objectionable assertion with authorial endorsement. Analyze how a voice presents itself and how the composition lets a reader assess that presentation. A narrator’s insistence can reveal an anxiety that the narrator does not intend to expose.
steps: Identify the narrator’s listener from direct address without inventing a name or institutional setting the excerpt does not establish.
Separate the narrator’s intended self-portrait from the details offered as proof. Ask how insistence, punctuation, and repetition affect your assessment.
Write with distinct subjects: “the narrator claims”; “the description suggests”; “Poe constructs.” Each phrase attributes the observation to the appropriate level.

worked.observation: The narrator denies madness and offers unusually acute hearing as evidence, including sounds in heaven, earth, and hell.
worked.inference: The effort to establish rational authority also gives readers reason to question the account.
worked.commentary: The extravagance of the supporting claim undermines the reassurance it is meant to provide. Poe thus builds a gap between the narrator’s desired effect and the effect of the language on a critical reader.
worked.qualification: Recognizing this gap does not provide an exact medical diagnosis or identify the unnamed listener.

lessons.pitfall: Do not write “Poe wants to murder the old man.” Nor should you assume every claim is false once reliability becomes doubtful. Evaluate particular assertions against particular details.

practice.task: Rewrite “Poe explains that his patience proves he is sane” so that it distinguishes composition from the narrator’s reasoning.
practice.response: The narrator presents his patience as proof of sanity, while Poe’s repeated descriptions of obsessive vigilance complicate that self-defense. This version distinguishes the voice’s argument from the author’s construction of its limits.

terms: Author: the historical maker of a work.
Narrator: the voice that tells a narrative.
Narratee: the person or audience addressed within the telling.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Tell-Tale Heart.” Write an essay analyzing how Poe uses literary elements and techniques to create tension between the narrator’s self-presentation and the account the narrator gives.

lessons.definition: Point of view concerns the position from which a narrative is told and the access it provides to experience. First person can offer intimate thought while limiting knowledge of other minds. Third person can be limited to one character, move among characters, or offer wider commentary. Grammatical person is a useful clue, but the central question is what the narration lets readers know and how.
lessons.importance: A narrator may tell events long after participating in them. This creates two positions within first-person narration: the experiencing self and the later telling self. Their knowledge, vocabulary, and judgments may differ. Ask when a sentence recalls a child’s immediate perception and when it adds hindsight. Neither first person nor third person automatically determines reliability.
steps: Mark what Jane sees, feels, remembers, and quotes. Distinguish her report of Mrs. Reed’s speech from direct access to Mrs. Reed’s thoughts.
Find explicit signs of retrospective knowledge, such as the later discovery of the sources of Bessie’s stories.
Explain one effect of this access: the passage can preserve the child’s uncertainty while giving the older narrator language for interpreting exclusion.

worked.observation: Jane recalls stories whose literary sources she discovered “at a later period.”
worked.inference: The telling self knows things unavailable to the child in the scene.
worked.commentary: The parenthetical time distinction makes memory a reconstruction rather than a recording made in the moment. Readers receive the child’s fascination alongside an adult clarification of its materials.
worked.qualification: This retrospective knowledge does not grant the narrator unrestricted access to every other character’s mind.

lessons.pitfall: Do not equate “I” with a diary written immediately after events. Also avoid saying a narrator is omniscient merely because the narration includes a strong judgment about another character; a judgment can be inferred from behavior.

practice.task: Describe one thing this passage lets us know about Jane that it does not let us know in the same way about Mrs. Reed.
practice.response: We receive Jane’s stated relief at avoiding the walk and her private pleasure in the book. Mrs. Reed’s reasons arrive through quoted speech and Jane’s account of conduct; we do not enter her unspoken thoughts directly.

terms: First person: narration by an “I” or “we.”
Focalization: the perspective organizing what is perceived.
Retrospective narration: telling an earlier experience from a later position.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Jane Eyre. Write an essay analyzing how Brontë uses narrative perspective and other literary techniques to develop Jane’s recollection of her childhood experience.

lessons.definition: An analytical paragraph advances one part of a larger interpretation. Its claim should identify a relationship worth explaining, not merely announce a topic. Evidence makes that claim answerable to the work; commentary explains the relationship between them. A paragraph can use several details when each develops the same reasoning, and it can qualify a claim when a detail complicates it.
lessons.importance: There is no required number of sentences or quotations. A useful test is whether the paragraph moves: does the second piece of evidence refine the first, establish a cause, reveal a contrast, or trace a change? If every sentence independently says that a character feels sad, the paragraph may accumulate support without developing an argument.
steps: Begin with a claim about change: Estella’s judgment becomes part of Pip’s own self-perception. This is more precise than “Dickens uses diction.”
Pair the insult about his hands with his statement that he had never been ashamed of them. Explain the before-and-after relation.
Add the infectious metaphor and then the admission that he may want to see Estella again. Use the latter to complicate the account of rejection.

worked.observation: Pip first hears his hands condemned, then calls the contempt “infectious,” and finally remains unsure that he wants to avoid Estella.
worked.inference: Social humiliation reshapes his self-judgment without eliminating his attraction to its source.
worked.commentary: The infection metaphor makes contempt something he absorbs rather than merely witnesses. His hesitant final response prevents the paragraph from ending with a simple desire to escape, revealing the mixed power of the encounter.
worked.qualification: The excerpt establishes this emerging mixture; a claim about Pip’s eventual adult values would require later scenes.

lessons.pitfall: A commentary sentence should not merely translate the quotation into synonyms. Ask what the wording reveals about the relation between the characters or about a change across the passage. Avoid a final universal moral detached from that reasoning.

practice.task: Write a four-to-six-sentence paragraph explaining the function of the repeated “Anything else?” Keep each sentence connected to one claim.
practice.response: A defensible paragraph could argue that Miss Havisham’s repeated prompt turns Pip’s discomfort into a performance for her observation. His answers move from pride to beauty to insult and escape, exposing conflicting responses. The final question about seeing Estella again draws out the attraction that makes the humiliation consequential.

terms: Claim: a proposition the paragraph develops.
Commentary: reasoning about how the evidence supports the claim.
Line of reasoning: connected claims that advance an interpretation.

frq.prompt: Read the selection from chapter VIII of Great Expectations. Write an essay analyzing how Dickens uses literary elements and techniques to portray Pip’s complex response to Estella’s treatment of him.

lessons.definition: A poetic speaker is the voice a poem constructs. Determine what that voice observes, addresses, remembers, claims, or withholds before identifying it with the historical poet. A speaker can be a participant, an observer, an imagined character, or a collective voice. Pronouns help locate the voice, but the more important question is the relationship between that voice and the experience represented.
lessons.importance: Speaker analysis changes how you treat apparent statements of fact. “I knew” is a claim of knowledge made by a voice; its certainty may exceed what an observer can verify. A poem can distinguish its speaker from a crowd while also exposing the limits of the speaker’s own gaze. Preserve these differences instead of assuming that sympathetic observation provides transparent access to another person.
steps: Identify the crowd, the dancer, and the observing speaker separately. Record what each does and which figure supplies the descriptions.
Locate “To me” and “I knew.” Compare the degrees of certainty in these phrases and what kind of evidence supports each.

Read the final couplet against the preceding visual attention. Explain how the speaker’s account distinguishes outward performance from inward selfhood without claiming access to the dancer’s own speech.

worked.observation: The speaker calls the dancer a storm-tested palm and later interprets her smile as false.
worked.inference: The speaker attempts to perceive an inward life that the crowd’s appetite overlooks.
worked.commentary: The resilient tree comparison grants the dancer a history of endurance, while the final turn separates bodily presence from the “self.” The speaker’s claimed recognition thus contests the crowd’s consumption of her appearance.
worked.qualification: The dancer does not speak about her feelings. The certainty of “I knew” remains the observer’s claim, a limit worth acknowledging.

lessons.pitfall: Do not automatically assign the speaker the poet’s biography, gender, or beliefs. Also avoid making the dancer’s silence proof of one specific private emotion. Explain what the voice infers and how the poem frames that inference.

practice.task: Compare “To me she seemed” with “I knew.” What changes in the speaker’s presentation of authority?
practice.response: “Seemed” marks an interpretation as perspectival, whereas “knew” presents the final judgment as certain. The change strengthens the speaker’s separation from the crowd but also invites a reader to consider the limit of knowing another person through appearance.

terms: Speaker: the voice constructed by a poem.
Address: the person or entity toward which speech is directed.
Perspective: the position and assumptions shaping an account.

frq.prompt: Read Claude McKay’s “The Harlem Dancer” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how McKay uses literary elements and techniques to develop the speaker’s complex perception of the dancer.

lessons.definition: A poem’s dramatic situation is the circumstance of its utterance: who speaks, to whom, about what, at what apparent moment, and under what pressure. Some of these conditions remain unspecified. Distinguish an explicit addressee from the actual reader, and distinguish a question that requests unknown information from one that guides a listener toward an answer the speaker already holds.
lessons.importance: A lyric need not have a plot to contain a changing situation. Speech can move from questioning to instruction, from distance to identification, or from complaint to blessing. Tracking that movement helps you explain why a poem repeats a phrase or changes pronouns. It also prevents you from treating every line as an isolated proposition.
steps: List the opening questions and the qualities of the creature they accompany. Identify what the speaker seems to want the lamb to recognize.
Notice when the speaker announces an answer. Track the movement among “thee,” “He,” “I,” and “we.”

Explain how the closing blessing changes the relationship established by the opening question. Use the speaker’s self-identification as a child without assuming the historical poet is literally a child.

worked.observation: The first stanza repeatedly asks who made the lamb; the second says “I’ll tell thee” and joins child and lamb through “we.”
worked.inference: The encounter moves from a lesson about origin toward a shared identity under a benevolent creator.
worked.commentary: The speaker initially occupies the role of questioner and then teacher, but the shared name reduces the distance between teacher and creature. The blessing performs the affectionate relation that the explanation describes.
worked.qualification: The displayed edition’s wording and punctuation are editorially transmitted; the analysis concerns this text rather than a claim about every original visual detail.

lessons.pitfall: Do not infer that a question proves confusion. A speaker can ask rhetorically, pedagogically, or ceremonially. Likewise, the person addressed need not be capable of answering in ordinary speech for the address to have a function.

practice.task: Explain why “I a child, and thou a lamb” matters to the situation rather than merely supplying two labels.
practice.response: The parallel phrasing places the speaker and addressee together within the poem’s account of creation. The child’s explanation becomes a claim of kinship, preparing the shared “we” and the repeated blessing.

terms: Dramatic situation: the circumstances of speaking.
Addressee: the person or entity addressed.
Rhetorical question: a question whose function exceeds a request for information.

frq.prompt: Read William Blake’s “The Lamb” as printed in this edition. Write an essay analyzing how Blake uses literary elements and techniques to develop the relationship between the speaker, the lamb, and the creator.

lessons.definition: Diction is word choice. Denotation is a word’s central referential meaning; connotation includes associations a word carries in a particular context. Analysis asks why a selected word matters beside plausible alternatives. Words also form patterns: nourishment can become injury, vigor can coexist with hate, and grandeur can become vulnerability. Trace such relationships instead of listing “positive” and “negative” words.
lessons.importance: A word’s effect depends on its syntax, speaker, and surroundings. An approving noun paired with a disturbing modifier can sustain contradiction rather than cancel either value. When answering a question about diction, distinguish the word’s meaning in context from the larger function of the phrase. Avoid treating an association as a universal symbolic code.
steps: Make two columns for language of sustenance and language of injury. Identify words that belong to both patterns in context.
Read “cultured hell” as a combination, not two unrelated labels. Explain what admiration remains present within condemnation.
Track the final vocabulary of monuments, value, and disappearance. Ask how this diction changes the scale of the speaker’s response from present struggle to historical time.

worked.observation: The country feeds the speaker “bread of bitterness,” while its vigor enters the speaker’s blood as strength.
worked.inference: The speaker experiences the nation as both damaging and energizing.
worked.commentary: Nourishment is made bitter rather than simply withdrawn, so the phrasing binds dependence to injury. The later language of strength prevents the hostile imagery from producing an uncomplicated rejection.
worked.qualification: The speaker’s refusal of terror or malice does not erase the country’s hate; the poem differentiates the speaker’s stance from the forces being resisted.

lessons.pitfall: Do not replace an argument with a string of tone adjectives. Explain the relationship between particular word groups and the speaker’s position. A phrase such as “cultured hell” does not mean that “cultured” has ceased to carry its favorable associations.

practice.task: Compare the effect of “priceless treasures” with a hypothetical phrase “worthless ruins” in the final image. What would the substitution lose?
practice.response: “Priceless treasures” retains admiration and value even as the monuments sink. “Worthless ruins” would make disappearance feel like simple dismissal. The actual diction sustains attachment while placing power under time’s pressure.

terms: Diction: word choice.
Connotation: contextual associations beyond central reference.
Semantic pattern: related words that develop a field of meaning.

frq.prompt: Read Claude McKay’s “America” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how McKay uses literary elements and techniques to develop the speaker’s complex relationship with the country.

lessons.definition: Imagery evokes sensory experience: sight, sound, touch, taste, smell, or bodily movement. An image can be literal, figurative, or both. Begin by identifying what a reader is asked to perceive, then explain how that perception changes across the poem. A sequence of images may carry a movement from a present object into memory and finally into an emotional response.
lessons.importance: Do not assume that beautiful imagery produces happiness. A vividly pleasurable remembered place can intensify the pain of absence. Sensory detail may also change function: fruit can be something to eat, a display to look at, a trigger of remembered landscape, and the occasion for a hunger that food cannot satisfy. The analysis lies in that development.
steps: Identify the present location of the fruit and distinguish it from the remembered place. The title and the later mention of a window help establish this difference.
Track the sensory movement from visible produce to sound, moisture, sky, and bodily longing. Note how the second stanza enlarges the first.
Explain why the speaker stops looking. Connect the bodily response to the poem’s transformed use of hunger rather than treating tears as an isolated ending.

worked.observation: Fruit in a window brings memories of streams and hills; the speaker later becomes “hungry for the old, familiar ways.”
worked.inference: The display awakens a desire for a whole way of life rather than merely for the food itself.
worked.commentary: The movement from tangible produce to an enveloping remembered landscape expands the object’s significance. The final hunger transfers a bodily need into longing for familiarity, making the act of turning away a response to absence made vivid.
worked.qualification: The poem does not specify a complete personal history or name every remembered place; those details should not be invented.

lessons.pitfall: Naming a sense is not a full explanation. “This is visual imagery” should lead to what the visible detail makes present, what it excludes, and how it contributes to the poem’s movement. Resist reducing the memory to a postcard of an objectively perfect homeland.

practice.task: Explain the relationship between the fruit’s apparent abundance and the speaker’s final hunger.
practice.response: The visible food is abundant, yet it cannot satisfy the desire it produces. Hunger becomes a figure for missing familiar ways of life, so material presence intensifies emotional absence rather than resolving it.

terms: Imagery: language that evokes sensory experience.
Sensory pattern: recurring or related perceptions.
Embodied response: emotion represented through bodily feeling or action.

frq.prompt: Read Claude McKay’s “The Tropics in New York” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how McKay uses imagery and other literary techniques to develop the speaker’s response to the fruit displayed in the window.

lessons.definition: A simile makes an explicit comparison, often using “like” or “as.” Identify both things being compared and the quality the comparison makes salient. Then ask what the comparison does in context: it can make the unfamiliar approachable, reveal a perspective, join distant places, or change the emotional force of an object. Not every occurrence of “like” or “as” introduces a simile.
lessons.importance: A useful analysis preserves the limits of the comparison. Snow likened to moths does not become literally alive, and a comparison to familiar tropical images may reveal more about the observer than about the weather. When several similes occur, consider whether they reinforce one another or mark stages in a changing response.
steps: Read the first stanza as advice to an addressed newcomer. Identify the unfamiliar sight and the familiar images used to imagine it.
Compare the playful first-stanza images with the chilly, raw conditions of the second. Explain what changes without claiming the first impression was simply false.
Distinguish “Like me” from the earlier snow comparisons. The phrase links the addressee to the speaker’s experience and supports the poem’s predictive voice.

worked.observation: Snow is compared to white moths and flowing hill water before the poem describes raw cold and homesickness.
worked.inference: The speaker predicts that initial enchantment will be tested by a less welcoming experience.
worked.commentary: Familiar graceful movements make snow appear delightful to a tropical imagination. The later bodily cold qualifies that first response, while the final spring turn prevents homesickness from becoming the only possible ending.
worked.qualification: The speaker offers a forecast based on experience, not a guarantee that every migrant will feel the same sequence.

lessons.pitfall: Do not stop at “the poet compares snow to moths.” Specify what the comparison carries—color, motion, delicacy, familiarity—and why that matters to this addressee. Avoid importing every property of the comparison’s vehicle into the scene.

practice.task: Explain what the moth comparison contributes that “the snow is white” would not.
practice.response: The comparison adds delicate, trembling motion and connects northern snow to an image associated with tropical air. It conveys the newcomer’s imaginative route into an unfamiliar experience, not merely its color.

terms: Simile: an explicit comparison.
Tenor: the subject being understood through a comparison.
Vehicle: the image or term through which it is understood.

frq.prompt: Read Claude McKay’s “To One Coming North” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how McKay uses comparisons and other literary techniques to develop the speaker’s complex account of adjusting to a new place.

lessons.definition: Metaphor presents one thing through the terms of another without requiring an explicit “like” or “as.” It can compress an argument: describing an aging self as late autumn selects decline, exposure, and approaching winter while leaving other aspects of aging outside the comparison. Identify the subject, the imagined terms, and the relation that makes the comparison meaningful.
lessons.importance: A poem may build several metaphors for the same subject. Do not treat them as interchangeable decorations. Ask what each adds and how their order changes the scale, urgency, or implications of the argument. A final turn can then use what the images establish to make a claim about another person’s response.
steps: Track the three “in me” images: season, twilight, and fire. For each, identify what remains and what is disappearing.
Compare the time spans implied by a year, a day, and a dying fire. Explain how the sequence concentrates the awareness of an ending.
Read the final couplet as a claim about the addressee’s love. Show how the preceding images prepare that claim rather than merely repeating that life is short.

worked.observation: The speaker moves from almost bare branches to fading twilight and then a fire lying on the ashes of its youth.
worked.inference: The metaphors make remaining life seem progressively more immediate and self-consuming.
worked.commentary: The fire image adds a paradox absent from a simple calendar: what sustained the flame becomes the material on which it expires. The couplet turns this recognition of loss into a reason for intensified love.
worked.qualification: The poem’s imagined self-presentation is not a reliable basis for calculating the historical poet’s age.

lessons.pitfall: Avoid assigning a single fixed meaning to every image. “Fire means passion” may overlook the ash, nourishment, and expiration that organize this particular fire. Explain the comparison’s selected relations and the argument they enable.

practice.task: How does the fire image complicate an account in which death arrives only as an external enemy?
practice.response: The flame expires on the ashes of what once nourished it. Its ending is linked to its own consumption of sustaining material, so decline appears built into the process of living rather than caused solely by an outside attacker.

terms: Metaphor: a comparison expressed through transferred terms.
Extended comparison: a relation developed through several connected details.
Figurative implication: the meaning made possible by the comparison.

frq.prompt: Read Shakespeare’s Sonnet 73 carefully. Write an essay analyzing how Shakespeare uses metaphor and other literary techniques to develop the speaker’s account of mortality and its relationship to love.

lessons.definition: Tone is the attitude conveyed by a voice toward its subject, addressee, or situation. Infer it from choices such as diction, syntax, imagery, rhythm, and qualification. A tone word should be precise enough to distinguish this response from nearby possibilities: weary observation differs from detached description; sorrow can coexist with accusation. A poem may sustain several attitudes or move among them.
lessons.importance: Do not confuse tone with the emotion a reader happens to feel, or with the general atmosphere of a setting. Explain whose attitude you are describing and what it concerns. Support a tonal claim through a pattern rather than one emotionally charged word. When a poem intensifies, identify the new object or scale of judgment that produces the change.
steps: Read the speaker’s route from faces to cries to institutions and finally intimate relations. Track what becomes the object of judgment at each stage.
Collect repeated words and the increasingly forceful verbs. Ask whether the speaker merely observes suffering or also implies causes and responsibility.
Choose a two-part tonal description and test it against the final image. Explain how lament and indictment can coexist without reducing the poem to either one.

worked.observation: The speaker hears repeated cries and then connects the soldier’s sigh to blood on palace walls.
worked.inference: The voice’s sorrow for suffering develops into an accusation directed toward institutions of power.
worked.commentary: The bodily trace on the palace makes misery appear connected to authority rather than isolated in individual weakness. The poem’s repeated universals sustain the pressure of this indictment across the city.
worked.qualification: The poem’s sweeping perspective is a constructed vision; it should not be treated as a statistical report about every inhabitant.

lessons.pitfall: Calling the tone “negative” is too broad to explain a choice. Nor does a dark image automatically make a voice frightened. Ask whether the speaker fears, condemns, grieves, mocks, or combines these responses, and support the distinction.

practice.task: Would “detached curiosity” adequately describe the speaker’s tone? Use two features to test the phrase.
practice.response: The repeated suffering and the violent verbs “blasts” and “blights” give the account moral and emotional urgency. The link between cries and powerful institutions also exceeds neutral curiosity by implying responsibility.

terms: Tone: a voice’s conveyed attitude.
Atmosphere: a work’s felt environment.
Tonal tension: attitudes that coexist or resist simple resolution.

frq.prompt: Read William Blake’s “London” as printed in this edition. Write an essay analyzing how Blake uses literary elements and techniques to develop the speaker’s response to the city and its inhabitants.

lessons.definition: A stanza is a group of verse lines separated as a unit. Its function depends on what happens within and between such groups: a stanza may establish a contrast, elaborate an image, advance an event, or revise a judgment. Describe those functions in verbs rather than merely reporting that a poem has four stanzas. Formal regularity can coexist with disturbing developments.
lessons.importance: Structure is an account of relationships, not a list of parts. Ask why one stage follows another and what a reader can infer at each boundary. A recurring rhyme or stanza length may lend a smooth, memorable surface to an increasingly troubling action. The effect emerges from the relation between regular form and changing content.
steps: Give each stanza a functional label: contrast, cultivation, fruition, consequence. Check each label against what the speaker actually says.
Follow the pronoun “it” back to the wrath it develops. Explain how the tree metaphor connects rather than replaces the emotional sequence.
Read the final stanza back against the first. Ask what the opening alternative of speaking anger allows readers to judge about the later cultivation.

worked.observation: The first stanza contrasts expressed and concealed anger; the next two develop cultivation and fruit; the last presents the foe beneath the tree.
worked.inference: The poem makes the ending the result of a sustained process rather than an isolated accident.
worked.commentary: The stanza sequence gives concealed wrath a life cycle. Because the opening supplies an alternative that ends anger, the later acts of tending and deception become consequential choices within the structure.
worked.qualification: The ending presents the foe “outstretched” and the speaker glad; analysis should distinguish the strongly implied outcome from details the poem does not explicitly narrate.

lessons.pitfall: Do not assume every stanza break marks a change of speaker or a complete sentence. Follow syntax across the boundary. Also avoid treating an orderly form as proof that the voice’s values deserve endorsement.

practice.task: What would be lost if the opening friend/foe contrast were removed?
practice.response: The poem would lose its explicit alternative to cultivating anger. The ending might then appear merely as a mysterious outcome rather than a result readers can compare with the earlier possibility of speaking and ending wrath.

terms: Stanza: a grouped unit of verse.
Sequence: the order in which developments are presented.
Structural contrast: a difference made consequential by arrangement.

frq.prompt: Read William Blake’s “A Poison Tree” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how Blake uses structure and other literary techniques to develop the relationship between concealed anger and its consequences.

lessons.definition: A shift changes a poem’s direction: subject, addressee, image pattern, time, emotional stance, or reasoning. A volta is a consequential turn, often discussed in sonnets. Locate a possible turn through a connective such as “yet,” but verify that the content actually changes. A poem may have a major turn and smaller movements within or after it.
lessons.importance: Explaining a turn requires an account of both sides and their relationship. Does the later movement reject, qualify, revalue, or intensify the earlier one? The initial condition may remain materially unchanged even when its meaning changes for the speaker. This is different from a plot in which external circumstances are magically repaired.
steps: Trace the opening verbs of complaint and comparison. Identify what the speaker believes others possess and what makes the speaker dissatisfied.
Locate “Yet” and the recollection that follows. Explain what triggers the change rather than treating the connective alone as the turn.
Compare the repeated word “state” at the opening, turn, and close. Decide what kind of wealth the final couplet claims.

worked.observation: The speaker moves from envying others to remembering the addressee’s love and refusing to exchange states with kings.
worked.inference: The turn changes the speaker’s valuation of the self rather than documenting a sudden material promotion.
worked.commentary: The rising lark transforms the earlier ineffective appeal to heaven into song. The repeated “state” connects social condition with inward condition, allowing remembered love to overturn the hierarchy that initially produces envy.
worked.qualification: The poem’s emotional transformation does not establish that every external source of exclusion has disappeared.

lessons.pitfall: Do not write “the tone changes at line nine” and stop. Specify the prior and later positions, the trigger, and the effect. Avoid forcing every sonnet to turn at exactly the same line regardless of its actual syntax.

practice.task: Explain why the final comparison with kings belongs to the poem’s reasoning rather than serving only as exaggeration.
practice.response: The opening measures the speaker against others’ advantages. The final comparison returns to that scale at its highest social point and refuses the exchange, demonstrating the revaluation produced by remembered love.

terms: Shift: a change in a poem’s movement.
Volta: a consequential turn in thought or feeling.
Revaluation: a change in what something is understood to be worth.

frq.prompt: Read Shakespeare’s Sonnet 29 carefully. Write an essay analyzing how Shakespeare uses literary elements and techniques to develop the change in the speaker’s response to the speaker’s own condition.

lessons.definition: A poetry-analysis essay explains how a poem’s choices develop an interpretation of a particular experience, relationship, or tension. Start with the literal situation and a provisional account of the poem’s movement. Then select features whose effects you can demonstrate. A thesis naming imagery, diction, and structure is incomplete unless it states what those choices help the poem mean.
lessons.importance: Read the whole poem before committing to a claim. Endings can qualify apparent promises, and confident exhortation can coexist with acknowledged danger. Organize paragraphs around developments in your interpretation rather than one device per paragraph by habit. A formal feature belongs in the essay when explaining it helps the reasoning, not because a checklist demands it.
steps: Identify the collective speaker, the addressed companions, and the threatening opponents. Use the poem’s language without inventing a specific scene it does not name.
Track the movement from avoiding an ignoble death to demanding courageous resistance. Notice that the speaker does not promise survival.
Build an interpretation around dignity under constraint. Select the animal comparisons, direct address, and closing participles according to how each advances that reading.

worked.observation: The poem begins with the possibility of death and ends with the collective still “dying, but fighting back.”
worked.inference: The speaker locates dignity in the manner of resistance rather than in guaranteed victory.
worked.commentary: The movement from hunted animals to human defiance changes the terms on which the group is imagined. Direct address turns this redefinition into an appeal for shared conduct, while the final concession preserves the danger the appeal confronts.
worked.qualification: The poem’s defiance does not make suffering desirable in itself; it responds to a threatened condition represented as already imposed.

lessons.pitfall: Do not let historical background replace analysis of the poem supplied. Context can clarify, but every major claim in a passage essay needs textual support. Also avoid treating a forceful voice as emotionally simple: resolve can be shaped by fear and acknowledged vulnerability.

practice.task: Draft a thesis that accounts for both “nobly die” and “Pressed to the wall” without listing three techniques.
practice.response: A defensible thesis could argue that the poem transforms threatened helplessness into collective resolve by defining dignity through resistance, while its persistent acknowledgment of death prevents that resolve from becoming a promise of rescue.

terms: Interpretation: an evidence-based account of meaning.
Line of reasoning: connected claims that develop an interpretation.
Complexity: a consequential tension or qualification sustained by the analysis.

frq.prompt: Read Claude McKay’s “If We Must Die” carefully. Write an essay analyzing how McKay uses literary elements and techniques to develop the speaker’s response to the situation facing the speaker and the addressed companions.

lessons.definition: Plot is the arrangement of consequential events. Causality concerns the connections that make one event enable, pressure, or prevent another. A sequence tells what happened next; a causal account explains why the next event becomes possible or significant. Causes can include material circumstances, a character’s interpretation, a threat, a mistaken assumption, or a choice made under pressure.
lessons.importance: Literary causality is often layered. A person may claim one reason for acting while the scene supplies another pressure. Distinguish a condition that permits an action from a motive that drives it, and distinguish a character’s explanation from the narrative’s broader pattern. This precision prevents plot summary from masquerading as analysis.
steps: List the encounter’s events without interpretation: mention of the blacksmith, glance at the iron, physical tilting, demand, threat, promise, release.
Join the events with specific causal verbs: enables, intensifies, motivates, enforces. Explain what changes if a link is described merely as “then.”
Separate the practical aim of the demand from the story the stranger tells to secure compliance. Ask what Pip can verify and what fear makes effective anyway.

worked.observation: The stranger looks at his iron after hearing “blacksmith,” then demands a file and food while repeatedly tilting Pip.
worked.inference: A newly available means of obtaining a tool combines with physical coercion to produce Pip’s promise.
worked.commentary: The glance links household information to the stranger’s practical need. Repeated tilting converts the request into a bodily experience of danger, so agreement cannot be read as freely chosen generosity alone.
worked.qualification: The stranger’s story about another threatening young man is a claim within the encounter, not independently verified information in this selection.

lessons.pitfall: Do not assume that an outcome proves a character intended every consequence. Also avoid making one motive explain everything. A material opportunity, fear, and an imaginative story can operate together without being identical causes.

practice.task: Explain why the reference to the blacksmith matters more to this sequence than a neutral detail about the village’s appearance would.
practice.response: It identifies possible access to a file, which the iron on the stranger’s leg makes useful. The immediate downward glance makes the connection visible before the demand is spoken, turning family information into a practical opportunity.

terms: Causality: a consequential connection between events.
Condition: a circumstance that enables or limits action.
Consequence: an outcome whose significance depends on what precedes it.

frq.prompt: Read the selection from chapter I of Great Expectations. Write an essay analyzing how Dickens uses literary elements and techniques to portray the pressures that lead Pip to make a promise to the stranger.

lessons.definition: Exposition supplies information a reader needs to understand a narrative situation. It can appear through direct explanation, dialogue, objects, or retrospective clarification. Its placement is a choice: an opening may tell readers what characters do not know, delay a fact that changes earlier events, or supply only enough background to make a present conflict legible.
lessons.importance: Ask who knows what and when. Withholding from a character is different from withholding from the reader. If readers already know a secret, their interest may lie in how it will be disclosed and how others will respond. Exposition therefore participates in suspense, irony, characterization, and pace rather than functioning as a detachable packet of background.
steps: Separate the order of events from the order of disclosure. Mr. Bennet’s visit occurs before the evening conversation, and the narrator reveals it before the family learns it.
Track remarks that have one meaning for the uninformed family and another for the informed reader.
Explain the final change in Mrs. Bennet’s evaluation. Use the opening information to assess her account of how the visit came about.

worked.observation: The narrator says Mr. Bennet had always intended to visit, but Mrs. Bennet later congratulates herself on persuading him.
worked.inference: The reader can see a gap between her explanation of the outcome and the information already supplied.
worked.commentary: Early exposition makes the disclosure comic rather than simply surprising. His teasing remarks become a performance whose destination readers know, while her triumphant explanation reveals her limited access to his intentions.
worked.qualification: Knowing this intention does not require readers to approve every effect of his teasing on the family.

lessons.pitfall: Do not call every withheld fact a mystery for the reader. Identify whose information is limited. Nor should you assume that moving exposition later always improves a story; it changes the kind of attention the story invites.

practice.task: What would change if the opening sentence revealing the visit were removed until the moment Mr. Bennet announces it?
practice.response: Readers would share more of the family’s surprise and would have less basis for reading his earlier remarks as deliberate teasing around a known secret. The scene would trade some dramatic irony for a delayed revelation.

terms: Exposition: presentation of necessary background or circumstances.
Disclosure: the moment information becomes available.
Information gap: a difference in what characters or readers know.

frq.prompt: Read the selection from chapter II of Pride and Prejudice. Write an essay analyzing how Austen’s handling of information and other literary techniques develops the family’s response to Mr. Bennet’s visit.

lessons.definition: Tension is a sustained pressure among incompatible possibilities, desires, or expectations. Suspense concerns uncertainty about what will happen or become known. Horror can contribute to suspense, but the two are not identical: a disturbing description may hold attention through revulsion even after an event is certain. Explain which uncertainty or pressure the passage sustains.
lessons.importance: Pacing, restricted perception, interrupted action, and delayed information can make an ordinary movement consequential. A narrative may also frustrate an expected climax: achieving a long-sought aim can produce terror rather than satisfaction. Track the relation between expectation and result, and distinguish what a narrator fears from what another character demonstrably does.
steps: Establish Victor’s earlier aim and the result he now calls a catastrophe. Explain the reversal before cataloging atmospheric details.
Track the sequence of waking creation, attempted sleep, nightmare, encounter at the bed, and flight. Ask how each attempted escape changes rather than ends the pressure.
Mark uncertain interpretations such as “seemingly to detain me.” Distinguish an observed gesture from the hostile intention Victor assigns to it.

worked.observation: The creature opens its mouth and reaches out, but Victor does not hear what it may say and immediately escapes.
worked.inference: The encounter remains unresolved partly because Victor’s fear interrupts any exchange.
worked.commentary: The restricted account turns an ambiguous gesture into anticipated pursuit. His later listening for every sound sustains suspense through expectation even when the creature is not visibly acting.
worked.qualification: The passage gives strong evidence of Victor’s terror, but weaker evidence of a definite intention to harm him at this moment.

lessons.pitfall: Avoid saying darkness automatically creates suspense. Specify what limited light prevents a character or reader from knowing. Likewise, calling a creature monstrous is a narrator’s evaluative act that should be examined alongside the actions described.

practice.task: Explain how the dream changes the meaning of Victor’s attempt to rest.
practice.response: Sleep initially promises forgetfulness, but the dream transforms an embrace of Elizabeth into contact with his dead mother. Rest reproduces the collapse of hoped-for life into death, so the attempted refuge intensifies rather than relieves his distress.

terms: Tension: pressure among incompatible possibilities or desires.
Suspense: attention sustained by uncertainty about an outcome.
Pacing: the narrative allocation of time and detail.

frq.prompt: Read the creation scene from Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein. Write an essay analyzing how Shelley uses literary elements and techniques to develop Victor’s response to the fulfillment of his ambition.

lessons.definition: Agency is a character’s capacity to choose and act within constraints. It is not identical to freedom, success, or moral correctness. A character can resist while remaining vulnerable, or comply while making a limited strategic choice. Analyze the available options, the costs attached to them, and the way the narration represents the moment of action.
lessons.importance: Power can operate through property, status, bodily force, family rules, or the authority to name another person’s behavior. A scene may show an act of resistance and then show observers redefining that act as misconduct. The interpretation should account for both the action and the unequal conditions under which it is judged.
steps: Identify the grounds on which John claims authority over Jane and the book. Separate his assertions about dependence from the force he then uses.
Trace Jane’s movement from compliance to alarm, verbal accusation, and physical resistance. Locate the change in feeling that makes resistance possible.
Compare Jane’s account of the assault with the household’s descriptions of her response. Explain how the final punishment limits the immediate result of her action.

worked.observation: John invokes ownership and dependence before throwing the book; the adults later call Jane’s resistance a “picture of passion.”
worked.inference: Jane can act against the hierarchy without controlling the terms by which that action is judged.
worked.commentary: The narrative gives readers access to the injury and fear that precede her resistance, while the adults’ labels detach her conduct from that cause. The resulting punishment shows the difference between asserting agency and possessing institutional power.
worked.qualification: Explaining the conditions of resistance does not require claiming that Jane acts with complete calm or a fully planned strategy.

lessons.pitfall: Do not equate a punished choice with an absence of agency. Nor should a moment of defiance become proof of complete liberation. Account for the action’s local effect and the constraints that remain afterward.

practice.task: Explain why Jane’s literary comparison to Roman emperors matters to her action.
practice.response: Reading has supplied a vocabulary for interpreting domination. A parallel she previously held in silence becomes a spoken accusation, so imaginative knowledge contributes to an act of resistance even though it does not protect her from punishment.

terms: Agency: the capacity to act within conditions.
Constraint: a force limiting available choices or their consequences.
Power: the capacity to shape action, resources, or the terms of judgment.

frq.prompt: Read the closing selection from chapter I of Jane Eyre. Write an essay analyzing how Brontë uses literary elements and techniques to portray Jane’s resistance and the limits placed upon it.

lessons.definition: Character development concerns change and continuity in a person’s understanding, values, relationships, or conduct. A moment of recognition is not automatically a complete transformation. Establish an earlier position, identify the pressure that unsettles it, and examine what changes in response. Then ask which habits or commitments remain visible.
lessons.importance: The strongest account of development explains a mechanism. New evidence may acquire force because a person rereads old details, recognizes a bias, or sees consequences that were previously ignored. A declaration of self-knowledge should itself be examined: later behavior can support, qualify, or contradict it. In a whole-work argument, use separated moments rather than treating one speech as the entire arc.
steps: List details Elizabeth remembers differently after the letter. Distinguish new facts from old facts receiving a new interpretation.
Trace her movement from judging Wickham and Darcy to judging her own discernment. Explain why the latter is more than a change of preference.
Examine the return home. Her wish to appear cheerful shows an immediate social response, not a complete record of her future development.

worked.observation: Elizabeth recognizes that praise from one man and neglect from another shaped what she accepted as evidence.
worked.inference: The change reaches her method of judgment, not only her opinion of the two men.
worked.commentary: Her repeated “I” turns the scrutiny inward. The recognition that vanity directed her reasoning makes the letter consequential as a challenge to the self-image of superior discernment.
worked.qualification: Her powerful claim that she never knew herself marks a recognition; whether it produces durable change must be tested against the rest of the novel.

lessons.pitfall: Avoid a simple before/after adjective pair such as “proud, then humble.” Specify what belief is revised and how. Do not assume a character becomes the opposite of everything previously shown.

practice.task: Explain how Elizabeth’s reassessment of Jane extends the change beyond her own romantic preference.
practice.response: She reconsiders the visibility of Jane’s feelings and the plausibility of Darcy’s account. The revision thus affects how she interprets other people’s perceptions, showing a broader reconsideration of evidence and judgment.

terms: Development: consequential change alongside continuity.
Recognition: a new understanding of a situation or self.
Character arc: a pattern of change across a work.

frq.prompt: Choose a novel or play in which a character must reconsider a judgment that has shaped the character’s understanding of self or others. Write an essay analyzing how that reconsideration contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. You may use Pride and Prejudice or another appropriate work you know well. Do not merely summarize the events.

lessons.definition: Social setting comprises the expectations, institutions, economic conditions, and hierarchies that organize a fictional world. It appears through concrete details: prices, clothing, forms of address, work, access to rooms, or assumptions about duty. These details shape what a choice means to a character and how others are likely to judge it.
lessons.importance: Context is not a substitute for close reading. Rather than announcing that a story is about class or gender, explain how a particular arrangement produces pressure. A small purchase may carry large significance when it interrupts a routine of scarcity and care. At the same time, avoid treating every person in a social position as interchangeable.
steps: Track what fifteen dollars can accomplish in Mrs. Sommers’s initial plan. Notice the labor of patching, darning, waiting, and calculation that the money might reduce.
Compare her worn possessions with the silk and the department store’s spaces. Explain how material contrasts affect her perception of herself.
Read the clerks’ responses and her changing demands. Distinguish a temporary consumer experience from a permanent change in economic position.

worked.observation: The small silk parcel seems lost in her shabby bag, and a clerk cannot reconcile her shoes with her stockings.
worked.inference: Her chosen luxury disrupts visible signals of the social position others expect her to occupy.
worked.commentary: The mismatched objects make class legible through appearance while exposing the instability of such quick judgments. Her new insistence on fit and style marks a temporary change in how she claims attention.
worked.qualification: The purchase does not establish that her family’s material needs or her long-term financial constraints have disappeared.

lessons.pitfall: Do not reduce the character to a verdict such as selfish consumer or selfless mother. The scene provides evidence of care, fatigue, desire, and constrained resources; an interpretation should explain how these pressures interact.

practice.task: Explain why the narrator’s correction about the missed lunch matters to the social setting.
practice.response: The correction connects bodily depletion to the work of feeding the children and preparing the household. Her encounter with luxury begins within a routine that has displaced attention to her own needs, giving the purchase a social and bodily context.

terms: Social setting: the economic and institutional circumstances of a work.
Status: a position recognized within a hierarchy.
Material detail: an object or condition through which social relations become visible.

frq.prompt: Read the opening selection from Kate Chopin’s “A Pair of Silk Stockings.” Write an essay analyzing how Chopin uses literary elements and techniques to portray the relationship between Mrs. Sommers’s circumstances and her changing response to the shopping experience.

lessons.definition: Dramatic dialogue is action conducted through speech. A line can accuse, evade, redefine, concede, command, or test another person’s position. Subtext consists of implications and pressures not exhausted by the literal topic. Read a reply in relation to the line it answers: a character may answer a different question, reject a term, or change the basis of the dispute.
lessons.importance: Because a play often lacks a narrator who explains motives, patterns of response become crucial evidence. Repeated words can expose incompatible definitions: one person’s happiness may be another’s mere merriment; one person’s solution may repeat the problem. Stage directions also affect the exchange, but interpretation should remain grounded in what the script permits.
steps: Annotate the exchange with verbs describing what each line does. Track Nora’s distinctions between love and pleasantness, happiness and merriment, education and self-education.
Examine Torvald’s partial concession. Ask whether his proposed “lesson-time” changes the hierarchy Nora criticizes.
Trace the point at which the conversation becomes a decision about departure. Explain how the final commands meet a different kind of response from Nora.

worked.observation: Torvald agrees that there is some truth in Nora’s account but proposes to educate both her and the children.
worked.inference: His attempted solution preserves the unequal relation she has identified.
worked.commentary: The reply changes play into lessons while retaining him as the governing teacher. Nora’s question about whose lessons makes the assumption audible, and her subsequent claim to self-education rejects the proposed terms.
worked.qualification: Her account of the marriage is a character’s forceful interpretation within the scene; analysis can examine its support without treating dialogue as an omniscient verdict.

lessons.pitfall: Do not treat a concession as complete agreement. Read what follows it. Also avoid adding a tone or gesture that the text cannot support merely because it suits a preferred interpretation.

practice.task: Explain how “No, only merry” changes the terms of Torvald’s question about happiness.
practice.response: Nora refuses to let visible cheerfulness stand as proof of deeper fulfillment. The distinction permits her to acknowledge pleasant moments while challenging the structure of the marriage, making her answer more precise than a denial of every past pleasure.

terms: Dialogue: an exchange whose responses perform actions.
Subtext: pressures or meanings implied beneath explicit speech.
Reframing: changing the terms on which a question or conflict is understood.

frq.prompt: Read the selected dialogue from act III of A Doll’s House, translated by R. Farquharson Sharp. Write an essay analyzing how Ibsen uses dramatic elements and techniques to develop the conflict between Nora’s and Torvald’s understandings of their marriage.

lessons.definition: Stage directions specify elements of a play’s visible or audible action: movement, gesture, entrances, props, setting, and delivery. They are part of the literary text, not optional packaging around dialogue. Ask what an audience can see before a character knows it, how bodies occupy space, and what changes when an object moves from one person to another.
lessons.importance: Distinguish a direction printed in the source from an interpretive staging choice you propose. Multiple productions can make different defensible choices, but not every staging is equally answerable to the script. Explain how a direction changes the force of a line, creates an information gap, or gives a relationship a physical form.
