The repeated form helps connect them.
Formal neatness accompanies the growth of concealed hostility.

questions.stem: Which account best describes the poem’s structural development?
choices: A result is announced first and then disproved by a flashback.
An initial alternative is followed by cultivation, attraction, and a troubling consequence.
Two speakers alternate until they agree to reconcile.
A natural description remains separate from the emotional situation.
rationales: The poem proceeds toward the result rather than disproving it.
Each stanza advances a stage of the concealed wrath’s development.
Only one voice narrates, and reconciliation with the foe is absent.
The tree grows from the wrath and cannot be separated from it.

questions.stem: The opening “When” establishes the speaker’s distress as
choices: a condition whose significance will be developed by the sentence that follows
an announcement that the speaker no longer remembers suffering
a completed event unrelated to the rest of the poem
a command addressed to a crowd
rationales: The syntax prepares a movement from a state of distress toward a later response.
The suffering is vividly represented.
The distress supplies the condition for the turn.
The opening is conditional description, not a command.

questions.stem: The accumulation of “beweep,” “trouble,” “look,” and “curse” chiefly establishes
choices: an exchange that restores the speaker through the addressee’s direct reassurance
a calm assessment free of emotional investment
a sustained pattern of self-directed complaint before the turn
a sequence of successful public achievements
rationales: Restoration comes through thought of the addressee; no spoken reassurance or reply is represented.
The verbs are emotionally charged.
The verbs build the opening state of dissatisfaction.
The actions express distress rather than achievement.

questions.stem: The speaker’s comparisons with other people in lines 5–8 primarily develop
choices: a detailed plan to acquire a particular occupation
envy that makes even existing pleasures unsatisfying
gratitude for the uniqueness of the speaker’s circumstances
a refusal to value social recognition at any point
rationales: No specific plan is formed.
The speaker desires others’ qualities and becomes least content with usual enjoyment.
The comparisons intensify dissatisfaction.
The opening is strongly shaped by others’ advantages.

questions.stem: “With what I most enjoy contented least” most clearly marks
choices: a return to the confidence expressed in the opening
a new addressee who interrupts the speaker
an assurance that the speaker has no remaining interests
the depth of dissatisfaction reached before the change
rationales: The opening is already distressed, not confident.
The same voice continues.
The line refers to things ordinarily enjoyed.
Even the speaker’s own sources of enjoyment lose their force.

questions.stem: The word “Yet” in line 9 signals a turn whose immediate trigger is
choices: a reply spoken aloud by a king
the discovery that the earlier distress was fabricated
the speaker’s thought of the addressed person
a sudden increase in material wealth
rationales: No king speaks in the poem.
The poem does not invalidate that distress.
“Haply I think on thee” supplies the change’s occasion.
No external financial event occurs.

questions.stem: The lark’s ascent chiefly transforms the earlier image of appeals to “deaf heaven” by
choices: recasting ineffective crying as an upward, celebratory song
confirming that every appeal remains unheard and unchanged
removing all relation between earthly and heavenly imagery
announcing the speaker’s literal ability to fly
rationales: The bird rises from sullen earth to sing at heaven’s gate.
The emotional and musical qualities change.
The ascent explicitly joins them.
The comparison is figurative.

questions.stem: The recurrence of “state” across the poem chiefly connects
choices: a political explanation of why wealth should be distributed equally
three unrelated geographical locations
two speakers whose contrasting fortunes are finally reconciled
social condition with the speaker’s changing inward valuation
rationales: The comparison concerns the speaker’s valuation of remembered love, not a developed doctrine of distribution.
The word does not name locations here.
The same speaker moves from comparison and discontent to a changed valuation; no second speaker takes over.
Outcast state becomes an altered state and finally one not exchanged with kings.

questions.stem: The remembered love’s “wealth” chiefly redefines value as
choices: a reward granted by the people who rejected the speaker
something that can outweigh the advantages previously envied
proof that the speaker has become socially powerful
a literal inheritance announced in the final couplet
rationales: The source is the remembered addressee’s love.
The recollection produces a refusal to exchange conditions with kings.
The change is in valuation, not documented rank.
No inheritance is described.

questions.stem: The final reference to kings most clearly completes the turn by
choices: returning to social comparison and reversing its earlier outcome
proving that the speaker’s friends have become monarchs
abandoning comparison altogether
restoring the opening conviction of worthlessness
rationales: The speaker now rejects an exchange with the highest imagined status.
No such event is reported.
The final line is itself a comparison.
The final stance is the opposite.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best preserves the limits of the poem’s transformation?
choices: The addressee directly persuades the speaker through an extended speech.
Every practical problem disappears as soon as the speaker recalls the addressee.
Remembered love changes the speaker’s response without proving that external exclusion has ended.
The speaker’s emotional condition remains entirely unchanged.
rationales: The addressee never speaks.
The text does not establish that result.
The poem reports an inward revaluation rather than a changed social situation.
The lark and final refusal clearly mark change.

questions.stem: The repeated conditional “If we must die” primarily establishes
choices: the possibility of death as a premise for deciding how to respond
a detached speculation unrelated to the addressees
a guarantee that no member of the group will die
a wish to seek death regardless of circumstances
rationales: The speaker argues about the manner and meaning of resistance under danger.
The collective “we” makes the situation shared.
The condition preserves the danger.
The poem responds to imposed threat rather than freely seeking it.

questions.stem: The opening comparison to hunted hogs chiefly presents the threatened group as
choices: content with the security provided by enclosure
naturally incapable of any collective action
confined and treated as less than fully human
responsible for organizing the attackers’ conduct
rationales: The enclosure is threatening and inglorious.
The rest of the poem urges such action.
Hunting and penning make helplessness and degradation central.
The group is pursued, not directing the pursuit.

questions.stem: The description of the opponents as “mad and hungry dogs” chiefly contributes to
choices: a claim that the conflict is literally between farm animals
a portrayal of predatory violence that the speaker refuses to accept passively
an expectation that the attackers will soon become sympathetic
an admiration for the opponents’ reasoned judgment
rationales: The comparisons frame a human appeal.
The animal imagery characterizes the attackers’ appetite and aggression.
The poem demands dignity and resistance under threat rather than predicting the attackers’ moral conversion.
“Mad” resists rational admiration.

questions.stem: The transition to “nobly die” most clearly shifts attention toward
choices: the certainty that social rank guarantees survival
a detailed description of funeral customs
the rejection of all concern for the group’s honor
the dignity that might be asserted despite an unchanged mortal danger
rationales: No such guarantee is given.
The phrase concerns conduct and meaning.
Honor becomes more explicit.
The speaker changes the terms of response rather than promising safety.

questions.stem: The claim that opponents will be “constrained to honor us” chiefly imagines
choices: a retreat that prevents the opponents from seeing any action
a voluntary friendship already established with the opponents
resistance compelling recognition even from hostile observers
a legal agreement the groups have signed
rationales: The poem urges confrontation.
Hostility remains present.
The speaker seeks a response that enemies cannot freely dismiss.
No agreement is described.

questions.stem: The direct address “O kinsmen!” chiefly strengthens
choices: the appeal to collective identity and mutual obligation
the introduction of a neutral narrator outside the conflict
the claim that only documented blood relatives may resist
the separation of the speaker from all companions
rationales: The address gathers the threatened group into a shared response.
The speaker remains involved.
The address functions as solidarity, not a genealogical rule.
The speaker includes the self in “we.”

questions.stem: The contrast between “their thousand blows” and “one death-blow” chiefly emphasizes
choices: the certainty that victory will require no sacrifice
the equality of the two sides’ resources
the speaker’s preference for careful statistical reporting
resistance under an acknowledged imbalance of force
rationales: The open grave remains before them.
The figures explicitly stress inequality.
The numbers function rhetorically rather than as a verified count.
The numerical disparity accompanies the admission of being outnumbered.

questions.stem: The question “What though before us lies the open grave?” chiefly functions as
choices: a request for directions to a burial ground
a challenge to let acknowledged danger determine submission
a promise that the grave is merely an illusion
an admission that the speaker has forgotten the opening premise
rationales: The grave is part of the poem’s argument.
The question presses the argument that courage remains possible despite death.
The danger is not dismissed as unreal.
It returns to that premise.

questions.stem: The final contrast between “Like men” and the “pack” chiefly advances
choices: the poem’s redefinition of dignity through the group’s chosen response
a return to the opening image of unquestioning helplessness
a claim that the opponents deserve admiration for restraint
a reconciliation in which both groups abandon hostility
rationales: Human courage is asserted against the attackers’ animalized violence.
The group now fights back.
They remain murderous and cowardly.
The confrontation continues.

questions.stem: Which thesis best accounts for the poem’s final “dying, but fighting back”?
choices: The poem rejects solidarity because individual escape is always preferable.
The poem celebrates certain military victory as the only source of human worth.
The poem asserts dignity through collective resistance while refusing to erase the possibility of defeat.
The poem treats courage as the absence of any awareness of danger.
rationales: The collective appeal runs throughout.
Victory is not guaranteed.
The ending sustains both mortal vulnerability and active defiance.
Danger remains explicit to the final line.

questions.stem: The stranger’s glance at his leg after hearing “blacksmith” most clearly prepares for
choices: his decision to ask Pip for medical treatment
his attempt to identify the owner of the tombstone
his recognition that Pip has already brought supplies
a demand for a blacksmith’s tool
rationales: The subsequent demand concerns a file and food, not treatment.
The glance concerns his own leg and practical need.
The supplies are requested for the following morning.
The iron and the blacksmith connection make a file practically relevant.

questions.stem: The movement from questions about a file and food to commands chiefly shows the stranger
choices: correcting an earlier mistaken account of Pip’s family
establishing Pip’s understanding before specifying the required action
offering Pip several equally acceptable choices
abandoning his practical purpose in favor of idle conversation
rationales: No correction of family information occurs.
Pip’s affirmative replies precede the direct demands.
The commands narrow rather than expand his options.
The questions prepare that purpose.

questions.stem: The repeated tilting interspersed with the demands most clearly makes
choices: physical pressure reinforce each part of the verbal instruction
the delivery instructions less consequential than the setting
Pip’s agreement appear independent of the surrounding threat
the stranger’s uncertainty about his demands increasingly apparent
rationales: The repeated action accompanies the tool, food, delivery, and threat.
The motion intensifies attention to the instructions.
The action makes coercion inseparable from agreement.
The demands remain explicit and consistent.

questions.stem: Pip’s request to be held upright chiefly attempts to
choices: delay the conversation until another adult arrives
reject the stranger’s authority through open defiance
gain relief while appearing cooperative
persuade the stranger that he cannot understand ordinary speech
rationales: He proposes no such delay or rescue.
His deferential language seeks accommodation within the threat.
He frames bodily relief as improved attention to the stranger’s demands.
He asks for conditions in which he can attend more.

questions.stem: The stranger’s description of the hidden young man primarily extends the threat by
choices: explaining why the stranger must cancel the requested delivery
making danger seem to continue beyond the immediate encounter
showing that the stranger is unable to influence what happens next
giving Pip an independently verified reason to trust him
rationales: The story enforces rather than cancels the demand.
The imagined pursuer can reach Pip even behind a locked bedroom door.
He claims to be holding the young man back.
The young man’s existence is asserted only by the stranger.

questions.stem: The imagined sequence of locking a door, getting into bed, and hiding under the covers chiefly serves to
choices: establish that Pip has already attempted and failed to hide
shift the account toward the stranger’s own childhood memories
offer practical advice about how Pip can avoid the delivery
invalidate successive forms of safety Pip might expect at home
rationales: These are hypothetical possibilities.
The focus remains on frightening Pip.
The sequence denies escape rather than advising it.
Each familiar protection is declared ineffective against the pursuer.

questions.stem: By claiming to restrain the young man, the stranger presents himself as
choices: an uninvolved observer who cannot affect the outcome
a reliable witness whose benevolence has been independently confirmed
a threatening but supposedly necessary protector
a person whose need for food has completely disappeared
rationales: He claims active restraint of the pursuer.
No independent confirmation supports the claim.
He threatens Pip while making continued safety depend on his intervention.
The practical demand remains in force.

questions.stem: Pip’s promise to bring “what broken bits of food I could” most clearly indicates
choices: an attempt to comply within the resources he imagines available
a recognition that the stranger’s account has been disproved
a confident plan to provide an elaborate meal
a negotiation that makes food conditional on relief from the tool demand
rationales: The qualification limits the food promise without rejecting the demand.
He continues to respond fearfully.
“Broken bits” suggests modest available scraps.
Pip agrees to bring both requested items; he does not bargain by making one depend on withdrawing the other.

questions.stem: The oath demanded after Pip’s promise chiefly functions to
choices: acknowledge that the stranger no longer needs the promised supplies
give Pip a socially equal role in negotiating the terms
replace the earlier demands with an unrelated religious debate
add another form of pressure to an agreement already secured by threats
rationales: The final reminder preserves the undertaking.
He is directed to repeat the words.
The oath remains tied to the same promise.
The stranger reinforces compliance before releasing him.

questions.stem: The final reminder of the undertaking and the young man chiefly links
choices: Pip’s release with the cancellation of every obligation
the practical task with the imagined consequence of failing it
the present encounter with a completed delivery
the stranger’s bodily weakness with a withdrawal of his earlier threats
rationales: Release follows a reiterated obligation.
Both the demand and its enforcing story are repeated before Pip leaves.
The delivery remains in the future.
The physical vulnerability complicates his threatening presence without canceling the coercive demands.

questions.stem: The opening disclosure that Mr. Bennet has already visited Bingley primarily
choices: removes interest in how the family will react
makes readers share the family’s complete ignorance until the announcement
lets readers interpret the conversation with knowledge his family lacks
presents the visit as a reluctant response to the evening’s persuasion
rationales: The known fact redirects interest toward the manner and effect of disclosure.
The narrator explicitly prevents that ignorance.
The family’s uncertainty unfolds after readers learn the fact and intention.
The visit precedes the conversation and was always intended.

questions.stem: The information that Mr. Bennet “had always intended” to visit most directly qualifies
choices: Mrs. Bennet’s later claim that she persuaded him
Lydia’s claim to be the tallest sister
Kitty’s denial that she coughs for amusement
Elizabeth’s expectation of meeting Bingley at an assembly
rationales: Her causal explanation conflicts with the intention already supplied.
The visit’s intention does not bear on height.
The intention supplies no correction of Kitty’s claim.
That expectation is not contradicted by his prior intention.

questions.stem: Mr. Bennet’s opening comment about Elizabeth’s hat is best understood, given the exposition, as
choices: a straightforward report of Bingley’s stated taste in hats
an unplanned disclosure of a fact he wishes permanently to conceal
an attempt to prevent further discussion of the newcomer
an indirect way to introduce the topic whose secret he controls
rationales: No such statement by Bingley is reported.
The narrator says the ensuing astonishment is what he wants.
He repeatedly returns to the topic.
He knows the visit has occurred while the family assumes it has not.

questions.stem: Mrs. Bennet’s judgment of Mrs. Long most clearly reveals how
choices: the narrator confirms every aspect of Mrs. Long’s character
perceived competition shapes her account of a possible introduction
the family has abandoned its interest in social access
Mr. Bennet has informed her of a broken agreement
rationales: The judgment belongs to Mrs. Bennet.
The nieces are offered as the reason Mrs. Long will not serve the Bennets.
Her complaint arises from continued interest in access.
No such information has been supplied.

questions.stem: The digression about Kitty’s cough chiefly allows the scene to
choices: displace frustration while prolonging the withheld information
introduce a medical explanation for the entire family conflict
establish that Kitty intentionally controls the timing of the visit
resolve the question of who will introduce Bingley
rationales: Mrs. Bennet turns from the unresolved introduction to scolding Kitty.
The scene treats the cough within domestic irritation and teasing.
She has no such control and denies coughing for amusement.
The cough does not settle that question.

questions.stem: Mr. Bennet’s suggestion that his wife might introduce Bingley to Mrs. Long carries an implication readers can recognize because
choices: Mrs. Long’s social influence has become more important to him than his own visit
Bingley has already become engaged to Elizabeth
his own visit has already made an introduction possible
his wife has independently met Bingley without remembering it
rationales: Mr. Bennet already possesses the decisive acquaintance and uses the discussion to prolong its disclosure.
No engagement is established.
Readers know the basis for a suggestion his wife calls impossible.
The passage supplies no such meeting.

questions.stem: The appeal to Mary as a reader of “great books” chiefly introduces
choices: a shift to Mary as the scene’s principal narrator
a comic test of Mary’s intellectual reputation
an authoritative judgment that resolves the introduction debate
a reliable account of Bingley’s literary preferences
rationales: The external narrator continues.
The narrator immediately reports her wish to sound sensible and failure to find words.
Mary supplies no judgment.
The comment concerns Mary.

questions.stem: The announcement of the visit is timed to follow Mrs. Bennet’s claim that she is “sick of Mr. Bingley,” primarily so that
choices: the narrator can retract the opening report as mistaken
readers will first learn that the family knows Bingley’s character well
the family will reasonably conclude that the visit must be undone
Mr. Bennet can make welcome news sound inconvenient
rationales: The announcement confirms it.
The announcement concerns access, not established knowledge of character.
The acquaintance cannot be escaped, he says teasingly.
His mock regret exploits the contrast between her outburst and her actual interest.

questions.stem: Mrs. Bennet’s claim that she expected the visit “all the while” is qualified most directly by
choices: the information that Bingley has servants
Lydia’s confidence about dancing at the ball
the narrator’s report of her surpassing astonishment
Mr. Bennet’s inability to remember whether he visited
rationales: That information belongs to a different concern.
Lydia’s confidence does not establish the mother’s earlier expectation.
The juxtaposition exposes a revision of her own prior state of knowledge.
He is certain that he did.

questions.stem: The final sentence changes the family’s activity from
choices: disputing access to anticipating an established acquaintance
anticipating an introduction to reconsidering whether the acquaintance is desirable
celebrating an engagement to regretting its cancellation
debating social forms to rejecting all future contact
rationales: They turn to the return visit and a future dinner.
The revealed visit secures access, and the family turns toward its practical consequences rather than rejecting its desirability.
No engagement has occurred.
They plan further contact rather than reject it.

questions.stem: The word “accomplishment” followed by “catastrophe” chiefly establishes
choices: a distinction between two unrelated experiments
a steady satisfaction temporarily interrupted by weather
a failure to achieve any sign of life
Victor’s reversal of judgment about his achievement
rationales: The terms refer to the same creation.
His response becomes horror, not sustained satisfaction.
The creature opens its eye and breathes.
The long-sought animation becomes the event he recoils from.

questions.stem: The nearly extinguished candle contributes to the opening chiefly by
choices: offering a stable source of comfort throughout the night
limiting the visual conditions under which the first signs of life appear
explaining the technical mechanism that animates the creature
proving that Victor intends to conceal the result from Walton
rationales: The light is failing and the night remains distressing.
Glimmering light accompanies the eye’s opening and convulsive movement.
The passage does not supply such a mechanism.
The immediate scene does not establish that intention.

questions.stem: Victor’s exclamation “Beautiful! Great God!” chiefly marks
choices: the failure of Victor’s earlier aesthetic judgment
a request that the creature explain its appearance
a calm comparison between several equally successful designs
his renewed confidence that the creature will be admired
rationales: The features chosen as beautiful now intensify a horrid whole.
He does not address the creature in that way.
The punctuation and wording are agitated.
The ensuing description is horrified.

questions.stem: The contrast between lustrous hair, white teeth, and the surrounding bodily details chiefly suggests that
choices: the creature’s appearance is irrelevant to his response
Victor had deliberately planned every feature to repel observers
pleasing parts fail to form a pleasing whole
the narrative has shifted to the creature’s self-description
rationales: Appearance repeatedly triggers his revulsion.
He says he selected features as beautiful.
The selected luxuriances worsen the contrast with eyes and skin.
Victor remains the perceiving narrator.

questions.stem: The reference to nearly two years of deprivation chiefly intensifies
choices: the impression that Victor acted without prior commitment
the disparity between sustained anticipation and immediate revulsion
the suggestion that the experiment’s result was entirely accidental
the certainty that the creature shares Victor’s memories
rationales: The account stresses prolonged commitment.
The duration and cost of work make the abrupt reversal more consequential.
Victor pursued the purpose for years.
No shared memory is established.

questions.stem: The dream of Elizabeth changing into Victor’s dead mother chiefly
choices: confirms that Elizabeth has literally entered the room
offers an independent explanation of the creature’s intentions
provides a reassuring prediction that the creation will restore his family
joins desired intimacy with death and decay
rationales: The scene is explicitly a dream.
It concerns Victor’s experience, not the creature’s mind.
The dream is disturbing rather than reassuring.
An embrace becomes contact with a corpse, repeating the collapse of expectation.

questions.stem: The phrases “He might have spoken” and “seemingly to detain me” most clearly reveal
choices: a narrator who has heard and accurately reported a complete threat
a creature whose hostile plan is explained without ambiguity
uncertainty within Victor’s interpretation of the creature’s gestures
a deliberate agreement between creator and creation to separate
rationales: Victor says he did not hear.
The qualifying language resists that certainty.
Possible speech and apparent intention are not fully established.
No exchange reaches agreement.

questions.stem: Victor’s repeated flight from room to courtyard to streets chiefly develops
choices: fear that outlasts the creature’s visible presence
a sequence in which each new location supplies reliable safety
a carefully planned effort to find assistance for the creature
a gradual restoration of complete physical composure
rationales: Anticipated pursuit governs him even when he no longer sees the creature.
He remains apprehensive in every location.
No assistance is sought in the selection.
Palpitations and irregular movement continue.

questions.stem: The arrival of morning chiefly qualifies an expectation of relief because
choices: Victor decides to resume the experiment immediately
the weather becomes bright and reassuring
the creature has disappeared from Victor’s memory
daylight brings ordinary landmarks without resolving Victor’s dread
rationales: He does not dare return to the apartment.
The morning remains dismal and wet.
He fears seeing it at every turn.
The church and clock return the scene to routine time while he still fears an encounter.

questions.stem: Which account best describes how the passage sustains tension after animation occurs?
choices: The narrative withholds whether any life has actually been produced.
Success becomes a source of dread that Victor repeatedly evades.
The creature repeatedly states a detailed plan of revenge.
Victor’s scientific explanation steadily replaces his emotional response.
rationales: Breathing and movement establish animation.
The climax of creation opens unresolved emotional and interpersonal pressures.
No intelligible speech or plan is reported.
The account remains dominated by horror and flight.

questions.stem: John’s references to money, meals, and clothing chiefly establish his attempt to
choices: acknowledge that Jane has the same claim to the books as he does
offer a neutral explanation of household accounting
turn Jane’s dependence into a justification for his authority
persuade Jane to accept a gift without embarrassment
rationales: He explicitly denies that claim.
The speech is accusatory and exclusionary.
He uses material support to deny her equal access and standing.
He asserts ownership rather than giving.

questions.stem: The qualification that the house belongs to John “or will do in a few years” most clearly suggests that
choices: he treats anticipated ownership as a basis for present domination
the narrator accepts his authority as morally sufficient
Jane has agreed to transfer the house to him
his lack of present ownership makes him abandon the commands
rationales: Future property rights are invoked to support immediate commands.
The narration exposes its coercive use.
No such agreement exists.
He continues to direct Jane.

questions.stem: Jane’s initial fetching of the book and movement toward the door chiefly show
choices: a successful negotiation over the use of the room
a calculated invitation for John to attack her
a refusal to recognize any household hierarchy
compliance before she fully understands the intended assault
rationales: John gives orders rather than negotiates.
Her alarm contradicts that intention.
She initially follows his commands.
She obeys and then recognizes the poised book as a threat.

questions.stem: The statement that Jane’s terror “had passed its climax” chiefly prepares for
choices: a return to the earlier pleasure of reading
a movement from fear toward active resistance
a decision to forgive John before he responds
a loss of all awareness of bodily pain
rationales: The scene moves into confrontation.
Other feelings succeed terror before she speaks against John.
No forgiveness is offered.
Pain is explicitly described and later remains influential.

questions.stem: Jane’s comparison of John to Roman emperors most clearly turns
choices: private reading into a vocabulary for publicly judging domination
a family quarrel into an accurate record of ancient events
her accusation into an admission that John’s authority is rightful
historical knowledge into proof that John holds legal office
rationales: The narrator explains that previously silent parallels are now spoken.
The history helps interpret the present encounter.
The comparison condemns tyranny.
The comparison is figurative.

questions.stem: John’s appeal to his sisters after Jane’s accusation chiefly reveals
choices: his willingness to consider whether her criticism is justified
his uncertainty about whether Jane is physically present
his outrage that she has challenged his assumed position
his wish to keep the encounter hidden from the family
rationales: He attacks rather than considers it.
He addresses her immediately afterward.
“Did she say that to me?” makes the breached hierarchy central.
He seeks witnesses and invokes their mother.

questions.stem: Jane’s description of sensations temporarily predominating over fear chiefly presents her resistance as
choices: a response made possible by the adults’ explicit encouragement
a bodily reaction exceeding deliberate calculation
a detached application of a previously rehearsed plan
an action she later denies having taken at all
rationales: The adults condemn her conduct.
Pain and desperation precede an action she cannot precisely reconstruct.
She does not clearly know what she did with her hands.
She acknowledges resistance while qualifying its details.

questions.stem: The adults’ descriptions of Jane as a “fury” and a “picture of passion” chiefly
choices: repeat Jane’s own evaluation of John in agreement with her
grant her a recognized right to answer force with force
confirm that they witnessed and condemned John’s initial assault
reframe her resistance without acknowledging the preceding injury
rationales: They direct the labels at Jane.
Their response leads to punishment.
They do not condemn him in the quoted responses.
Their labels focus on her behavior after the narration has supplied its cause.

questions.stem: The command to lock Jane in the red-room chiefly demonstrates
choices: a voluntary retreat Jane has requested
the immediate success of Jane’s effort to change the family’s rules
the household’s power to impose consequences despite her moment of resistance
the adults’ uncertainty about who controls the house
rationales: She is taken away by force.
The hierarchy remains operative.
The scene ends with confinement ordered by Mrs. Reed.
The order is promptly executed.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the relation between agency and constraint in the passage?
choices: Jane acts against domination but cannot control how the household names or punishes her action.
Jane’s ability to speak removes the material conditions of dependence.
John’s authority rests solely on physical size, without social support.
Jane’s punishment proves that she has made no consequential choice.
rationales: Resistance and continuing unequal power coexist.
The household’s control persists.
His property claims and the adults’ intervention add social power.
Her accusation and resistance remain actions despite their cost.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s memory of Wickham avoiding the ball chiefly becomes significant because
choices: she learns for the first time that the ball occurred
an old event now conflicts with a claim she previously accepted
the event proves that every statement in Darcy’s letter is accurate
she decides that attendance is the only measure of character
rationales: She recalls an event already known.
His avoidance undermines his assertion that he did not fear Darcy.
It supports reassessment without proving every claim.
Her review uses several kinds of evidence.

questions.stem: The repeated references to what Elizabeth “remembered” chiefly portray change as
choices: a simple accumulation of facts with no change in judgment
a replacement of memory by an unrelated fantasy
a refusal to consider any new perspective
a reorganization of existing evidence under a revised understanding
rationales: Her judgments change substantially.
The account remains anchored in remembered conduct.
The letter prompts a new reading of the past.
Past conversations acquire implications she previously missed.

questions.stem: The changing interpretation of Wickham’s interest in Miss King chiefly shows that
choices: Elizabeth now regards financial motives as impossible
Wickham has openly explained his motives to Elizabeth
questioning a motive changes the meaning of familiar evidence
Elizabeth has obtained a new numerical account of the fortune
rationales: She increasingly suspects them.
She infers motives from conduct.
A modest fortune once suggested moderation and now suggests opportunism.
The amount is not revised in this selection.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s recognition that Darcy’s manners were “proud and repulsive” while his conduct was not evidently unjust chiefly indicates
choices: a growing distinction between personal agreeableness and moral character
a complete reversal in which she now finds every manner attractive
a decision that outward manners never affect relationships
a belief that moral conduct can be judged without any evidence
rationales: She separates the dislike of manners from evidence of principle.
The negative description remains.
She does not deny their effect.
She reviews specific relationships and actions.

questions.stem: The transition from reviewing the men to “She grew absolutely ashamed of herself” chiefly shifts the reassessment toward
choices: an effort to protect her earlier opinion by refusing further evidence
an assurance that she had always understood both men correctly
a comparison of the men’s social rank alone
the reliability of her own methods of judgment
rationales: Her continued rereading tests and undermines the former judgment rather than shielding it from evidence.
She condemns her earlier partiality.
The focus turns to bias and vanity.
Her former discernment becomes an object of scrutiny.

questions.stem: The repeated “I, who” in Elizabeth’s speech chiefly emphasizes
choices: a new confidence that she is incapable of error
the contrast between her valued self-image and her recognized conduct
her desire to imitate Jane’s exact manner of speaking
her certainty that no other person has contributed to the situation
rationales: The speech confesses error.
Claims of discernment are set against acknowledged blindness.
No such imitation occurs.
She later considers the family and others.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s distinction between vanity and love most clearly revises
choices: her account of the motive that shaped her earlier judgments
the facts of the first conversations themselves
her belief that Wickham and Darcy are the same person
the narrator’s statement that she has no emotional response
rationales: Praise and neglect, rather than romantic attachment alone, become central to her explanation.
She reinterprets rather than rewrites the events.
No confusion of identity exists.
The narration describes intense emotion.

questions.stem: Her return to the part of the letter concerning Jane and Bingley chiefly suggests that
choices: her attention has shifted away from evidence toward appearance alone
she considers each claim wholly unrelated to all others
one corrected judgment prompts her to reconsider a related judgment
she accepts the entire letter without rereading it
rationales: She considers Jane’s visible feelings and prior observations as evidence.
The narration explicitly links them.
Credit given to Darcy in one matter affects how she weighs another.
She reads that section again.

questions.stem: The statement that a compliment “soothed, but it could not console” Elizabeth chiefly shows
choices: a decision that Darcy’s letter contains no valid criticism
reassurance cannot undo the injury she recognizes
a complete return to the vanity she has just identified
an inability to register any favorable statement at all
rationales: She accepts the reproach as merited.
The family’s conduct and Jane’s disappointment remain painful.
The reassurance cannot override her larger concern.
The compliment is “not unfelt.”

questions.stem: The effort to appear cheerful on returning home chiefly qualifies the scene’s recognition by
choices: showing that all distress has already disappeared
establishing that every later judgment will be impartial
proving that the letter has produced no change
separating inward upheaval from the outward conduct she must manage
rationales: The wish to conceal it implies its persistence.
The excerpt ends before that can be tested.
The preceding reassessment is extensive.
She suppresses reflections that would disrupt conversation.

questions.stem: The contrast between fifteen dollars and the worn purse chiefly establishes
choices: a permanent transition into secure wealth
her unfamiliarity with any form of financial calculation
the sum’s unusual importance within a constrained life
her indifference to the appearance of her possessions
rationales: The sum is limited and the wider circumstances remain.
The next paragraphs show careful calculation.
The money bulges in an old purse and restores a long-absent sense of importance.
The material contrast carries significance.

questions.stem: The detailed plan for shoes, fabric, and stockings chiefly reveals
choices: how economic decisions are intertwined with care and repeated household labor
a preference for decorative goods unrelated to family needs
a desire to conceal the money from every family member
a refusal to consider the cost of any purchase
rationales: Durability, patching, and darning shape the anticipated purchases.
The list is largely practical and child-centered.
No such concealment is established.
She calculates the allocation closely.

questions.stem: The imagined reduction in darning chiefly makes the new stockings valuable as
choices: a symbol whose meaning is independent of domestic work
a means of improving the children’s public reputation more than their comfort
proof that the children have rejected all old clothing
relief from labor as well as new material possessions
rationales: The meaning arises partly from that work.
The reduced darning emphasizes household work and practical use rather than chiefly public display.
Their opinions are not reported.
The purchase would save recurring repair work.

questions.stem: The neighbors’ references to “better days” chiefly provide
choices: a reliable prediction that prosperity will soon return
a comparison with her more prosperous past
a detailed explanation of how she acquired the fifteen dollars
evidence that she spends her days absorbed in nostalgia
rationales: No such prediction is offered.
The comments introduce a past she has little time to revisit.
The money’s origin remains unspecified.
The narrator explicitly denies time for that.

questions.stem: The description of bargain shopping as a struggle through a crowd chiefly presents thrift as
choices: labor demanding physical endurance and determination
a practice she has always refused on principle
a leisurely pleasure requiring little effort
an unusual incompetence specific to Mrs. Sommers
rationales: Clutching, holding, and elbowing make obtaining value laborious.
She knows bargains and has pursued them persistently.
The diction emphasizes effort and competition.
She is described as skilled at it.

questions.stem: The correction that she has not eaten lunch chiefly links her fatigue to
choices: an inability to obtain any food in the city
the immediate effect of purchasing the stockings
the priority given to feeding the children and preparing the household
a deliberate fasting practice she explains to the clerk
rationales: The passage identifies overlooked self-care, not absolute unavailability.
The fatigue precedes the purchase.
The routine has displaced her own meal.
No such practice or explanation appears.

questions.stem: Her smile at the invitation to inspect silk hosiery, as though offered a diamond tiara, chiefly reveals
choices: her contempt for the clerk’s lack of taste
luxury’s apparent distance from her ordinary means
her expert knowledge that silk and diamonds cost the same
a settled intention formed before entering the store
rationales: The account does not assign that motive.
The comparison makes the modest invitation feel extravagantly beyond expectation.
The comparison concerns perceived luxury, not equivalent price.
The tactile encounter precedes the decision.

questions.stem: The small parcel seeming lost in the shabby bag chiefly makes visible
choices: the complete disappearance of her previous economic identity
her immediate regret and return of the stockings
a practical error in the clerk’s packaging
luxury’s incongruity with her usual material circumstances
rationales: The old bag remains present.
She keeps and wears them.
No packaging error is described.
The juxtaposition places the new purchase within continuing worn circumstances.

questions.stem: The shoe clerk’s inability to reconcile her shoes with her stockings chiefly illustrates
choices: Mrs. Sommers’s success in explaining her entire personal history
a narrator who regards outward appearance as infallible evidence
clothing’s role in rapid judgments of status
his inability to distinguish shoes from hosiery
rationales: She does not provide that history.
The mismatch exposes the limits of the clerk’s assumptions.
The mismatched items disrupt his expectations.
He recognizes the items but cannot reconcile their apparent status.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the social significance of Mrs. Sommers’s changing demands?
choices: A temporary experience of luxury alters how she claims attention without removing her underlying constraints.
Her fatigue makes all social and economic details irrelevant to the decision.
Her purchases establish that the family’s economic difficulties have ended.
Her initial family plans prove that personal desire has no role in her behavior.
rationales: Her new insistence on style coexists with the established context of scarcity and care.
Those details help explain the fatigue and the purchase’s meaning.
The passage provides no such resolution.
The later purchases reveal its force.

questions.stem: Torvald’s question about whether an earnest discussion would have benefited Nora chiefly reveals
choices: his limited estimate of her intellectual participation
a concession that he has always misunderstood her
a willingness to let her define the subject without challenge
a request for specific business advice
rationales: His reply questions its value to her, prompting her accusation of misunderstanding.
He has not yet conceded that claim.
He immediately challenges the proposed value.
She has explicitly excluded business matters.

questions.stem: Nora’s distinction between loving her and finding it pleasant to be in love with her chiefly challenges
choices: his claim that her father treated her differently from him
the fact that Torvald has ever used affectionate language
his identification of enjoyment with love
the possibility that the marriage has contained any pleasant moments
rationales: He has grouped himself with the father.
The distinction concerns the meaning of affection, not its vocabulary alone.
She separates his pleasurable feeling from understanding and care directed toward her.
She later acknowledges merriment and kindness.

questions.stem: Torvald’s interruption about Nora’s expression “came to live with you” chiefly shows his concern with
choices: her inability to remember the house’s location
the terms in which she is redefining their marriage
the exact date on which she moved
the practical arrangements for an already agreed departure
rationales: No such memory problem appears.
He objects to wording that unsettles the expected marital description.
The objection is to the expression, not chronology.
Departure has not yet been announced.

questions.stem: Nora’s uncertainty about whether she shared Torvald’s tastes or merely pretended chiefly suggests
choices: that she cannot remember any events of the marriage
that the distinction has no consequence for her present decision
that Torvald has explicitly invited independent disagreement
adaptation has obscured her independent preferences
rationales: She supplies an extensive account of its pattern.
Self-understanding becomes central to leaving.
Her account says he arranged everything to his taste.
She cannot cleanly separate assimilation from performance.

questions.stem: The distinction between being “happy” and being “merry” chiefly allows Nora to
choices: prove that Torvald knowingly intended every harm she describes
claim that the children have never enjoyed playing
acknowledge surface pleasure while disputing deeper fulfillment
withdraw her criticism because entertainment is sufficient
rationales: The distinction concerns her experience, not complete access to his intention.
She says they found it fun.
She does not need to deny every pleasant moment to challenge the marriage.
She continues to reject the relationship’s structure.

questions.stem: The progression from “doll-child” to “doll-wife” to the children as dolls chiefly
choices: extends the pattern of unequal treatment across successive relationships
isolates the problem entirely in her father’s household
establishes that Nora bears no relation to the pattern she criticizes
turns the conversation away from family relations toward craftsmanship
rationales: Nora recognizes both being treated as a doll and reproducing that relation.
The pattern continues in marriage and parenting.
She includes her own treatment of the children.
The doll language remains metaphorical.

questions.stem: Torvald’s concession followed by “lesson-time shall begin” chiefly demonstrates
choices: an abandonment of every assumption about gender and marriage
a complete acceptance of her claim to self-education
a decision to place himself under Nora’s instruction
a proposed reform that retains his authority over Nora
rationales: His proposal preserves the governing hierarchy.
He offers to educate her rather than recognize independence.
He specifies lessons for her and the children.
He changes the activity from play to instruction while remaining teacher.

questions.stem: Nora’s question “Whose lessons?” chiefly works to
choices: avoid the subject of her own development
make explicit the hierarchy implied by Torvald’s proposed solution
shift attention to a teacher outside the household
request a timetable for an arrangement she has already accepted
rationales: The question leads directly to it.
The answer groups her with the children as pupils.
No outside teacher has yet been introduced.

questions.stem: Nora’s reuse of Torvald’s earlier claim that she cannot raise the children chiefly
choices: makes his criticism support her need for self-education
proves that he now consistently maintains the same judgment
shows that she has forgotten the earlier dispute
ends the conversation by agreeing to remain unchanged
rationales: She accepts the need for preparation while rejecting him as its provider.
He dismisses it as a moment of anger.
She quotes its substance back to him.
It leads to her decision to leave.

questions.stem: The final exchange between prohibition and “It is no use forbidding me” chiefly marks
choices: an admission that Nora has no intention of acting on her decision
a negotiated agreement about every consequence of departure
a change in Nora’s acceptance of the authority Torvald’s commands assume
a return to the earlier playful manner without alteration

The exchange remains conflictual and incomplete.
His familiar form of control no longer secures compliance.
The command is directly refused.

questions.stem: The opening bell, entrance, humming, and parcels chiefly establish
choices: a silent household in which no activity is permitted
domestic liveliness preceding concealment and disagreement
the outcome of the financial dispute before it begins
a formally controlled household in which spontaneous pleasure is absent
rationales: The opening is active and audible.
Festive movement precedes the later tensions.
The dispute has not yet unfolded.
Humming, parcels, and lively entrance establish animation rather than an absence of spontaneous pleasure.

questions.stem: The visible Christmas tree and instruction to hide it primarily establish
choices: a stage object with no relation to household relationships
an immediate threat to Torvald’s professional position
proof that every hidden object in the scene has the same motive
one ordinary form of concealment that can be compared with Nora’s later secrecy
rationales: The tree is concealed specifically for the children.
No such threat is attached to the tree here.
The objects invite comparison without establishing identical purposes.
A festive surprise precedes the more cautious concealment of the sweets.

questions.stem: Nora’s listening at Torvald’s door after eating macaroons chiefly gives the action
choices: the appearance of complete indifference to his presence
the certainty of an open disagreement already underway
caution beneath her apparent cheerfulness
a meaning available only through Torvald’s spoken explanation
rationales: She deliberately checks whether he is there.
The main conversation has not yet begun.
The direction places vigilance beside humming and laughter.
The audience can infer caution from the action itself.

questions.stem: Torvald’s first calls from his room chiefly allow the scene to
choices: establish a relationship through voice before the characters share the visible space
confirm that he has seen every action Nora performs
show that Nora has left the house before he speaks
remove the significance of the study door
rationales: His endearments cross the boundary of the study.
His position limits what he visibly observes.
She remains with the parcels.
The offstage voice makes the separation noticeable.

questions.stem: The direction that Nora pockets the macaroons and wipes her mouth chiefly supplies
choices: proof that Torvald has already discovered the packet
a resolution of the tension between Nora’s private acts and Torvald’s expectations
a direct statement of the historical author’s opinion about food
a contrast between concealed eating and displayed purchases
rationales: His discovery is not shown.
Concealing the sweets maintains the difference between private behavior and what she openly displays.
The direction stages behavior rather than authorial commentary.
The visible concealment qualifies the apparent openness of the invitation.

questions.stem: Torvald’s entrance with a pen in hand chiefly reinforces
choices: a completed legal agreement about household spending
his association with work rather than shopping
the idea that he has been helping Nora wrap gifts
the narrator’s access to his private thoughts
rationales: No agreement is written in the scene.
The prop connects him to the study as he scrutinizes purchases.
The pen accompanies his work-room entrance, not shared wrapping.
A visible prop does not supply direct mental access.

questions.stem: The playful handling of Nora’s ear chiefly gives the exchange
choices: a physical form that can combine affection with correction
an unambiguous equality of bodily and financial control
a direction requiring a production to portray open hatred
a break in which all spoken disagreement ceases permanently
rationales: The gesture accompanies his rebuke about borrowing.
He corrects and handles her in the same moment.
“Playfully” preserves an affectionate surface.
The argument about debt continues.

questions.stem: Nora’s putting her hands over Torvald’s mouth chiefly
choices: proves that she controls every later turn of the conversation
replaces the need to attend to the dialogue that surrounds it
makes her attempt to stop the imagined death physically visible
shows her acceptance of the example without discomfort
rationales: He resumes the example and the argument.
Its significance depends on that dialogue.
The gesture interrupts his hypothetical account before her spoken objection.
She objects to the horrid thought.

questions.stem: The movement toward the stove and Torvald’s following most clearly stages
choices: a change to an entirely different room and scene
a withdrawal and an effort to restore the exchange
a resolution in which neither character needs further contact
a purely decorative movement unrelated to their disagreement
rationales: The action remains in the same room.
Her compliance is followed by retreat, and he approaches with reassurance and money.
He immediately follows and speaks.

questions.stem: Nora’s quick turn at the mention of Torvald’s purse chiefly makes visible
choices: her refusal to accept any money from him
the permanent resolution of the underlying disagreement about authority
his loss of all influence over the conversation
her renewed animation at the prospect of money
rationales: She accepts and thanks him.
The moment restores mood without proving structural change.
His gesture successfully redirects it.
Her immediate response and counting follow the earlier withdrawal.

questions.stem: The mountain setting and Victor’s initial search for elevated consolation chiefly prepare a contrast with
choices: a confrontation that interrupts his sought-for refuge
a narrator who has no emotional investment in the meeting
a peaceful agreement that both characters reach before speaking
the creature’s complete acceptance of exclusion
rationales: The creature appears within a landscape Victor hopes will restore peace.
Victor’s response is intensely involved.
The encounter begins with hostility.

questions.stem: Victor’s initial labels for the creature most clearly function to
choices: establish a neutral vocabulary both speakers accept
separate the encounter from the history of creation
deny a relation that the creature then insists upon
acknowledge the creature’s account before hearing it

That history becomes central to the dispute.
Terms of abhorrence meet the counterclaim “thy creature.”

questions.stem: The creature’s reminder that Victor is his creator chiefly turns the argument toward
choices: a request that Victor judge only outward appearance
the duties that creation establishes
the idea that power alone establishes moral innocence
the creature’s claim to have designed Victor’s experiment
rationales: The appeal challenges that reduction.
The appeal makes creation relevant to present duties.
The creature invokes duties and suffering, not only force.
No such reversal of origin is asserted.

questions.stem: The contrast between “thy Adam” and “the fallen angel” chiefly presents the creature’s condition as
choices: a claim that he has never heard any account of creation
a statement that all responsibility belongs to fate alone
a simple assertion that the two figures have identical relations to their creator
exclusion from an expected place of care
rationales: The comparison demonstrates familiarity with such accounts.
The creature addresses Victor’s conduct directly.
The contrast depends on their different positions.
The allusion opposes an intended relation of care to being driven from joy.

questions.stem: The claim “I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend” chiefly asks Victor to consider
choices: a rejection of any distinction between benevolence and malice
an admission that suffering has had no effect on him
misery as a cause of changed conduct
a guarantee that every later act will be harmless
rationales: The distinction structures the claim.
He explicitly makes suffering causal.

questions.stem: The request to hear the creature’s tale chiefly makes the immediate ethical question one of
choices: whether condemnation will precede or follow attention to an account
whether the landscape can permanently separate the two figures
whether the creature can erase every harmful consequence by speaking
whether Victor can supply an exact medical classification

They move toward conversation rather than separation.
A hearing does not itself erase consequences.
No classification is the task at stake.

questions.stem: The creature’s acknowledgment of Victor’s power over him most clearly complicates
choices: the claim that Victor has any connection to his origin
the fact that the creature can move across the ice
the possibility that either speaker experiences anger
the assumption that physical superiority alone determines the encounter
rationales: The connection is repeatedly affirmed.
That ability remains visible.
Both anger and appeal are present.
He can evade attack yet still seeks the creator’s recognition and aid.

questions.stem: Victor’s eventual decision to listen most clearly represents
choices: a complete acceptance of every claim the creature will make
a concession to hearing rather than reconciliation
a return to the initial refusal without modification
an abandonment of the question of responsibility
rationales: He has not yet heard the tale.
He follows while weighing arguments and retains troubled feelings.
His behavior changes from rejection to hearing.
Listening begins engagement with it.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the coexistence of the creature’s appeal and his threatening language?
choices: The desire for recognition is entangled with coercion and injury rather than presented as uncomplicated innocence.
The appeal proves that the creature has no capacity to cause harm.
The two modes belong to unrelated speakers in separate episodes.
The threatening language makes every claim about suffering irrelevant.
rationales: The encounter contains both an appeal to duty and hostile pressure.
The scene does not establish that innocence.
They coexist within the same confrontation.
It complicates rather than automatically nullifies the appeal.

questions.stem: Which thematic claim is most fully supported by the encounter?
choices: Listening to an account necessarily settles every conflict between the participants.
A creator’s revulsion automatically cancels every duty toward a creation.
Responsibility becomes difficult to evade when a rejected creation insists on being heard, even amid justified fears and unresolved injuries.
Suffering always guarantees the moral correctness of every response to it.
rationales: The encounter moves toward narration without complete settlement.
The creature’s successful demand for a hearing challenges that claim.
The scene stages an obligation under pressure rather than a simple verdict.
The passage retains threats and contested responsibility.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best connects Elizabeth’s rereading of Wickham’s conduct with her self-accusation?
choices: The correction proves that her earlier observations were entirely fabricated.

Her distress arises solely from discovering that Darcy is wealthier.
Her self-accusation replaces any need to examine evidence.
rationales: The events remain; their interpretation changes.
The passage moves from remembered inconsistencies to vanity and partiality.
Wealth alone does not explain the reassessment.
The accusation grows from detailed review.

questions.stem: Which claim best accounts for the phrase “How differently did everything now appear”?
choices: A new narrator contradicts the preceding narrator’s report.
Elizabeth decides that appearances can never provide any useful evidence.
The physical setting has suddenly become unfamiliar to her.
A changed interpretive frame reorganizes details that Elizabeth already knows.
rationales: The perspective remains continuous.
She continues to interpret conduct and manners.
The change concerns Wickham and judgment.
The paragraph revalues remembered conduct under new assumptions.

questions.stem: The account of Darcy’s affection for his sister most directly supports an interpretation that
choices: Elizabeth now treats social charm as the only measure of virtue
Darcy’s family ties make all criticism of him impossible
conduct begins to challenge her impression of manners
Wickham has never acknowledged any favorable quality in Darcy
rationales: The detail helps her move beyond charm.
The passage uses the detail as evidence, not immunity.
The remembered affection complicates a judgment based on pride and repulsiveness.
The paragraph says even Wickham allowed merit as a brother.

questions.stem: Which claim best explains the importance of Elizabeth’s comparison with Jane’s “generous candour”?
choices: Her recognition challenges the superiority she had assigned to her own skeptical discernment.
She abandons concern for Jane after reviewing her own conduct.
She decides that Jane’s judgment must be correct in every circumstance.
She concludes that distrust and generosity have identical effects.
rationales: She admits having disdained a quality that now exposes her vanity.
Her thoughts return directly to Jane.
No universal guarantee follows.
The comparison depends on a difference.

questions.stem: The phrase “Yet, how just a humiliation!” most clearly supports which interpretation?
choices: She enjoys humiliation without any competing response.
Her distress proves that the letter contains no valid information.
Her shame is entirely imposed by others without her agreement.
She accepts correction without escaping its pain.
rationales: The surrounding language is wretched and painful.
The phrase accepts rather than rejects the correction.
She explicitly endorses its justice.
The exclamation joins emotional cost with acknowledged justice.

questions.stem: Which claim best accounts for the relation between “Pleased with the preference of one” and “offended by the neglect of the other”?
choices: The two men have behaved identically toward her.
Opposite social experiences have produced a similar bias in her reasoning.
Her judgments arose from two fully independent and impartial investigations.
Elizabeth has never valued either man’s opinion.
rationales: Their differing treatment is central.
Praise and neglect both shape her willingness to believe.
She names personal feeling as a cause.
The admission shows that their treatment mattered.

questions.stem: The description of Jane’s feelings as fervent but little displayed most clearly helps develop
choices: the difference between felt and observable emotion
a claim that Jane has deliberately deceived everyone about Bingley
a denial that observers’ perspectives matter to the reassessment
a conclusion that strong feeling must always be obvious
rationales: Elizabeth reconsiders how Darcy might have read Jane’s manner.
Limited display does not establish deliberate deception.
That perspective is the reason the distinction becomes relevant.
The passage explicitly separates feeling from display.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the family’s role in Elizabeth’s later distress?
choices: She concludes that family conduct has no effect on social judgment.
She accepts the family’s behavior as wholly beyond criticism.
Recognition makes family consequences part of her personal distress.
Her shame remains confined to one private conversation with Wickham.
rationales: She explicitly sees such effects.
She regards the reproach as merited.
She connects family impropriety with Jane’s disappointment and their shared credit.
The concerns broaden substantially.

questions.stem: The final phrase “as well as she could” chiefly supports a qualification that
choices: Elizabeth has refused to reconsider any prior belief
reconciliation to the changed understanding remains difficult and incomplete
the narrator regards her new interpretation as necessarily final and perfect
fatigue has erased the significance of the letter
rationales: The passage records extensive reconsideration.
The phrase limits the ease of the process before her return home.
The wording preserves difficulty rather than perfection.
The effort to manage her thoughts shows continuing significance.

questions.stem: Which thesis most fully accounts for the passage’s movement from recollection to managed outward cheerfulness?
choices: A single letter permanently frees Elizabeth from every source of prejudice and distress.
Elizabeth learns that agreeable manners always reveal reliable character.
Austen uses dialogue and description to show that Elizabeth has feelings.
Reassessing evidence forces Elizabeth to confront the vanity behind her discernment, producing an insight whose emotional cost she must conceal socially.
rationales: The excerpt establishes recognition, not complete permanent resolution.
Her reassessment specifically challenges that assumption.
This identifies features without explaining the consequential relationship.
The claim connects evidence, self-judgment, and the closing behavior.

questions.stem: The qualification that Mr. Hurst “merely looked the gentleman” chiefly establishes
choices: the narrator’s confidence that appearance reliably establishes character
an explanation of why the assembly prefers him to Darcy
a distinction between an appearance of status and substantive qualities
a close similarity between his conduct and Bingley’s friendliness
rationales: The qualification makes appearance insufficient.
No such preference is reported.
“Merely” limits what outward presentation can establish.
His conduct is not developed in that comparison.

questions.stem: The rapid circulation of Darcy’s income chiefly characterizes the company’s initial attention as
choices: responsive to wealth as well as physical appearance
indifferent to information about a stranger’s social position
based primarily on knowledge of his private generosity
skeptical of every favorable report about a newcomer
rationales: The fortune joins height, features, and bearing in generating admiration.
The income report quickly affects attention.
No such private history is supplied.
The initial response is admiring.

questions.stem: The change in descriptions of Darcy’s countenance chiefly suggests that
choices: the company distinguishes appearance from conduct without allowing either to affect the other
his physical features visibly change during the evening
the narrator has confused Darcy with another guest
judgment of behavior alters how observers perceive appearance
rationales: The account shows their evaluations interacting.
The shift concerns appraisal rather than literal transformation.
The same man remains the subject.

questions.stem: Bingley’s anger that the ball closes early chiefly reveals
choices: a wish that Darcy had occupied more of the available partners
enthusiasm for the company and activity he wishes to continue
a wish to withdraw from people he finds tiresome
resentment that the hosts have failed to honor his rank
rationales: Bingley’s complaint about the early ending reflects his own enjoyment, not a wish for Darcy to monopolize partners.

He wants more of the gathering.

questions.stem: Darcy’s choice to speak mainly with his own party chiefly supplies indirect evidence of
choices: his restricted willingness to enter the wider social gathering
his desire to discover the views of every local guest
his inability to recognize anyone he already knows
his complete silence throughout the evening
rationales: His companions and limited dances reinforce selective participation.
He declines new introductions.

questions.stem: Darcy’s description of dancing with other women as a “punishment” chiefly reveals
choices: a shared rule that the assembly imposes on reluctant guests
a humorous exaggeration everyone present openly enjoys
his tendency to frame social participation through his own standards of acceptability
his concern that the women would suffer by dancing with him
rationales: The phrasing expresses his judgment, not a stated rule.
Elizabeth’s response shows injury rather than shared amusement.
The word makes an ordinary invitation feel intolerable to him.

questions.stem: Darcy’s withdrawal of his gaze after meeting Elizabeth’s eye chiefly contributes to
choices: a sign that he cannot distinguish Elizabeth from Jane
the impression of a cool refusal to engage with the person being judged
a demonstration that Elizabeth has already accepted an invitation
a tactful effort to repair the effect of his dismissive assessment
rationales: He distinguishes them in his evaluation.
The gesture precedes his dismissive evaluation.
No invitation is made to her by Darcy.

questions.stem: The phrase “give consequence” most clearly implies that Darcy regards his attention as
choices: a duty he owes equally to every guest
a courtesy whose value is independent of social distinction
a favor whose value depends entirely on Elizabeth’s approval
something capable of conferring social importance
rationales: He explicitly refuses to distribute it that way.
Darcy treats his attention as conferring standing, so the phrase depends on hierarchy rather than neutral courtesy.
His phrasing centers his own power to confer it.
He treats a dance as bestowing status rather than merely sharing an activity.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s decision to retell the slight “with great spirit” chiefly adds to her portrayal
choices: a desire to conceal the encounter from every acquaintance
an absence of any negative feeling about Darcy’s conduct
an ability to convert an unwelcome experience into social amusement
a willingness to accept Darcy’s assessment as an objective truth
rationales: She tells friends about it.
The narrator states that she feels no cordiality toward him.
The retelling follows hurt but draws on her delight in the ridiculous.

questions.stem: The assertion “His character was decided” most clearly invites attention to
choices: the speed with which a public performance becomes a comprehensive social verdict
the narrator’s refusal to report the community’s opinions
the completion of a long investigation into his private conduct
Darcy’s explicit announcement that he intends to change his character
rationales: A single evening produces a sweeping judgment of Darcy.
Those opinions shape the account.
The verdict arises during the assembly.
He makes no such announcement.

questions.stem: Placing Bingley and Darcy at the same assembly chiefly allows their differences to emerge through
choices: a comparison between entirely unrelated periods of their lives
contrasting responses to shared social opportunities
separate accounts that never bring the men into interaction
the effects of substantially different weather conditions
rationales: The actions occur in one evening.
Both can dance and meet guests, but they participate differently.
Bingley directly urges Darcy to join the dance.

questions.stem: The community’s eventual preference for Bingley chiefly emphasizes that
choices: Bingley has established moral superiority through a complete personal history

wealth has no influence on anyone’s first impression

rationales: The scene offers public conduct, not a full history.

The opening explicitly shows its influence.
Darcy’s estate cannot preserve the approval his manners lose.

questions.stem: The contrast between Bingley dancing every dance and Darcy dancing only with his own party chiefly makes visible
choices: a difference in whether either man knows any woman present
a shared intention to avoid the local guests
openness to new company versus reliance on an existing circle
a difference explained solely by one man’s inability to dance
rationales: Both know people in their party.
Bingley actively joins them.
The distribution of partners gives the contrast concrete form.
No inability is reported.

questions.stem: Bingley’s description of Darcy’s “stupid manner,” compared with Darcy’s dismissal of the women, chiefly contrasts
choices: criticism of a friend’s withdrawal with criticism of the available company
a formal dispute over which man owns the assembly room
two identical explanations for why Darcy should remain alone
Bingley’s indifference to Darcy with Darcy’s concern for Bingley’s loneliness
rationales: Bingley locates the problem in Darcy’s conduct; Darcy locates it in the partners.
No ownership dispute appears.
They disagree about the reason and response.
Bingley is the one trying to draw his friend in.

questions.stem: The men’s shared admiration for Jane chiefly qualifies the contrast by
choices: making Bingley’s praise of other women insincere
proving that both intend to marry her immediately
eliminating every difference in their behavior toward the company
showing that divergent social attitudes do not make all their judgments opposite
rationales: He praises Jane while also finding others agreeable.
No such intention is stated here.
Their participation still differs sharply.
Both find Jane beautiful despite broader disagreement.

questions.stem: Bingley’s offer to arrange an introduction chiefly reveals his role as
choices: a rival seeking to prevent Darcy from meeting Elizabeth
a social connector whose action exposes Darcy’s resistance to connection
an impartial judge who refuses to influence either person
a spokesman who repeats Darcy’s evaluation without modification
rationales: He proposes that meeting.
He proposes a practical way for his friend to participate.
He actively encourages the introduction.
He describes Elizabeth as pretty and likely agreeable.

questions.stem: Darcy’s refusal after Bingley’s offer chiefly makes their contrast consequential because
choices: one man’s openness becomes the occasion for the other’s injurious judgment
the conversation resolves their differing attitudes into agreement
Bingley accepts that every woman except Jane is unworthy
Elizabeth is prevented from hearing any part of the exchange
rationales: The attempted introduction leads to the slight Elizabeth overhears.
The disagreement remains.
He has already rejected that assessment.
She hears enough to feel the slight.

questions.stem: The final separation of Bingley and Darcy chiefly carries their contrast into
choices: a movement toward agreement about the pleasures of the assembly
a common preference for withdrawing from an unsatisfactory gathering
different movements within the social space
a permanent end to their friendship
rationales: Their separate movements sustain the difference between Bingley’s participation and Darcy’s reserve.
Bingley continues to enjoy participation while Darcy withdraws; they do not express a shared preference for leaving.
Bingley returns to his partner while Darcy walks away.
The excerpt does not establish a rupture.

questions.stem: Mrs. Bennet’s sharpened resentment chiefly shows that the foil contrast is received through
choices: a perspective wholly detached from family interests
personal stakes as well as judgments of general conduct
a complete lack of awareness of either man’s behavior
an equal hostility toward both men regardless of their actions
rationales: Her daughter’s treatment matters directly.
Darcy’s slight to her daughter intensifies her wider dislike.
She responds to that behavior.
Bingley’s attention produces approval.

questions.stem: Which qualification best preserves the complexity of the foil relationship?
choices: Their friendship means the apparent differences cannot be meaningful.
The community’s preference makes all future evidence about Darcy unnecessary.
The contrast proves that each man lacks any quality the other possesses.
The scene contrasts public behavior without supplying an equally complete inward history of both men.
rationales: Friendship makes the juxtaposition more visible rather than impossible.
Later evidence can qualify an initial verdict.
They share some judgments and social circumstances.
A first encounter cannot establish every motive or later development.

questions.stem: Torvald’s reference to “what people will say” chiefly introduces
choices: a shift away from the relationship toward an unrelated public event
an account of opinions already collected from the neighbors
public reputation as a pressure on Nora’s private decision
a concern Nora treats as the decisive reason to remain
rationales: Reputation is invoked to constrain the departure.
No consultation is reported.
He places anticipated social judgment beside home and family obligations.
She refuses to let it govern her decision.

questions.stem: Nora’s question about her “most sacred duties” chiefly makes possible
choices: a challenge to a definition Torvald assumes is self-evident
an agreement that duties have no importance in her decision
a concession that Torvald alone can determine every obligation
a request for factual information about household tasks
rationales: He treats wifehood and motherhood as the complete answer; she introduces duties to self.
She calls other duties equally sacred.
She questions and revises his definition.
The dispute concerns moral priorities.

questions.stem: The disagreement over whether Nora is “before all else” a wife and mother chiefly concerns
choices: whether Torvald can remember the names of the children
whether she has ever legally married or had children
which household activity should be completed first that evening
which identity should have priority in defining her obligations
