rationales: The exchange concerns roles, not memory.
Those facts are not disputed.
The priority is ethical and personal, not a schedule.
Nora asserts a prior claim to being a reasonable human being.

questions.stem: Nora’s qualification “or, at all events, that I must try and become one” chiefly complicates her assertion by
choices: withdrawing every claim that she can act independently
joining a claim to equal personhood with acknowledgment of unfinished development
claiming that she has already answered every moral question
accepting Torvald’s definition without any remaining objection
rationales: She continues to insist on self-directed inquiry.
She asserts human standing while recognizing work still needed.
It explicitly leaves learning unfinished.
The qualification does not restore his hierarchy.

questions.stem: Her response to widely held opinions and books most clearly establishes a desire to
choices: test inherited judgments through her own reasoning
replace Torvald’s authority with unquestioned obedience to another person
deny that the surrounding society has any influence on her
reject every possible source of knowledge before examining it
rationales: She acknowledges common views but refuses to be satisfied by repetition alone.
She seeks an independent assessment.
Her need to examine it acknowledges its influence.
She proposes thinking and understanding, not automatic rejection.

questions.stem: The exchange about religion chiefly reveals a difference between
choices: a shared decision that religious questions are already settled
Torvald’s lack of confidence that religion can guide conduct
received formulas and an understanding Nora intends to examine for herself
Nora’s claim to possess a complete alternative theology
rationales: The discussion exposes uncertainty.
He invokes it as a reliable guide.
She recalls what she was taught but questions whether it is right for her.
She admits she does not yet know.

questions.stem: Nora’s reply to the charge that she does not understand the world chiefly
choices: avoids the question by returning to Christmas preparations
turns an accusation of ignorance into a reason for inquiry
proves that she considers the world entirely irrelevant
concedes that she must remain because understanding is impossible
rationales: The response stays with the disputed condition.
She accepts the limitation while announcing an effort to judge the world and herself.
She intends to examine whether it is right.
She states the opposite intention.

questions.stem: The contrast between Torvald’s descriptions of illness and Nora’s claim of clarity chiefly shows
choices: a disagreement already resolved by a third-party authority
a shared recognition that Nora’s judgment must be postponed
a narrator’s independent confirmation of Torvald’s diagnosis
competing interpretations of the same decision
rationales: No third party resolves it.
Torvald questions her condition, while Nora asserts clarity and a present need to decide.
The play supplies conflicting speech, not an external diagnosis.
He treats departure as evidence of disorder; she treats it as considered necessity.

questions.stem: Torvald’s conclusion that Nora no longer loves him chiefly marks
choices: a claim that Nora denies while agreeing to remain
the first indication that any personal relationship exists
a shift from disputing duties and understanding to naming the loss of attachment
an account of an unrelated romance Nora has confessed
rationales: She confirms the loss of love.
The marriage is central throughout.
He reaches a different explanation after failing to persuade her through other authorities.
No other romance is introduced in this selection.

questions.stem: Nora’s statement that his kindness makes the admission painful chiefly preserves
choices: the coexistence of gratitude or affectional memory with the decision to leave
a claim that painful decisions are necessarily mistaken
a simple account in which every past interaction was cruel
an immediate reversal of her clear intention to depart
rationales: Past kindness does not restore the love she says she has lost.
The pain accompanies rather than invalidates her conviction.
She explicitly acknowledges kindness.
She reiterates why she will not stay.

questions.stem: The narrator’s initial relief that the baby is not in the room chiefly shows her
choices: reporting a decision the baby has independently explained
describing a move to a different room that has already occurred
accepting that the wallpaper has no troubling effect on anyone
reinterpreting her own confinement as protection for someone more vulnerable
rationales: The baby supplies no account.
She remains in the nursery.
She continues to call it horrid.
She calls her occupancy lucky because she believes she can endure the room better.

questions.stem: The claim that the wallpaper contains things “nobody knows but me” chiefly establishes
choices: a willingness to submit every perception to John’s judgment
a sense of privileged knowledge unavailable to the other characters
a detached account whose interpretation is shared by the household
independent confirmation by another observer
rationales: She says she no longer mentions it.
The narrator presents her perception as exclusive.
The interpretation remains private.
The claim explicitly excludes other knowers.

questions.stem: The phrases “like a woman” and “seemed to shake” most clearly mark
choices: comparisons and appearances rather than externally verified events
a second narrator’s correction of the first account
a certainty that the figure has spoken intelligibly
a refusal to give any sensory description at all
rationales: The qualifying language matters to the status of the perceived figure.
The same voice supplies the qualifications.
No speech from the figure is reported.
The narrator describes perceived shapes and movement.

questions.stem: The sequence “I wonder—I begin to think—I wish” chiefly reveals
choices: a direct report of John’s private reasoning
a completed explanation accepted by both spouses
a movement from uncertain interpretation toward a desire for removal
a loss of interest in the wallpaper’s pattern
rationales: The first-person sequence concerns her response.
No shared explanation follows.
The interrupted thought culminates in wishing John would take her away.
Her attention remains intense.

questions.stem: The narrator’s explanation that talking to John is hard because he is wise and loving chiefly creates
choices: an external narrator’s guarantee that his interpretation is correct
a tension between reassuring descriptions and the difficulty of being heard
a statement that she has never attempted to speak with him
an uncomplicated account of successful communication
rationales: The description belongs to her account.
The positive terms accompany an obstacle to expressing her experience.
She says she tried the previous night.
The conversation that follows remains unequal.

questions.stem: John’s claim that she is better “whether you can see it or not” chiefly asserts
choices: an admission that he has observed no relevant signs
a willingness to leave the question open until she agrees
a distinction the narrator has already accepted without reservation
the priority of his assessment over her reported experience
rationales: He cites flesh, color, and appetite.
He states the conclusion confidently.
She immediately disputes weight and qualifies appetite.
He makes professional authority decisive despite her contrary perception.

questions.stem: The narrator’s distinction between evening and morning appetite chiefly contributes
choices: a complete rejection of every observation he has made
a shift to an issue unrelated to the disputed condition
specific experiential evidence that complicates John’s general improvement claim
a claim that he has never been present during a meal
rationales: She allows that appetite may improve in the evening.
Appetite is one of his cited measures.
She links appetite to times when he is present or absent.
She explicitly places him in the evening.

questions.stem: Her stopping after “Better in body perhaps” chiefly makes visible
choices: the interruption of a distinction she is trying to introduce
a sudden inability to remember the room’s appearance
a narrator who no longer has access to her own intention
her completed agreement that bodily improvement settles every concern
rationales: John’s stern look prevents her from developing the contrast.
The wallpaper remains central to her attention.
She records the attempted distinction and its interruption.
The unfinished phrase points beyond the body.

questions.stem: The report that John thought she slept first, while she remained awake, chiefly gives readers
choices: proof that John has read her private account
a reason to assume every statement by John is knowingly false
a new omniscient viewpoint entering both minds directly
access to a discrepancy between outward appearance and private attention
rationales: No reading of it is reported.
The discrepancy concerns his mistaken perception here.
His belief is reported from her limited account.
Her hidden wakefulness is unavailable to his presumed understanding.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best respects the passage’s restricted access?
choices: John’s professional title makes every account of her experience irrelevant.
The account makes the narrator’s distress available while leaving the wallpaper’s literal status unverified.
The conflicting views require readers to discard every detail in the passage.
The narrator’s sincerity establishes that the figure must exist physically.
rationales: His authority is part of the conflict, not an external resolution.
Intimate access to feeling does not independently confirm the perceived movement.
Particular claims can be evaluated without total rejection.
Sincerity and external verification are different.

questions.stem: The narrator’s statement about Mr. Bennet’s long-standing intention chiefly provides
choices: only an external description of his visible posture
access to a motive not yet available to the other participants
a claim Mr. Bennet has just openly announced to the room
an inference explicitly attributed to Mrs. Bennet
rationales: The information concerns intention.
The family does not know he has always intended to visit.
The narrator supplies it before the dialogue unfolds.
Her later explanation differs from it.

questions.stem: The opening account of both the visit and Mrs. Bennet’s ignorance chiefly positions readers
choices: within Mrs. Bennet’s belief that the visit has not occurred
as recipients of a letter written by Elizabeth
entirely inside Mrs. Bennet’s mistaken expectation
across a knowledge gap that no single family response expresses
rationales: The narrator tells readers that the visit has occurred while also reporting her ignorance of it.
No letter frames the passage.
The visit has already been disclosed to them.
Readers know the event and the wife’s lack of knowledge simultaneously.

questions.stem: The report that Mrs. Bennet cannot contain herself before scolding Kitty chiefly
choices: limits itself to dialogue without explanatory framing
gives Kitty’s private diagnosis of her mother
interprets the emotional pressure behind an outward action
establishes that the cough is deliberately timed to provoke her
rationales: The sentence explicitly supplies framing.
The statement is narratorial.
The narrator links silence and redirected irritation.
Kitty later denies coughing for amusement.

questions.stem: The sentence about Mary wishing to speak sensibly but not knowing how chiefly demonstrates
choices: a brief movement into a character’s unspoken aspiration and difficulty
a complete replacement of the scene by Mary’s life history
a first-person confession Mary makes to the family
a conclusion Mr. Bennet has independently verified in conversation
rationales: The narrator supplies more than the observable silence.
The access is momentary and local.
She does not speak the thought.
The narrator, not Mr. Bennet, gives the inward account.

questions.stem: The narrator’s report that the ladies’ astonishment is what Mr. Bennet wishes chiefly
choices: attributes the plan to the surprised daughters
endorses his behavior as unquestionably considerate
leaves his purpose wholly unspecified
connects the observed reaction with his private purpose
rationales: The wish belongs to Mr. Bennet.
Knowledge of purpose does not establish moral approval.
The desired astonishment is identified.
The effect of the disclosure is related to an intention.

questions.stem: The juxtaposition of Mrs. Bennet’s astonishment with her later claim of expectation chiefly enables
choices: a confirmation that Mr. Bennet has misremembered the visit
a narratorial irony based on access to both reaction and self-presentation
a neutral repetition of two perfectly consistent statements
a shift to a narrator who knows less than every participant
rationales: His visit is not in doubt.
Readers see her immediate surprise and subsequent revised account.
Surprise and claimed prior certainty are in tension.
The narrator supplies wider knowledge.

questions.stem: The description of Mr. Bennet leaving “fatigued with the raptures of his wife” chiefly adds
choices: an account of his response to the enthusiasm he has helped produce
a complete explanation supplied in Mr. Bennet’s spoken farewell
a judgment that every family member experiences identical feelings
proof that the wife’s joy is deliberately feigned
rationales: The narrator connects departure with an inward reaction.
He speaks about Kitty’s cough, not his fatigue.
The scene differentiates their responses.
The narration does not establish feigning.

questions.stem: Which detail most clearly goes beyond what an external observer could report without inference?
choices: Mr. Bennet’s departure from the room
Lydia’s spoken claim to be tallest
Mary’s unspoken wish to say something sensible
Kitty’s audible complaint about her cough
rationales: An observer could see him leave.
An observer could hear the statement.
The narration directly supplies an inward aspiration.
An observer could hear the spoken complaint.

questions.stem: The narrator’s selective access to several minds chiefly contributes to
choices: a claim that all characters share one identical interpretation
comedy produced by differences among intention, awareness, and self-description
an absence of any limits on what readers must still infer
a requirement that the narrator approve each character equally
rationales: The narration repeatedly exposes differences.
The scene’s effects depend on unevenly distributed knowledge.
Readers still interpret motives and consequences beyond supplied facts.
Access and approval are separate matters.

questions.stem: Which account most precisely describes the passage’s narrative scope?
choices: It reports every possible thought of every character continuously.
It avoids all interpretation in favor of a transcript of speech.
It remains entirely within Elizabeth’s immediate perceptions.
It moves beyond one character’s knowledge while choosing particular intentions and thoughts to reveal.
rationales: The passage offers brief selected access, not exhaustive knowledge.
Narratorial framing and mental access are substantial.
Mr. Bennet’s intention and Mary’s wish exceed that position.
The reported minds are plural, but disclosure remains selective.

questions.stem: The account of purchases that “should” be made chiefly brings the narration close to
choices: a store manager’s independent sales forecast
the children’s spoken demands during the shopping trip
a formal instruction imposed by an external narrator
Mrs. Sommers’s planning and sense of appropriate use
rationales: No manager supplies the plan.
Their speech is not reported.
The passage presents the character’s projected use of money.
The modal phrasing follows her calculations and imagined family benefits.

questions.stem: The exclamation about how much darning new stockings would save chiefly
choices: separates the narrator completely from Mrs. Sommers’s concerns
gives the third-person plan the immediacy of a character’s anticipated relief
establishes the children’s own assessment of the household’s work
introduces a direct conversation with the clerk
rationales: The phrasing is closely aligned with those concerns.
The exclamation conveys the felt value of reduced labor.
The thought is presented through Mrs. Sommers’s planning, not as an expressed judgment by the children.
The clerk has not yet entered the scene.

questions.stem: The sentence “She had no time—no second of time to devote to the past” chiefly produces
choices: emphatic proximity to the pressure of her present obligations
a detached chronology with no evaluative coloring
an explicit quotation from a neighbor’s speech
a claim that she is incapable of remembering anything
rationales: The repetition intensifies the experience of time being absorbed.
The insistence carries an experiential emphasis.
The neighbors’ comments are separately introduced.
The sentence concerns available attention, not total memory loss.

questions.stem: The correction “no!” in the account of lunch chiefly
choices: removes the narrator from all access to the character’s awareness
signals that a different character interrupts aloud
lets the narration enact Mrs. Sommers’s realization as it occurs
corrects the reader for misunderstanding a completed dialogue
rationales: It brings the narration closer to that awareness.
No new speaker is introduced.
The account revises an assumption in the rhythm of her thought.
The correction concerns her own recollection.

questions.stem: The comparison between inspecting stockings and buying a diamond tiara most clearly reflects
choices: the narrator’s assertion that no one could reasonably buy stockings
the extravagance the invitation seems to hold for Mrs. Sommers
a memory of a specific tiara she once bought
an actual pricing equivalence established by the clerk
rationales: The extravagance is contextual rather than universal.
Her smile is explained through a comparison scaled to her circumstances.
No such purchase is narrated.
The comparison is not a price report.

questions.stem: “What a very small parcel it was!” chiefly changes a plain description into
choices: a correction that the stockings were never purchased
an instruction telling the clerk to use a larger package
an external inventory indifferent to the customer’s response
an immediate evaluation colored by the purchase’s significance to the character
rationales: The purchase has occurred.
No spoken instruction is given.
The phrasing is affectively charged.
The exclamation conveys the felt disproportion between desire and physical size.

questions.stem: The sentence “How good was the touch of the raw silk to her flesh!” most clearly
choices: reports a judgment made by the shoe clerk
withdraws all access to the reasons the purchase matters
draws the narration into the character’s sensory pleasure
establishes a general rule that silk feels identical to everyone
rationales: The clerk is not the source of the sensation.
The pleasure helps explain its significance.
The exclamatory evaluation conveys bodily immediacy.
The sentence is tied to her experience.

questions.stem: The explicit statement that she was “not thinking at all” differs from the nearby exclamations chiefly because it
choices: reports a mental condition rather than enacting a moment of evaluation
introduces Mrs. Sommers’s direct spoken confession
eliminates the possibility of analyzing narrative proximity
proves that every later action is invented by the narrator
rationales: The narration names a state while the exclamations echo felt perception.
The statement remains third-person narration.
The contrast makes proximity worth examining.
That conclusion does not follow.

questions.stem: The account of the clerk’s inability to reconcile shoes and stockings chiefly widens the passage beyond
choices: the store’s material setting altogether
all interest in how social position is read
the narrator’s ability to report inward responses
Mrs. Sommers’s own sensory absorption
rationales: The clerk’s judgment depends on material details.
His puzzlement makes that reading visible.
It adds another inward response.
The narration briefly supplies another person’s puzzlement about her appearance.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the shifts between narrated explanation and character-colored exclamation?
choices: Every sentence must be assigned exclusively to either the narrator or the character.
The passage lets readers experience the purchase’s immediacy while also seeing conditions the character does not fully analyze.
Narrative closeness requires readers to endorse every purchase without question.
The exclamations prove that the whole story is a first-person diary.
rationales: Blending can make that separation uncertain.
Closeness and contextual framing coexist.
Access to experience does not compel unqualified approval.
The grammar and narrative frame remain third person.

questions.stem: The unspecified “thousand injuries” chiefly limits the reader’s ability to
choices: understand that Fortunato values expertise in wine
recognize that the narrator intends revenge
independently assess the grounds of the narrator’s grievance
distinguish the speaker from Fortunato
rationales: The passage clearly describes that pride.
That intention is explicit.
The narrator asserts repeated injury without detailing it.
Their roles remain distinct.

questions.stem: The appeal to a listener who knows “the nature of my soul” chiefly seeks to
choices: make familiarity stand in place of a fuller justification
provide a documented account of the listener’s identity
establish that the narrative is addressed directly to Fortunato
invite the listener to correct every remembered detail
rationales: The narrator invokes presumed understanding before explaining the plan.
The listener remains unnamed.
That identification is not supplied.
The voice anticipates agreement rather than correction.

questions.stem: The assertion that punishment must occur “with impunity” chiefly reveals
choices: an independent legal principle verified outside the account
a decision to abandon revenge because it carries risk
a willingness to accept equal accountability for both participants
a definition of justice shaped by the narrator’s own exemption from consequences
rationales: The principle is the narrator’s assertion.
Risk is to be avoided while revenge proceeds.
The narrator explicitly rejects that condition.
Successful redress is made dependent on avoiding retribution.

questions.stem: The claim that an avenger must make himself felt as such chiefly suggests
choices: that the narrator is indifferent to what Fortunato understands
that the narrator wants recognition of his power as well as an outcome
that the narrator plans to tell Fortunato the whole story immediately
that the narrator seeks reconciliation through mutual apology
rationales: Recognition is part of his stated requirement.
The wrong must be knowingly answered by the avenger.
He continues to conceal hostility.
The stated aim is punishment.

questions.stem: The narrator’s admission that his smile conceals thoughts of “immolation” chiefly
choices: makes his deception of Fortunato explicit to the reader
shows that Fortunato has correctly interpreted the smile
proves that he conceals the revenge intention equally from the reader
establishes that all narrated physical events must therefore be false
rationales: The account openly distinguishes performed goodwill from hostile intention.
The narrator says Fortunato does not perceive its changed meaning.
He has already announced it.
Deception within the story does not invalidate every reported fact.

questions.stem: The acknowledgment that Fortunato is respected, feared, and sincere about wine chiefly complicates
choices: the narrator’s claim to share any interest with him
the reader’s knowledge that a carnival is occurring
a portrait that might otherwise reduce him to an entirely contemptible target
the fact that the narrator plans to exploit his pride
rationales: The narrator explicitly shares wine expertise.
The assessment does not alter the setting.
The narrator grants real standing and expertise while identifying a vulnerability.
The concession helps explain the exploitable strength.

questions.stem: The narrator’s warm greeting after announcing revenge chiefly creates
choices: an apparent reconciliation that the narrator now accepts as sincere
a gap between the social performance and the motive readers have been given
a clear withdrawal of the revenge plan
an account in which neither reader nor Fortunato knows the narrator’s intention
rationales: The announced revenge makes the warm greeting part of concealed hostility rather than accepted reconciliation.
The hand-wringing pleasure is informed by the earlier hostile purpose.
No withdrawal is announced.
Readers know it while Fortunato apparently does not.

questions.stem: The repeated claim of doubt about the wine chiefly functions as
choices: a verified confession that the narrator knows nothing about wine
a request that Fortunato leave the matter to the narrator alone
a deferential acknowledgment that ends the competition over expertise
a lure that offers Fortunato a chance to display the expertise he values
rationales: He has already claimed substantial expertise.
The exchange draws him further into it.
The repeated doubt draws Fortunato further into demonstrating expertise instead of closing that pressure.
The uncertainty invites his judgment and plays upon established pride.

questions.stem: The reference to Luchesi chiefly pressures Fortunato by
choices: revealing that Luchesi has already settled the wine’s authenticity
proving that Fortunato has no interest in comparative status
introducing a rival evaluator whose competence he feels compelled to dispute
offering an impartial witness who can verify the original injuries
rationales: The consultation is only proposed.
His dismissal of Luchesi shows the opposite.
Fortunato immediately rejects Luchesi’s ability and proposes going.
The rivalry concerns wine, not the grievance.

questions.stem: Which judgment most carefully distinguishes the account’s different kinds of reliability?
choices: The narrator reports his manipulations openly while leaving the moral warrant for revenge insufficiently demonstrated.
Because the narrator sounds methodical, his grievance must be proportionate and just.
Because the injuries are unspecified, readers can prove that no injury ever occurred.
Because the narrator deceives Fortunato, every word addressed to the reader must be false.
rationales: Factual candor about tactics can coexist with self-serving ethical claims.
Planning does not establish moral justification.
Lack of substantiation is not proof of nonoccurrence.
The account openly supplies information Fortunato lacks.

questions.stem: The phrase “my infant tongue” chiefly places the naming of Pip within
choices: a later voice’s reconstruction of an early limitation
an account supplied entirely by the stranger in the marshes
a claim that the narrator has forgotten the name’s origin
a transcript recorded by the infant at the moment of naming
rationales: The narrator explains the child’s abbreviated name from a retrospective position.
The stranger has not yet appeared.
The origin is explicitly reconstructed.
The explanatory language is retrospective.

questions.stem: The reference to the tombstone and sister as “authority” chiefly creates
choices: an assurance that the childhood portraits were empirically accurate
a rejection of all information provided by family members
a reflective account of how knowledge about absent parents was assembled
an authoritative family account that removes the need for childish inference
rationales: He later calls them unreasonable fancies.
The sister is cited as a source.
The narrator identifies sources where direct memory is unavailable.
The limited sources prompt Pip’s imaginative conclusions; they do not supply a complete family history.

questions.stem: The parenthetical explanation about photographs chiefly signals
choices: a refusal to distinguish memory from visual evidence
a later perspective clarifying a condition of the remembered childhood
a discovery the child makes during the encounter with the stranger
an indication that the whole episode occurs in a photographic studio
rationales: The explanation makes that distinction explicit.
The narrator explains why no likeness was available.
The comment belongs to the retrospective account.
The setting is a churchyard.

questions.stem: Calling the tombstone-derived portraits “unreasonable” chiefly allows the narrator to
choices: give the child complete adult knowledge of his family
dismiss the parents as irrelevant to the child’s experience
certify the portraits as accurate descriptions of the parents
acknowledge the child’s faulty reasoning without erasing its vividness
rationales: The difference in knowledge remains.
Their absence motivates the fancies.
The evaluation denies that certainty.
The account both evaluates and reconstructs the imaginative inference.

questions.stem: The description of the dead brothers as giving up the struggle for a living chiefly combines
choices: a factual account of the infants’ conscious struggle to earn money
a literal claim that the infants chose paid occupations
adult verbal irony with the child’s encounter with loss
an account entirely free of retrospective interpretation
rationales: The adult economic idiom is imaginatively applied to infants, not reported as a literal livelihood.
The phrasing is figurative and ironic.
The idiom humorously reframes early deaths without making them disappear.
The adult idiom adds interpretive distance.

questions.stem: The long sentence identifying churchyard, marshes, river, sea, and Pip chiefly moves
choices: from an expansive ordering of the world to the child’s small, frightened place within it
from the child’s confidence to an adult narrator’s inability to name any object
from bodily fear to a complete disappearance of emotion
from a present urban scene to an unrelated historical landscape
rationales: The final identification makes the scale personal.
The objects are named precisely.
The child ends crying and shivering.
The same remembered setting continues.

questions.stem: The abrupt dialogue after the expansive landscape description chiefly reduces the felt distance by
choices: replacing the child’s fear with an impersonal summary
confirming that the narrator wrote the dialogue during the encounter
removing Pip’s participation from the narrated event
placing readers within the immediate pressure of command and frightened reply
rationales: The speech makes fear audible.
Immediate presentation does not establish contemporaneous writing.
He is directly addressed and answers.
The scene shifts from reflective description to urgent exchange.

questions.stem: The correction “for he was so sudden and strong” within the upside-down church account chiefly
choices: denies that Pip was ever physically moved
adds a later explanatory frame to the child’s disoriented perception
attributes the inversion to an independently verified supernatural force
makes the church’s apparent movement unrelated to Pip’s body
rationales: The explanation confirms the movement.
The narrator explains the physical cause while preserving the inverted experience.
The cause is the stranger’s handling.
The two are directly connected.

questions.stem: The phrase “I believe they were fat” in response to the stranger’s comment chiefly conveys
choices: a measured retrospective concession rather than an unqualified adoption of the aggressor’s view
a new accusation that the stranger has deliberately described another child
a certainty that the stranger’s every perception was accurate
an inability to remember any aspect of childhood appearance
rationales: The narrator grants the cheeks’ appearance while qualifying his overall strength.
No mistaken identity is suggested.
The concession is local and followed by qualification.
He supplies a limited remembered assessment.

questions.stem: Which account best describes the effect of the narrative distance in the selection?
choices: The narrator treats every childhood conclusion as equally reliable with later knowledge.
The adult narrator’s irony removes any basis for sympathy with the child.
The older voice can expose childish errors while preserving the vulnerability that made them meaningful.
The child’s immediate perception excludes all later commentary.
rationales: He explicitly marks some as unreasonable or childish.
The family loss and physical threat sustain sympathy.
Humor, explanation, and immediate fear coexist.
Retrospective qualifications appear repeatedly.

questions.stem: The opening reference to arriving “yesterday” chiefly anchors
choices: the letter’s present position before it expands into hopes and recollections
a chronology that begins with Walton’s earliest childhood
an event whose timing is deliberately impossible to determine
a retrospective account written after the expedition has ended
rationales: The recent arrival locates the moment of writing.
Childhood appears later in the telling.
The relative time is explicitly supplied.
The voyage remains ahead.

questions.stem: The movement from the present breeze to imagined polar beauty chiefly
choices: reports discoveries Walton has already completed at the pole
replaces present experience with an unrelated childhood anecdote
turns a current sensation into anticipation of a desired future
establishes that every prediction has been independently confirmed
rationales: He has not yet reached it.
The immediate shift is toward the proposed voyage.
The wind gives a “foretaste” that energizes his projections.
The passage retains conjectural language.

questions.stem: The extended account of possible discoveries before the childhood history chiefly
choices: makes the past irrelevant to the present decision
foregrounds the ambition’s attraction before explaining its origins
preserves the exact chronological order of Walton’s life
conceals the fact that a voyage is being planned until the end
rationales: The subsequent history justifies the decision.
Readers first encounter the desired future and then its development.
Childhood necessarily precedes the present projections.
The undertaking is announced at the start.

questions.stem: The statement that writing these reflections has dispelled agitation chiefly reveals
choices: a narrator unable to distinguish writing time from childhood
the calming effect of advice already received from Margaret
a condition fixed long before the letter began
a change occurring during the act of composing the letter
rationales: The temporal relation is clear.
Walton attributes the relief to writing his own reflections, not to a reply or advice from his sister.
He explicitly contrasts the beginning with the present.
The imagined future affects the writer’s present emotional state.

questions.stem: The return to childhood reading chiefly provides
choices: a correction that Walton has never cared about exploration
a complete explanation of every practical obstacle the voyage will face
a retrospective origin for the present expedition’s imaginative appeal
a separate narrative whose connection to ambition remains absent
rationales: The memory demonstrates long-standing interest.
The reading history does not supply that forecast.
The voyage accounts explain an early recurring dream.
The connection is explicit.

questions.stem: The episode of poetic ambition chiefly complicates a simple story of uninterrupted preparation by
choices: introducing a different pursuit before the earlier desire returns
showing that Walton has already achieved the fame he seeks
removing literary imagination from the development of his ambitions
establishing that the expedition was invented only the previous day
rationales: The maritime visions fade, poetry fails, and inheritance redirects him.
He reports failure and disappointment.
Poetry remains part of that development.
The account gives a much longer history.

questions.stem: The inheritance’s placement after poetic disappointment chiefly identifies
choices: an event that prevents all further preparation
a fact Walton withholds until after Margaret answers him
a reward earned by successful completion of the polar voyage
a material circumstance that helps redirect an earlier aspiration into renewed action
rationales: Six years of preparation follow.
It is included in the present letter.
The voyage has not occurred.
The fortune coincides with the return to maritime ambition.

questions.stem: The summary of six years’ hardship chiefly functions to
choices: give each day of preparation the same narrative space as the opening breeze
compress sustained preparation into evidence for his present claim of deserving achievement
prove that the projected discoveries are already accomplished
replace the earlier ambitions with a wish for permanent leisure
rationales: Years are summarized rather than narrated day by day.
The record supports the question about a great purpose.
Preparation does not equal discovery.
He contrasts labor and glory with available luxury.

questions.stem: The final admission that hopes fluctuate chiefly qualifies
choices: the confident future projected earlier in the letter
the claim that the voyage will require endurance
the fact that Walton has undertaken any preparation
the identity of the person to whom he is writing
rationales: Firm resolution coexists with unstable hope and a need for encouragement.
The admission reinforces that demand.
He does not retract the preparation.
Margaret remains the addressee.

questions.stem: Which account most accurately distinguishes chronology from narrative order here?
choices: The letter contains only future events and no remembered experience.
The letter narrates every event in the order it occurred.
The letter moves from present and projected future into selected past episodes, then returns to imminent departure.
The projected discoveries can be treated as confirmed outcomes because they are described vividly.
rationales: Several paragraphs recount the past.
The early future projection and later childhood history contradict that.
The arrangement serves Walton’s explanation of ambition.
Vivid anticipation remains anticipation.

questions.stem: The narrator’s distinction between ordinary poetic desolation and “insufferable” gloom chiefly establishes
choices: a preference for cheerful scenery that excludes all interest in the sublime
an objective proof that the house contains a supernatural agent
an experience that resists the aesthetic pleasure he might normally find in darkness
a familiar landscape whose effect he fully understands at once
rationales: He recognizes a usual pleasure in stern images.
The statement concerns his response, not an established cause.
He explicitly denies the usual half-pleasurable response.
He repeatedly questions the cause.

questions.stem: The repeated movement from “I looked” through particular features chiefly
choices: accumulates an impression while also exposing the narrator’s attempt to locate its cause
provides a neutral survey unaffected by the observer’s state
delays any indication of the narrator’s feelings until the final paragraph
establishes that one isolated object completely explains the response
rationales: The inventory joins perception to analysis.
The features are emotionally charged.
The feelings appear from the first glimpse.
He remains unable to identify a sufficient cause.

questions.stem: The comparison to the aftermath of an opium dream chiefly conveys
choices: a medical explanation supplied by Roderick before the visit
a confirmed account of the narrator taking opium during the journey
a pleasant escape that removes his discomfort
a painful collapse from imaginative elevation into dreary actuality
rationales: The comparison belongs to the narrator’s description.
The passage uses a comparison, not that report.
The analogy emphasizes the unpleasant aftermath.
The “bitter lapse” and falling veil stress disillusioned descent.

questions.stem: The attempt to view the house in the tarn chiefly tests
choices: whether the surrounding landscape lacks any reflected image
whether changing the arrangement of visible details can change their emotional effect
whether Roderick has sent a forged invitation
whether the house has physically moved across the water
rationales: The reflection is plainly visible.
The narrator proposes rearrangement as a possible remedy.
The experiment concerns visual impression.
No movement is the stated hypothesis.

questions.stem: The reflection’s intensification of the shudder chiefly suggests that
choices: the narrator’s effort to master the impression becomes part of its deepening
the landscape has been objectively transformed by a supernatural act
the original description was entirely unemotional
the narrator has achieved the detachment he sought
rationales: The attempted alteration fails to neutralize the response.
The effect is reported through perception.
The first impression was already overwhelming.
His disturbance increases.

questions.stem: The account of Roderick’s letter chiefly explains
choices: why the narrator has no prior connection with the household
why the narrator already possesses complete knowledge of Roderick’s condition
why the narrator enters despite the aversive impression
why every aspect of the visit is freely chosen without relational pressure
rationales: He recalls a childhood friendship.
He reports the letter’s claims and acknowledges limited acquaintance.
The apparent sincerity of a friend’s appeal makes a personal response compelling.
The request leaves him feeling little room for hesitation.

questions.stem: The admission that the narrator knew little of his intimate boyhood companion chiefly
choices: eliminates the emotional force of the request
complicates the assumption that longstanding association guarantees understanding
establishes that every family detail he later reports is invented
proves that the letter came from an entirely unknown person
rationales: He still feels compelled to answer.
Closeness in childhood coexists with Roderick’s reserve.
Limited personal knowledge does not establish fabrication.
The friendship is real within the account.

questions.stem: The double meaning of “House of Usher” chiefly helps connect
choices: two unrelated households with no shared history
the narrator’s family with the local peasantry
a legal dispute that the narrator has already resolved
the physical estate with the family’s apparently enclosed continuity
rationales: The account stresses their identification.
The phrase concerns the Ushers and their estate.
No such dispute is described.
The name gathers mansion and lineage into one interpretive pattern.

questions.stem: The acknowledgment that awareness of increasing superstition accelerates it chiefly develops
choices: a claim that the physical setting has no role in the response
a successful elimination of superstition through reason alone
a self-conscious account in which reflection can intensify the feeling it examines
an external narrator’s correction of the first-person account
rationales: The setting continues to supply images and impressions.
The fear continues and grows.
The narrator identifies a feedback within fear.
The same narrator makes the observation.

questions.stem: Which thesis best accounts for both the house descriptions and the narrator’s explanations?
choices: The passage makes the house unsettling through a mind whose attempts at analysis repeatedly deepen rather than settle its disturbance.
The narrator’s friendship with Roderick removes all uncertainty from the visit.
The setting functions only as background to a fully explained social obligation.
The passage proves a supernatural cause by excluding every psychological explanation.
rationales: The described object and interpreting consciousness develop together.
The account repeatedly acknowledges limits.
The setting actively shapes the experience and its interpretation.
The narrator explicitly considers the mind’s contribution.

questions.stem: The opening sentence primarily establishes the speaker's position by
choices: conceding that mutual affection cannot overcome social barriers
asking the beloved to explain a change in feeling
distinguishing an earlier attraction from a more mature attachment
refusing to acknowledge an obstacle to a particular kind of union
rationales: The refusal does not concede the power of such barriers, and the sentence does not specify social circumstances.
The speaker makes an assertion rather than requesting an explanation from a particular beloved.
The opening contains no account of successive personal attachments.
The negative construction presents an ideal of united minds through the speaker's refusal to admit impediments.

questions.stem: In “Love is not love / Which alters,” the relative clause primarily serves to
choices: describe a temporary obstacle to an otherwise stable relationship
exclude a changeable attachment from the speaker's definition
explain why the speaker has ceased to value affection
introduce an exception that the speaker later accepts
rationales: The construction denies the name of love to what alters, making more than a temporary qualification.
The clause specifies the kind of apparent love that the speaker refuses to recognize as true love.
The sentence defines the ideal more strictly rather than rejecting affection altogether.
Changeability remains excluded throughout the poem rather than becoming an accepted exception.

questions.stem: The interjection “O, no!” most directly contributes to the transition from
choices: rejecting inadequate definitions to presenting an affirmative image
expressing certainty to acknowledging a personal mistake
addressing a beloved to addressing an adversary
describing a failed relationship to mourning its consequences
rationales: The preceding clauses exclude alteration; the following sentence offers the fixed mark as a positive representation.
The emphatic denial strengthens the speaker's position rather than retracting it.
The interjection changes emphasis without identifying a new addressee.
No failed relationship is narrated, and the next lines present a durable ideal.

questions.stem: The clause “although his height be taken” qualifies the claim about the star by distinguishing
choices: the star's apparent motion from its actual movement
the reliability of navigation from the unreliability of sight
the possibility of measurement from the adequacy of valuation
the speaker's knowledge from the beloved's ignorance
rationales: The clause concerns height and worth rather than a correction about motion.
The poem does not discredit navigation or sight; it separates practical measurement from full worth.
A star's height can be measured even when its worth remains unknown; the concession limits what measurement establishes.
No contrast between these two people's knowledge is specified.

questions.stem: The grammatical relationship between “Love's not Time's fool” and “though rosy lips and cheeks” emphasizes that
choices: physical beauty is protected whenever affection remains constant
bodily change can be acknowledged without conceding love's submission to time
time briefly defeats love before love regains its earlier power
love's resistance depends on denying the existence of aging
rationales: The sickle explicitly reaches rosy lips and cheeks, so the poem does not exempt the body.
The concessive clause admits time's reach over beauty while maintaining a different claim for love.
The syntax maintains love's constancy and supplies no sequence of defeat and recovery.
The concession acknowledges physical vulnerability rather than denying it.

questions.stem: In lines 11–12, the conjunction “But” primarily sets
choices: a youthful ideal against an older speaker's disillusionment
the certainty of death against uncertainty about the beloved
a lover's private experience against a public misunderstanding
endurance against alteration under temporal pressure
rationales: The speaker's age and a history of disillusionment are not given.
The contrast concerns love's response to time, not doubt about a specific beloved.
Neither clause introduces a public audience or its mistaken account.
The second clause contrasts bearing love out with changing according to time's brief intervals.

questions.stem: Which account best describes the function of the conditional sentence in the final couplet?
choices: It narrows the definition to relationships the speaker has personally witnessed.
It supplies an example demonstrating that the preceding definition has already failed.
It stakes the speaker's authority on an exceptionally absolute consequence.
It invites the reader to choose freely among several equally valid definitions.
rationales: The consequence expands to “no man ever” rather than restricting the claim to personal observation.
The hypothetical condition is not presented as an event that has occurred.
If the definition is proved wrong, the speaker denies both his writing and anyone's having loved, giving the claim a deliberately extreme wager.
The speaker challenges refutation rather than endorsing equivalent alternatives.

questions.stem: Across the poem, the repeated negative constructions primarily enable the speaker to
choices: define constancy through the pressures and behaviors it resists
catalogue the faults of a beloved whose conduct has changed
avoid making a claim specific enough to be challenged
express an uncertainty that steadily replaces the initial confidence
rationales: Not altering, not being shaken, and not serving time build an ideal through sustained exclusions.
No particular beloved's conduct is recounted; the statements concern an idealized category.
The exclusions culminate in an exceptionally strong, explicitly challengeable claim.
The tone grows emphatic; qualifications concern pressures on love rather than an abandonment of confidence.

questions.stem: Which interpretation of the poem is best supported by the relation between its concessions and its main assertions?
choices: The ideal depends on removing every reference to bodily or material experience.
The argument becomes convincing chiefly by presenting a sequence of remembered events.
The speaker gradually discovers that every earlier claim requires withdrawal.
The speaker's ideal gains force by acknowledging conditions that ordinarily cause change.
rationales: Lips, cheeks, storms, navigation, and time's sickle give the ideal concrete pressures and analogies.
The poem uses definitions and figures rather than a narrative of remembered experiences.
The concessions refine the ideal but do not retract its central assertion.
Tempests, alteration, and time are admitted as pressures while the principal clauses insist on constancy.

questions.stem: The movement from “Let me not” at the opening to “I never writ” at the close most clearly
choices: replaces a universal claim with an apology for an individual failure
connects an initial act of definition with a final assertion of personal authority
shifts responsibility for the argument from the speaker to the beloved
reveals that the speaker is quoting a belief that he privately rejects
rationales: The ending intensifies the universal claim and contains no apology.
The first-person framing makes the speaker's refusal and concluding wager part of one committed position.
The speaker retains responsibility by invoking his own writing in the final challenge.
Nothing marks the central definition as a rejected quotation.

questions.stem: The relation between the first line and the following three lines primarily establishes
choices: an impulsive declaration that the speaker immediately regrets
a firm outward resolve supported by an inwardly sustained feeling
an account of physical confinement followed by a plan for escape
a public accusation that gives way to a description of reconciliation
rationales: The following lines sustain rather than retract the resolve.
The opening refusal to bend is followed by the secret chambers in which the speaker cultivates and bears hatred.
The chambers belong figuratively to the heart, and the opening is a declaration rather than an escape narrative.
The speaker's private hostility remains active; no reconciliation is described.

questions.stem: The continuation from “Deep in the secret chambers of my heart” to “I muse my life-long hate” primarily allows the poem to
choices: separate the speaker's heart from a hatred attributed to someone else
present hatred as an accidental feeling soon replaced by reflection
suggest that the heart's contents are inaccessible even to the speaker
place the feeling within an inward space before naming the speaker's activity there
rationales: The first-person possessives and verb identify the same speaker throughout.
The feeling is life-long and deliberately contemplated rather than briefly superseded.
The speaker directly names and reflects on the feeling.
The line ending leaves the locative phrase awaiting its action, which the following line supplies.

questions.stem: Read together, lines 5–8 characterize the “dark Passion” as
choices: a destructive force that has already deprived the speaker of all vitality
an inherited habit the speaker intends to relinquish
a sustaining force whose absence would empty the speaker's life
a disguise that conceals the speaker's indifference to the city
rationales: The imagined emptiness is conditional on the passion's absence, not its presence.
No intention to relinquish it appears; the speaker presents it as essential.
The conditional sentence says the self would be a skeleton or shell if the passion did not supply vital blood.
The language emphasizes intense engagement, not indifference.

questions.stem: The delay of “Did not forever feed me vital blood” until line 8 most directly makes the reader
choices: wait for the condition that explains the imagined emptiness of the self
recognize that the preceding three lines form unrelated fragments
revise an earlier assertion that the speaker is literally starving
identify a new speaker who answers the opening declaration
rationales: The intervening relative clause delays the main action of the conditional phrase, completing why the self would otherwise be a shell.
The delayed verb completes their shared grammatical construction.
The earlier language is figurative and conditional, not a report of literal hunger.
The same first-person speaker continues the sentence.

questions.stem: The opposition between “my heaven” and “the white world's hell” chiefly develops
choices: an argument that private feeling has no relationship to public experience
the speaker's acceptance of the world's definition of happiness
a contrast between a remembered homeland and an anticipated destination
the difference between the speaker's inward sustenance and an oppressive surrounding world
rationales: The phrase places the speaker's inward condition within, and in response to, the surrounding world.
The conflicting evaluations resist a shared definition of well-being.
The lines do not identify two geographical places or a journey between them.
The possessive heaven exists within the hostile world's hell, making passion a paradoxical source of life.

questions.stem: The catalogue beginning with “The strident trains” acquires its governing evaluation only when
choices: the “fortressed port” reveals the literal location of the speaker's home
the final line supplies “Are sweet” and its unexpected cause
the phrase “vapor-kissed” proves that the city is entirely benevolent
the speaker abandons first-person perception for an impersonal description
rationales: The catalogue supplies no address or domestic location for the speaker.
The listed urban features become the subject of the delayed predicate, which links their sweetness to hatred.
That single image does not settle the catalogue's overall significance.
First-person seeing and contemplating frame the catalogue and its final judgment.

questions.stem: The movement from “The tides, the wharves, the dens I contemplate” into the last line chiefly produces
choices: a concluding reinterpretation of the accumulated urban details
a chronological explanation of how the city was constructed
a resolution in which the speaker's hatred finally disappears
a shift from the city's present condition to a prediction of its destruction
rationales: The final predicate evaluates the catalogue through the speaker's paradoxical relation between sweetness and hatred.
The objects are accumulated spatial impressions, not stages of construction.
The last words explicitly preserve hatred as the cause of the response.
The conclusion concerns present feeling and gives no destruction narrative.

questions.stem: In the phrase “the goaded mass,” “goaded” most nearly suggests that the city's people are
choices: concealed from the speaker by the city's mist
moving slowly because they have lost interest in work
driven by pressures that diminish their freedom of movement
united by their admiration for the city's beauty
rationales: Mist affects perception, but “goaded” describes the people as driven.
The trains speed, and the pressure implied by “goaded” does not suggest leisurely indifference.
The word presents the mass as urged or driven onward, complicating the apparent energy of the speeding trains.
The diction suggests pressure, not a common aesthetic enthusiasm.

questions.stem: Which account best explains the poem's combination of a completed opening assertion and a delayed final judgment?
choices: The syntax enacts the speaker's steady withdrawal from feeling into neutral observation.
The syntax moves from declared resolve toward a more entangled account of what that resolve sustains.
The syntax replaces the speaker's private experience with an objective verdict on every city resident.
The syntax shows that the speaker can state a motive only after another person supplies it.
rationales: The conclusion remains intensely evaluative and first-person.
The opening is firm, while the final catalogue and causal clause make the relationship between hatred, vitality, and attraction more complex.
The final judgment concerns the speaker's perception and feeling, not a comprehensive account of residents.
No other speaker intervenes or explains the motive.

questions.stem: The final phrase “because I hate” most significantly challenges the expectation that
choices: a sonnet must contain a speaker who observes the external world
private emotion would be expressed through first-person language
the city's industrial movement would be described through sensory details
attraction to the city's sights would require affection for the social world they embody
rationales: The poem readily satisfies that condition; the surprise lies in the causal relation.
The poem uses first-person language from its opening, so that feature is not the concluding challenge.
Trains, towers, and ports already provide sensory particulars without creating the final paradox.
The causal relation makes the sights sweet through hatred rather than through reconciliation with the city.

questions.stem: The firm stops after the first two lines help establish a pattern in which the speaker
choices: interrupts a story to supply background about the relationship
tries unsuccessfully to complete a description of the beloved
offers separate corrections to conventional idealizing comparisons
gradually withdraws an accusation against the beloved
rationales: No narrative sequence is underway.
The comparisons are completed clearly; their limitation is deliberate.
Eyes and lips receive distinct, plainly bounded refusals of exaggerated likeness.
The opening offers descriptions rather than an accusation later retracted.

questions.stem: The internal pause in “If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun” chiefly separates
choices: an accepted standard of comparison from the corrective observation it prompts
a question addressed to the beloved from her implied reply
a remembered description from a prediction about future change
a literal account of weather from a reflection on the seasons
rationales: The conditional whiteness of snow is followed by a conclusion refusing to assign that quality to the beloved.
Both parts belong to the speaker, and no answer from the beloved is supplied.
The line compares present qualities rather than stages in time.
Snow functions as a comparative standard, not as reported weather.

questions.stem: The transition from “I have seen roses damask'd, red and white” to “But no such roses see I in her cheeks” primarily
choices: concedes that the beloved resembles roses more closely than expected
suggests that the beloved's beauty changes whenever flowers bloom
contrasts an unreliable memory with a newly accurate perception
uses a familiar beautiful object to sharpen a refusal of figurative exaggeration
rationales: The explicit negative denies that resemblance.
No seasonal change in the beloved is described.
The remembered roses are not discredited; the rejected step is the comparison.
The speaker acknowledges actual roses before denying their conventional transfer to cheeks.

questions.stem: In “I love to hear her speak, yet well I know,” the internal turn allows the speaker to
choices: correct an earlier assertion that the beloved never speaks
retain affection while qualifying a claim of sensory superiority
suggest that affection has made accurate judgment impossible
replace a personal preference with indifference to all sound
rationales: No earlier claim of silence appears.
The speaker loves hearing her but acknowledges that music has a more pleasing sound.
The speaker presents affection and accurate comparison as compatible.
The preference remains; the line does not erase responsiveness to sound.

questions.stem: The completion of the sentence in line 10 chiefly demonstrates that the continuation beyond line 9
choices: supplies the content of the acknowledgment introduced by “yet well I know”
turns the beloved into a speaker who judges the poet's song
contradicts the speaker's statement that he enjoys the beloved's voice
introduces an unrelated complaint about the beloved's education
rationales: The music comparison completes the knowledge clause and clarifies the concession.
The grammatical speaker remains unchanged.
Enjoyment need not imply that the voice surpasses music, so the two claims can coexist.
The sentence concerns sound rather than education.

questions.stem: The pause after “My mistress” in line 12 most directly draws attention to
choices: the beloved's refusal to walk in the speaker's presence
a change in addressee from the beloved to an assembled audience
the beloved as an embodied person whose movement contrasts with a goddess's imagined movement
the speaker's uncertainty about whether he knows the beloved
rationales: No refusal or particular encounter is reported.
The line remains a third-person description and specifies no new audience.
Naming her before the walking clause grounds the contrast in ordinary human action.
The possessive identifies an established relation rather than uncertainty about identity.

questions.stem: The phrase “And yet” at the beginning of the couplet primarily
choices: introduces the beloved's objection to the speaker's account
reframes the preceding denials as compatible with a high valuation of love
announces that every earlier physical description was inaccurate
concedes that conventional praise would have been more sincere
rationales: No second voice enters the poem.
The final assertion of rarity follows, rather than cancels, the rejection of false comparisons.
The speaker defends truthful description and does not retract the details.
The ending calls such comparisons false, not more sincere.

questions.stem: In the final line, “belied with false compare” most clearly criticizes
choices: a beloved who has deliberately concealed her identity
a poet who chooses ordinary language because he lacks imagination
a listener who refuses to appreciate musical skill
praise that misrepresents its object through conventional exaggeration
rationales: The falsehood belongs to the comparison, not to an act of concealment by the beloved.
The poem uses deliberate comparison to question a convention, not to confess an inability.
Music is an earlier standard of comparison, not the target of the final criticism.
The phrase distinguishes the speaker's love from descriptions that falsify the person praised.

questions.stem: Which description best accounts for the relationship between the poem's pauses and its argument?
choices: Every internal pause marks a moment when the speaker abandons his previous position.
The final pause leaves an interrupted narrative event unresolved.
Distinct corrective statements accumulate before a concluding concession makes their purpose clearer.
Frequent pauses prevent the speaker from stating any definite judgment.
rationales: The pauses articulate contrasts and qualifications without systematic abandonment.
The poem concludes an argument about praise rather than interrupting a narrative event.
Stops organize the refusals, while internal and final turns show how affection survives those refusals.
The speaker repeatedly makes definite comparisons and ends with a definite valuation.

questions.stem: The tone of the poem as a whole is best described as
choices: candidly corrective while ultimately affirming
resentful toward a beloved who has rejected the speaker
ceremonially reverent while carefully avoiding criticism
embarrassed by an affection the speaker wishes to conceal
rationales: Plain refusals of idealized comparisons lead to an assertion of the love's rarity.
No rejection by the beloved or resulting resentment is established.
The speaker openly criticizes false comparison rather than avoiding it.
The speaker directly acknowledges love and enjoyment of the beloved's voice.

questions.stem: The opening question chiefly serves to
choices: announce a seasonal narrative that proceeds in chronological order
request information that the beloved later provides
introduce a comparison whose adequacy the poem proceeds to revise
express uncertainty about whether the speaker has met the beloved
rationales: The poem develops an argument about comparison and endurance, not a seasonal plot.
The beloved supplies no answer; the speaker develops the comparison.
Summer initially offers a standard, but its defects lead toward the claim for preservation in verse.
The poem addresses the beloved directly without such uncertainty.

questions.stem: The phrase “summer's lease” primarily characterizes summer's beauty as
choices: a possession limited by an allotted term
a burden the speaker hopes the beloved will relinquish
a promise that guarantees favorable weather
a gift whose value increases through ownership
rationales: The metaphor of a lease emphasizes temporary tenure and a definite ending.
Summer's beauty is desirable but brief, not an unwanted burden assigned to the beloved.
The surrounding rough winds and excessive heat undermine any such guarantee.
The emphasis falls on duration rather than rising value.

questions.stem: The descriptions of the sun in lines 5–6 contribute to the argument chiefly by
choices: implying that the beloved has caused an alteration in the weather
establishing that the speaker prefers darkness to all forms of beauty
introducing a conflict between two competing divine beings
showing that even a prominent source of natural beauty is variable
rationales: No causal power over weather is attributed to the beloved.
The lines identify variability without expressing that general preference.
The figurative sun is not placed in a narrative conflict with another deity.
The sun can be too hot or dimmed, making summer an imperfect standard.

questions.stem: The repetition of “fair” in “every fair from fair sometime declines” primarily emphasizes
choices: the speaker's uncertainty about the meaning of physical attractiveness
the vulnerability of beautiful things to a loss of beauty
the beloved's preference for one season over another
a distinction between moral fairness and social injustice
rationales: The line makes a general claim rather than seeking a definition.
The repeated term links what possesses beauty with the quality it cannot permanently retain.
No preference belonging to the beloved is expressed.
The context concerns beauty's decline, not legal or moral equity.

questions.stem: The turn introduced by “But” in line 9 depends on a distinction between
choices: natural beauty's decline and the beloved's proposed endurance through poetry
a harsh summer remembered in youth and a mild summer in the present
the beauty of the body and the complete absence of beauty in nature
the speaker's earlier ignorance and a fact supplied by the beloved
rationales: The preceding examples of change are answered by the promise later grounded in “eternal lines.”
The seasons are comparative figures rather than dated autobiographical episodes.
Nature supplies beauty whose duration and consistency are limited, not an absence of beauty.
No exchange of information with the beloved occurs.

questions.stem: The repeated “Nor” constructions in lines 10–11 primarily
choices: weaken the initial promise by conceding that it cannot be fulfilled
identify two objections the beloved has spoken aloud
extend the assurance by excluding successive forms of loss
shift attention from the beloved to unrelated public concerns
rationales: The constructions reinforce rather than retract the promise.
No speech by the beloved is presented.
The parallel negatives rule out losing beauty and falling under death's boast.
Both lines remain directed toward the beloved's proposed endurance.

questions.stem: In line 13, the rising pattern in “so LONG / as MEN / can BREATHE / or EYES / can SEE” most clearly works with the syntax to
choices: imitate the rough winds described earlier through an abrupt breakdown of pattern
give measured emphasis to the human capacities on which the closing assurance depends
suggest that the speaker can no longer complete a coherent thought
make breathing and seeing appear incompatible activities
rationales: The cited reading illustrates the recurring rising framework rather than a breakdown.
The recurrent stresses support a balanced condition linking continued life and perception to the verse's survival.
The line forms a coherent condition completed by the next line.
The alternatives broaden the condition rather than establish incompatibility.

questions.stem: The repeated opening “So long” in the final couplet primarily
choices: introduces a correction of the poem's earlier use of time imagery
creates hesitation about whether the speaker wishes to finish the poem
marks two unrelated predictions about different beloveds
makes the relation between a condition and its claimed consequence audible
rationales: The ending develops that imagery into its central claim rather than merely correcting a usage.
The parallelism gives the conclusion balance rather than reluctance.
The same beloved and the same poem remain the focus.
The first line gives the condition of human life and perception; the second links it to the poem's continuance.

questions.stem: In the final line, “this” most plausibly refers to
choices: the beloved's physical body surviving unchanged
the summer whose brief duration the speaker has lamented
the poem that preserves and renews the beloved in acts of reading
the sun's ability to maintain a constant brightness
rationales: The poem locates preservation in lines and future readers rather than bodily stasis.
Summer's brevity makes it the inadequate standard the poem moves beyond.
The nearby “eternal lines” and the claim that “this gives life” identify the verse as the means of endurance.
The earlier account explicitly denies such constancy.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the poem's formal closure and its final condition?
choices: The balanced ending sounds assured while making poetic endurance depend on continuing readers.
The closing condition cancels the value of every comparison that precedes it.
The measured ending abandons the beloved in favor of an unrelated celebration of nature.
The final rhyme proves that the beloved cannot experience physical death.
rationales: The repeated structure supports confidence, but breathing and seeing remain conditions of the claim.
The earlier comparisons establish the temporal problem the verse claims to answer.
The final “thee” returns explicitly to the beloved.
Formal closure supports the assertion rhetorically; it cannot establish literal biological immunity.

questions.stem: The repetition of “Tiger” and the clustered sounds in “burning bright” chiefly make the opening address
choices: hesitant about whether the creature deserves notice
conversationally casual about an ordinary household encounter
primarily concerned with correcting the creature's name
insistent and vividly focused on the creature's presence
rationales: The direct repeated address is forceful rather than hesitant.
Night, fire, and fearful symmetry create a heightened encounter rather than domestic casualness.
The repetition intensifies address and supplies no naming dispute.
The repeated name and linked initial sounds concentrate attention before the question about its making.

questions.stem: The paired endings “bright/night” most significantly connect
choices: a peaceful setting with the speaker's wish to remain there
the creature's fiery intensity with the darkness surrounding it
two successive times when the speaker observes a change in the creature
the speaker's confidence with the creature's submissiveness
rationales: The diction is fearful and intense, not an uncomplicated statement of peace.
The sound link reinforces the visible contrast between burning brightness and nocturnal forest.
The pair describes a single imagined scene rather than successive observations.
The creature is not characterized as submissive, and the speaker asks unresolved questions.

questions.stem: The repeated interrogative openings across the poem primarily
choices: sustain an inquiry that grows through successive images of creation
demonstrate that the speaker has forgotten information known at the beginning
gradually establish a practical method for building a machine
allow several named witnesses to offer competing explanations
rationales: What, in what, and did introduce different aspects of making without supplying a definitive answer.
The opening already asks about the maker; no earlier knowledge is lost.
Industrial images figure creation, but the poem supplies questions rather than instructions.
Only one questioning voice is presented; no witnesses answer.

questions.stem: The short questions “What the hammer? what the chain?” most directly contribute to
choices: an explanation of how the tiger was captured
a calm inventory of objects the speaker owns
a concentrated, forceful imagining of the means by which the creature was formed
a dismissal of manual skill as irrelevant to the poem's subject
rationales: The surrounding furnace and anvil concern making its brain and body, not capturing it.
The objects belong to an imagined act of creation, not a stated personal collection.
The compressed syntax and tool names give the inquiry a striking, labor-intensive emphasis.
The tools make skill and force central to the imagined creation.

questions.stem: The sequence “hammer,” “furnace,” and “anvil” chiefly presents creation through the language of
choices: gentle cultivation and patient seasonal growth
powerful and potentially dangerous craftsmanship
musical performance before an appreciative audience
legal judgment and the enforcement of a sentence
rationales: These are forging images rather than horticultural ones.
The industrial implements suggest shaping through heat and force, matching the creature's terrors.
No performance or listening audience is described by the tools.
A chain alone might suggest punishment, but the sequence concerns fabrication.

questions.stem: The rhyme linking “spears” and “tears” reinforces a movement from
choices: the creature's youth toward its eventual aging
earthly craftsmanship toward a rejection of all celestial imagery
the speaker's fear toward a clearly stated victory
an image of armed power toward an image of grief or surrender
rationales: The stars' actions do not narrate the tiger's life cycle.
The stars and heaven explicitly extend the celestial imagery.
No victory is established, and the stars' actions remain part of an unresolved vision.
The stars throw down weapons and water heaven with tears, placing the two actions in a linked pair.

questions.stem: The question about the maker of the lamb most directly intensifies the poem's concern with
choices: whether the tiger can be trained to live peacefully among people
whether the speaker should abandon the forest for a farm
whether apparently different forms of creation can share an origin
whether the lamb's appearance has been accurately described
rationales: The question concerns making rather than domestication.
The contrast supplies no travel decision.
The lamb introduces a contrasting creature into the inquiry about the tiger's formidable maker.
The poem does not offer a physical description of the lamb for verification.

questions.stem: The change from “Could” in the opening stanza to “Dare” in the final stanza chiefly shifts emphasis from
choices: capacity to the audacity of the creative act
a future possibility to a remembered historical event
uncertainty to a confirmed identification of the maker
fear of the creature to indifference about its origin
rationales: The returning question now stresses daring to make such a creature, intensifying the moral and imaginative pressure.
The modal change does not establish a dated event in the speaker's past.
The maker remains unidentified and the final sentence remains a question.
The renewed address and stronger modal preserve concern.

questions.stem: The phrase “fearful symmetry” is significant chiefly because it
choices: resolves the poem's questions by proving that beauty excludes danger
contrasts the speaker's fear with the creature's inability to act
explains that the creature's body is visibly incomplete
holds formal coherence and a capacity to inspire dread together
rationales: The phrase joins the qualities instead of making them mutually exclusive.
No incapacity is attributed to the tiger.
Symmetry implies a patterned form, not incompleteness.
Symmetry suggests ordered form while fearful makes that order unsettling rather than simply reassuring.

questions.stem: The return of the opening sounds and images at the end most clearly produces
choices: a new setting that displaces the forest introduced earlier
formal completion without a final explanatory answer
a complete reversal in which the creature becomes harmless
an interruption that prevents the poem from revisiting its central concern
rationales: The forest of the night returns rather than being displaced.
The refrain closes the pattern, but the changed question leaves the mystery of creation active.
The fearful symmetry and daring remain, offering no harmless transformation.
The ending explicitly revisits the maker and the creature's form.

questions.stem: The opening personification chiefly makes Death appear as
