choices: a familiar friend whose identity has already been fully explained
a courteous agent who accommodates the speaker's inability to stop
an angry rival whose demands the speaker openly resists
a passive condition that the speaker can indefinitely postpone
rationales: The courteous manner does not supply a history of friendship or a full explanation of the figure.
Death's kindly stopping reverses the speaker's inability and establishes a social encounter.
The tone emphasizes kindness and civility, and the speaker reports no open resistance.
Death acts by stopping and directing the journey; it is not passive or indefinitely deferred.

questions.stem: The presence of Immortality in the carriage most directly
choices: introduces a second driver who disputes Death's control
confirms that the speaker expects to return home before nightfall
explains why Death cannot find room for the speaker
extends the apparently ordinary ride beyond the scale of a social outing
rationales: Immortality is a passenger, not a competing driver in the displayed text.
No return home is promised, and immortality enlarges rather than limits the time scale.
The carriage holds the figures described; no shortage of room is stated.
An abstraction associated with endless existence accompanies the speaker and Death, qualifying the familiar carriage scene.

questions.stem: The phrase “he knew no haste” chiefly characterizes Death's conduct as
choices: uncertain because the route is unfamiliar
reluctant because the speaker has ordered him to continue
unhurried in a way that makes the journey seem composed
careless about an appointment that the speaker wants to keep
rationales: No uncertainty about direction is expressed by Death.
The speaker issues no such order, and Death initiates the encounter.
The slow drive and absence of haste support the courteous social framing.
No appointment or impatience from the speaker is supplied.

questions.stem: The speaker's putting away both “labor” and “leisure” suggests
choices: a relinquishment that encompasses opposing parts of ordinary life
a complaint that Death has refused to allow any rest
an assurance that the journey will not interrupt established habits
a decision to replace hard work with a more enjoyable occupation
rationales: Work and recreation together indicate the breadth of what the speaker leaves behind.
The poem represents accommodation to civility rather than a complaint about rest.
The relinquishment explicitly interrupts the activities that organized ordinary life.
Both labor and leisure are put away, not exchanged for each other.

questions.stem: The explanation “For his civility” most significantly
choices: proves that Death's intentions and destination are entirely reassuring
reveals that the speaker has consciously deceived Death
turns the ride into a dispute about the proper rules of conversation
represents an immense transition through the obligations of polite behavior
rationales: Courteous conduct does not fully explain or guarantee the meaning of the journey.
No deception by the speaker is described.
The phrase supplies a motive for accommodation rather than an overt dispute.
The speaker gives up ordinary activities in response to Death's manners, making a familiar social code mediate an unfamiliar departure.

questions.stem: The repeated “We passed” chiefly contributes to
choices: an increasingly detailed explanation of the speaker's childhood
a steady sequence of familiar scenes receding during the journey
a series of returns to the same place after failed departures
a contrast between the speaker's movement and Death's refusal to move
rationales: The school may invite a life-stage association, but no personal childhood narrative is given.
School, fields, and setting sun are encountered through the same passing action, giving the ride continuity.
The objects change and no circular return is reported.
The plural subject includes the carriage's occupants in the same movement.

questions.stem: In “the fields of gazing grain,” the human quality assigned to the grain primarily
choices: makes the landscape appear attentive within the passing scene
establishes that the harvest has failed because the crop cannot grow
shows that the speaker has mistaken a crowd of people for crops
identifies the grain as the speaker's actual traveling companion
rationales: Gazing gives the nonhuman field an observing quality rather than leaving it inert.
No agricultural failure is described.
The language is personification, not an explicit correction of a perceptual error.
The grain remains in the fields and does not enter the carriage.

questions.stem: The description of the “house” as a swelling of the ground most strongly suggests
choices: the school building mentioned in the previous stanza
a temporary shelter that Death intends to repair
a grave rendered through the familiar language of habitation
a grand estate whose scale astonishes the speaker
rationales: The school and the ground-level house occupy different stages of the passage.
No repair plan or temporary stay is stated.
The scarcely visible roof and mound make the house a grave-like destination while preserving domestic vocabulary.
The low, scarcely visible features undermine the notion of grandeur.

questions.stem: The final stanza changes the reader's understanding of the narrated ride chiefly by
choices: revealing that no journey occurred outside an afternoon dream
placing its remembered duration against a vastly enlarged temporal perspective
replacing the first-person speaker with Death as narrator
showing that the speaker has returned to the earlier school
rationales: The text offers no waking explanation that cancels the journey.
Centuries feel shorter than the day, transforming the scale on which the journey is recalled.
The first-person recollection continues in “I first surmised.”
The stanza concerns retrospective time and eternity, not a return to the school.

questions.stem: The verb “surmised” most significantly qualifies the ending by
choices: suggesting that Death has explicitly announced every stage of the route
establishing that the speaker now rejects the earlier interpretation of the journey
confirming that the horses have stopped before reaching the house
presenting the direction toward eternity as an inference reached by the speaker
rationales: Death does not speak, and surmising differs from receiving an explicit announcement.
No rejection follows the surmise.
The verb concerns the speaker's understanding of direction, not a confirmed stopping point for the horses.
The word marks a realization or supposition rather than a destination fully described and mastered.

questions.stem: The opening address to the rose primarily establishes
choices: a dispute in which the rose answers the speaker's accusation
a celebration of the rose's recovery from an earlier illness
a detached explanation of a general gardening procedure
an intimate diagnosis whose significance the remaining lines complicate
rationales: The rose receives an address but never answers.
The sickness is present and the ending describes destruction rather than recovery.
The exclamation and address are immediate, while the poem supplies no practical instructions.
The direct address names sickness before the worm, joy, and destructive love develop its implications.

questions.stem: The worm's invisibility, together with its movement at night, chiefly emphasizes
choices: the harmlessness of an organism too small to be observed
the concealed operation of the force harming the rose
the speaker's inability to notice that the rose is sick
the rose's deliberate effort to protect the worm from danger
rationales: The ending attributes destruction to the worm's love, so concealment does not imply harmlessness.
The hidden creature and nocturnal setting support the later language of dark secrecy.
The speaker explicitly diagnoses sickness at the opening.
No protective action by the rose is described.

questions.stem: The phrase “crimson joy” most directly creates a tension between
choices: sensuous vitality and the destruction that enters its place
the speaker's happiness and the rose's expressed resentment
the worm's fear of discovery and its wish to escape the storm
a color perceived at night and the absence of color during the day
rationales: The positive, vivid phrase describes the bed that the worm finds, making the later damage more troubling.
The rose does not speak, and the joy is not directly assigned to the speaker.
The poem does not give the worm that emotional conflict.
No day scene or colorless counterpart appears.

questions.stem: The relationship between “love” and “destroy” in the final two lines most strongly supports a reading of
choices: secrecy as necessary to protect every valuable relationship
sickness as an illusion produced by the speaker's jealousy
intimacy as capable of carrying concealed harm
affection as a guarantee of restoration
rationales: The secrecy here accompanies damage, not a general protective rule.
Neither an illusion nor jealousy on the speaker's part is established.
A term associated with attachment becomes the agency of destruction, creating the poem's disturbing symbolic relation.
The verb destroy prevents a straightforward restorative account.

questions.stem: Which claim most carefully respects the poem's symbolic openness?
choices: The worm can signify only one identifiable person in the poet's biography.
The poem supports a pattern of hidden destructive intimacy without fixing a single human analogue.
The rose must represent innocence because roses have that meaning in every poem.
The poem cannot suggest any human relation because its nouns name natural objects.
rationales: No biographical identification is supplied by the text.
Night, secrecy, joy, love, and destruction establish a relation, while the poem leaves its exact application unstated.
A universal symbolic dictionary replaces the particular poem's evidence with an unsupported rule.
The language of bed, joy, and secret love invites significance beyond literal botany.

questions.stem: The contrast between “what I never had seen” and “Where I used to play” primarily establishes
choices: an argument that childhood play was forbidden before the chapel appeared
the speaker's uncertainty about whether the garden has ever existed
a preference for the new building over the earlier open space
a changed place measured against the speaker's remembered freedom
rationales: The remembered activity is play, while prohibition is attached to the present chapel.
The speaker treats the past garden as remembered experience, not a doubtful invention.
The later shut gates and bound desires complicate rather than support such a preference.
The new chapel occupies the site of earlier play, making memory the basis for recognizing transformation.

questions.stem: The shut gates and the words “Thou shalt not” function together chiefly as
choices: instructions explaining how the speaker can enter the garden
contrasting signs that make the chapel's invitation ambiguous
visible and verbal forms of exclusion
evidence of a temporary repair to an otherwise welcoming building
rationales: The inscription denies rather than offers a procedure for entry.
Both details restrict rather than one inviting and one excluding.
The barrier and prohibition reinforce each other, characterizing access to the chapel through restriction.
No repair or promised reopening is described.

questions.stem: The replacement of flowers by graves chiefly gives the garden's transformation
choices: a movement from remembered vitality toward death and restriction
a clear explanation of the historical events that caused the deaths
a movement from disorder toward an order the speaker celebrates
a distinction between cultivated flowers and more valuable wild plants
rationales: The speaker explicitly sees tombstones where flowers should be, making loss a spatial and symbolic substitution.
No history of the graves' occupants is provided.
The ending associates the new order with binding joys and desires rather than celebration.
The contrast is with graves and tombstones, not another kind of vegetation.

questions.stem: The priests' binding of “my joys and desires” with briars most clearly
choices: shows the speaker willingly exchanging desire for religious office
resolves the poem by restoring the play remembered at the opening
describes a successful effort to protect flowers from being picked
turns a physical action into an image of constraint on inward life
rationales: The speaker does not volunteer or become a priest.
The final action constrains rather than restores that freedom.
The flowers have been displaced and the binding targets joys and desires.
The objects bound are abstract feelings, so the action joins the garden's material imagery to the speaker's psychic restriction.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for both the garden's name and its final condition?
choices: The final scene makes the garden's promised welcome fully available.
A place associated with love becomes the site of institutions and practices that constrict desire.
The garden teaches the speaker to reject every form of human attachment.
The speaker discovers that the remembered garden was always a cemetery.
rationales: Closed gates and binding briars contradict a fulfilled welcome.
The name persists while chapel, graves, and binding priests transform the speaker's relation to the place.
The focus is the restriction of joy and desire, not a stated rejection of all attachment.
The poem presents a perceived change and contrasts present graves with earlier flowers and play.

questions.stem: With the supplied gloss of Lethe in mind, the phrase “Lethe-wards had sunk” primarily presents the opening sensation as
choices: a confident preparation for heroic combat
a return to an accurately remembered childhood home
an accusation that the bird has deliberately deceived the speaker
a movement toward numbness and forgetting
rationales: Neither the local imagery nor the gloss introduces battle or confident readiness.
The movement is toward oblivion, not autobiographical recollection.
The speaker describes an internal sensation without attributing intentional deception to the bird.
The allusion's association with forgetting works with hemlock, opiate, and drowsiness to characterize the speaker's condition.

questions.stem: Calling the bird a “light-winged Dryad of the trees” chiefly
choices: suggests that the song is a mechanical repetition without feeling
gives its natural music an imaginatively enchanted presence
establishes that the speaker has literally identified a human performer
turns the forest into an urban place of public entertainment
rationales: The language of full-throated ease and enchantment points away from mechanical emptiness.
The tree-nymph allusion transforms the singer into a figure of woodland vitality while remaining connected to its habitat.
The description is figurative, and the subject remains the bird.
The surrounding beechen green and shadows retain a woodland setting.

questions.stem: The reference to “Flora” in the imagined draught chiefly
choices: concentrates the pleasures of vegetation and seasonal abundance in the desired drink
explains a dispute between two gods over ownership of the forest
identifies the person to whom the speaker intends to give the drink
warns that the wine has been contaminated by poisonous flowers
rationales: The flower-goddess allusion accompanies country green, dance, and mirth, making the wine carry a richly imagined environment.
No divine dispute is narrated.
Flora is an allusive association, not a stated recipient.
Poison appears in the opening simile, but this passage presents a desired, pleasurable draught.

questions.stem: The allusion to Hippocrene is particularly significant because it
choices: contrasts poetry with every form of pleasure in the preceding lines
proves that the speaker has physically traveled to the spring
brings poetic inspiration into the speaker's imagined means of departure
provides a precise geographical location for the bird's nest
rationales: The allusion enters a sequence of pleasurable associations rather than rejecting all of them.
The passage expresses a wish, not a completed journey.
The spring of the Muses associates the desired draught with poetry before the later explicit turn to Poesy.
The reference concerns inspiration and drink, not the bird's location.

questions.stem: The shift from “Bacchus and his pards” to “the viewless wings of Poesy” primarily
choices: abandons the desire to join the bird altogether
revises the proposed means of escape from intoxication to imaginative flight
returns the speaker to a purely factual description of the room
claims that poetic creation requires a literal winged vehicle
rationales: The speaker says “I will fly to thee,” retaining the desired destination.
The explicit “Not … But” construction replaces the wine god's vehicle with poetry's unseen wings.
The passage intensifies imaginative movement rather than describing a room.
The wings are viewless and figurative, not a practical apparatus.

questions.stem: The clause “Though the dull brain perplexes and retards” qualifies the turn to Poesy by
choices: proving that the earlier wish for wine has been fulfilled
making the bird responsible for the speaker's intellectual confusion
showing that the speaker has forgotten the bird entirely
acknowledging a mental impediment even as the speaker attempts imaginative release
rationales: No drinking event is reported; the clause concerns the mind.
The dull brain is the speaker's impediment, not an action attributed to the bird.
The next line asserts being already with the bird.
The concession introduces resistance within the mind that seeks to fly.

questions.stem: The imagined continuity of the song across “emperor and clown” chiefly
choices: establishes that the bird sings differently for rulers and ordinary people
introduces a contest in which the emperor defeats the clown
extends its reach across differences in status and historical time
shows that only privileged listeners can appreciate the music
rationales: The speaker emphasizes the same voice rather than separate tailored songs.
No contest or interaction between the two figures is described.
The paired social positions and ancient days make the voice seem available across human distinctions and generations.
The inclusion of the clown broadens rather than restricts the audience.

questions.stem: The word “Perhaps” before the reference to Ruth is important because it
choices: marks the proposed connection between the present song and a distant sorrow as imaginative speculation
announces that the following account is a direct quotation from Ruth
dismisses Ruth's homesickness as unworthy of attention
suggests that the speaker doubts whether the bird is singing now
rationales: The speaker envisages continuity without claiming documented certainty that Ruth heard this song.
No quoted speech by Ruth appears.
The sad heart and tears make her sorrow part of the song's imagined human reach.
The present song is heard; the uncertainty concerns its imagined past connection.

questions.stem: The repetition of “forlorn” across the seventh and eighth stanzas chiefly
choices: supplies the historical name of the place where Ruth lived
introduces a new bird whose call replaces the nightingale's
confirms that the speaker has successfully remained in the faery lands
turns a word within the imagined distant scene into the stimulus for a return to the solitary self
rationales: Forlorn is an emotional descriptor, not a place name.
The change occurs in the speaker's response to a word, not in the identity of the bird.
The explicit return “to my sole self” reverses that possibility.
The word first describes faery lands and then tolls like a bell that recalls the speaker from the bird.

questions.stem: Taken together, the classical, biblical, and fairy-tale references chiefly allow the poem to
choices: establish a single consistent mythology that resolves the speaker's questions
enlarge the song's imagined reach while testing the limits of imaginative escape
replace the speaker's immediate sensations with a detached historical survey
prove that human suffering has vanished wherever the song is heard
rationales: The references come from varied traditions and culminate in unresolved questions.
The allusions move through pleasure, inspiration, shared sorrow, and enchantment before the speaker returns to uncertainty.
Bodily ache, sensory guessing, listening, and self-return remain central.
Ruth's tears and the speaker's mortality remain within the imagined reach of the music.

questions.stem: The assertion that the brain is “wider than the sky” most plausibly depends on a distinction between
choices: the sky's daytime appearance and its larger appearance at night
a mature person's intelligence and a child's limited knowledge
the actual width of the brain and an error in measuring the sky
physical dimensions and the mind's capacity to represent what exceeds the body
rationales: No day-night contrast is introduced.
The poem makes no age-based comparison.
The figurative comparison does not offer a scientific measurement correction.
The following inclusion of sky and observer suggests mental comprehensiveness rather than literal anatomical size.

questions.stem: The addition of “and you beside” in the first stanza chiefly
choices: limits the claim to an isolated private memory of a friend
extends the mind's capacity to include the observer as well as the observed world
excludes the addressee from the mental space being described
reveals that two speakers have been arguing about the sky
rationales: The poem offers a general comparison, not a narrated memory.
The mind contains the sky and the person placed beside it, enlarging the initial comparison.
The phrase adds rather than excludes the addressee.
No second speaker's argument is presented.

questions.stem: The sponge and bucket comparison chiefly makes the brain's relation to the sea seem like
choices: a capacity to take in or contain what appears physically immense
a literal account of the brain's composition from water and fabric
a warning that knowledge must be removed before thought can occur
a struggle in which the sea repeatedly defeats human thought
rationales: Absorption and containment give a concrete form to the mind's figurative depth.
The simile does not propose an anatomical composition.
The image concerns taking in rather than emptying knowledge.
The brain is presented as including the sea, not being defeated by it.

questions.stem: The phrase “if they do” in the final stanza chiefly
choices: confirms that the speaker has performed an actual weighing experiment
withdraws every comparison made in the preceding stanzas
leaves the asserted distinction open rather than making it wholly secure
identifies an audience whose agreement the speaker has already obtained
rationales: The imagined comparison is not a report of empirical procedure.
It qualifies the final difference without explicitly canceling the earlier comparisons.
The conditional qualification interrupts a simple claim that brain and God differ in a definite way.
No audience response is supplied.

questions.stem: The ending's comparison of “syllable” and “sound” most strongly invites readers to consider
choices: a contest in which language proves that the sea is physically shallow
a relation between a formed unit and a broader medium that complicates simple separation
the speaker's preference for silence over every form of thought
the complete absence of any relation between mind and divinity
rationales: The ending moves to brain and God, not an empirical verdict about ocean depth.
A syllable is shaped sound, making difference and relation coexist rather than providing a wholly independent pair.
No preference for silence is stated.
The comparison and qualification make the relation open and connected rather than absent.

questions.stem: The comparison of light with “the weight / Of cathedral tunes” primarily
choices: suggests that the speaker hears a cheerful song whenever winter ends
distinguishes an outdoor scene from an unrelated memory of worship
explains the exact physical cause of an architectural collapse
translates a visual impression into an oppressive bodily and auditory experience
rationales: The setting is winter afternoon and the feeling is oppression.
The simile connects the experiences instead of leaving them unrelated.
The comparison is experiential, not an engineering account.
Weight and music make the slant of light felt across senses, emphasizing pressure rather than simple illumination.

questions.stem: The phrase “Heavenly hurt” chiefly creates a tension between
choices: the speaker's public happiness and a concealed wish for wealth
an injury suffered in childhood and its complete healing in adulthood
an association with elevation or sacredness and an experience of pain
a literal sky wound and the landscape's medical treatment
rationales: Neither public happiness nor wealth is established.
No biographical sequence or completed healing appears.
The adjective does not cancel the hurt; their conjunction makes the experience difficult to classify as simply consoling.
The poem uses figurative experience rather than a literal medical scene.

questions.stem: The contrast between “no scar” and “internal difference” most directly suggests that
choices: the experience changes inward meaning without leaving an observable bodily mark
the light's influence can be verified only through a visible wound
the speaker has discovered that the experience had no effect
physical pain is easier to remember than emotional happiness
rationales: The poem distinguishes external evidence of injury from a transformation where meanings reside.
The absence of a scar makes that proposed verification inadequate.
Internal difference explicitly asserts an effect.
The lines do not compare those kinds of memory.

questions.stem: Calling the experience an “imperial affliction” primarily emphasizes
choices: its brief insignificance compared with ordinary tasks
its value as a reward for a completed religious duty
its origin in a documented political decree
its commanding force over the person who undergoes it
rationales: The elevated diction magnifies rather than diminishes the experience.
Affliction and despair resist a straightforward reward reading.
No actual ruler or decree is identified.
Imperial associates the affliction with authority and domination rather than voluntary choice.

questions.stem: The final image, “the distance / On the look of death,” chiefly leaves the experience with
choices: a precise measurement of the speaker's distance from a grave
an unsettling sense of remoteness that resists a fully concrete explanation
a clear assurance that the speaker's earlier pain has ended permanently
a return to the cheerful landscape described at the beginning
rationales: The poem supplies no measurable location or actual grave.
Distance is associated with a look of death, sustaining the inward and difficult-to-define quality of the affliction.
Departure of the light receives a disturbing comparison, not a guarantee of lasting relief.
The opening landscape was oppressive rather than cheerful.

questions.stem: The opening comparison between waves and minutes chiefly establishes
choices: a belief that individual moments can reverse their direction
a recurring forward movement in which each unit gives way to another
a remembered voyage that the speaker later describes in detail
a distinction between nature's permanence and time's complete stillness
rationales: The lines emphasize forward contention and replacement, not reversal.
The waves' sequence provides a figure for minutes hastening toward their end.
The wave image supports an analogy rather than a narrated voyage.
Both terms of the comparison are defined through movement.

questions.stem: The phrase “In sequent toil” most directly complicates the opening natural image by
choices: identifying the speaker's occupation as a sailor
suggesting that the waves have ceased to move
presenting time as a leisurely pleasure free of struggle
making successive motion seem laborious rather than merely graceful
rationales: No occupation is supplied.
The line explicitly describes forward contention.
Toil and contend work against that account.
Toil gives the waves' and minutes' forward movement a sense of effort and pressure.

questions.stem: The second quatrain shifts the poem's focus from
choices: a public disaster to a private reconciliation
the beloved's childhood to a detailed account of the speaker's old age
repeated units of time to the course of a life under time's power
a hostile landscape to a refuge beyond time
rationales: Neither event structures the transition.
The language is generalized, not a pair of biographical narratives.
Nativity, maturity, and the loss of glory translate the opening sequence into a human life pattern.
The new image remains subject to time's destruction.

questions.stem: The movement from “Crawls to maturity” to “being crown'd” primarily
choices: presents growth as an attainment whose triumph is immediately threatened
identifies a literal coronation that resolves a political dispute
makes childhood appear more powerful than every later stage
suggests that maturity removes the subject from all temporal change
rationales: Maturity receives a crown, but eclipses and Time's confounding follow the apparent achievement.
The language figures life stages without narrating a political succession.
Crawling and crowning suggest development rather than childhood's supremacy.
The following lines explicitly expose the crowned condition to loss.

questions.stem: The claim that Time “gave” and then “his gift confound” chiefly portrays Time as
choices: an impartial observer who never affects the natural world
a force whose destructive powers have been permanently exhausted
a benefactor whose gifts remain untouched by later events
both the source of development and the agent that undoes its results
rationales: Time acts directly in giving and confounding.
The next quatrain intensifies those powers.
The verb confound denies that permanence.
The repeated agent supplies and disrupts the gift, giving time a double role.

questions.stem: The third quatrain's sequence of verbs—“transfix,” “delves,” and “Feeds”—primarily
choices: shows that destruction occurs only when people resist natural change
intensifies time's action into a sustained assault on youth and beauty
slows the poem into a neutral catalogue of farming techniques
introduces three independent characters who oppose Time
rationales: The passage gives no such condition limiting time's action.
Piercing, carving, and consuming accumulate forms of damage before the scythe image.
The verbs act on youth and beauty through personification rather than practical farming description.
Time remains the acting subject across the sequence.

questions.stem: The image of “parallels in beauty's brow” most plausibly refers to
choices: lines of aging rendered as marks cut by Time
the lines of the poem already granting the beloved immortality
two equal arguments about the beloved's moral character
paths through a landscape that lead away from the sea
rationales: The brow and the verb delves suggest wrinkles as evidence of time's active damage.
Poetic lines appear in the couplet; these marks belong to the damaged brow.
Parallels here are figurative marks rather than rival propositions.
The image concerns beauty's brow, not geographic routes.

questions.stem: The phrase “And nothing stands but for his scythe to mow” prepares the couplet by
choices: resolving the earlier tension by proving time cannot touch beauty
announcing that the poem has already abandoned its subject
making the proposed endurance of verse answer an apparently universal threat
restricting time's power to agricultural objects
rationales: The line asserts time's reach over standing things rather than immunity.
The threat leads directly to the beloved's worth and the verse's purpose.
The sweep of “nothing” gives force to the following “And yet” and its hope that verse will stand.
The preceding youth, brow, and nature's rarities extend the scythe beyond literal crops.

questions.stem: The words “in hope” are important to the final couplet because they
choices: make the preceding account of time a confirmed misunderstanding
qualify the assertion of poetic endurance without extinguishing its resistance
show that the speaker intends to stop praising the beloved
identify Hope as a new character who physically defeats Time
rationales: The threat remains active and is not exposed as false.
The verse “shall stand,” but the phrase frames that confidence as a hope opposed to Time's cruel hand.
The final line explicitly continues the purpose of praise.
Hope is the speaker's stance, not an enacted victory by a new character.

questions.stem: Which account best explains the sonnet's overall structural movement?
choices: Four equally reassuring images establish that natural beauty never changes.
A scientific explanation of tides is interrupted by an unrelated love complaint.
A personal quarrel moves through accusation and apology toward reconciliation.
Three developing accounts of temporal destruction culminate in a qualified counterclaim for verse.
rationales: The quatrains repeatedly describe change and damage.
The waves begin a sustained analogy about time that leads coherently to the final praise.
No quarrel or apology is narrated.
Waves, life stages, and Time's assault build the pressure that the couplet answers with hopeful poetic endurance.

questions.stem: The opening description of candlelight without daylight primarily establishes
choices: a practical shortage that Pip immediately volunteers to remedy
a contrast between the visitor's wealth and the inhabitant's poverty
a festive occasion that the narrator understands without uncertainty
an environment separated from the ordinary conditions outside it
rationales: Pip does not offer a repair or identify the condition as a temporary shortage.
The room's rich furnishings do not establish poverty, and Pip's wealth is not the contrast.
The narrator repeatedly marks uncertainty, and the apparent festivity becomes disturbing.
Artificial illumination and excluded daylight prepare the room's larger pattern of withdrawal and arrested routine.

questions.stem: The account of the dressing table in the first two paragraphs most clearly reveals
choices: the child's deliberate effort to flatter Miss Havisham through admiration
the narrator's attention to how the child's recognition depended on context
the child's complete familiarity with every object in the room
the narrator's conviction that the room contains no useful objects
rationales: The passage reports perception rather than a spoken compliment.
The older voice questions whether Pip would have recognized the table without the lady seated there.
The passage explicitly says that many forms and uses were unknown to him.
Unfamiliarity does not establish uselessness, and several objects are recognized.

questions.stem: The repeated references to white in paragraph 3 are significantly revised when
choices: the next paragraph distinguishes former whiteness from present fading and yellowing
the narrator withdraws the claim that the woman is wearing bridal clothing
Pip realizes that the room is illuminated by daylight
Miss Havisham explains that she has recently purchased new clothes
rationales: The descriptive sequence first invokes bridal whiteness and then exposes its altered condition.
The bridal identity remains central; it is the condition of the clothing that changes.
The room excludes daylight throughout the selection.
No such explanation appears.

questions.stem: The one shoe, half-arranged veil, and unused accessories together suggest
choices: a child's misunderstanding of clothing that is actually complete
a woman selecting among several outfits for an imminent journey
preparation interrupted and left materially unfinished
a room intentionally cleared of evidence of the past
rationales: The narrator describes concrete incompletion rather than correcting it as an error.
Trunks are present, but no current selection or imminent departure is narrated.
The clustered incomplete actions make the dressing process appear suspended.
The scattered objects preserve rather than remove such evidence.

questions.stem: The comparison between the withered bride and her dress chiefly
choices: contrasts a healthy body with objects that alone have decayed
joins the condition of the inhabitant to the condition of her preserved surroundings
explains that the dress was made specifically for the woman's present figure
suggests that Pip cannot distinguish a person from a garment at all
rationales: The woman is described as shrunken and withered as well.
Both body and clothing bear the effects of time within an arrangement that appears arrested.
The narrator contrasts its original fit on a young figure with its present looseness.
He recognizes the woman, while figurative comparison makes her appearance disturbing.

questions.stem: The movement from waxwork and skeleton to eyes that “moved and looked at me” primarily
choices: introduces two additional visitors hidden in the room
turns the encounter into a reassuring recognition of a familiar friend
corrects Pip's belief that the woman is actually absent
makes signs associated with lifeless display disturbingly animate
rationales: The waxwork and skeleton are remembered comparisons, not new occupants.
The child is frightened almost to the point of crying out.
He has already seen her; the comparison concerns the uncanny quality of her presence.
Pip's remembered images of death or imitation acquire living eyes in his perception of Miss Havisham.

questions.stem: The watch and clock stopped at the same time chiefly give the room's temporal pattern
choices: a contradiction proving that Pip has misread both instruments
an explanation of how long Pip has already spent in the house
a coordinated specificity beyond a general impression of age
a sign that ordinary household routines continue unaffected
rationales: Their agreement supplies no such contradiction.
The stopped instruments do not measure the visit's elapsed time.
Two instruments agree on a precise moment, making arrested time a deliberate-looking feature of the environment.
The stoppage participates in the suspension of ordinary routine.

questions.stem: Miss Havisham's emphatic “Broken!” complicates her self-presentation because
choices: her expression combines suffering with something resembling pride in that suffering
she offers a clear chronological explanation of every object in the room
she immediately denies that any emotional injury has occurred
she uses the word to accuse Pip of damaging the clock
rationales: The eager look and smile with a kind of boast qualify the declaration of a broken heart.
The single declaration suggests a connection but supplies no full history.
She emphatically names the injury rather than denying it.
The gesture identifies her heart, not an object Pip has broken.

questions.stem: The repeated commands to “play” chiefly expose a contradiction between
choices: Miss Havisham's wish to leave the room and Pip's insistence on remaining
the narrator's belief that children should work and Pip's refusal to do so
Pip's enthusiasm for performance and Miss Havisham's wish for silence
the demand for spontaneous diversion and the intimidating conditions imposed on the child
rationales: Neither intention is stated.
The passage presents fear of work as another pressure, not the narrator's educational doctrine.
Pip feels unable to perform, while she demands diversion.
The room and Miss Havisham's manner make the requested play difficult, as the narrator explicitly observes.

questions.stem: The final question about sullenness and obstinacy most directly shows how
choices: the room's earlier strangeness has ceased to influence the encounter
the child's inhibited response can be misread as a willful disposition
the adult narrator endorses Miss Havisham's judgment without reservation
the child has successfully explained the cause of his discomfort
rationales: The fear generated by the room and its inhabitant continues to shape Pip's behavior.
Pip attributes his stillness to fear and inability, while Miss Havisham interprets it through blame.
The retrospective account supplies reasons that complicate her judgment.
He has not given that explanation to her.

questions.stem: Walton's opening address to Margaret chiefly positions his letter as
choices: an effort to communicate the emotional force of a story she has received through him
a request that Margaret supply the missing ending of Victor's story
an accusation that Margaret has knowingly altered his notes
a neutral inventory designed to exclude all personal response
rationales: He asks whether her blood congeals as his does, linking her reading to his experience of hearing.
Walton says she has read the story and does not ask her to complete it.
No alteration by Margaret is alleged.
The direct appeal and bodily imagery foreground feeling.

questions.stem: The changing account of Victor's voice and expression primarily presents his storytelling as
choices: an entirely consistent display of calm detachment
a failed effort to speak a language Walton cannot understand
a performance that alternates between control and eruptions of anguish
a deliberate imitation of another named storyteller's manner
rationales: The passage repeatedly describes agony, sorrow, and sudden rage.
Difficulty comes from emotion, not a stated language barrier.
Tranquil narration and suppressed agitation give way to volcanic rage, making delivery part of Walton's experience.
No model for imitation is identified.

questions.stem: The volcano comparison most directly emphasizes
choices: the narrator's certainty that every reported event is false
the sudden emergence of emotion after visible restraint
the gradual disappearance of Victor's interest in his story
the physical danger posed by the ship's location near an active volcano
rationales: The image concerns delivery, not a verdict of fabrication.
The eruption follows an account of suppressed agitation and a tranquil voice.
The image magnifies passion rather than its fading.
The comparison describes a face and voice, not the ship's geography.

questions.stem: Walton's reference to the letters and the sighting from the ship chiefly
choices: proves that Margaret has already rejected the existence of the creature
establishes that he regards emotional delivery as the only basis for belief
shows that he has independently witnessed every event Victor recounts
distinguishes corroborating evidence from the persuasive force of Victor's assertions
rationales: No response from Margaret is presented.
He explicitly identifies a stronger source of conviction.
The evidence corroborates aspects of the account, not its entire sequence.
He says those items gave him greater conviction than earnest, connected narration alone.

questions.stem: Victor's refusal to explain the particulars of the creature's formation primarily
choices: confirms that the creature's existence has been entirely disproved
suggests that Walton has no interest in the experiment
sets a limit on the knowledge he is willing to transmit through his story
shows that Victor intends to invite the sailors to reproduce the experiment
rationales: The refusal concerns particulars of formation, not a retraction of existence.
Walton explicitly asks about it.
He answers Walton's curiosity with a warning against repeating his misery rather than a technical explanation.
His warning discourages such repetition.

questions.stem: The report that Victor “corrected and augmented” the notes most significantly
choices: makes the transmitted account an acknowledged product of revision by its central participant
guarantees that the notes preserve the exact wording of every original conversation
removes Victor's concern about how future readers will judge him
reveals that Walton never heard Victor speak
rationales: Victor helps shape Walton's written record, particularly reported conversations with his enemy.
Revision by an interested participant does not independently establish verbatim accuracy.
His reference to posterity makes that concern more visible.
Walton's hearing and note-taking are explicitly described.

questions.stem: Victor's objection to a “mutilated” narration most directly suggests
choices: an admission that he has intentionally destroyed Walton's manuscript
a belief that only Margaret can supply the missing facts
a refusal to allow any record of his history to survive
an investment in the completeness and future form of his remembered account
rationales: No destruction is reported.
He himself corrects and enlarges the notes.
He accepts preservation while revising its form.
He wants the preserved narrative to carry what he regards as its life and spirit into posterity.

questions.stem: Walton's statement that his thoughts and feelings have been “drunk up” by interest in his guest chiefly
choices: establishes that he has lost all memory of the narrated events
reveals the extent to which sympathy absorbs his attention
indicates that Victor's story is primarily about drinking
introduces a detached reconsideration that cancels his earlier admiration
rationales: Absorption in interest does not mean amnesia.
The figurative consumption makes his emotional investment in Victor explicit.
The phrase describes Walton's response, not the subject of the story.
The surrounding language continues to admire and pity Victor.

questions.stem: Walton's account of Victor's dreams is qualified most clearly by
choices: his distinction between their imposing effect and their uncertain status as truth
his claim that Margaret has verified each dream through correspondence
his assertion that he has personally met the dead friends aboard the ship
his insistence that the dreams provide no comfort to Victor
rationales: He describes the faith as offspring of solitude and delirium and says the reveries are almost as interesting as truth.
No verification by Margaret appears.
No such encounter is reported.
He explicitly describes consolation and excitement to vengeance.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for the selection's framing of Victor?
choices: His account is rejected as soon as he attempts to revise the notes.
His account becomes independent of every teller once it is written down.
His account reaches the reader through a listener who seeks some corroboration while becoming deeply invested in him.
His account is presented through a recorder whose identity and feelings remain entirely concealed.
rationales: Walton reports revision without rejecting the narrative.
The selection explicitly describes the roles of speaker, recorder, reviser, and recipient.
Walton distinguishes evidence from assertion, yet admiration and emotional absorption shape the record.
The letter foregrounds Walton's voice and response.

questions.stem: The opening claim that “all occasions” inform against Hamlet primarily frames the expedition as
choices: an interruption that has no bearing on his central concern
one more external event converted into evidence for self-accusation
a welcome distraction from every question of action
a reliable report of a legal trial already underway
rationales: The opening immediately connects the occasion to revenge.
Hamlet treats what he encounters as a witness against his delayed revenge.
The occasion intensifies rather than suspends that question.
The language is figurative accusation, not a described courtroom event.

questions.stem: The description of human beings as more than creatures that “sleep and feed” chiefly establishes
choices: a preference for animal life as morally superior to human life
a practical explanation of why the army lacks provisions
a claim that physical needs make every deliberate action impossible
a standard of purposeful capacity against which Hamlet judges his inactivity
rationales: He uses beast as a diminished condition to be avoided.
The passage does not discuss the army's food supply.
The argument distinguishes higher capacities rather than denying action because of bodily need.
He invokes reason and forethought as powers that should not remain unused.

questions.stem: The contrast between the army's “mass and charge” and its “delicate and tender prince” primarily
choices: shows that the prince has refused to accompany the expedition
proves that the army has already been defeated
makes the scale and risk of the enterprise seem striking beside the leader's apparent vulnerability
suggests that Hamlet considers the expedition too small to notice
rationales: He is described as leading it.
No battle outcome is reported.
The substantial force is led by a prince described in terms that contrast with its weight and danger.
He calls it an example gross as earth and dwells on its scale.

questions.stem: The image “Even for an eggshell” chiefly emphasizes
choices: the disproportion between what is risked and the apparent value of the object sought
the certainty that the disputed land contains valuable resources
the soldiers' inability to recognize one another
the prince's skill at protecting his followers from danger
rationales: Mortal vulnerability and great danger are set against a fragile, slight object.
The image diminishes rather than establishes material value.
The image concerns the campaign's object, not personal recognition.
The passage emphasizes exposure to danger rather than reliable protection.

questions.stem: The claim about finding quarrel “in a straw / When honour's at the stake” primarily attempts to
choices: prove that the prince knows the outcome of the campaign in advance
show that the soldiers are motivated solely by immediate financial profit
withdraw every earlier criticism of Hamlet's delay
justify great action for a small material object by invoking a different kind of value
rationales: The invisible event remains uncertain.
The stated value is honor, not direct payment.
The speech uses the claim to intensify self-reproach.
Honor supplies the ground on which a seemingly trivial occasion might warrant resolve.

questions.stem: The question “How stand I then” chiefly turns the parallel action toward
choices: a calculation of Hamlet's formal military rank
a comparison between Hamlet's substantial personal motives and the army's slight occasion
a request for the captain to describe the safest route home
an explanation of why Hamlet has chosen to join the army
rationales: The phrase concerns his moral and practical position, not rank.
His murdered father and dishonored mother are placed against the previously diminished object of the campaign.
No captain answers within the speech, and the question is self-directed.
No enlistment or decision to join occurs.

questions.stem: The phrase “a fantasy and trick of fame” complicates Hamlet's use of the soldiers as an example by
choices: casting doubt on the substance of the glory for which they risk death
establishing that every soldier has been told the campaign is fictional
replacing all admiration with a settled rejection of decisive action
proving that the prince has no ambitions beyond survival
rationales: The diction makes fame seem insubstantial even as their action shames him.
The campaign is treated as real; the phrase evaluates its reward.
The final resolution still presses toward action, preserving the tension.
The speech explicitly attributes ambition to the prince.

questions.stem: The comparison “Go to their graves like beds” chiefly
choices: describes the comfort of the army's temporary lodgings
suggests that Hamlet has forgotten the purpose of the expedition
makes the soldiers' acceptance of death seem disturbingly familiar or easy
assures the audience that no soldiers will actually face danger
rationales: The comparison concerns graves, not a literal lodging report.
He continues to connect the deaths to the disputed plot.
The ordinary place of rest is joined to the grave, sharpening the scale of sacrifice.
The speech explicitly imagines imminent deaths.

questions.stem: The description of land too small to contain the slain primarily reinforces
choices: the practical superiority of this territory over surrounding land
the mismatch between the campaign's material object and its human cost
the idea that the battle has already occurred and been fully counted
the speaker's belief that burial customs are the expedition's chief cause
rationales: The point diminishes its adequacy rather than praising it.
The plot cannot even hold the bodies of those who may die for it.
The deaths are anticipated, not reported as a completed tally.
The grave image evaluates cost rather than identifies the motive.

questions.stem: As a parallel to Hamlet's central conflict, the expedition chiefly functions in this speech to
choices: provide an unqualified demonstration that any action is better than reflection
settle the future outcome of Hamlet's revenge by matching it to a completed victory
remove the need to consider Hamlet's personal motives
press him toward resolution while exposing unresolved questions about what makes action worthwhile
rationales: The speech's own diminishing images resist that simple conclusion.
Neither a military victory nor Hamlet's eventual result is established in the selection.
He explicitly restates those motives through father and mother.
The soldiers' movement rebukes delay, but eggshell, straw, and fantasy complicate their value as a model.

questions.stem: Claudius's opening description of his offence as something that “smells to heaven” primarily
choices: announces that he has already received a clear pardon
explains a literal odor that distracts him from an unrelated concern
suggests that he believes no one beyond the room could judge him
represents guilt as impossible to confine to a merely private interior
rationales: The speech proceeds through inability and uncertainty, not confirmed forgiveness.
The smell figures moral corruption rather than a practical sensory problem.
He invokes heaven as a sphere his guilt reaches.
The sensory image projects the offence upward and outward before the attempt to pray.

questions.stem: The image of a man “to double business bound” chiefly describes Claudius's
choices: resentment that Hamlet has assigned him too much work
division between competing demands that prevents completion of either
confidence that two duties can be completed without conflict
belief that practical efficiency will erase the murder
rationales: No task assignment by Hamlet is stated.
He pauses between the desire to pray and the guilt he cannot relinquish, neglecting both tasks.
The image emphasizes paralysis rather than confident coordination.
The conflict is moral and inward, not an efficiency problem.

questions.stem: The list “My crown, mine own ambition, and my queen” chiefly identifies
choices: the retained benefits that obstruct the repentance Claudius seeks
the sacrifices Claudius has already made in order to repent
the only things Hamlet knows about the murder
three witnesses who can independently confirm his innocence
rationales: He recognizes that he still possesses what motivated the murder, making pardon problematic.
He explicitly says he remains possessed of them.
The speech concerns Claudius's condition rather than a list of Hamlet's knowledge.
The list names rewards and motives, not witnesses.

questions.stem: Claudius's contrast between earthly and heavenly judgment primarily rests on
choices: his expectation that heavenly judgment will overlook intention entirely
a belief that earthly law has already punished him adequately
the difference between purchasable evasion and an exposure that cannot be bargained away
a claim that both courts accept exactly the same kinds of payment
rationales: His final problem concerns thoughts and inability to repent.
No completed earthly punishment is described.
Gilded offence can buy out worldly law, whereas above there is no shuffling and the action appears in its true nature.
He expressly distinguishes the two.

questions.stem: The image of the “limed soul” struggling to be free chiefly presents Claudius as
choices: already liberated from the rewards of the murder
increasingly entangled by the very struggle to escape his condition
unaware that his own conduct caused the problem
confident that merely changing his physical location will resolve guilt
rationales: He has just acknowledged retaining those rewards.
The birdlime image joins effort toward freedom with being more engaged or caught.
The confession repeatedly recognizes his offence.
The problem remains inward despite the later movement to kneel.

questions.stem: The stage direction that Claudius kneels is especially important because it
choices: removes all difference between what Hamlet and the audience know
announces that Claudius's inner conflict has been conclusively resolved
allows Hamlet to hear the entire confession that preceded his entrance
creates an outward sign that Hamlet interprets more confidently than the audience can
rationales: The earlier speech has created a difference that the posture does not erase.
The concluding words deny a successful union of words and thoughts.
Hamlet enters only after the kneeling direction.
The audience has heard the failed reasoning about repentance before Hamlet sees the posture.

questions.stem: Hamlet's description of killing Claudius at this moment as “hire and salary” chiefly implies that
choices: he believes a public trial will pay his father's debts
he has abandoned every desire to avenge his father
he fears rewarding the king spiritually instead of achieving the revenge he wants
he expects to receive money from Claudius for postponing the act
rationales: The phrase concerns spiritual consequence, not a trial or financial account.
He seeks a more damaging opportunity instead.
Sending the praying king to heaven would, in Hamlet's reasoning, benefit rather than adequately punish him.
No monetary bargain occurs between them.

questions.stem: Hamlet's acknowledgment that only heaven knows his father's “audit” qualifies his reasoning by
choices: admitting uncertainty within the comparison he nevertheless uses to justify delay
establishing that his father left a written confession Hamlet has read
proving that he knows Claudius's thoughts more accurately than the audience does
showing that he no longer considers his father's death relevant
rationales: He cannot fully know his father's spiritual account, yet reasons from the circumstances of the death.
No written confession is identified.
His uncertainty about his father does not grant access to Claudius's mind.
The father's condition remains central to the comparison.

questions.stem: The final distinction between words flying up and thoughts remaining below chiefly
choices: reveals that Hamlet secretly heard and understood every earlier word
turns the preceding scene into a dream experienced by the king
confirms that the prayer has removed the guilt Hamlet fears rewarding
confirms the gap between visible prayer and inward repentance that Hamlet's decision overlooks
rationales: Hamlet has exited, and no concealed hearing is supplied.
The text supplies no dream frame.
Claudius distinguishes outward words from inward repentance, undermining the assumption that prayer has cleansed him.
Claudius's last words tell the audience that the apparent prayer has not become the purification Hamlet imagines.

questions.stem: The sequence of private speech, observed posture, and final private speech most strongly invites the audience to
choices: accept physical posture as an infallible measure of inward intention
evaluate a consequential decision made from an incomplete reading of appearances
ignore Claudius's guilt because Hamlet cannot see it directly
conclude that postponing revenge necessarily produces the best possible outcome
rationales: The scene demonstrates the inadequacy of that assumption.
The audience receives inward information before and after Hamlet acts on the kneeling sign.
The audience has explicit knowledge of the guilt.
The scene exposes grounds for delay without establishing such an outcome.

questions.stem: Polonius's opening instructions to Gertrude chiefly establish the encounter as
choices: a public hearing whose witnesses are openly identified to Hamlet
an accidental meeting in which no one expects Hamlet
a planned confrontation supported by concealed observation
a reconciliation in which Gertrude has already agreed to every accusation
rationales: Polonius conceals himself rather than announcing his presence.
The instructions and Hamlet's anticipated arrival show preparation.
He advises a forceful rebuke and then hides to hear it.
The opening prepares correction of Hamlet, not acceptance of his case.

questions.stem: The stage direction placing Polonius behind the arras chiefly gives the audience
choices: specific knowledge of the hidden person's identity before Hamlet acts
certainty that Hamlet has been told who is hiding
evidence that Gertrude cannot know anyone is behind the curtain
a reason to believe the hidden person is Claudius
rationales: The audience sees the concealment, making the later uncertain thrust consequentially different for it.
No such communication to Hamlet is shown.
She tells Polonius to withdraw and is present for the plan.
The direction explicitly names Polonius.

questions.stem: The exchange over who has offended “father” most directly reveals
choices: Hamlet's inability to remember the identities of his relatives
a shift from family conflict to an unrelated political report
agreement that the same action has offended the same person
a conflict over which paternal relationship defines the accusation
rationales: His later identification of his mother and her marriage shows deliberate relational emphasis.
The political and familial relations remain intertwined in the exchange.
The mirrored wording sharpens a difference rather than agreement.
Gertrude refers to the current king, while Hamlet redirects the language toward his murdered father.

questions.stem: The mirrored phrases about an “idle tongue” and a “wicked tongue” chiefly
choices: show that Hamlet is trying to imitate Gertrude's pronunciation
turn a rebuke of Hamlet's manner into his counteraccusation about Gertrude's conduct
establish a calm agreement about appropriate conversation
signal that Polonius has begun speaking in Gertrude's place
rationales: The parallel concerns accusation and reversal, not accent.
He preserves her sentence pattern while intensifying the moral charge.
The exchange is antagonistic and escalating.
The speaker labels keep the exchange between mother and son.

questions.stem: Hamlet's promise to set up a “glass” in which Gertrude may see her “inmost part” chiefly presents his intended role as
choices: forcing an inward moral recognition through a figurative act of reflection
agreeing to end the conversation before any accusation is made
helping her prepare her appearance for a public celebration
offering an objective medical diagnosis based on physical symptoms
rationales: The mirror image claims access to the self she must confront.
He insists she remain until the confrontation occurs.
The inmost part and confrontation make this more than grooming.
The language concerns moral scrutiny, not a clinical examination.

questions.stem: Gertrude's call for help after asking whether Hamlet will murder her most directly
choices: reveals a secret agreement to invite Claudius into the room
demonstrates that Hamlet has explicitly announced a plan to murder her
shows that his insistence on keeping her seated has become physically threatening to her
confirms that she knows Hamlet has already killed Polonius
rationales: No such agreement is shown.
She asks about a feared intention; he has not stated that plan.
The question and cry reveal her perception of danger before Polonius responds.
The killing follows her cry and his response.

questions.stem: The order of Hamlet's thrust and his question “Is it the King?” chiefly establishes that
choices: he has already abandoned any suspicion that the king might be present
he acts fatally before confirming the identity of the person concealed
he verifies the victim's identity before drawing his weapon
he intends only to frighten the hidden person without risking injury
rationales: His question still entertains that possibility.
The question follows the blow and the report of death.
The sequence is the reverse.
The thrust, cry of death, and fatal result contradict a merely harmless gesture.

questions.stem: Hamlet's response “Almost as bad” to Gertrude's condemnation chiefly
choices: offers an unqualified apology that ends the confrontation
abandons the theme of wrongdoing for a neutral description of the room
proves that Gertrude has confessed to arranging the murder
redirects evaluation of his deed toward the offence he attributes to her relationship with Claudius
rationales: No apology or ending follows.
The exchange remains intensely accusatory.
Her startled question does not constitute such a confession.
He acknowledges a bloody deed but immediately compares it with killing a king and marrying the brother.

questions.stem: The address to Polonius as a “rash, intruding fool” most significantly
choices: reveals that Polonius had openly challenged Hamlet to a duel
confirms that the audience had mistaken the hidden person's identity
assigns blame to the victim's interference after Hamlet's own unverified action
shows that Hamlet refuses to explain the death in any way
rationales: Polonius was hidden and called for help; no duel is proposed.
The audience's earlier identification is confirmed, not corrected.
The description makes intrusion an explanation for the fate, inviting scrutiny of how responsibility is distributed.
He supplies a pointed characterization and consequence.

questions.stem: The scene's return from the dead Polonius to Hamlet's effort to “wring” Gertrude's heart chiefly
choices: shows the confrontation continuing even though an irreversible consequence has intervened
proves that Gertrude has ceased to be affected by the killing
indicates that the killing has been revealed as a harmless performance
restores the situation to exactly what it was before Hamlet entered
rationales: Hamlet resumes his moral pressure, but the staged death remains part of the scene's changed conditions.
The command to stop wringing her hands suggests continued distress.
The stage direction says Polonius falls and dies; no reversal is supplied.
The death prevents an unchanged restoration.

questions.stem: Elizabeth's opening questions about Darcy's falling in love chiefly establish a tone of
choices: playful inquiry made possible by the security of their present relationship
formal gratitude directed toward a benefactor she still fears
detached curiosity about a relationship that no longer concerns her
anxious interrogation prompted by a new suspicion of his sincerity
rationales: The narrator explicitly notes returning playfulness, and the questions revisit difficulty from within an engagement.
Her teasing and impertinent self-description exceed a deferential expression of thanks.
The inquiry is intimate and concerns their continuing attachment.
The selection does not introduce a new suspicion; the narrator frames the exchange as playful.

questions.stem: Darcy's statement that he was “in the middle” before knowing he had begun primarily
choices: avoids admitting affection because he still considers it socially improper
attributes his attraction to a deliberate plan Elizabeth successfully carried out
resists locating affection in a single, consciously recognized origin
suggests that his feelings arose only after the engagement was settled
rationales: He acknowledges the attachment and offers an account of its gradual recognition.
He identifies no plan of hers in the reply.
He cannot fix an hour, place, look, or word and describes recognition as arriving after involvement.
He places the beginning too far back to locate, not after the present engagement.

questions.stem: The difference between Elizabeth's “impertinence” and Darcy's “liveliness of your mind” chiefly
choices: reveals that Elizabeth has stopped valuing the independence she displayed
shows the same conduct receiving a more affectionate valuation
establishes that they are recalling entirely different conversations
suggests that Darcy wishes to correct her speech before marriage
rationales: Her continuing teasing preserves that independence even while questioning its earlier form.
Her provocative behavior becomes, in his phrasing, an engaging intellectual quality.
The exchange concerns competing descriptions of her behavior toward him.
His reply praises rather than prescribes a change in her manner.

questions.stem: Elizabeth's contrast between herself and women seeking Darcy's approbation primarily
choices: treats his former reserve as evidence that he never noticed her conduct
suggests that he has always preferred open hostility to affection
attributes his preference chiefly to her superior social rank
presents resistance to deference as part of what made her interesting to him
rationales: Her explanation assumes that she roused and interested him.
She distinguishes lively opposition from the possibility that an unamiable man would have hated it.
Her account concerns manner and independence, not a claim to higher rank.
She explains attraction through being unlike those whose conduct is directed toward pleasing him.

questions.stem: Darcy's reference to Elizabeth's care for Jane chiefly
choices: concedes that he admired her only because Jane recommended her
redirects the conversation away from Elizabeth because he regrets the proposal
supplies a concrete instance of goodness that qualifies her teasing self-deprecation
criticizes Elizabeth for having neglected her own interests at Netherfield
rationales: No recommendation from Jane is cited.
The example remains a reason for valuing Elizabeth.
He answers her claim that he knows no actual good of her with an observed act of affection.
He treats the conduct as good rather than as a fault requiring correction.

questions.stem: Elizabeth's assignment of exaggeration to Darcy and teasing to herself chiefly
choices: turns their differing habits into an imagined pattern of affectionate exchange
sets enforceable conditions designed to prevent future disagreement
reveals a settled belief that Darcy's praise has no basis in observation
acknowledges that she must suppress her independence once married
rationales: The playful division gives each a role within the relationship and continues her lively manner.
The tone and immediate teasing make this a playful arrangement, not a guarantee against conflict.
His example of her care for Jane has just supplied such a basis.
She claims a continuing right to tease and quarrel.

questions.stem: The brief sequence “But I was embarrassed” and “And so was I” chiefly
choices: reopens the earlier quarrel by treating embarrassment as an accusation
suggests that neither speaker can remember the encounter clearly enough to discuss it
shows that one speaker accepts blame while the other refuses responsibility
makes a formerly misleading difference in behavior recognizable as a shared feeling
rationales: The exchange explains past difficulty within a playful present.
They can identify their feelings and the behavior being interpreted.
The matching admissions establish similarity rather than that asymmetry.
Each had read reserve through uncertainty; the paired admissions reveal mutual embarrassment.

questions.stem: Darcy's reply “A man who had felt less might” most directly reverses the assumption that
choices: a reserved manner can ever be sincere
greater feeling should necessarily produce more fluent or frequent speech
Elizabeth's questions require a serious answer
love begins before either person recognizes it
rationales: His reply defends the sincerity behind reserve rather than denying it.
He makes intense feeling an explanation for inhibited conversation.
He gives a serious reason within their playful exchange.
The reply is compatible with his earlier account of unrecognized beginnings.

questions.stem: The discussion of Lady Catherine's intervention chiefly produces irony through
choices: the difference between the separation she intended and the confidence her information gave Darcy
the discovery that Lady Catherine had secretly planned the engagement from the beginning
the contrast between a marriage the couple desires and one they have decided to reject
the difference between Elizabeth's gratitude and Darcy's refusal to credit his aunt at all
rationales: Her obstructive action removed doubts and helped make the union possible.
The text calls her efforts attempts to separate them, not a hidden plan to unite them.
They remain engaged and discuss their happiness.
Darcy explicitly credits the intervention's unintended usefulness.

questions.stem: Darcy's distinction between his “real purpose” and what he “avowed to myself” chiefly suggests
choices: a refusal to explain himself now that the engagement is secure
an accusation that Elizabeth knowingly misrepresented the reason for his visit
a retrospective recognition that his stated explanation partly concealed a more personal motive
a claim that concern for Bingley played no role in any of his actions
rationales: The distinction is itself a revealing explanation.
He analyzes his own purposes rather than accusing her.
He separates the desire to see Elizabeth from the account centered on Bingley and Jane, including self-avowal in that distinction.
He reports making a confession to Bingley, so the secondary purpose need not be wholly fictitious.

questions.stem: Hamlet's use of the verbs “inform” and “spur” in the opening primarily makes his surroundings seem to
choices: accuse him and press him toward action
confirm that he has already completed his duty
offer him a refuge from the demands of revenge
invite a dispassionate survey of other people's motives
rationales: The occasions become witnesses and goads in his self-directed argument.
He calls his revenge dull and the task still to do.
The verbs intensify those demands rather than suspend them.
The opening turns observation immediately toward his own conduct.

questions.stem: The passage about “godlike reason” chiefly gives Hamlet a basis for criticizing
choices: the belief that careful thought should ever precede action
the soldiers' lack of access to scholarly education
the failure to use a human capacity for more than passive bodily existence
the willingness to consider the past when making a decision
rationales: He criticizes unused or excessively scrupulous thought, while initially valuing reason as a capacity.
No educational history of the soldiers is given.
Reason, foresight, and retrospection are contrasted with merely sleeping and feeding.
Looking before and after is part of the valued capability.

questions.stem: The alternatives “Bestial oblivion” and “some craven scruple” primarily show Hamlet
choices: distinguishing his own courage from the soldiers' excessive caution
testing opposed explanations for delay while finding both degrading
accepting that a moral scruple fully excuses his continued postponement
settling confidently on forgetfulness as the sole cause of inaction
rationales: The alternatives concern his own conduct, and the soldiers are presented as exposing themselves to danger.
He considers thoughtlessness and overprecise thinking, then admits he does not know why he still delays.
He calls it craven and disproportionately cowardly, refusing a simple excuse.
The alternative and “I do not know” prevent that settled conclusion.

questions.stem: The division of a thought into “one part wisdom” and “three parts coward” chiefly functions as
choices: a measured result that resolves his uncertainty through objective evidence
a generous concession that careful reasoning chiefly explains his delay
a description of four advisers whose competing counsel he has received
a severe self-evaluation that reduces the credit due to caution
rationales: The ratio is rhetorical self-judgment, not an empirical finding.
Wisdom receives the smaller portion.
The parts belong to a thought, not to four named people.
The imagined proportions make cowardice dominate the account of overthinking.

questions.stem: The list “cause, and will, and strength, and means” primarily
choices: announces that he has abandoned the need for a justifying cause
identifies the resources the prince has and Hamlet lacks
accumulates reasons that make continued inaction seem harder for Hamlet to explain
reduces revenge to a purely physical challenge unrelated to intention
rationales: Cause remains first in the list.
Hamlet says “I have,” assigning the list to himself.
He presents the usual requirements for action as available, sharpening the question of delay.
Cause and will include motive and intention alongside strength and means.

questions.stem: The movement from self-questioning to “Witness this army” chiefly
choices: introduces an external example into an argument Hamlet is conducting with himself
shifts the speech into an official report intended for the king
marks the end of Hamlet's concern with his own conduct
invites the soldiers to answer questions as a speaking chorus
rationales: The army becomes evidence in his effort to judge and redirect his own behavior.
The speech remains self-directed rather than a report to Claudius.
He soon asks how he stands in comparison.
The phrase calls them as figurative evidence; no response follows.

questions.stem: The phrase “Makes mouths at the invisible event” most plausibly characterizes the prince as
choices: trying to conceal his fear through silence
possessing secret knowledge that guarantees military success
refusing to act until every consequence has been calculated
defying an outcome he cannot fully foresee
rationales: The image is a gesture of defiance rather than silence.
Invisible stresses an outcome beyond secure knowledge.
He exposes mortal life to fortune, death, and danger.
The mocking gesture toward an unseen event presents boldness under uncertainty.

questions.stem: Hamlet's reference to the excitements of both “reason” and “blood” chiefly
choices: separates a rational wish to forgive from an entirely unrelated bodily illness
presents his motives as engaging judgment and passionate kinship together
attributes his uncertainty solely to an inherited physical weakness
suggests that emotion has displaced every capacity for reflection
rationales: No illness or wish to forgive is supplied here.
The murdered father and stained mother move both his thinking and his feeling.
Blood here participates in motive and feeling rather than a diagnosis.
Reason remains explicitly part of the motive.

questions.stem: The closing command that his thoughts be bloody or worthless chiefly
choices: tries to force the unsettled reasoning into an uncompromising resolution
withdraws the earlier comparison because the army has ceased to matter
turns the speech into a request that another character make the decision
records a completed act of revenge already visible to the audience
rationales: The imperative supplies a severe criterion for future thought after a speech of questions and comparisons.
The resolution emerges from that comparison rather than discarding it.
