Hamlet directs the command toward his own thoughts.
The speech declares an intention, not an accomplished revenge.

questions.stem: Which description best accounts for the speech as an act of private reasoning?
choices: Hamlet neutrally reports his feelings without attempting to alter them.
Hamlet steadily develops a single explanation that remains unchanged from the opening.
Hamlet alternates between explanation and accusation before attempting to bind himself to action.
Hamlet receives a clear answer from an external authority and repeats it.
rationales: The spurring examples and final command show an effort to redirect conduct.
The alternative causes and unstable valuation of the army make the progression less uniform.
The speech tests causes, invokes examples, reproaches the self, and ends in a resolution whose fulfillment lies beyond the selection.
No external authority speaks an answer within the soliloquy.

questions.stem: Krogstad's initial question about the date of Nora's father's death chiefly serves to
choices: invite her to choose a date that would make the document easier to defend
show that he has forgotten the basis of their financial arrangement
establish a fact he already knows before confronting her with its implication
seek comfort from Nora about a loss he has just learned of
rationales: He already possesses the date and uses it to constrain the explanation.
The questioning reveals detailed knowledge of the document.
He confirms that he has ascertained the date himself and then produces the discrepancy.
His next action concerns the bond rather than condolence.

questions.stem: The paper taken from Krogstad's pocket primarily functions as
choices: a material object through which private knowledge can become enforceable pressure
a token of friendship that reassures Nora about his intentions
a record whose meaning both characters immediately accept in the same way
an irrelevant formality that disappears once repayment is promised
rationales: The bond links the discrepancy to the possibility of court and to his later threat.
It exposes her vulnerability rather than simply offering reassurance.
They dispute the relation between signature, motive, and judgment.
Nora's promise of money does not end Krogstad's challenge.

questions.stem: Krogstad's proposed explanation that someone else may have dated a genuine signature chiefly
choices: proves that he cannot recognize any of the handwriting on the bond
withdraws his concern about the document's validity
shows that he has accepted Nora's innocence without needing an answer
narrows the issue so that Nora must confront the authenticity of the name itself
rationales: He says the date resembles handwriting he thinks he knows.
He immediately asks about the signature, preserving the challenge.
He continues questioning and calls the confession dangerous.
He offers a possible account of the date before pressing whether her father actually signed.

questions.stem: Nora's gesture of raising her head before admitting the signature chiefly
choices: signals an attempt to ask her absent father for assistance
gives her confession a defiance that contrasts with her preceding silence
establishes that she already understands every legal consequence
shows that she has decided to deny having written the name
rationales: The gesture is directed toward Krogstad in the confrontation.
The stage direction shifts from pauses and silence to direct acknowledgment.
Her next reply about repayment shows that she has not accepted Krogstad's account of the danger.
Her words explicitly admit it.

questions.stem: Nora's reply “You shall have your money soon” most directly reveals that she initially
choices: treats repayment as an answer to a problem Krogstad defines more broadly
believes that Krogstad borrowed the money from her father
agrees that motive has no relevance to judging her action
intends to abandon the obligation as soon as he leaves
rationales: She responds to the danger of the confession with financial assurance, while he presses the forgery and its consequences.
The exchange concerns her debt and the signature on its bond.
Her later explanation repeatedly appeals to motive.
The promise affirms an intention to repay, whatever its adequacy to the threat.

questions.stem: Nora's repeated use of “impossible” in explaining the signature and the journey chiefly
choices: offers evidence that no physical means of sending a letter existed
shows that she regards her husband's welfare as less important than her own comfort
presents her action as a response to duties she could not bring herself to abandon
acknowledges that Krogstad had explicitly authorized her to sign
rationales: Her stated impossibility concerns the consequences of asking, not postal logistics.
Her explanation centers his life and her father's distress.
She could neither distress her dying father nor give up the trip she believed would save her husband.
No such authorization is claimed.

questions.stem: The difference between Krogstad's comparison of their offences and Nora's reply chiefly turns on
choices: whether either character remembers the amount of the loan
whether similarity of act or the purpose behind it should determine judgment
whether Nora will admit writing the signature at all
whether the two signatures were written with the same pen
rationales: The disagreement concerns culpability rather than the sum.
He equates the false step; she asks whether his motive was the bravery of saving a wife.
She has already admitted it; the argument shifts to significance.
No physical comparison of instruments is made.

questions.stem: Nora's criticism of a law that would forbid protecting father or husband chiefly
choices: demonstrates that she has consulted a legal text proving Krogstad wrong
expresses indifference to the effects of her conduct on family members
shows that she accepts public judgment as more important than her own reasons
exposes a conflict between her understanding of familial duty and the authority Krogstad invokes
rationales: She admits limited legal knowledge and argues from what she believes ought to be permitted.
Concern for those effects is the basis of her objection.
She questions the judgment rather than ranking it above those reasons.
She assumes law should permit the acts she sees as caring, while he insists it can judge her regardless.

questions.stem: Krogstad's final threat to make Nora lose her position if he loses his chiefly
choices: abandons his concern for employment in favor of a purely abstract moral debate
promises to protect Nora's reputation in exchange for no action from her
connects his threatened social standing with his power to expose hers
concedes that Nora alone has the power to decide what the law means
rationales: His threatened position returns the dispute to concrete interests.
The condition is coercive rather than an unconditional promise of protection.
The reciprocal phrasing makes the document a means of linking their fates and exerting pressure.
He relies on exposure and institutional judgment, not her legal authority.

questions.stem: Nora's interrupted domestic activity after Krogstad leaves chiefly
choices: makes the disturbance visible despite her repeated verbal dismissal of the threat
establishes that she has already made a settled plan to reveal the loan to Helmer
confirms that the conversation has had no continuing effect on her
shows that the children understand the financial problem better than she does
rationales: The pauses, unfinished sewing, and repeated denials show unease entering ordinary household actions.
She tells the children not to mention the visitor, including to their father.
Her disrupted actions and “And yet” contradict that certainty.
They report the man's departure and ask to play, without displaying such knowledge.

questions.stem: The contrast between the room's grandeur and its infrequent use chiefly establishes
choices: an impressive space whose social and emotional associations keep it isolated
a refuge Jane has freely chosen for privacy
a familiar nursery whose comforts immediately reassure the child
a room neglected because the family cannot afford to maintain it
rationales: The room is stately but rarely entered, with the death history explaining its special separation.
She has been confined there after punishment.
The room is remote from the nursery and becomes threatening rather than comforting.
Regular cleaning and preserved valuables do not support that financial explanation.

questions.stem: The bed's comparison to a “tabernacle” and the chair's to a “pale throne” chiefly
choices: establishes that Jane knows the room was once used as a public chapel
shows that the furnishings are small enough for a child's play
gives ordinary furnishings an imposing, almost ceremonial authority
presents the room as a place where Jane expects to inherit political power
rationales: The comparisons do not supply such a literal history.
Their scale and authority work against diminishment into toys.
The comparisons magnify their presence in a room already associated with solemnity and death.
No such expectation is voiced.

questions.stem: The sequence explaining why the room is chill, silent, and solemn primarily
choices: replaces description with an unrelated account of the servants' daily schedule
grounds its atmosphere in material arrangement and established household practice
corrects the child by showing that none of her sensations has a basis
suggests that the room changes its physical properties whenever Jane enters
rationales: The housekeeping details contribute directly to the room's isolation.
Lack of fire, distance from busy rooms, and infrequent entry provide causes before the death history deepens them.
The explanations support rather than disprove the sensations.
The causes preexist her confinement.

questions.stem: The revelation of Mr. Reed's death in the room chiefly
choices: resolves Jane's fear by assuring her that the room carries no memory
establishes that the family has removed every reminder of him
shows that Jane has invented the family's reluctance to enter
supplies a history that makes its preserved solitude more intelligible
rationales: The history increases its charge rather than erasing memory.
His miniature and other preserved objects remain.
The narrated history supports that reluctance.
The place of death, lying in state, and removal of the coffin explain its dreary consecration.

questions.stem: Jane's act of checking the door chiefly adds to the setting
choices: a successful attempt to summon a sympathetic adult
evidence that she can leave whenever she wishes
a verified restriction of movement that precedes her heightened imaginative response
proof that the room's apparent confinement exists only in reflection
rationales: She checks the door but does not obtain help in this moment.
The check confirms the opposite.
She confirms that it is locked before returning past the mirror.
The locked door is distinct from the later reflected image.

questions.stem: The mirror episode chiefly makes Jane's own figure appear
choices: estranged from her through the room's darkness and the stories shaping her perception
confidently dominant over the room's larger furnishings
unchanged by the emotional circumstances of confinement
recognizable as an actual visitor who has entered without opening the door
rationales: She sees a strange small figure like a phantom, linking reflected features to Bessie's tales.
The figure is small and frightened amid vacant majesty.
Fear and imaginative comparison shape the appearance.
The passage identifies the figure as her reflection.

questions.stem: The sentence delaying superstition's “complete victory” primarily suggests that
choices: Jane has already overcome every disturbing association of the place
the child intends to entertain herself by inventing a harmless ghost story
the narrator has established that a supernatural force literally controls the room
anger and resistance still compete with the child's growing fear
rationales: The present remains dismal and the fear continues to develop.
The struggle is distressing and tied to actual confinement.
The personification describes her mental struggle rather than proving a spirit's presence.
Warm blood and the mood of revolt continue to brace Jane before she quails.

questions.stem: The comparison of family grievances to a dark deposit in a turbid well chiefly
choices: suggests that Jane has forgotten the particular actions that caused her resentment
presents remembered mistreatment as material stirred up within an already disturbed mind
makes the family's conduct appear purified by distance and reflection
establishes that a physical well outside the room caused her punishment
rationales: The passage immediately supplies detailed examples.
The image connects the rush of memories with the inward agitation produced by the scene.
Dark deposit and turbid water resist a cleansing interpretation.
The well is a comparison for memory and mental disturbance.

questions.stem: The extended contrast between John Reed's permitted cruelty and Jane's condemned resistance chiefly
choices: gives concrete evidence for her sense that household judgment is unequally distributed
suggests that her resentment arises solely from envy of Georgiana's appearance
shows that both children receive the same penalties for similar acts
explains that Jane admires John's freedom enough to excuse his violence
rationales: His acts go unpunished while her attempt to resist violence receives blame.
Beauty is one example within a broader pattern including violence and partiality.
The passage emphasizes unequal treatment.
She presents the disparity as unjust rather than excusing him.

questions.stem: The final distinction between the child's unanswered “why” and the older narrator's clearer sight chiefly
choices: gives the reader a complete historical explanation within this selection
suggests that the older voice has no connection to the child described
preserves the intensity of the experience while qualifying the child's ability to explain it
withdraws the claim that the child suffered at all
rationales: The narrator asserts clearer sight but the excerpt ends before fully developing it.
The first-person continuity and retrospective reflection maintain that connection.
The narrator recalls tumult and ignorance, then marks the greater understanding of retrospective distance.
The suffering remains explicit and serious.

questions.stem: The movement from the mountain's “awful majesty” to the creature's arrival primarily
choices: suggests that the creature arrives only because Victor has consciously summoned him
confirms that the landscape has permanently freed Victor from his earlier suffering
interrupts a fragile recovery of feeling with a confrontation Victor cannot keep outside it
introduces a new narrator who views the landscape without Victor's emotions
rationales: Victor addresses wandering spirits, not a deliberate invitation to the creature.
The confrontation immediately unsettles that relief.
Victor's faint happiness is quickly displaced by rage and horror at the approaching figure.
Victor continues to narrate the scene through his responses.

questions.stem: Victor's change from “Begone” to “Or rather, stay” chiefly reveals
choices: opposed impulses to reject the creature's presence and to destroy him
uncertainty about whether the approaching figure is his creation
a decision to hear the creature's full account before judging
a calm effort to negotiate the terms of a meeting
rationales: The correction turns expulsion into the wish to trample him, exposing conflict within the rage.
He has already recognized the creature and reacts to that recognition.
At this point Victor threatens rather than agrees to listen.
The surrounding invective and threat are not calm negotiation.

questions.stem: The creature's assertion that creator and creature are bound by ties chiefly attempts to
choices: deny that either of them can harm the other
prove that Victor has no choices left in responding to him
treat their encounter as a temporary agreement between unrelated strangers
make Victor's responsibility persist despite his desire to disown the relation
rationales: The same speech recognizes killing and threatens further violence.
The creature makes demands and conditions, still addressing possible choices.
The appeal rests on creation as a continuing relation.
The claim establishes a bond that disgust and rejection cannot simply dissolve.

questions.stem: The creature's promise of peace and threat against Victor's friends most significantly complicate his appeal by
choices: showing that he has abandoned any wish to influence Victor's response
combining a demand for reciprocal duty with coercive pressure
establishing that he has already carried out every future harm he mentions
making his motives identical to Victor's without any remaining difference
rationales: The conditions are designed to influence that response.
Conditional peace is paired with threatened bloodshed, preventing a reading of the appeal as purely vulnerable petition.
The threatened harm is conditional and prospective within the speech.
Their positions and claims remain distinct despite shared anger.

questions.stem: The creature's emphasis on his greater height and strength, followed by a promise of docility, chiefly
choices: presents restraint as a choice made conditional on Victor's reciprocal conduct
withdraws the claim that Victor has any special responsibility toward him
shows that his earlier appeal for compassion was addressed to the mountains rather than Victor
concedes that he cannot physically defend himself under any circumstances
rationales: He notes his capacity to resist but offers mildness if Victor performs his part.
The promise invokes Victor as natural lord and king and insists on what is owed.
The appeal remains directed to his creator.
He explicitly says he will defend life and is more powerful.

questions.stem: The claim “misery made me a fiend” chiefly asks Victor to reconsider
choices: whether the creature has ever experienced any negative feeling
whether the creature is physically the same being Victor created
the relation between suffering and the conduct he condemns
whether Victor should ignore every consequence of the creature's acts
rationales: Misery is central to the claim rather than denied.
The argument concerns moral development, not mistaken identity.
The creature offers a causal history that challenges an account of evil as simply original or self-explanatory.
A causal explanation invites scrutiny but does not itself erase consequences or responsibility.

questions.stem: The creature's contrast between bleak skies and hostile human beings chiefly
choices: proves that Victor experiences the landscape in exactly the same way
reverses ordinary expectations of where shelter and kindness might be found
establishes that he prefers isolation independently of others' treatment
suggests that the mountain climate has removed his desire for companionship
rationales: Victor initially finds temporary uplift, while the creature describes a refuge forced by rejection.
Ice and desolation become a refuge because people reject him, making the natural harshness comparatively kinder.
He repeatedly laments exclusion and links the refuge to human hostility.
His plea for compassion and account of loneliness remain active.

questions.stem: The appeal to the accused person's opportunity to speak in defence chiefly
choices: shows that the creature seeks only an audience for a story with no bearing on judgment
replaces the personal relation with an admission that Victor owes him nothing
claims that a court has already found the creature innocent
recasts listening as a minimum standard of justice before condemnation
rationales: He explicitly asks Victor to hear and then judge whether to abandon or commiserate him.
The appeal supplements, rather than cancels, the claim on the creator.
No completed trial or verdict is described.
The creature invokes a procedure available even to the guilty to challenge Victor's refusal to hear him.

questions.stem: The gesture of covering Victor's eyes most directly
choices: shows that the creature intends to end the conversation without telling his story
establishes that Victor has permanently lost the ability to see
separates the demand to hear from the visual disgust that obstructs it
confirms that appearance is irrelevant to Victor's response from the beginning
rationales: The gesture accompanies renewed insistence on hearing it.
Victor flings the hands away; no lasting blindness is reported.
The creature removes the abhorred sight momentarily while insisting that Victor can still listen.
Victor's repeated disgust makes appearance an important obstacle.

questions.stem: Victor's final decision to listen is best characterized as
choices: a limited change produced by several motives while hostility remains
a purely strategic delay without any acknowledged concern for the creature
a complete reconciliation in which he withdraws every suspicion
an unconditional acceptance of the creature's entire explanation before hearing it
rationales: Curiosity, compassion, a wish to verify an accusation, and a new sense of duty coexist with odious labels and a heavy heart.
Victor explicitly reports compassion and duties of a creator.
He still seeks confirmation or denial of murder and retains hostility.
He agrees to hear and consider, not to accept all claims in advance.

questions.stem: Collins's account of his former reluctance to reconcile chiefly reveals
choices: a fear that Mr. Bennet will demand repayment of a specific debt
a suspicion that his father secretly wished the quarrel to end
a strained effort to make inherited hostility appear dutiful
a principled refusal to seek advantage from a family connection
rationales: The letter describes a family breach, not a stated financial debt to Bennet.
Collins represents his father as having pleased himself with being at variance.
He worries that friendship with his father's enemy would disrespect the father's memory.
He now proposes reconciliation while anticipating inheritance and mentioning possible amends.

questions.stem: The prominence given to Lady Catherine in a letter about reconciliation chiefly suggests
choices: that patronage occupies an excessive place in Collins's self-presentation
that Collins considers his clerical position an embarrassment to conceal
that the family has specifically requested a full report of her household
that Collins intends to criticize her interference before seeking Bennet's advice
rationales: Her titles, bounty, approval, and control of his absences recur beyond what the family purpose requires.
He advertises ordination and the valuable rectory rather than concealing them.
No such request is described in the context or letter.
His language expresses deference and gratitude rather than an appeal against her.

questions.stem: The phrase “I flatter myself” is particularly revealing when followed by “highly commendable” because it
choices: introduces a judgment supplied by Lady Catherine rather than Collins himself
turns a modest apology into an explicit refusal to make peace
shows that Collins doubts whether any benefit could follow from the visit
makes a declaration of goodwill also an act of self-congratulation
rationales: The first-person phrase directly claims the judgment as his own.
He still offers reconciliation; the irony concerns how he values the offer.
He anticipates satisfaction and calls his intentions commendable.
Collins praises the merit of his own overtures while presenting them as a duty.

questions.stem: Collins's apology for being next in the entail creates a comic difficulty chiefly because
choices: it reveals that Collins believes Longbourn already belongs to Lady Catherine
it treats an inherited position as though a personal apology could settle its effects
it conceals the fact of the inheritance from everyone except Mr. Bennet
it proposes a clear legal solution that the family refuses to consider
rationales: He identifies himself as next in the entail, not his patron as owner.
Elizabeth questions the apology, while the family's material concern remains unresolved.
The letter openly names the position and is read to the family.
The letter promises unspecified amends rather than a legal alteration of the entail.

questions.stem: The detailed proposal for a visit in the letter chiefly adds to Collins's portrayal by
choices: joining elaborate politeness with a substantial presumption on hospitality
suggesting that he expects the family to be absent throughout his stay
showing a practical concern that overrides his interest in making an impression
establishing that he has been invited repeatedly and is only confirming arrangements
rationales: He conditionally asks to be received but specifies arrival and a lengthy stay as his proposed satisfaction.
He explicitly proposes visiting Bennet and the family.
The schedule remains embedded in formal self-presentation and discussion of his patron.
The letter presents an overture and proposed visit, not a response to repeated invitations.

questions.stem: Mr. Bennet's praise of the “peace-making gentleman” is best understood in light of his later statement that
choices: he expects Collins to become the family's most reliable financial adviser
he considers Lady Catherine's permission the chief obstacle to welcoming Collins
he hopes Collins will prove entertainingly unlike a sensible man
he regrets having doubted the sincerity of the offered reconciliation
rationales: No such advisory role is proposed.
His reference to her indulgence participates in the mock praise.
His hope for the reverse of sense reveals the amusement beneath the apparent commendation.
His explicit account of servility and self-importance maintains critical distance.

questions.stem: Jane's response to the promised amends chiefly distinguishes her from Elizabeth by emphasizing
choices: interest in the letter's conventional imagery rather than its personal implications
credit for the intention despite uncertainty about its practical meaning
resentment at the family's willingness to entertain a future heir
suspicion about the writer's motives before considering any possible kindness
rationales: Mary, rather than Jane, comments chiefly on composition and the olive branch.
Jane cannot identify the proposed atonement but values the wish, whereas Elizabeth questions judgment and style.
Jane does not express that resentment in the selection.
That reverses Jane's charitable response.

questions.stem: The narrator's account of Elizabeth being struck by Collins's willingness to perform ordinary clerical rites chiefly
choices: endorses Collins as unusually generous for accepting duties other clergy avoid
suggests that Elizabeth has mistaken the nature of his profession
reveals a conflict between Elizabeth's preferred ceremonies and Lady Catherine's
exposes the disproportion between routine duties and their self-important announcement
rationales: The text does not establish that other clergy refuse those duties.
Her comment targets the manner of presenting familiar duties rather than showing ignorance of the role.
No competing ceremonial preference is described.
His stated readiness to christen, marry, and bury becomes notable because he advertises what the role ordinarily requires.

questions.stem: Mary's qualified approval of the olive-branch image primarily reveals her tendency to
choices: agree with Elizabeth that the letter's style proves its writer insensible
reject figurative language whenever it has appeared in an earlier work
evaluate conventional expression without closely examining the writer's judgment
defend Collins because she has privately received a separate explanation from him
rationales: Mary calls the composition not defective, a different emphasis from Elizabeth's concern.
She acknowledges its lack of novelty but still calls it well expressed.
She discusses novelty and composition while others consider character, motive, or benefit.
No separate correspondence is supplied.

questions.stem: The closing contrast among the younger sisters' indifference and their mother's softened attitude chiefly shows
choices: how different interests govern responses to the same prospective visitor
how Mr. Bennet's amusement has removed the practical stakes of inheritance
how Collins's letter has brought the entire family to a single judgment
how literary style matters more to every reader than social circumstance
rationales: The sisters value military company, while the mother responds to possible amends for her daughters.
Those stakes continue to shape Mrs. Bennet's response despite his amusement.
The varied responses demonstrate the opposite.
That emphasis belongs chiefly to Mary, not to all the family.

questions.stem: The abrupt transition from putting the writing away to “We have been here two weeks” chiefly makes visible
choices: a correction proving that the first sentence was written before the family arrived
a deliberate attempt to narrate the same afternoon from two separate viewpoints
a break in the record as part of the narrator's circumstances
a new speaker taking over the account after the narrator loses access to it
rationales: Both statements concern the stay, and no such pre-arrival correction is offered.
The time statement marks elapsed days, and the narrator remains the same.
The preserved sequence moves from interruption to a later resumption rather than narrating each intervening day.
The first-person voice continues without a change of speaker.

questions.stem: The phrase “save lack of strength” chiefly qualifies the narrator's apparent freedom to write by
choices: distinguishing an opportunity from the capacity to use it
suggesting that John's permission is now the only obstacle she faces
showing that she no longer has ideas she wishes to express
establishing that writing has become an effortless substitute for social contact
rationales: John's absence removes an immediate hindrance, but the narrator still reports exhaustion.
The stated limit is her own strength, not only permission.
She later describes the press of ideas, so the issue is not absence of material.
She explicitly reports difficulty and later longs for companionship about her work.

questions.stem: The juxtaposition of “I am glad my case is not serious!” and “But these nervous troubles are dreadfully depressing” chiefly
choices: shows that the narrator regards the other patients' suffering as imaginary
establishes that the narrator has deliberately fabricated all her symptoms
resolves the narrator's earlier disagreement with John about her condition
sets a reassuring classification against the severity of lived distress
rationales: She gives no such account of John's other cases.
The text reports distress and conflicting explanations, not an admission of fabrication.
The contrast preserves tension rather than resolving it.
The second statement complicates the first without requiring the reader to supply an external diagnosis.

questions.stem: The claim that John knows there is “no reason to suffer” primarily exposes a difference between
choices: his secret fear of the illness and his public refusal to discuss medical work
his explanatory certainty and her experience of suffering
her confidence in his diagnosis and her indifference to its consequences
her knowledge of medicine and his lack of any professional training
rationales: No secret fear or public performance is established here.
His satisfaction with an explanation does not encompass what she says he fails to know.
She says he does not know how much she suffers.
The passage identifies his cases and does not establish that reversal of expertise.

questions.stem: The movement from nervousness to failing in “duty” and becoming a “burden” chiefly shows
choices: the narrator interpreting distress through expectations of service to others
the narrator dismissing the value of every relation within the household
the narrator planning to replace domestic responsibilities with paid employment
John explicitly ordering her to describe herself in those precise words
rationales: She measures herself against being a help, rest, and comfort to John.
She expresses concern for John and affection for the baby despite difficulty.
No such employment plan appears.
The language appears in her account; the passage does not quote that order.

questions.stem: The statements about the baby chiefly complicate the narrator's account by placing
choices: a remembered childhood experience beside an unrelated description of the present
complete confidence in her health beside a lack of interest in household life
expressed affection beside an inability to sustain the expected closeness
resentment of the child beside a plan to dismiss the person caring for him
rationales: Both statements concern her present situation with the baby.
The difficulty with the baby is another sign of distress, not confidence in health.
She calls the baby dear and values Mary's care, yet says she cannot be with him because of nervousness.
She praises both the child and Mary's care rather than proposing dismissal.

questions.stem: John's prediction that changing the paper would lead to objections about bed, windows, and stairs chiefly
choices: invites the narrator to choose the single renovation she considers most important
turns a specific complaint into evidence of a supposedly expanding tendency
acknowledges that each feature is unsafe and promises to replace it
shows that he has already inspected and repaired each object on the list
rationales: The response resists renovation rather than offering a choice.
He frames accommodation as giving way to fancies that will move from one feature to another.
He uses the sequence to justify not making the change.
No completed repairs are reported.

questions.stem: The narrator's request to go downstairs and John's response about the cellar chiefly create
choices: a clear agreement to move into the room she has identified
a practical discussion in which both speakers rank available rooms by size
a mutual joke that removes every remaining objection to the wallpaper
a gap between the accommodation she requests and the affectionate answer he gives
rationales: The narration does not report the requested move.
The exchange concerns preference and reassurance rather than a shared size calculation.
She continues to call the paper horrid and to consider its effects.
His embrace and exaggerated offer do not enact her proposal to occupy the pretty rooms downstairs.

questions.stem: The narrator's statement that she would not make John uncomfortable “just for a whim” chiefly
choices: expresses a new belief that John should leave the house while she stays
confirms that the earlier request was intended only as a test of his affection
recasts her own discomfort in the minimizing terms used to reject it
shows that she has independently discovered the wallpaper is physically harmless
rationales: No separation plan is proposed.
The text presents the request as a response to her discomfort, not an admitted test.
The self-description follows his resistance and makes concern for his comfort a reason to suppress the request.
She supplies no such independent discovery.

questions.stem: The final wish for advice and companionship about her work most clearly deepens the account of writing as
choices: an activity constrained by isolation as well as interruption and fatigue
a professional obligation imposed on her by visitors she would rather avoid
a private pleasure she consistently wishes to keep separate from other people
an activity whose benefits she has conclusively proved to John through evidence
rationales: The narrator wants exchange about her work, while the promised visitors are deferred because John calls them stimulating.
No such obligation is stated, and she welcomes the prospect of company.
She explicitly desires companionship and advice.
She believes writing might relieve her but has not established agreement with him.

questions.stem: The account of Edna's earlier swimming lessons chiefly establishes
choices: a competition in which Robert has repeatedly prevented her from succeeding
a deliberate refusal to accept instruction from anyone younger than herself
a persistent dependence on nearby reassurance
a practical skill she has mastered but is unwilling to demonstrate publicly
rationales: Robert teaches her regularly and becomes discouraged by the lack of progress.
She receives instruction even from children; refusal is not the stated obstacle.
The first paragraph describes repeated instruction and dread unless a helping hand is close.
The passage presents the new success as an unlooked-for achievement.

questions.stem: The comparison with a child first walking chiefly makes Edna's discovery seem
choices: like an emergence into independent movement, with confidence exceeding experience
like a regression that leaves her less capable than before the lessons
like the completion of a carefully predicted sequence of formal exercises
like a performance undertaken chiefly to amuse the watching group
rationales: The child moves alone boldly and with over-confidence, anticipating both exhilaration and risk.
The comparison accompanies a new ability, not a loss of one.
The realization is sudden after repeated difficulty, rather than a planned culmination.
Edna's joy and later solitude emphasize her experience rather than an entertaining display.

questions.stem: The movement from “She could have shouted” to “She did shout” chiefly
choices: shifts from the narrator's account to an instruction spoken by Robert
contrasts what Edna remembers with what another witness says occurred
qualifies the joy by suggesting that Edna decides to conceal it
turns imagined intensity into an enacted expression of joy
rationales: The narrator continues describing Edna's response.
No competing witness account is introduced by the two sentences.
She gives it overt expression rather than suppressing it.
The immediate correction makes the emotional force audible in an actual action.

questions.stem: The phrase “her body and her soul” chiefly expands the achievement into
choices: an objective demonstration that Edna has overcome every social constraint
a perceived power over the self beyond the practical act of swimming
a religious conversion whose doctrine the narrator later explains
a separation in which bodily success has no effect on inward experience
rationales: The narrator describes a feeling and soon introduces its limits.
The wording makes the discovery feel significant to inward as well as bodily life.
No doctrine or conversion narrative is supplied.
The phrase explicitly joins the two dimensions.

questions.stem: The narrator's statement that Edna is “overestimating her strength” primarily
choices: qualifies her exultation before fear interrupts it
shows that the other swimmers have refused to acknowledge her achievement
withdraws the earlier claim that she has actually learned to swim
confirms that Robert is deliberately exaggerating the danger
rationales: The narration gives the reader a caution that Edna's intoxication with power does not fully register.
They applaud and congratulate themselves on contributing to it.
The ability is real even though its extent is overestimated.
The qualification belongs to the narrator, not to a reported warning from Robert.

questions.stem: The observers' tendency to credit their own teaching chiefly contrasts
choices: their shared fear of the water with her longstanding confidence in it
their accurate prediction of the event with her stated plan to fail
their self-congratulation with Edna's inward sense of discovery
their indifference to Edna with her desire to receive their admiration
rationales: The opening establishes Edna's earlier dread, not theirs.
Neither a prediction nor a plan to fail is given.
The group interprets the event through its instructional contribution, while Edna experiences new personal power.
They do admire her, but she soon declines their group activity.

questions.stem: Edna's refusal to join the group's sports chiefly gives her new capacity
choices: a practical purpose of rescuing someone beyond the group
a direction toward solitary experience rather than continued collective play
a direction toward teaching the children who had helped her
a social purpose of publicly disproving her husband's earlier instructions
rationales: No person needing rescue is introduced.
She swims out alone to encounter space and solitude.
No teaching activity follows.
The passage does not state such an intention or quote those instructions.

questions.stem: The qualification about the distance being small for an experienced swimmer chiefly distinguishes
choices: the narrator's disbelief in the sea's existence from Edna's confidence in it
a remembered danger from a present situation in which she feels entirely safe
Robert's route from the shorter route Edna was instructed to take
measurable distance from its significance to Edna's unaccustomed perception
rationales: The qualification concerns scale and experience, not whether the sea exists.
The fear occurs within the present narrated swim.
No two prescribed routes are compared.
The same stretch is modest in one frame and a seemingly insurmountable barrier in hers.

questions.stem: Her husband's response that he was watching chiefly reveals
choices: an understanding of her experience more fully articulated than her own account
an accusation that she has lied about having learned to swim
a reassuring external account that does not encompass her inward encounter with terror
a confession that he intentionally left her without any possible help
rationales: His brief reassurance does not describe the inward transformation and fear the narration has supplied.
He disputes the apparent distance and danger rather than the new ability itself.
He measures proximity and observation while she has experienced possible death and unaided effort.
He says he watched; the passage does not establish a plan to abandon her.

questions.stem: The final characterization of Edna as “capricious” chiefly places
choices: a social label beside an experience the reader has been allowed to see more fully
a shared celebration of her independence after everyone understands its cause
the narrator's definitive explanation above every earlier account of the swim
Edna's own description of her motives beside her agreement to rejoin the group
rationales: The observers explain her abrupt departure through temperament, while the narration has shown exhilaration and terror.
The observers focus on disrupted pleasure and apparent caprice rather than that understanding.
The label belongs to Madame Lebrun and her husband, not an unqualified narratorial verdict.
She does not use the label and continues away despite their calls.

questions.stem: Nora's return with cloak, hat, and bag chiefly gives the conversation
choices: the appearance of a brief errand both characters have agreed upon
evidence that Nora expects to remain in the room throughout the night
a pause in which Helmer assumes control of the household arrangements
visible preparation that makes departure an action already underway
rationales: Helmer asks her not to go, and their exchange concerns separation.
She explicitly says she cannot spend the night there.
Nora continues to direct her preparations and explain what will happen.
The objects and dressing accompany the decision, preventing it from remaining merely hypothetical speech.

questions.stem: Calling Helmer a “strange man” primarily indicates
choices: a claim that he has only recently moved into the house
a changed understanding of the relation beneath their familiar domestic roles
an attempt to disguise his name from someone listening outside
a failure to recognize his physical identity after the long conversation
rationales: Their established marriage is part of the context and dialogue.
The phrase recasts her husband as someone from whom she now feels estranged.
No such hidden listener or concealment plan is supplied.
She continues to address Torvald and discuss their shared life.

questions.stem: Nora's response to the possibility of “some day” chiefly distinguishes
choices: uncertainty about her future from determination about leaving now
a settled plan to return from a reluctance to reveal its date
confidence in future reconciliation from doubt about the present marriage
an intention to punish Helmer briefly from a willingness to resume ordinary life
rationales: She cannot say what will become of her but continues the practical departure.
She says she has no idea, offering no evidence of a concealed schedule.
The future remains unconfirmed rather than confidently reconciliatory.
The text does not define the departure as a brief punitive tactic.

questions.stem: The exchange of rings most directly gives material form to
choices: a division of household valuables according to their monetary worth
Helmer's proposal that they continue living as brother and sister
Nora's demand for release from reciprocal obligation
a renewed promise that both will preserve the marriage unchanged
rationales: The dialogue emphasizes relational obligation, not appraisal of the rings' price.
Nora rejects that proposal before demanding the exchange.
She connects the returned rings with perfect freedom on both sides.
The exchange accompanies separation rather than renewed vows.

questions.stem: The details about keys, servants, and Christine chiefly
choices: delay the separation until Helmer agrees to each logistical detail
combine practical continuity in the household with Nora's removal from her former place
establish that Christine has ordered the departure on Nora's behalf
show that the household will immediately cease to function without Nora
rationales: Nora presents arrangements and continues toward departure without that agreement.
She explains how tasks and belongings will be managed after she leaves.
Christine is assigned a practical task, not represented as making Nora's decision.
She explicitly names people who know the arrangements and will handle her things.

questions.stem: Nora's statement that she will think of Helmer, the children, and the house chiefly
choices: suggests that she expects to forget the family's existence as soon as she departs
retracts the decision to leave because attachment has returned
makes memory conditional on Helmer providing financial support
preserves a continuing mental relation without promising renewed cohabitation
rationales: The statement says the opposite.
She continues to refuse offers and then exits.
She refuses support rather than linking remembrance to it.
Remembering is acknowledged alongside her refusal to stay or accept contact on his terms.

questions.stem: The successive refusals of letters, gifts, and help chiefly
choices: invite Helmer to choose the form of assistance she will accept
establish that Helmer has withdrawn all willingness to support her
define present boundaries against forms of continued dependence or connection
show that Nora believes she can predict every future material need
rationales: Each offered form is refused.
He makes the offers; she rejects them.
The series narrows what Helmer may continue to provide after the departure.
She has already admitted uncertainty about what will become of her.

questions.stem: The condition that both would have to change chiefly makes possible reunion depend on
choices: a transformed relationship rather than a simple reversal of the departure
Nora's acceptance that the present marriage already satisfies her ideal
the completion of a practical errand that Christine will perform tomorrow
Helmer's single promise to stop asking questions that evening
rationales: Nora names a real wedlock as the result of changes in both, not merely returning to the same arrangement.
Her conditional language indicates that it does not.
The condition concerns the couple, not the packing of belongings.
The required change is broader and reciprocal.

questions.stem: Helmer's final flash of hope is best understood as
choices: the narrator's independent guarantee that Nora will soon return
Nora's final assurance that she still expects their marriage to continue
evidence that the departure has already been canceled offstage
his response to an unfulfilled condition whose realization remains uncertain
rationales: Drama here supplies his action and thought, not an external forecast.
She exits after defining a change she says she no longer believes will happen.
The final sound confirms a closing door, not a canceled exit.
The stage direction locates hope in him, while the play supplies no future fulfillment.

questions.stem: The last sound of the door shutting chiefly
choices: answers Helmer's question by proving that reconciliation is impossible under every future condition
closes the performed action while leaving the proposed future change unverified
signals that Nora has silently reentered the same room to resume the conversation
replaces the visible departure with an explanation that it was only a rehearsal
rationales: The sound confirms the present separation, not every imaginable future.
The departure reaches a material endpoint after Helmer's unanswered question.
The direction locates the shutting door below after her exit through the hall.
No rehearsal frame is introduced.

questions.stem: The narrator's repeated attention to changing light chiefly makes the wallpaper
choices: a practical clock that the household uses to coordinate meals
a decoration the narrator studies only because Jennie has requested an explanation
an object whose apparent identity varies with conditions of perception
a stable reference point unaffected by the narrator's changing habits
rationales: The passage associates it with observation and rest but does not give it that agreed function.
She pursues the pattern independently and guards her interpretation from Jennie.
Sunlight, moonlight, and other illumination yield different appearances and levels of recognition.
Its apparent transformations are precisely what she continually watches.

questions.stem: The statement “That is why I watch it always” chiefly reveals
choices: a recurring cycle in which puzzlement sustains attention
a decision to stop looking once the first sunlight enters
a method designed to reassure John that she has abandoned imaginative activity
a shared household routine in which everyone studies the paper together
rationales: The rapid change is hard to believe, and that uncertainty becomes the reason for continual watching.
The phrase explicitly insists on continued attention.
She does not present the watching as a report intended for him.
She claims a peculiarity others do not seem to notice.

questions.stem: The change from a “dim sub-pattern” to certainty that it is a woman chiefly marks
choices: a loss of interest in the wallpaper once its pattern is identified
the discovery of a printed label explaining the manufacturer's design
a correction supplied by John after he examines the wall
an increasing definiteness in the narrator's interpretation
rationales: Her interest and protective attention continue to intensify.
No label or external explanation is reported.
The narrator claims the recognition herself.
She contrasts earlier uncertainty with being now quite sure, without an independent witness confirming it.

questions.stem: The proximity of “It keeps her so still” and “It keeps me quiet by the hour” chiefly invites
choices: a claim that the narrator has deliberately taught the woman to rest
a connection between the perceived woman's condition and the narrator's own routine
a literal identification independently verified by another character in the room
a distinction proving that the woman has complete freedom while the narrator lacks it
rationales: No act of instruction is described.
The repeated agency of the pattern links the two states of stillness.
The relation arises within the narrator's account, not external verification.
Both statements emphasize being kept still or quiet.

questions.stem: The account of compulsory rest followed by concealed wakefulness chiefly develops a pattern of
choices: outward compliance accompanied by private divergence
shared agreement that wakefulness is the intended result of treatment
open refusal that immediately persuades John to change the routine
complete inactivity in which the narrator no longer observes the room
rationales: She lies down as instructed but does not sleep and does not tell them she is awake.
John tells her to sleep, and she calls the habit bad because she does not.
She conceals rather than announces the divergence.
Watching and thinking about the paper remain active during the stillness.

questions.stem: The recurring acts of watching John and “catching” Jennie chiefly
choices: establish that both have confessed to plotting against her
replace the wallpaper with a wholly unrelated concern about household theft
turn the narrator into an observer who suspects others of concealed interest
show that she now accepts their explanations without qualification
rationales: She interprets their behavior, but no confession is supplied.
Her suspicion continues to center on the wallpaper and its secret.
She monitors them without their knowledge and treats their contact with the paper as evidence.
She explicitly rejects Jennie's apparent innocence.

questions.stem: Jennie's explanation about yellow marks chiefly introduces
choices: an authoritative confirmation of the hidden woman’s physical existence
a practical account that competes with the narrator's preferred interpretation
evidence that the narrator has stopped caring who understands the pattern
independent confirmation that a woman is moving inside the wallpaper
rationales: Jennie comments on yellow marks; that observation does not independently verify the narrator’s perceived woman.
Staining clothes offers a reason for touching the paper, while the narrator insists Jennie was studying the pattern.
She becomes determined that no one else shall find it out.
Jennie mentions stains, not a woman.

questions.stem: The contrast between improving “in spite of” and “because of” the wallpaper chiefly
choices: shows that John has adopted the narrator's interpretation without admitting it
resolves the conflict by proving that the paper has no relation to her condition
establishes that the narrator wants John to take her away immediately
makes the same outward change support opposing causal accounts
rationales: The phrases mark a difference, and no concealed agreement is established.
Both accounts remain interpretations rather than a conclusive external finding.
She withholds her explanation partly because he might remove her.
John and the narrator agree that she appears better but assign the paper different roles.

questions.stem: The catalogue of yellow things excludes buttercups chiefly to
choices: replace the paper's color with a neutral technical description
suggest that the narrator can no longer distinguish yellow from other colors
narrow the color's associations toward corruption and aversion
show that the garden has physically changed to match the room
rationales: The adjectives remain strongly evaluative rather than neutral.
She discriminates among associations within yellow, not between wavelengths.
She rejects a beautiful yellow example and chooses old, foul, bad things.
The comparison concerns remembered yellow things, not a reported transformation outside.

questions.stem: The smell described as hovering, skulking, and lying in wait chiefly
choices: extends the paper's presence through the house with an apparent agency of pursuit
provides an agreed explanation from John for every earlier visual impression
converts the narrator's suspicion into a verified report of another person's movements
confines the narrator's attention more strictly to a single visible patch
rationales: The personifying verbs make an odor seem mobile and watchful beyond the wall.
No such explanation by John appears.
The verbs characterize the smell figuratively, not a confirmed human intruder.
The smell moves through multiple rooms and stairs in her account.

questions.stem: The sequence of grounds, gates, stairs, and roof chiefly organizes Jane's movement as
choices: a journey whose destination she has already reached through employment
a search for a wider range of vision and experience
a retreat from contact with others because she considers society worthless
a practical inspection of the household duties she has been assigned
rationales: She describes experience she still lacks despite her position at Thornfield.
Her successive positions culminate in wishing to see beyond the visible limit into a busier world.
She explicitly desires more intercourse with people and variety of character.
The movements are connected to longing and perception rather than a list of assigned chores.

questions.stem: The wish for vision that could “overpass that limit” chiefly makes the horizon
choices: a precise route she expects to follow on the following morning
a sign that Jane distrusts every account of places she has not visited
an obstacle whose removal would require rejecting all present relationships
a boundary between known surroundings and desired possibilities
rationales: The passage gives a desire, not a scheduled journey.
She wishes to encounter them rather than dismissing their existence.
She continues to value Mrs. Fairfax and Adèle while wanting more.
The limit of sight corresponds to places and forms of life she has heard of but not experienced.

questions.stem: Jane's acknowledgment of goodness in her present companions chiefly qualifies her desire by
choices: conceding that her restlessness has no basis and should be abandoned
establishing that the household fully satisfies every intellectual need she has
separating a wish for more from a denial of what she already values
suggesting that she seeks a new position only to improve her income
rationales: She proceeds to defend the need for fuller activity and experience.
Her continuing longing explicitly indicates otherwise.
She affirms their goodness while imagining other, more vivid kinds beyond her reach.
The stated desire concerns experience and varied character, not wages.

questions.stem: The corridor's function differs from that of the outward view chiefly because it
choices: provides a protected place for inward movement when outward experience is limited
requires Jane to perform duties that prevent her from imagining anything else
proves that physical enclosure necessarily extinguishes creative activity
offers direct access to the distant towns visible from the roof
rationales: Back-and-forth walking accompanies the mind's eye, inward ear, and self-created narrative.
She uses its solitude to imagine rather than describing assigned work there.
The corridor supports an active imaginative life.
It remains an interior space rather than a route to those towns.

questions.stem: The “tale that was never ended” chiefly represents
choices: a published novel whose ending Jane cannot remember accurately
a report from another servant that she suspects is partly untrue
a plan whose every episode she has already decided to carry out
an imaginative supply of the incident and feeling missing from daily life
rationales: The passage says her imagination creates and continuously narrates it.
It is an inward tale, distinct from later attempts at conversation.
The imagined narrative is not presented as a fixed program of future action.
Jane explicitly connects its contents with what she desired and lacked in actual existence.

questions.stem: The movement from “Who blames me?” to a claim about human beings generally chiefly
choices: replaces the desire for experience with acceptance that stillness is always preferable
extends a personal defense into an argument about capacities needing exercise
withdraws the personal experience because it cannot support any broader reflection
asks the reader to identify a particular person who has lodged a formal accusation
rationales: The following argument explicitly rejects compulsory satisfaction with tranquility.
Jane answers anticipated criticism by placing her restlessness within a wider human need for action.
The experience becomes a basis for reflection rather than being withdrawn.
The question addresses anticipated judgment, not a specified proceeding.

questions.stem: The reference to “rebellions besides political rebellions” chiefly
choices: enlarges the idea of revolt to include unrecognized discontent within ordinary lives
confirms that every discontented person will eventually become a political leader
argues that public political events have no relationship to private experience
claims that Jane is organizing an armed campaign among the servants
rationales: The passage connects silent inward resistance with the constraints placed on people's capacities.
The claim concerns the existence of silent revolt, not a guaranteed career.
The analogy draws a relation while distinguishing kinds of rebellion.
No such action is narrated.

questions.stem: The list of puddings, stockings, piano playing, and embroidery chiefly
choices: describes the precise timetable that Adèle follows under Jane's instruction
establishes that Jane regards each activity as inherently worthless in every context
makes a conventional restriction of women's activity concrete
proves that the household has prohibited women from all forms of artistic expression
rationales: The list functions in a general argument about women rather than as a student's schedule.
Her objection is to confinement to them, not a universal ban on their value.
The examples show the range custom treats as sufficient while Jane argues for fuller use of faculties.
Piano playing and embroidery are allowed within the narrow range being criticized.

questions.stem: The contrast between the unsettling laugh and Grace Poole's ordinary appearance chiefly
choices: independently resolves the sound's true source for the entire novel
checks the expectation of romance raised by an unexplained sound
makes Grace's appearance seem more fantastic than the sound that preceded it
shows that Jane no longer has any curiosity about the household
rationales: The selection presents Jane's understanding at this stage, not a complete verification.
Jane's attribution and curiosity encounter a staid figure carrying commonplace objects and porter.
The narrator says the appearance dampens rather than heightens interest.
She attempts conversation and still cannot account for some sounds.

questions.stem: The closing account of Sophie's unsatisfying answers chiefly returns the passage to
choices: a conclusion that imagined experience is necessarily superior to actual travel
a new certainty that her present surroundings contain nothing worth valuing
a claim that language differences make every conversation impossible
the difficulty of obtaining a wider world through the available companions
rationales: The passage reports frustrated inquiry without establishing that general hierarchy.
Earlier appreciation remains, while the ending emphasizes a particular unmet desire.
Jane speaks French with Sophie; the limitation is descriptive and narrative interest.
Jane asks about France but receives responses that check rather than encourage inquiry.

questions.stem: The opening account of the disease chiefly makes its horror both
choices: private and easily concealed, since the symptoms leave no outward sign
remote and historical, since the narrator says the danger has already passed
gradual and predictable, since the victims have ample time to prepare
bodily and social, since visible symptoms cut victims off from aid
rationales: The scarlet stains are conspicuous and socially consequential.
The following retreat and revel occur while the pestilence continues.
The account compresses seizure through death into half an hour.
The blood and rapid decline are joined to exclusion from sympathy and assistance.

questions.stem: The transition beginning “But the Prince Prospero was happy” chiefly
choices: shows that the prince's grief has caused him to abandon every pleasure
sets privileged confidence against the devastation already described
confirms that the prince has discovered a cure available to all his subjects
suggests that the narrator has forgotten the disease and begun an unrelated tale
rationales: He supplies an elaborate range of entertainment and abundance.
The prince's mood and selected company contrast with a country being depopulated.
He withdraws with selected healthy friends rather than distributing a cure.
The retreat is explicitly a response to the pestilence.

questions.stem: The welded gates complicate the refuge chiefly because they
choices: exclude danger while also preventing exit in moments of despair
show that the prince expects his guests to leave before the festivities begin
make the abbey vulnerable by leaving its doors visibly open
allow the courtiers to move freely between the abbey and the afflicted population
rationales: The text explicitly names both ingress and egress as blocked.
The guests seal themselves in for prolonged seclusion.
The welding emphasizes closure.
The gates are sealed, not designed for free movement.

questions.stem: The statement that the external world could take care of itself chiefly exposes
choices: a promise that the abbey will soon open to anyone seeking shelter
a practical confidence that the prince's public relief program is succeeding
the indifference implicit in the courtiers' claim to protected pleasure
the narrator's demonstration that the disease cannot affect anyone beyond the walls
rationales: The surrounding details emphasize exclusion and selected admission.
No relief program is described.
The line places those outside beyond the concerns of the selected company.
The disease is precisely what remains outside and continues to rage.

questions.stem: The arrangement of the seven rooms chiefly affects perception by
choices: making every chamber visible from a single central position
limiting a continuous view and forcing successive encounters with new effects
ensuring that the final room can be reached without passing any other chamber
concealing the differences in color so that the rooms seem identical
rationales: The passage explicitly denies such comprehensive sight.
Sharp turns prevent the long, unobstructed vista common to other suites.
No such separate route is stated; the emphasis is a winding suite.
Each turn creates a novel effect and the chambers have distinct colors.

questions.stem: The final chamber's relation between decoration and window color is exceptional because
choices: its blue windows repeat the exact scheme of the eastern room
its lamps remove the effects produced elsewhere by the corridor fires
its white furnishings reflect ordinary daylight from open windows
its black interior is illuminated through blood-red glass
rationales: Blue belongs to the first room, not the final one.
No lamps or candles burn within any of the chambers.
The chamber is black and the illumination comes through tinted glass from braziers.
Unlike the other rooms, the window color does not match the prevailing decoration.

questions.stem: The courtiers' reluctance to enter the black chamber chiefly shows
choices: a shared objection to the room's lack of expensive furnishings
a practical concern that the room lies outside the welded gates
an unease produced within the prince's own designed refuge
a refusal to obey the prince's explicit order that everyone gather there
rationales: The issue is its effect, not a shortage of luxury.
The chamber belongs to the interior suite.
The ghastly light and transformed faces make part of the protected interior difficult to inhabit.
The selection gives no such order.

questions.stem: The clock's “brazen lungs” chiefly turn a familiar object into
choices: an apparently animate voice capable of interrupting the company
a decorative imitation that has no effect on the revelers' actions
a reassuring companion whose sound blends unnoticed with the orchestra
an unreliable instrument whose silence prevents anyone from knowing the hour
rationales: The personification gives its sound a force that halts music and dance.
Its effect on their actions is repeatedly described.
The musicians must pause and the company becomes disconcerted.
The clock repeatedly and emphatically marks each hour.

questions.stem: The laughter after each chime chiefly functions as
choices: a sign that the courtiers never noticed the interruption in the first place
an organized response the prince has rehearsed as part of the entertainment
a successful release that permanently removes the company’s fear
an effort to dismiss a disturbance that the next recurrence renews
rationales: They stop, grow pale, reflect, and then laugh after the echoes cease.
No rehearsal or instruction explains the laughter.
The recurring disconcert disproves permanence.
The guests smile at their nervousness and promise not to repeat it, yet the same reaction returns.

questions.stem: The parenthetical conversion of an hour into thousands of seconds chiefly
choices: assures the reader that the company has unlimited time to remain secure
draws attention to accumulated time despite the revelers' attempted distraction
changes the scene from a nighttime celebration to a morning ceremony
explains that the clock is running too slowly to keep accurate time
rationales: The emphatic passage of time undermines a feeling of timeless safety.
The numerical expansion makes the interval conspicuous before the next chime repeats the disturbance.
The parenthesis measures duration rather than changing the occasion.
The conversion is accurate and no mechanical fault is alleged.

questions.stem: Walton's movement from being touched to renewed indignation chiefly depends on
choices: new evidence that the creature has lied about his physical presence
the interaction of the creature's speech with loyalty and remembered warning
a request from Margaret that he refuse to listen further
the creature's withdrawal of every admission of wrongdoing
rationales: No such factual discovery occurs in the moment.
He recalls Victor's account of persuasive powers and looks at his friend's body before responding.
Margaret is the letter's recipient but does not issue that request here.
The creature continues to acknowledge crimes rather than retracting them all.

questions.stem: Walton's analogy of burning buildings and lamenting their ruins chiefly
choices: credits the creature with saving others from a danger created by Victor
distinguishes accidental harm from a destruction no one could have foreseen
suggests that the creature has tried successfully to repair the damage
casts grief as compromised by responsibility for producing the loss
rationales: The creature is cast as the destroyer within Walton's analogy.
Throwing a torch into buildings implies agency rather than unforeseeable accident.
The ruins remain and the analogy offers no repair.
The image accuses the creature of mourning a desolation he has caused.

questions.stem: Walton's claim that Victor would remain a target if alive chiefly
choices: establishes an outcome the narrative has independently tested
accepts the creature's account of remorse without reservation
interprets the mourning through a hypothetical continuation of vengeance
reports an observed attempt to attack Victor after this conversation
rationales: The condition is counterfactual, so it remains Walton's judgment.
The claim directly questions that account.
He imagines what the creature would do if the victim were still available.
Victor is already dead and no later observed attack is described.

questions.stem: The creature's concession about the impression conveyed by his actions chiefly
choices: acknowledges the grounds of Walton's reading while contesting its completeness
withdraws his admission that the actions themselves occurred
agrees that Walton has accurately described every motive he has ever had
shows that he is interested only in whether his voice sounds persuasive
rationales: He says the actions can produce that impression but proceeds to distinguish inward experience.
He disputes their purport, not their occurrence.
The ensuing account explicitly complicates Walton's explanation.
He addresses the meaning of conduct and suffering rather than sound alone.

questions.stem: The repeated “Once” in the creature's account chiefly organizes
choices: a sequence of successful reconciliations that restored his original confidence
a gradual reduction of responsibility until no wrongdoing remains admitted
a list of claims Walton has already verified through independent testimony
a contrast between former hopes and present degradation
rationales: The sequence emphasizes lost hopes, not completed reconciliation.
The passage explicitly names degradation through crime and a catalogue of sins.
The memories remain the creature's account in this exchange.
Earlier virtue, affection, honor, and imagined fellowship are measured against current despair and crime.

questions.stem: The comparison with a fallen figure who nevertheless had companions chiefly intensifies
choices: a claim that wrongdoing necessarily produces friendship and social acceptance
the creature's sense of isolation even within an account of moral fall
a denial that he ever wished to possess qualities admired by others
his confidence that companions will soon join him on Walton's ship
rationales: The comparison concerns a particular contrast, not a universal rule.
He invokes a being associated with hostility and fall, then distinguishes his own lack of associates.
The preceding account is full of those earlier wishes.
No such future companionship is promised.

questions.stem: The distinction between Victor's account of crimes and the creature's “hours and months of misery” chiefly
choices: challenges whether a narrated sequence of harms contains the sufferer's duration
proves that Victor invented every event in the story he told Walton
asks Walton to ignore the consequences of the actions because they were brief
shows that the creature has no memory of the interval between his acts
rationales: The creature argues that knowledge of acts and Victor's misfortunes does not sum up his prolonged inward experience.
The creature does not deny the crimes themselves.
The argument adds a missing dimension; it does not establish that consequences vanish.
He describes that interval as enduring misery and unsatisfied desire.

questions.stem: The question whether he is the “only criminal” chiefly seeks to
choices: replace the question of responsibility with a purely geographical account of travel
establish that no one in the story has committed any wrong
widen the account of responsibility beyond the speaker's admitted acts
establish that shared guilt makes his own acts morally harmless
rationales: The examples remain moral accusations about others' conduct.
The question presupposes wrongdoing and disputes its exclusive allocation.
He names injuries and exclusions by others while continuing to acknowledge his own crimes.
The question challenges exclusive blame, but the creature also acknowledges innocent victims and his own wrongdoing.

questions.stem: The statement that innocent victims had not injured him chiefly places a limit on
choices: Victor's responsibility for having created a being capable of feeling
an explanation that might otherwise turn exclusion into complete justification
the reader's knowledge that the creature has committed any violence
Walton's ability to acknowledge that the creature suffered
rationales: The admission does not erase the creator relation, though it complicates blame for particular acts.
His own admission identifies harm directed at people he does not claim wronged him.
It confirms rather than removes that knowledge.
The admission complicates justification without making suffering impossible.

questions.stem: Which account best captures the ethical tension in the exchange?
choices: Walton's friendship with Victor makes every judgment he offers factually false.
An admission of guilt makes every account of prior exclusion irrelevant.
The most eloquent speaker acquires complete authority over the interpretation.
Recognition of suffering remains necessary but insufficient to settle responsibility.
rationales: Friendship shapes his response, but it does not by itself falsify each claim.
The text continues to give exclusion explanatory weight without making it exonerating.
Eloquence is explicitly questioned and does not settle the admitted facts.
Both speakers supply reasons to hear or distrust the account, while the creature joins complaint with confession.

questions.stem: The narrator's enjoyment of the newly bare room chiefly complicates a simple escape reading because
choices: she considers the room unchanged from the beginning of the stay
she values a changed interior while still refusing to leave it
she has accepted John's plan to restore the paper immediately
she has already reached an open space beyond the house
rationales: The bareness and removed things explicitly mark a changed condition.
The pleasure concerns the room's altered condition, and she repeatedly rejects going outside.
She removes the paper to prevent being put back, not to invite its restoration.
She remains in the room throughout the ending.

questions.stem: The locked door and discarded key chiefly support the inference that the narrator
choices: is following an explicit instruction John has given her for that evening
has accidentally lost every means by which anyone could enter
has made a settled plan to abandon the house without confronting John
temporarily controls access to a space in which she has herself been constrained
rationales: No such instruction is supplied.
She knows and repeatedly states the key's location.
She says she wants to astonish him and waits for his arrival.
She decides who may enter and makes John obtain the key rather than obeying his demand to open.

questions.stem: The movement from a woman who might escape to women who came out “as I did” chiefly
choices: provides independent testimony that several visitors were hidden in the walls
shows that she has stopped associating herself with the wallpaper
destabilizes the distinction between the narrator and the figure she has perceived
clarifies a conventional comparison that she explicitly identifies as merely decorative
rationales: The claim remains within her narration, not an external confirmation.
The phrasing intensifies that association.
Her account shifts from speaking of another woman to including herself in that imagined emergence.
She does not label it a detached ornament; it shapes her account of action.

questions.stem: The repeated refusal to go outside chiefly qualifies the claim of getting out by
choices: making escape from the pattern different from departure into an unrestricted world
proving that John has already granted every freedom she requested
suggesting that she believes the room contains no remaining physical limits
establishing that she has no preferences about where she will remain
rationales: She celebrates being out in the room while rejecting the road and ground outside.
The ending supplies no such agreement.
She encounters the immovable bed, bars, and the route around the wall.
Her refusals are emphatic and specific.

questions.stem: The fit between her shoulder and the mark around the wall chiefly connects
