choices: her movement with a newly opened route directly to the front gate
her body with evidence that John has physically carried her through the room
her declared freedom with the disappearance of every trace of earlier activity
her sense of secure movement with a repetitive path
rationales: The path remains around the room's wall.
No such action by John is reported here.
The existing mark guides the present movement rather than disappearing.
The mark lets her creep without losing the way, combining reassurance with circular constraint.

questions.stem: The contrast between John's pounding and the narrator's gentle instructions chiefly
choices: resolves the conflict through a mutually agreed explanation of the room
reverses the immediate distribution of composure and practical control
demonstrates that John now accepts her entire account of the woman in the paper
shows that the narrator has become unable to communicate any usable fact
rationales: The exchange secures access but no shared interpretation.
He is agitated outside the door, while she calmly repeats information he must use to enter.
He later reacts with alarm and questions what she is doing.
Her precise key instructions are usable and lead to entry.

questions.stem: The declaration “you can't put me back” is most carefully read as
choices: a claim of resistance whose extent must be tested against the continuing action
a withdrawal of the earlier wish to alter the room's condition
a literal report that John has previously enclosed her body inside the wall
an objective guarantee that the narrator will never again encounter any restriction
rationales: The removed paper and declaration matter, but the reader must also account for continued creeping in the room.
The declaration depends on having pulled off much of the paper.
The text gives her identification with the paper, not independent evidence of literal enclosure.
The ending supplies no such future guarantee.

questions.stem: John's collapse and the narrator's continued movement chiefly allow the ending to
choices: confirm that the narrator has left the house before he can respond
establish that he has voluntarily agreed to perform a game she proposed
reverse his immediate authority without resolving her condition
restore the ordinary household relationship described at the story's opening
rationales: She remains on the path by the wall.
The narrator is surprised that he fainted; no game agreement is shown.
He becomes an obstacle she moves over, yet the repetitive movement and enclosed setting continue.
The collapse and her response radically alter the immediate relation.

questions.stem: Which detail most directly challenges a reading of the ending as uncomplicated liberation?
choices: The narrator has supplied the key's location more than once.
The narrator repeatedly circles the room and refuses to go outside.
The narrator has removed much of the wallpaper from the walls.
John initially cannot open the locked door from the hallway.
rationales: That detail chiefly shows her control of entry; it does not by itself establish continued confinement.
The continuing route and rejection of the exterior qualify what getting out has achieved.
Removal supports resistance, though its significance must be read with the ongoing action.
His blocked access supports a temporary reversal of power more directly than it challenges liberation.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best accounts for both the declaration of escape and the final repeated movement?
choices: The ending reveals that the earlier conflict was a deliberate joke shared by the couple.
The ending guarantees a complete recovery that the narrator will describe in a later entry.
The ending makes the narrator entirely passive and without any effect on her surroundings.
The ending entangles an act of resistance with continuing distress and constraint.
rationales: No shared joke explains John's alarm or collapse.
No later account or guarantee is provided.
She changes the paper, controls entry, and affects John's position, even though her freedom remains qualified.
This account includes altered control and removal of paper while retaining the significance of circular movement and enclosure.

questions.stem: Joe's formal address and the comparison of Pip to someone “a long way off” chiefly establish
choices: a shared joke in which both men comfortably imitate strangers
a long-standing preference for official titles in their private friendship
a felt social distance within a physically close conversation
a literal problem of hearing caused by the size of the apartment
rationales: The surrounding awkwardness and later melting of formality complicate such ease.
The return to old chap suggests a more familiar prior relation.
The wording makes separation perceptible even while the two occupy the same room.
The comparison concerns the look and relation, not a measured distance or hearing impairment.

questions.stem: The narrator's comparison of Joe's manner to making a will chiefly
choices: makes an ordinary message sound unusually solemn and formal
indicates that Joe has arrived to announce his own imminent death
shows that Pip understands the message as legally binding
establishes that Joe has been trained to draft documents professionally
rationales: The legal-formality comparison characterizes the strained delivery of Miss Havisham's words.
No such announcement is made.
The message concerns Estella's return and wish to see Pip, not a legal obligation.
His craft identity is blacksmithing, and the comparison describes manner rather than training.

questions.stem: Pip's hope that consciousness of his earlier discouragement was a “remote cause” of his blush chiefly
choices: records Joe's explanation of Pip's expression as an established fact
asserts that remorse was certainly his only response to the message
denies that Estella's return has any importance to him
qualifies his own account of a morally flattering motive
rationales: The speculation belongs to Pip's narrating voice, not to Joe.
Remote cause and hope prevent that exclusive certainty.
His immediate reaction follows that news, leaving its personal force evident.
The retrospective voice admits only a tentative, partial role for that better explanation of the reaction.

questions.stem: Biddy's reported encouragement that Joe deliver the message in person chiefly
choices: establishes that Pip had personally requested the visit in a recent letter
places an expectation of welcome beside the awkwardness of the actual visit
proves that Biddy intended the encounter to punish both men
shows that Joe came only because he wished to avoid seeing Pip
rationales: The quoted encouragement comes from Biddy rather than a stated invitation from Pip.
She imagines Pip will be glad and recognizes Joe's wish to see him; the scene has not fulfilled that ease.
No punitive intention is reported.
Her words explicitly recognize his desire for the visit.

questions.stem: The brief exchange about leaving and returning to dinner chiefly
choices: shows Pip trying to prolong an encounter Joe has decided to end
confirms that both men had planned the departure at exactly this moment
shows Joe demanding an invitation that Pip repeatedly withholds
removes the social awkwardness through a detailed practical agreement
rationales: Pip makes two attempts to keep the visit open, and Joe replies with firm refusals.
Pip's questions express surprise or resistance to the timing.
Pip offers continued company; Joe declines.
The short replies preserve strain rather than negotiating a plan.

questions.stem: The phrase that all the “Sir” melted out of Joe's heart chiefly
choices: suggests that Joe has forgotten the name by which he should address Pip
shows that the narrator considers all respectful language inherently dishonest
makes the return of intimate address a change in emotional relation
establishes that Pip's improved social position has been legally revoked
rationales: He addresses Pip familiarly rather than losing his identity.
The phrase concerns this encounter's formality rather than a universal judgment.
The formal title gives way to dear old chap at the moment of eye contact and farewell.
The change is interpersonal and linguistic, not a legal event.

questions.stem: Joe's description of life as partings “welded together” chiefly
choices: reduces his attachment to Pip to an arrangement for sharing workshop tools
uses the language of his craft to express both connection and separation
imitates the legal vocabulary he used earlier without changing its effect
shows that he thinks personal relationships can be repaired without any difficulty
rationales: The metaphor addresses life and parting, not a literal tool agreement.
Welding joins what the sentence calls partings, making his occupational knowledge carry emotional insight.
The craft image shifts toward his own language and intimate reflection.
The speech accepts painful divisions and does not promise effortless repair.

questions.stem: Joe's claim that any fault is his chiefly needs to be read alongside
choices: the fact that Miss Havisham has invited Estella to return home
Joe's report that he cleaned himself before calling on Miss Havisham
the narrator's statement that Joe eventually leaves the apartment
Pip's earlier recognition that he had offered too little encouragement
rationales: Estella's return explains the message but does not directly determine fault in the visit.
That preparation does not resolve the interpersonal blame at issue.
Departure is relevant to the outcome, but Pip's acknowledged conduct more directly tests the self-blame.
That detail complicates taking Joe's self-blame as a complete allocation of responsibility.

questions.stem: The repeated invitation to imagine Joe at the forge chiefly
choices: establishes that Joe considers manual work inferior to London's social life
asks Pip to abandon every future ambition and become a blacksmith immediately
offers a setting in which his identity and dignity can be recognized without the awkward costume
suggests that Joe's affection exists only when Pip is useful in the workshop
rationales: He locates being right and recognizable in his own work rather than disowning it.
Joe invites recognition and possible visiting, not an explicit change of occupation.
Hammer, anvil, apron, and familiar work contrast with the clothes he calls wrong in London.
The blessing and dear old chap preserve affection beyond practical utility.

questions.stem: The final recognition of dignity followed by the unsuccessful search chiefly supports the interpretation that
choices: understanding arrives without an immediate opportunity to repair the encounter
Joe has refused a direct apology that Pip clearly speaks before he leaves
Pip remains wholly unmoved by the farewell despite the narrator's explicit claims
Pip has completed a permanent transformation whose later conduct cannot complicate it
rationales: Pip recognizes Joe's dignity and pursues him, but the departure has already made him unreachable in that moment.
No such spoken apology and refusal occur in the selection.
The recognition, emotional recovery, and search provide evidence of being moved.
The selection establishes a moment of recognition, not proof of every future action.

questions.stem: The “sessions” to which the speaker summons remembrance chiefly present reflection as
choices: a final verdict that prevents the speaker from revisiting old grievances
a public celebration whose guests are the friends named later in the poem
a spontaneous escape from every obligation associated with earlier experience
a formal gathering in which the past is called into consideration
rationales: The poem describes renewed grief rather than a permanently closed case.
The gathering is figurative and inward; the friends are not literally present.
The language organizes and reopens the past rather than escaping it.
Sessions and summon give private thought the character of an assembled hearing.

questions.stem: The relation between “old woes” and “new wail” chiefly establishes
choices: the speaker's inability to distinguish remembered people from present companions
the renewal of sorrow through the act of remembering
the replacement of earlier losses with unrelated recent misfortunes
the belief that grief becomes less intense whenever it is expressed
rationales: The lines concern renewed emotion, not mistaken personal identity.
Past grief becomes a present expression rather than remaining completed history.
The new wail arises from old woes, not a separate set of events.
The language emphasizes recurrence and renewed cost rather than steady diminution.

questions.stem: The phrase “an eye, unused to flow” chiefly qualifies the weeping as
choices: a renewed response that interrupts a usual restraint
a habitual public display the speaker performs without feeling
a sign that the speaker has permanently lost the capacity to mourn
a bodily injury unrelated to the friends the speaker remembers
rationales: The eye is unaccustomed to tears, yet remembrance makes it flow.
The phrase indicates lack of habitual tears and the context supplies felt loss.
The speaker can drown the eye and weep afresh.
The next line directly connects the weeping to dead friends.

questions.stem: The phrase “death's dateless night” chiefly gives the friends' absence
choices: a temporary darkness that the next morning will certainly end
a secrecy deliberately maintained by the friends themselves
a duration beyond the ordinary accounting of days
a specific anniversary that the speaker has forgotten to record
rationales: Death's night is not presented as an ordinary overnight interval.
The friends are hidden in death, not acting to conceal their whereabouts.
Dateless contrasts with the poem's temporal and financial reckoning.
No particular date or forgotten anniversary is identified.

questions.stem: The financial language of expense, account, and payment chiefly makes grief seem
choices: like a debt that another person has formally agreed to reimburse
like a cost repeatedly incurred for losses already suffered
like a practical calculation that eliminates emotional involvement
like a source of material profit that compensates for bereavement
rationales: No external debtor or repayment contract appears.
The speaker pays anew what was paid before, turning recollection into renewed expenditure.
The account is explicitly sad and filled with repeated woe.
The figures describe expenditure and loss, not literal enrichment.

questions.stem: The repeated “Then can I” constructions chiefly
choices: announce successive solutions that prevent grief from returning
divide the poem among several speakers offering conflicting accounts
mark a sequence of unrelated historical periods in the speaker's life
extend the consequences of the opening act of remembrance
rationales: They describe renewed tears and grief rather than solutions.
The first-person voice remains continuous.
The repetition organizes present recollection, not a dated chronology.
The clauses develop what becomes possible when the speaker summons the past.

questions.stem: The third quatrain's repetition of forms of “woe,” “grieve,” and “moan” chiefly
choices: shows that the speaker has found precise financial terms inadequate and abandoned them
suggests that the speaker is mocking the friends whose deaths are recalled
intensifies the sense of sorrow repeating its own earlier work
introduces a new feeling that has no connection with the earlier quatrains
rationales: Account and pay continue the financial field within the same quatrain.
The recurrence expresses burden, with no clear ridicule of the dead.
The lexical recurrence mirrors the described return to fore-bemoaned grief.
The vocabulary develops the established grief.

questions.stem: The final couplet's “But if” chiefly establishes
choices: a conditional interruption of the preceding cycle
a reason the speaker must stop thinking about the friend
a correction proving that the remembered losses never happened
a transition to a separate account of the friend's own bereavement
rationales: Thought of the friend can redirect the grieving sequence when it occurs.
The friend supplies the consoling possibility, not the prohibited thought.
The turn changes present response rather than historical fact.
The couplet remains about the speaker's losses and sorrows.

questions.stem: The word “restor'd” in the ending is best understood as
choices: a factual report that the dead friends have returned to the speaker's room
a withdrawal of affection from everyone except the addressed friend
a promise that the friend will repay the speaker's actual financial debts
a figurative recovery of value within the speaker's present feeling
rationales: The poem locates the change in thinking, not a bodily return.
The consolation does not explicitly require repudiating the remembered people.
The monetary language remains figurative.
The friend counters the sense of loss without literally reversing death or vanished time.

questions.stem: The relationship between the first twelve lines and the couplet chiefly gives the sonnet
choices: a series of balanced arguments left without any final change in direction
an accumulated burden answered by a compressed assurance
an initial confidence that steadily collapses into unresolved accusation
a narrative climax followed by a factual account of what happened years later
rationales: The couplet clearly turns through But if and restoration.
Three quatrains develop renewed loss before two lines offer the friend's counterforce.
The movement proceeds from sorrow toward consolation, not the reverse.
The poem organizes acts of thought rather than a chronological sequel.

questions.stem: The opening personification of autumn and the sun chiefly presents ripening as
choices: an accidental result that neither figure appears able to influence
a completed harvest whose produce has already been removed
a competition in which one force prevents the other's work
a cooperative abundance rather than a solitary seasonal act
rationales: The active verbs make the figures seem purposive.
The stanza dwells on swelling, filling, and continuing flowers.
The actions are collaborative rather than obstructive.
The close friendship and conspiracy join season and sun in loading and blessing fruit.

questions.stem: The bees' belief that warm days will never cease chiefly
choices: introduces a complaint that the flowers have ceased too soon
places a perception of endless plenty within a transient season
establishes the speaker's literal prediction that winter will not arrive
shows that the first stanza rejects sensory pleasure as deceptive and worthless
rationales: Flowers continue budding more and still more.
Their apparent confidence arises from abundance, while the poem's seasonal frame allows a reader to see its limit.
The belief is assigned to the bees, not offered as a verified forecast.
The stanza values abundance while permitting a limit to its appearance.

questions.stem: The second stanza's varied harvest figures chiefly
choices: give autumn several embodied forms of patient or suspended activity
replace the season with a single named farmer whose biography the poem recounts
turn the poem away from ripeness toward a completed scene of winter scarcity
contrast a wholly inactive autumn with workers who appear only in spring
rationales: Sitting, sleeping, carrying, and watching present different postures within harvest labor.
No named biographical subject replaces autumn.
The stanza remains amid stored and gathered produce.
The images belong to autumn's own harvest setting.

questions.stem: The response “thou hast thy music too” chiefly redirects attention toward
choices: a remembered human song that replaces the natural sounds around the speaker
a reassurance that the poem's references to decline were unintended mistakes
the present season's particular value rather than its failure to repeat spring
a competition in which autumn's music is objectively proved louder than spring's
rationales: The following catalogue consists of insects, birds, and lambs.
The soft-dying day remains part of the valued scene.
The speaker answers the question about spring by attending to autumn's sounds.
No quantitative or universal ranking is established.

questions.stem: The final stanza's conjunction of mourning sounds and active animal voices chiefly
choices: makes the season uniformly silent after the question about spring
allows decline and continuing life to belong to the same appreciation
confirms that every creature has already departed for another place
withdraws the poem's earlier praise in favor of an unqualified rejection of autumn
rationales: The stanza is filled with audible life.
Gnats mourn while other creatures bleat, sing, whistle, and gather.
Gathering swallows are present, along with multiple other sounding creatures.
The season's own music is affirmed despite its elegiac inflections.

questions.stem: The departure of herd and plowman in the first stanza chiefly
choices: introduces a conflict over who owns the land being cultivated
establishes that the villagers have permanently abandoned their homes
presents the speaker as an official directing the workers' departure
leaves the speaker in a landscape becoming solitary and dark
rationales: The opening concerns evening withdrawal rather than a property dispute.
The movements are ordinary returns home at day's end.
No command or office is attributed to the speaker.
Their homeward motion gives the remaining world to darkness and the observing self.

questions.stem: The sounds that qualify the “solemn stillness” chiefly
choices: establish an approaching danger that the villagers have failed to notice
show that the speaker has become unable to distinguish one sound from another
make quiet perceptible through small, isolated disturbances
replace the evening's quiet with a crowded public celebration
rationales: The passage does not turn these sounds into a confirmed warning of danger.
The poem identifies the sounds with specificity.
Beetle, distant bells, and owl are heard within the prevailing hush.
The sounds are sparse and subdued, not a festival.

questions.stem: The repeated “no more” in the descriptions of morning and home chiefly
choices: measures the dead villagers' absence against continuing ordinary routines
claims that domestic pleasures were never available to the people remembered
suggests that the entire village has ceased all work after the burials
turns the account into a direct accusation that the children caused the deaths
rationales: Calls, hearth, household care, and children can no longer rouse or welcome them.
The imagined loss presupposes the value of such relations.
The absence concerns those buried, not a verified end to village life.
No such causation is alleged.

questions.stem: The injunctions to Ambition and Grandeur chiefly
choices: urge the villagers to abandon their former work in pursuit of fame
ask the reader to forget the particular people and consider only political history
celebrate rank as the only reliable measure of a life’s worth
defend obscure lives against contempt based on status
rationales: The villagers are dead, and the injunction defends their lives rather than redirecting them.
The address arises from the remembered local lives and their value.
Rank and pomp are precisely what the passage subjects to a limit.
The speaker asks that useful labor and homely joy not be mocked by elevated social values.

questions.stem: The statement that paths of glory lead to the grave chiefly
choices: argues that only ambitious people are subject to death
places celebrated power within the same mortal limit as obscure life
withdraws the earlier respect for useful labor because every life ends
promises that fame will erase the distinction between living and dying
rationales: The preceding graves already establish mortality among the poor.
The inevitable hour qualifies heraldry, beauty, wealth, and power alongside the buried villagers.
Shared mortality supports the challenge to disdain, not a cancellation of value.
The grave limits glory rather than being erased by it.

questions.stem: The opening question about what a lively child should know of death chiefly
choices: records a conclusion the child herself has already accepted
establishes an adult assumption that the ensuing encounter can test
shows that the narrator intends only to count children without interpreting their knowledge
supplies a factual explanation of the causes of the siblings' deaths
rationales: The opening belongs to the adult framing voice.

establishes that the speaker regards Tom's distress as entirely unworthy of care
shows that Tom is punished because the speaker has reported his behavior
rationales: Bare hair cannot be spoiled by soot, but the reassurance does not alter the laboring situation.
The statement concerns soot and hair, not all danger.
The speaker addresses and tries to comfort him.
No reporting or punishment by the speaker is described.

questions.stem: The dream's black coffins and open green plain chiefly
choices: show that the children have physically escaped before morning
make the dream indistinguishable from the conditions of the following day
describe two workplaces that Tom is invited to choose between
contrast confinement in labor's imagery with imagined release
rationales: They wake and return to work.
The cold, dark return creates a contrast.
The scene is a dream of liberation, not an employment offer.
The sweepers leave coffins, bags, and blackness for movement, washing, and light.

questions.stem: The angel's condition that Tom be a good boy chiefly
choices: guarantees an immediate end to the children's earthly labor
ties promised care and joy to obedience within the dream
asks Tom to reject all authorities before accepting comfort
explains that the speaker has personally met and questioned the angel while awake
rationales: The next morning they resume work.
The conditional assurance makes goodness a prerequisite of the promised paternal relation.
The condition requires good behavior rather than rejection.
The angel belongs to Tom's reported dream.

questions.stem: The return to work while Tom feels warm chiefly
choices: distinguishes a consoling effect from a change in material conditions
establishes that the cold morning was only another dream
proves that the dream's promised freedom has already occurred literally
shows that the speaker now openly rejects every claim the angel made
rationales: Happiness and warmth coexist with cold morning labor.
The poem marks awakening before the return to work.
The bags, brushes, and work remain.
The final duty statement does not voice such a rejection, though readers can examine its tension.

questions.stem: The opening description of a “little black thing” against snow chiefly
choices: presents the snow as proof that the child's conditions are comfortable
identifies an object discarded after a chimney has been cleaned
makes the child's visibility depend on a stark and diminishing contrast
establishes that the questioner cannot hear any voice from the figure
rationales: The contrast and sorrow do not support simple comfort.
The ensuing dialogue identifies a child with parents.
The figure is small, dark, and initially called a thing within a white setting.
The next line gives the cry in notes of woe.

questions.stem: The question about the parents chiefly introduces
choices: an accusation that the child has deliberately concealed the parents from view
an expectation of care that the child's answer will put under pressure
a request for directions that the child answers without personal implication
a topic the child refuses to discuss at any point
rationales: No deliberate concealment by the child is stated.
Their absence at prayer becomes significant alongside the child's condition.
The answer develops a critique of parental conduct.
The child directly describes the parents and their actions.

questions.stem: The contrast between happiness on the heath and the “clothes of death” chiefly
choices: suggests that the child's visible joy makes imposed suffering less consequential
makes the child's account a neutral description of changing fashion
establishes that the clothes restore the freedom of the earlier scene
presents suffering as imposed upon an earlier capacity for joy
rationales: The contrast exposes how visible happiness is used to misread or excuse suffering, not to reduce its harm.
The diction is strongly evaluative and consequential.
The death imagery complicates rather than restores that freedom.
The child links being clothed and taught in woe to others' actions.

questions.stem: The repeated “because” in the child's explanation chiefly exposes
choices: a refusal to connect the parents' actions with the child's condition
a claim that the child has become incapable of any happiness at all
a troubling use of apparent happiness to justify adult conduct
a logical agreement in which the child accepts the parents' judgment as accurate
rationales: The causal phrasing explicitly connects them.
The poem says the child is happy and dances while questioning the inference drawn from it.
The parents treat happiness as compatible with, and evidence for, their denial of injury.
The child's account calls their heaven a product of misery.

questions.stem: The final phrase about making heaven from misery chiefly
choices: accuses religious and political authority of benefiting from suffering it disregards
withdraws the earlier criticism because prayer has repaired the injury
promises that the child's present work will soon be rewarded by an announced rescue
identifies the child's imagination as the sole cause of the harmful conditions
rationales: The child joins parents, priest, and king in an account of a consoling order built on misery.
The parents' prayer remains implicated in the critique.
The ending offers accusation rather than a narrated rescue.
The account names adult and institutional actions rather than private imagination alone.

questions.stem: The opening statement chiefly establishes a speaking situation in which
choices: the historical poet documents a medically verified event in her own life
a constructed voice reports the experience of its own dying
a living observer describes another person's death from outside
the fly becomes the narrator of the entire scene
rationales: The poem supplies a literary speaker, not such verification.
The first-person retrospective claim creates the poem's unusual perspective without proving autobiography.
The speaker says when I died and later reports its own failed sight.
The fly is heard and described rather than speaking.

questions.stem: The comparison of stillness to the interval between storm heaves chiefly
choices: shows that the speaker cannot distinguish silence from continuous loud noise
establishes that a literal outdoor storm has caused the death
suggests that the scene has ended before any expectation can form
makes quiet feel charged with an anticipated onset
rationales: The comparison emphasizes a pause within possible force.
The weather relation is a simile, not a stated cause.
Breaths gather and an onset is anticipated afterward.
The pause is framed by surrounding force rather than simple peaceful absence.

questions.stem: The eyes that have “wrung them dry” chiefly suggest
choices: a completed celebration that has removed every sense of loss
the speaker's deliberate refusal to let anyone observe the scene
exhausted weeping among those gathered nearby
a physical drought that has damaged the room's windows
rationales: The image carries mourning rather than an uncomplicated celebration.
Others remain beside the speaker.
The eyes stand for mourners whose tears have been spent.
The image concerns surrounding people and tears, not weather damage.

questions.stem: The gathered breaths before the king's expected power chiefly create
choices: a collective anticipation of a moment of commanding significance
a practical explanation of why the fly cannot move
a verified appearance of a named monarch who enters the room
a disagreement in which each observer states a different prediction
rationales: The stillness and gathering focus attention on an expected onset.
No physical restriction on the fly follows from the breaths.
The poem does not identify or stage a literal monarch's entrance.
The observers' separate speeches are not supplied.

questions.stem: The qualification “What portion of me I / Could make assignable” chiefly
choices: establishes that every aspect of the speaker has been legally transferred
proves that the observers are present only to contest an inheritance
suggests that the speaker has refused to leave any keepsakes to others
distinguishes transferable possessions from a self not wholly disposed of by a will
rationales: Portion and could explicitly qualify the scope.
No such motive is established for everyone gathered.
The speaker says those have been willed and signed away.
The keepsakes can be signed away, but the phrase limits what can be assigned.

questions.stem: The fly's arrival after “and then” chiefly
choices: reveals that the speaker has been describing a remembered childhood game
interrupts the anticipated sequence with an ordinary sensory presence
shows that the room's stillness was never noticed by the speaker
completes an explicit prediction that the mourners made earlier
rationales: No such frame replaces the death scene.
The interposition follows preparation and expected significance rather than fulfilling them in an explained way.
The opening carefully describes that stillness.
No prediction of a fly appears.

questions.stem: The adjectives “uncertain” and “stumbling” applied to the buzz chiefly
choices: give the sound an irregularity unlike the expected display of power
establish that the fly is consciously deciding whether to console the mourners
make the sound a clear verbal message whose meaning is fully explained
show that the speaker considers the interruption entirely irrelevant to the scene
rationales: The hesitant sensory quality complicates the gathered anticipation.
The poem personifies quality without supplying that intention.
The buzz remains nonverbal and uncertain.
It occupies the culminating sensory sequence.

questions.stem: The fly's position “Between the light and me” chiefly
choices: replaces the room with an independently narrated account of an afterlife
confirms that the fly has extinguished a particular lamp by physical contact
places an obstruction within the speaker's final perceptual relation
proves that the expected king has deliberately sent a messenger
rationales: The poem remains with the speaker's reported perception.
No lamp or such action is described.
The interposed presence precedes the failure of the windows and sight.
That agency is not identified in the text.

questions.stem: The final failure of the “windows” most strongly supports
choices: a claim that the mourners have stopped caring because the fly appeared
a reading centered on the limits of seeing and consciousness
a guarantee that the speaker now understands every earlier uncertainty
a factual conclusion that the house's glass panes have all shattered
rationales: Their later motives are not reported.
The surrounding light and final inability to see connect the image with perception.
The ending withdraws access rather than supplies comprehensive explanation.
No shattering is narrated, and the final line concerns seeing.

questions.stem: Which interpretation most carefully preserves the poem's limits?
choices: The final loss of sight reveals that the entire preceding event was unreal.
The king's anticipated arrival is confirmed by a clear speech explaining the fly.
The fly proves that no form of existence can occur after any person's death.
An expected moment of power gives way to uncertain sensation and a boundary of perception.
rationales: The ending marks a perceptual limit, not an explicit cancellation of the narrated experience.
No such arrival or speech is presented.
The poem's particular sensory scene does not establish that universal doctrine.
This accounts for anticipation, interruption, and the ending without asserting what lies beyond it.

questions.stem: The visitor’s questions about Pip’s income and guardian primarily serve to
choices: conceal his uncertainty about the lawyer who represents Pip
gradually disclose precise personal knowledge that supports his startling claim to have provided Pip’s fortune
invite Pip to correct an inaccurate account of his childhood
test whether Pip has managed his allowance responsibly
rationales: He deliberately supplies the initial and then Jaggers’s name as part of the revelation.
The accurate financial and personal details lead Pip toward recognizing the source of his expectations.
The questions concern Pip’s present arrangements and confirm rather than correct the visitor’s knowledge.
The visitor uses the details to identify his own involvement, not to audit Pip’s spending.

questions.stem: Pip’s comparison of his heartbeat to a “heavy hammer of disordered action” emphasizes his
choices: determination to regain control of an awkward social encounter
impatience with the visitor’s unnecessarily elaborate questioning
anger that his guardian has failed to protect his privacy
physical distress as recognition approaches
rationales: The disordered action registers lost control, not a settled plan to recover it.
The surrounding inability to breathe and speak indicates shock rather than irritation at delay.
The passage does not identify a breach of privacy as the cause of his reaction.
The hammering heart precedes the explicit realization and makes its disruptive force bodily.

questions.stem: The accumulation of “disappointments, dangers, disgraces, consequences” most clearly conveys
choices: the visitor’s inability to distinguish imagined threats from real ones
the gradual replacement of embarrassment with financial confidence
the simultaneous collapse of Pip’s personal hopes and his confidence in his social position
the narrator’s orderly classification of problems already resolved
rationales: These are Pip’s perceived consequences, not the visitor’s account of threats.
The accumulation intensifies distress and offers no movement toward confidence.
The sequence presents simultaneous personal, practical, and social implications of the discovery.
The rushing multitude and struggle for breath emphasize overwhelming simultaneity rather than order.

questions.stem: The visitor’s repetition of “I swore” in his account of earning money chiefly stresses
choices: the durability of his commitment to Pip
the uncertainty of his memory about how the fortune began
the resentment he feels at Pip’s demands for further support
the legal restrictions governing his investment of the money
rationales: The repeated vow connects successive earnings and later wealth to an enduring intention.
The repeated assertion is emphatic rather than tentative or forgetful.
Pip makes no demand here, and the visitor presents the support with pride.
The oath is a personal promise, not an explanation of investment law.

questions.stem: The paired phrases “lived rough” and “live smooth” reveal that Pip’s comfort
choices: has failed to meet the visitor’s hopes for social advancement
will be withdrawn unless Pip adopts the visitor’s habits
has taught the visitor to prefer luxury to physical labor
has been made possible by the labor and hardship of a person he regards with revulsion
rationales: The visitor celebrates having made Pip a gentleman rather than declaring the effort unsuccessful.
The speech announces what has already been given, not a condition of continued support.
The contrast concerns their different lives, not the visitor’s conversion to luxurious habits.
The antithesis makes the visitor’s deprivation the enabling condition of Pip’s ease.

questions.stem: When the visitor denies wanting Pip to “feel a obligation,” he is chiefly
choices: withdrawing a request for gratitude after Pip rejects it
presenting the gift as a source of personal pride
asking Pip to repay only the original amount invested
acknowledging that the gift has damaged their former friendship
rationales: Pip is unable to speak, so the denial does not answer an expressed rejection.
He follows the denial by celebrating the power of a hunted outcast to make a gentleman.
No financial repayment is proposed; the speech emphasizes what the gift proves to its maker.
He does not recognize Pip’s revulsion as damage to a friendship in this speech.

questions.stem: The visitor’s description of himself as a “hunted dunghill dog” chiefly contrasts
choices: his former social degradation with the achievement he celebrates in conferring the status of gentleman
a childish misunderstanding with a more accurate adult memory
past criminal success with present regret about his fortune
physical weakness with an intention to threaten Pip again
rationales: The lowly self-image is set against his achievement of making Pip a gentleman.
The visitor supplies the image himself; it is not identified as Pip’s childhood error.
He takes pride in the fortune’s use rather than regretting it.
The speech celebrates support and does not announce a renewed threat.

questions.stem: The action in which the visitor catches Pip and places him on the sofa complicates Pip’s reaction by
choices: making the visitor appear dependent on Pip’s protection
confirming that Pip’s alarm is caused by a fresh attack
showing care from the person he fears
establishing that Pip has accepted the visitor’s affection
rationales: Pip is the person needing immediate physical support in this exchange.
The action steadies Pip after he nearly collapses rather than assaulting him.
The visitor physically supports Pip even as Pip shudders at the proximity of his face.
Pip’s continuing repugnance prevents interpreting the assistance as mutual acceptance.

questions.stem: The final comparison to a “terrible beast” most strongly indicates that Pip
choices: has discovered evidence that the visitor’s story is false
responds to the truth through a revulsion that makes the visitor seem less than human
is recalling the precise appearance of an animal from childhood
understands the visitor’s hardship as similar to his own
rationales: Pip has recognized the truth; the comparison describes his reaction to it.
The comparison makes his abhorrence extreme despite the visitor’s account of devoted support.
The phrase is a hypothetical comparison, not the recollection of an actual beast.
The image creates distance and fear rather than an acknowledgment of shared experience.

questions.stem: Taken as a whole, the passage presents a revelation that
choices: reconciles Pip’s ambitions with the visitor’s hopes for repayment
transfers narrative authority from Pip to an impartial observer
resolves uncertainty by giving Pip a secure sense of belonging
exposes a conflict between benefit and social judgment
rationales: No repayment is requested, and Pip’s response is profoundly unreconciled.
Pip remains the retrospective narrator, and no impartial observer takes over.
The new knowledge disrupts his identity rather than securing belonging.
Pip learns that the comfort and status he values come from a man he regards with disgust.

questions.stem: The creature’s decision to remain hidden initially arises from a conflict between
choices: curiosity about wealth and resentment of domestic work
his desire to share the family’s companionship and his fear of suffering another hostile reception
a desire for solitude and a need to find warmer shelter
loyalty to Victor and suspicion of the cottagers
rationales: The opening emphasizes companionship and fear, not a wish to acquire property.
He admires the family’s gentleness but remembers the villagers’ violent treatment.
He explicitly longs to join the family rather than preferring isolation.
His stated reasons concern previous mistreatment and the family’s appealing manners.

questions.stem: The repeated attention to the cottagers’ daily work chiefly establishes
choices: a division of tasks that the narrator immediately understands fully
an atmosphere of leisure that makes the family’s sadness inexplicable
a monotonous life that the creature decides he must avoid
a domestic pattern the observer gradually learns to interpret
rationales: His later questions and discoveries show that his understanding develops over time.
The passage repeatedly describes labor, and poverty later explains part of the sadness.
He is attracted to the family and seeks participation rather than escape from its routine.
The routines become evidence through which he understands affection, poverty, and opportunities to help.

questions.stem: The old man’s smiles function in the passage as
choices: signals that he has discovered the hidden observer
attempts to conceal impatience with the family’s poverty
a reciprocal expression of affection in response to the younger people’s attentive care for him
expressions of amusement at the young people’s misunderstanding
rationales: The passage supplies no evidence that he knows the creature is nearby.
Neither impatience nor an intention to conceal it is attributed to him.
The smiles reward the affectionate services the young people perform for him.
The smiles are described as benevolent responses to duty, not mockery.

questions.stem: The parenthetical phrase “for such it was in my eyes” qualifies the description of the house by
choices: marking the limits of the creature’s perspective
suggesting that the family deliberately disguises its prosperity
correcting an earlier claim that the cottage was abandoned
distinguishing the present narrator’s sight from his former blindness
rationales: The phrase identifies delightfulness as his judgment, which later recognition of poverty complicates.
The passage reveals actual deprivation rather than concealed wealth.
No such claim appears in the selection.
The old man is blind; the creature’s limitation here is interpretive, not visual.

questions.stem: The questions about the cottagers’ tears primarily dramatize
choices: a detached investigation with little emotional involvement
confidence that their apparent unhappiness is merely pretended
resentment that the family refuses to explain its problems
an emotional response to suffering whose cause the observer has not yet learned to understand
rationales: He explicitly says that he is deeply affected by their unhappiness.
He is puzzled and searching, not certain that the tears are false.
He watches secretly and has not asked the family for an explanation.
The creature is affected by their sadness before he can explain its causes.

questions.stem: The discovery of the family’s poverty changes the significance of the earlier description of “every luxury” by
choices: confirming that the narrator has intentionally misled his listener
revealing how deprivation shapes the observer’s standards
showing that the family has rapidly lost its former fortune
suggesting that the family values comfort more than affection
rationales: His account openly presents his earlier misunderstanding and subsequent learning.
Food, warmth, and company initially seem luxurious to someone who lacks them.
The passage describes a correction of understanding, not a newly occurring financial collapse.
The young people’s sacrifice of food demonstrates affection despite material scarcity.

questions.stem: The creature’s decision to stop taking food most directly demonstrates
choices: a willingness to change his own behavior once he recognizes the pain it causes other people
obedience to a rule the young cottagers have explained
a wish to appear generous before asking the family for shelter
fear that the old man will identify and punish him
rationales: He changes his own means of survival after learning that his theft causes pain.
No rule has been communicated to him; the recognition comes through observation.
The action remains secret and is not presented as a strategy for a request.
The stated motive is the pain inflicted on the family, not anticipated punishment.

questions.stem: The secret delivery of firewood develops the creature’s characterization chiefly through
choices: an attempt to exchange stolen food for a promised reward
a demonstration that physical strength prevents intellectual growth
a practical response to the family’s burdens
an effort to prove that the youth is neglecting his duties
rationales: There is no agreement or expected reward in the passage.
The act depends on observation, learning the tools, and understanding its effect.
He identifies a laborious task and performs it, freeing the youth for other work.
The creature intends assistance and takes pleasure in its beneficial result.

questions.stem: The family’s surprise at the wood creates a difference between
choices: what the old man believes and what the young woman admits
the reader’s knowledge of the hidden helper and the family’s ignorance of the wood’s source
what the creature intends and the harm his action causes
what Victor predicts and what the creature refuses to reveal
rationales: The passage does not establish conflicting explanations within the family.
The reader has heard the creature’s account of supplying the wood; the family does not know its source.
The described effect is useful rather than harmful.
Victor offers no prediction within this selection.

questions.stem: The passage’s movement from puzzlement to assistance most strongly complicates a view of the creature as
choices: eager to find a place within human companionship
dependent on observation for knowledge of human society
unusually attentive to the details of ordinary life
incapable of moral learning
rationales: His desire for connection is explicit and remains important throughout.
Observation is precisely the means by which he learns here.
The passage supports, rather than challenges, his close attention.
He learns to recognize deprivation and changes his actions to reduce another’s burden.

questions.stem: The creature’s description of the books as “treasures” chiefly conveys
choices: his intention to sell the volumes for food and clothing
his preference for possessions over the cottagers’ company
his recognition that the books belong to a wealthy collector
his delight in acquiring a means of intellectual and emotional discovery beyond his immediate surroundings
rationales: The passage describes reading them, not converting them into money.
The books intensify his questions about relationship rather than replacing that desire.
The owner’s identity and wealth are not established.
He responds with delight and repeatedly studies the books as new sources of experience.

questions.stem: The contrast between “ecstasy” and “lowest dejection” suggests that reading
choices: gradually loses its appeal as the stories become familiar
enlarges feeling without securing contentment
allows the creature to separate imagined events from true history
corrects the creature’s tendency to respond too emotionally
rationales: The contrast describes powerful effects, not declining interest.
The books produce both exhilaration and distress rather than a stable escape from suffering.
He later says that he reads the volumes as true histories.
His emotional range grows; it is not replaced by detached judgment.

questions.stem: The statement that the creature weeps for Werter “without precisely understanding” his extinction emphasizes
choices: the strength of an emotional identification that exceeds his ability to explain the figure’s death
a deliberate refusal to consider the book’s moral questions
an inability to distinguish one character from another
a preference for the narrator’s explanation over the hero’s opinions
rationales: He is moved by a figure whose arguments and death he does not fully understand.
He expresses wonder and speculation, not a settled refusal to think.
The limitation concerns understanding the case, not identifying characters.
He says that he inclines toward the hero’s opinions.

questions.stem: The sequence “Who was I? What was I? Whence did I come?” marks a movement from
choices: asking Victor for information to accepting Victor’s account
doubting the books’ accuracy to rejecting their authors’ authority
reading others’ lives to questioning his own identity
remembering his childhood to reconstructing a forgotten family history
rationales: The questions describe recurring uncertainty during his reading, not a resolved exchange.
He does not conclude that the books are inaccurate or reject their authors.
The questions follow his comparison of himself with the beings described in books.
He lacks the ordinary relationships the questions seek to explain.

questions.stem: The contrast between Werter and Plutarch chiefly distinguishes
choices: private affection from a rejection of moral feeling altogether
a movement into private gloom with an elevation toward admiration of virtuous public action
simple language from a style too difficult for him to read
unreliable fiction from historical accounts he knows to be verified
rationales: Plutarch arouses admiration for virtue and aversion to vice, not a rejection of morality.
The creature says one deepens gloom while the other elevates him toward civic heroes.
The distinction concerns effects and subjects rather than reading difficulty.
He treats the volumes as histories and does not verify their reliability.

questions.stem: The creature’s reference to the cottage as his “only school” qualifies his response to Plutarch by
choices: explaining why he dismisses the possibility of civic virtue
establishing that the cottagers have formally taught him classical history
suggesting that his understanding exceeds that of the book’s subjects
showing the narrow experience through which he interprets it
rationales: He admires peaceable lawgivers and develops an ardor for virtue.
He learns secretly by observation; no formal instruction in Plutarch is described.
The passage emphasizes his limited experience, not his superiority to the historical figures.
He has little knowledge of cities or large groups, so domestic experience shapes his understanding of public life.

questions.stem: The imagined influence of a “young soldier” primarily introduces the possibility that
choices: military experience would have resolved his questions about his origin
the books give every reader an identical understanding of virtue
the values learned through books may be shaped by the human examples a reader has first encountered
the cottagers conceal a history of violence from him
rationales: The hypothetical concerns values and sensations, not the facts of his creation.
The hypothetical explicitly allows variation in response.
He suggests that a different introduction to humanity might have produced different feelings.
The passage provides no such information about the family.

questions.stem: The comparison with Adam becomes an account of difference when the creature emphasizes
choices: the care and companionship he has been denied
Victor’s possession of powers greater than those of God
his certainty that the two figures share a common ancestry
his own greater ability to interpret unfamiliar books
rationales: Adam’s guarded, happy condition contrasts with the creature’s helpless solitude.
The passage emphasizes inadequate care, not Victor’s greater power.
The comparison is interpretive rather than genealogical.
The contrast does not claim intellectual superiority over Adam.

questions.stem: Satan appears to the creature a “fitter emblem” chiefly because of
choices: a shared desire to become a peaceful lawgiver
a belief that he and Satan were created without physical bodies
a conviction that Victor has ordered him to imitate rebellion
his painful envy when he watches a happiness that he can recognize but cannot share
rationales: That admiration belongs to the discussion of Plutarch, not the Satan comparison.
The passage supplies no such belief and repeatedly concerns bodily difference.
Victor gives no such instruction in the selection.
The creature connects this identification to watching the cottagers’ bliss and feeling envy.

questions.stem: The discovery of Victor’s journal changes the reading sequence by
choices: providing the companionship that the earlier books could only imagine
making his creator’s disgust part of his self-understanding
replacing his emotional responses with a detached scientific account
correcting his mistaken belief that Victor had abandoned him
rationales: A written account of disgust deepens rather than relieves his isolation.
The record supplies a personal account of his origin whose language intensifies his horror.
He responds with sickness and agony, not detachment.
The journal confirms rejection in his understanding rather than disproving it.

questions.stem: The opening account of the Tuesday reception chiefly establishes
choices: the established social routine that gives Edna’s apparently simple decision to go out its disruptive force
an exceptional celebration requiring unusual household preparation
a newly adopted custom that neither spouse understands
a private pleasure that Edna has been prevented from enjoying
rationales: The detailed custom and its six-year duration make the later departure a recognizable change.
The reception occurs regularly, not as a singular celebration.
The routine has been followed throughout their marriage.
The passage presents a social obligation she leaves, not a desired event she is denied.

questions.stem: The word “religiously” in the description of Edna’s former conduct emphasizes
choices: the explicitly theological purpose of the visitors’ discussions
the narrator’s certainty that Edna approves every social expectation
the regularity of her observance
the spiritual transformation caused by the return from Grand Isle
rationales: No religious discussion is described at the receptions.
Regular observance does not establish inward approval of every expectation.
The word characterizes six years of following a social program with habitual fidelity.
The word refers to the preceding routine, not a new conversion.

questions.stem: Mr. Pontellier’s notice of Edna’s ordinary house dress serves as
choices: a reminder that he prefers her to avoid fashionable society
a visible departure from the familiar ritual that anticipates her explanation of the afternoon’s absence
proof that the visitors have already criticized her appearance
evidence that the household can no longer afford formal clothing
rationales: His subsequent insistence on social obligations contradicts that preference.
Her clothing differs from the customary reception gown before she explains her absence.
He notices the dress himself; no visitor’s criticism is reported.
The passage does not attribute the change to financial necessity.

questions.stem: Edna’s reply “I simply felt like going out, and I went out” most directly asserts
choices: an inability to remember what required her to leave
a wish to conceal an urgent obligation from her husband
agreement that the departure needed a carefully prepared excuse
personal desire as a sufficient reason for action
rationales: She does not claim forgetfulness; she clearly names her motive.
No hidden obligation is supplied by the statement or surrounding passage.
She follows the reply by saying she left no excuse.
She offers inclination itself rather than the external necessity her husband expects.

questions.stem: The repeated interruptions about the soup connect the social dispute with
choices: a mutual decision to postpone the dispute until after dinner
Edna’s growing fear that the food has been deliberately spoiled
Léonce’s broader expectation that the household should maintain the forms of service he considers proper
the servants’ explicit criticism of the couple’s argument
rationales: The complaints continue the tension rather than resolving to postpone it.
She eats with satisfaction and later tolerates the scorched fish.
His complaints move between missed calls and meals, treating both as failures in household management.
The servants do not offer such criticism in the passage.

questions.stem: The calling cards become especially important when Mr. Pontellier
choices: reads social relationships in terms of practical advantage
recognizes that the visitors have no connection to his work
uses them to apologize for missing his own reception duties
discovers that Edna has invented the existence of visitors
rationales: His comments connect callers with business dealings and financial importance.
He explicitly names connections to his business.
He criticizes Edna’s conduct and offers no apology.
The cards confirm that callers came; they do not expose fabrication.

questions.stem: The claim that Belthrop could “buy and sell us ten times over” primarily explains
choices: why the narrator regards Mrs. Belthrop as personally admirable
why Edna believes the family must reduce household spending
why the visitors have refused to return to the house
why a missed social courtesy seems to Léonce capable of endangering a financially valuable relationship
rationales: The valuation belongs to Léonce and concerns status, not the narrator’s moral endorsement.
Edna does not offer that financial conclusion.
No refusal to return is reported.
He uses Belthrop’s wealth and business value to justify attending carefully to his wife.

questions.stem: The disagreement about “seeming trifles” centers on whether
choices: the guests have accurately remembered the date of the reception
small social observances carry substantial obligations
the family should replace social calls with business meetings
the servants have delivered the wrong set of visiting cards
rationales: Neither spouse questions the scheduled day.
Léonce insists that such details count while Edna resists the seriousness he assigns them.
No such replacement is proposed; Léonce treats the spheres as connected.
The accuracy of the cards is not disputed.

questions.stem: The comparison between cooks and office clerks reveals that Mr. Pontellier
choices: treats household management as analogous to the supervision he considers necessary in his business
believes his own business would improve without close oversight
regards cooking as an art beyond his ability to evaluate
considers domestic workers more independent than business employees
rationales: He argues that employees in both settings require supervision to prevent disorder.
He predicts that unsupervised clerks would make a mess of it.
His repeated judgments about the meal indicate the opposite stance.
The analogy stresses a shared need for supervision.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole develops tension chiefly by
choices: moving from mutual misunderstanding toward a shared practical solution
revealing a secret financial crisis through apparently casual conversation
placing individual inclination within a network of social demands
contrasting a public quarrel with the couple’s private harmony
rationales: The selection ends with another assertion of supervision, not agreement.
No hidden crisis is disclosed; the issue is maintaining established expectations.
Edna’s afternoon choice becomes a dispute about visits, business, meals, and supervision.
The quarrel itself occurs privately, and no harmonious contrast is supplied.

questions.stem: Hamlet’s comparison of exaggerated delivery to a town-crier chiefly expresses
choices: his impatience with delivery that turns a performed speech into conspicuous noise rather than fitting expression
a wish to replace the players with an experienced messenger
admiration for performers who can project to distant listeners
concern that the speech contains information the town should hear
rationales: The comparison criticizes mouthing lines as public noise rather than nuanced performance.
The comparison rebukes a style rather than arranging a replacement.
His tone is critical, not approving of projection as an end in itself.
The issue is how the lines are spoken, not public access to their content.

questions.stem: The images “torrent,” “tempest,” and “whirlwind” make Hamlet’s demand for temperance seem
choices: an instruction to avoid portraying emotionally intense situations
a confession that he cannot understand the players’ language
a discipline exercised within powerful feeling
a preference for scenery that realistically imitates severe weather
rationales: He discusses how to perform passion, not how to exclude it.
The speech confidently evaluates performance rather than admitting incomprehension.
The turbulent images identify passion that requires control rather than complete removal.
The images are figurative descriptions of emotional force.

questions.stem: The warning “Be not too tame neither” chiefly
choices: signals that the First Player has refused his instructions
qualifies the attack on exaggeration by insisting that restraint should not become lifeless performance
introduces a separate concern about the actors’ personal courage
withdraws his objection to uncontrolled gesture
rationales: The player has agreed to them, not refused.
Hamlet rejects lifeless restraint as well as exaggerated display.
The warning concerns acting style, not courage outside performance.
He continues to require discretion and a fit between action and word.

questions.stem: The parallel commands about suiting action and word emphasize
choices: the superiority of gesture whenever language becomes difficult
the need to improvise actions that contradict the written speech
a division between actors who speak and actors who move
coordination between verbal and physical expression
rationales: The reciprocal structure gives neither element automatic priority.
Hamlet asks for fit, not deliberate contradiction.
The instruction concerns integrated performance rather than separate roles.
Each is to fit the other, so neither independently overwhelms the performance.

questions.stem: The “mirror up to nature” comparison presents playing as
choices: a way to replace moral judgment with visual spectacle
an exact duplication of appearances without selective judgment
a representation through which an audience can recognize human qualities and the character of its age
a private exercise with little relation to an audience
rationales: The mirror is linked to recognizing qualities, not abandoning judgment.
The surrounding instructions require discretion and distinguish successful from failed representation.
Hamlet names virtue, scorn, and the character of the age as things performance can show.
The speech repeatedly considers spectators and their responses.

questions.stem: Hamlet’s contrast between “the unskilful” and “the judicious” establishes
choices: a hierarchy of audience judgment
a belief that every spectator responds identically to excess
a preference for the larger group whenever reactions conflict
a difference between actors trained in comedy and tragedy
rationales: He gives the discerning viewer’s evaluation greater weight than a whole theatre of others.
He distinguishes laughter from grief at the same overdone performance.
He explicitly privileges the smaller discerning judgment over numbers.
The terms describe spectators’ responses, not the performers’ genres.

questions.stem: In context, the “censure” Hamlet says should “o’erweigh” other responses means
choices: public punishment
official prohibition
personal insult
an evaluation of the performance, especially the discerning judgment Hamlet values above general applause
rationales: The phrase evaluates audience response rather than prescribing a penalty.
No authority is banning the performance in this statement.
The term is broader than an abusive remark and is valued as assessment.
The passage concerns the weight of a discerning viewer’s evaluation.

questions.stem: The comparison to “Nature’s journeymen” chiefly ridicules actors whose performance
choices: shows insufficient knowledge of a particular manual trade
makes human behavior look badly manufactured
depends on elaborate costumes instead of spoken dialogue
reveals too much sympathy for ordinary working people
rationales: The craft comparison is figurative, not an assessment of vocational accuracy.
The imagined makers produce defective human imitations, matching the strutting and bellowing Hamlet criticizes.
The criticism concerns gait, accent, and exaggerated behavior, not costume expense.
No such sympathetic portrayal is described.

questions.stem: Hamlet objects to clowns’ added laughter primarily because it
choices: draws spectators toward the performer’s separate display while a consequential part of the play requires attention
makes serious spectators unable to hear the musical accompaniment
exposes the author’s uncertainty about the intended ending
prevents the actors from receiving sufficient applause
rationales: He says the audience may laugh while a necessary question of the play should be considered.
No musical accompaniment is mentioned.
The objection concerns unauthorized performer display, not the author’s indecision.
The problem is the kind and timing of attention, not too little acclaim.

questions.stem: The passage presents Hamlet’s ideal of performance as
choices: formal dignity maintained by suppressing comic material
emotional spontaneity protected from textual constraints
expressive action governed by judgment
popular amusement measured by the loudest response
rationales: He criticizes distracting clowning, not the existence of comedy itself.
He insists that clowns keep to what is written and that actors use discretion.
He asks for passion, restraint, coordination, and attention to the work’s purpose.
He distrusts noise and privileges discerning response over mass laughter.

questions.stem: The repeated opposition between “must go” and “must stay” initially establishes
choices: a direct conflict over whether Jane’s departure will be governed by her decision or Rochester’s insistence
Rochester’s acceptance that Jane has already decided to leave
a shared plan whose practical details remain uncertain
Jane’s inability to understand that Rochester is her employer
rationales: The speakers issue incompatible necessities concerning her departure.
His insistence that she stay resists that decision.
Their stated plans directly conflict rather than merely requiring details.
Her response contests his claim over her, not his identity or position.

questions.stem: Jane’s question about being an “automaton” challenges the assumption that she
choices: prefers mechanical routine to the uncertainties of affection
is incapable of carrying out her work independently
can be treated as if she lacks inward feeling
has secretly arranged to replace Rochester in the household
rationales: She asserts the depth of her feelings rather than a preference for routine.
Her challenge is not a confession of practical incompetence.
She immediately glosses the image as a machine without feelings.
The image concerns emotional personhood, not an employment scheme.

questions.stem: The images of bread and water make anticipated separation appear
choices: an opportunity to acquire greater material wealth
the loss of something essential to emotional life, figured through the removal of basic nourishment
a manageable inconvenience in Jane’s daily schedule
a punishment Jane believes she has earned
rationales: Nothing in the images promises enrichment.
The threatened loss is figured through basic nourishment.
The images intensify the loss rather than minimizing it.
She protests deprivation and does not concede deserving it.

questions.stem: The list “poor, obscure, plain, and little” prepares for Jane’s claim by
choices: showing that she accepts Rochester’s right to judge her value
establishing that her account of herself is physically impartial
explaining why affection cannot survive differences of income
separating social disadvantage from spiritual worth
rationales: The speech rejects the inference that those qualities make her lesser.
The list participates in an urgent argument, not an independent neutral assessment.
She declares the strength of affection despite unequal circumstances.
She follows the list by insisting that she possesses as much soul and heart as Rochester.

questions.stem: The imagined meeting at “God’s feet” chiefly permits Jane to
choices: deny that earthly choices have any moral significance
confirm Rochester’s superior authority in religious matters
assert an equality of personhood that she presents as independent of customary and material distinctions
postpone every demand for recognition until after death
rationales: She continues to judge Rochester’s proposed marriage and her own freedom.
No such authority is granted in the speech.
She explicitly moves beyond custom and mortal flesh to a relation between spirits.
She immediately insists that they are equal now: “as we are.”

questions.stem: Jane’s movement from “as we are” to “and yet not so” indicates that she
choices: qualifies equality by judging their present choices
withdraws her belief that she possesses a soul and heart
admits that Rochester has correctly understood her wish to stay
abandons moral judgment in favor of financial calculation
rationales: She affirms equal personhood but then condemns the union she believes he intends.
The qualification concerns conduct and circumstance, not her humanity.
She continues to demand release and departure.
Her objection concerns sympathy, love, and the union’s integrity.

questions.stem: The contrast between Rochester’s bird image and Jane’s response centers on
choices: whether a natural metaphor can accurately describe the weather
whether she prefers Ireland’s landscape to Thornfield’s gardens
whether her physical strength exceeds Rochester’s
whether Jane’s struggle is an irrational movement to be restrained or an expression of deliberate human freedom
rationales: The bird is applied to Jane, not to the surrounding conditions.
The images concern agency, not geographical preference.
The exchange contests the meaning of her struggle rather than measuring strength.
He describes a struggling bird; she rejects the image and names deliberate human freedom.

questions.stem: The statement that Jane stands “erect before him” gives physical form to
choices: her intention to leave without hearing another word
her asserted independence
her regret that she has spoken too forcefully
her willingness to accept restraint as reassurance
rationales: She remains in the exchange and responds to the offer.
It follows her declaration of will and her successful effort to free herself.
No regret is stated at that moment.
She has just escaped the embrace rather than accepted its restraint.

questions.stem: Rochester’s offer of his “hand,” “heart,” and “possessions” combines
choices: a declaration of love and marriage with an offer to share the material resources he possesses
spiritual equality with a rejection of worldly resources
an apology with a promise to dismiss Jane from employment
a demand for obedience with a refusal to discuss marriage
rationales: The sequence joins marriage and love to a share of property.
Possessions are explicitly included rather than rejected.
The offer asks for a shared life, not her dismissal.
The offer is a proposal, though its surrounding power relations remain open to analysis.

questions.stem: The pause marked by wind and birdsong changes the exchange by
choices: replacing the conflict with a natural assurance that their wishes coincide
confirming that both characters have resolved their doubts
creating space after the urgent contest of wills
showing that Jane has become indifferent to Rochester’s words
rationales: The pause permits renewed explanation but does not establish that their intentions are already identical.
Jane still needs explanation, and the passage does not establish settled agreement.
Speech gives way to listening, tears, and quiet before the invitation to explain.
Her tears and continued engagement indicate feeling, not indifference.

questions.stem: The phrase “got rid of her two most deserving daughters” gives the opening a tone of
choices: surprised disbelief
solemn moral instruction
unqualified sorrow
satisfaction sharpened by irony about the practical objective underlying Mrs. Bennet’s delight in the marriages
rationales: The marriages are treated as accomplished facts rather than doubtful events.
The phrasing is pointed and ironic, not a formal lesson addressed to the reader.
Mrs. Bennet is delighted, and the narrator’s phrasing is comic rather than mournful.
The blunt idiom complicates the celebration of marriage by exposing a practical maternal objective.

questions.stem: The narrator’s wish that Mrs. Bennet had become “sensible, amiable, well-informed” chiefly
choices: explains why Mr. Bennet no longer visits his daughters
raises an improvement that the account then denies
announces a transformation concealed from the other characters
attributes the daughters’ marriages to their mother’s education
rationales: The next paragraph describes his increased visits to Elizabeth.
The hypothetical desirable change contrasts with her continued nervousness and silliness.
The narrator explicitly says that her familiar traits persist.
No improved education is credited with producing the marriages.

questions.stem: The suggestion that Mr. Bennet might not relish “domestic felicity in so unusual a form” implies that
choices: long familiarity with his wife’s faults complicates the prospect of an ideally improved domestic relationship
he intends to prevent his wife from visiting their daughters
his daughters’ marriages have eliminated his enjoyment of irony
he has long concealed his admiration for his wife’s learning
rationales: The joke makes an ideal change potentially unsettling because it would be unfamiliar to him.
No such intention is stated.
The passage continues to characterize him through an ironic perspective.
The imagined learning is precisely what she has not acquired.

questions.stem: Mr. Bennet’s unexpected visits to Pemberley most directly demonstrate
choices: a determination to supervise Darcy’s management of the estate
a preference for formal invitations over familiar access
affection expressed through a changed habit
resentment that Elizabeth has acquired greater wealth than he has
rationales: No supervisory purpose is supplied.
He particularly enjoys arriving when least expected.
Missing Elizabeth draws him from home more often than other motives do.
The narrator explicitly names affection rather than financial resentment.

questions.stem: The account of Jane and Bingley’s move qualifies their amiability by
choices: revealing that their affection for Elizabeth has disappeared
suggesting that even their unusually generous temperaments do not make constant proximity to relations desirable
suggesting that their marriage is chiefly a financial arrangement
proving that they share the sisters’ hostility toward every neighbor
rationales: Their new home keeps the sisters within thirty miles and adds to their happiness.
The proximity of relations is undesirable even to his easy temper and her affectionate heart.
The paragraph does not make that claim.
The account identifies a particular difficulty, not universal hostility.

questions.stem: Kitty’s improvement is attributed most clearly to
choices: a new understanding produced by formal academic study
a sudden increase in inherited wealth
a private decision to abandon all family relationships
a changed social environment
rationales: The passage emphasizes society, attention, and management rather than schooling.
No inheritance is described as the cause.
