Her improvement occurs within different family relationships.
The narrator connects her progress with her older sisters’ company and removal from Lydia’s influence.

questions.stem: The repeated comparative forms “less irritable, less ignorant, and less insipid” characterize Kitty’s progress as
choices: a change in appearance that leaves character untouched
an achievement that makes her superior to every sister
a relative improvement defined by diminished faults rather than an uncomplicated arrival at perfection
a deterioration concealed by the narrator’s polite phrasing
rationales: The named qualities concern disposition and understanding, not appearance.
No comprehensive ranking of all the sisters follows.
The phrasing identifies reductions in faults rather than an idealized complete transformation.
The narrator explicitly calls the change advantageous and great improvement.

questions.stem: Mary’s changed circumstances are presented through a combination of
choices: social obligation and reduced unfavorable comparison
romantic disappointment and a refusal to remain at home
intellectual triumph and the admiration of a new audience
economic necessity and a plan to seek paid employment
rationales: She must keep her mother company and no longer faces the same comparison with her sisters’ beauty.
She remains at home, and no romantic disappointment is described.
Her continued moralizing is noted, but no triumph or admiring audience is established.
Neither employment nor financial necessity is given as her motive.

questions.stem: The assertion that Lydia and Wickham’s characters “suffered no revolution” chiefly
choices: introduces a political event that interrupts the family history
indicates that the narrator can no longer assess their motives
suggests that marriage has made them morally exemplary
sets their continuing habits and hopes against the changes reported in the lives of other family members
rationales: “Revolution” refers figuratively to character change.
The narrator immediately describes Wickham’s continuing hopes.
The surrounding account continues to expose ingratitude and opportunistic hopes.
Their unchanged expectations follow accounts of relocation and improvement elsewhere in the family.

questions.stem: The selection’s sequence of family outcomes supports an interpretation of the ending as
choices: a single transformation shared equally by every household
a differentiated account of change and continuity
a retreat from social observation into purely private emotion
a rejection of marriage as a possible source of happiness
rationales: The passage repeatedly distinguishes outcomes rather than making them uniform.
The narrator distributes happiness, adaptation, improvement, and persistent faults unevenly.
Relations, company, habits, and status remain central to the account.
Jane and Elizabeth’s happiness is acknowledged even as other consequences are qualified.

questions.stem: The account of deaths among the crew before their request chiefly
choices: explains why Walton has already abandoned the expedition
shows that the sailors have exaggerated an uneventful voyage
establishes the actual cost of the expedition before its dangers are redescribed as a test of courage
makes Victor responsible for every earlier navigational choice
rationales: He says that he has not yet conceived of returning if freed.
The described cold, ice, and deaths contradict that minimizing account.
The narrative establishes real losses before Victor calls their concern an imagination or trial of danger.
The passage does not assign him command of the voyage.

questions.stem: The crew’s demand is specifically conditional on
choices: the ship’s release from the ice
Victor’s recovery from his illness
a guarantee that no further hardship will occur
Walton’s receipt of permission from his sister
rationales: They ask that a free passage lead south rather than into renewed danger.
His health is not their stated condition.
They seek a direction of travel, not an impossible guarantee of safety.
No such permission is requested.

questions.stem: Walton’s question about refusing the demand “in justice, or even in possibility” reveals
choices: a decision to surrender command before hearing the sailors
indifference to the distinction between responsibility and ambition
certainty that the crew’s request violates an existing promise
pressure from both the justice of the request and the practical difficulty of refusing the crew
rationales: The hesitation occurs after their request and before his decision.
His hesitation makes that distinction consequential.
He does not identify such a promise and questions whether refusal is just.
He considers fairness and feasibility before Victor intervenes.

questions.stem: Victor’s account of why the expedition was “glorious” depends on the idea that
choices: scientific discovery matters only when it requires little sacrifice
danger gives achievement its claim to honor
the sailors’ names have already been publicly celebrated
the crew originally sought private wealth rather than public benefit
rationales: His reasoning makes difficulty and sacrifice central.
He says the undertaking was glorious because courage would confront terror and death.
He describes anticipated future acclaim rather than an accomplished reception.
He appeals to benefit for humanity and public honor, not private profit.

questions.stem: The imagined return to “warm firesides” functions in Victor’s speech as
choices: a deliberately diminishing picture of comfort used to make the alternative to continued danger seem shameful
a recollection of the expedition’s successful earlier homecoming
a compassionate acknowledgment of the sailors’ family obligations
a practical proposal for protecting the sickest crew members
rationales: He reduces retreat to seeking comfort and associates it with shame.
The return is imagined, not remembered.
His tone mocks the return rather than honoring its relational obligations.
The phrase belongs to an appeal to continue, not a care plan.

questions.stem: The contrast between mutable ice and firm hearts primarily
choices: suggests that the sailors should change their purpose as readily as ice changes
acknowledges that determination cannot affect the crew’s circumstances
turns a physical obstacle into a test of resolve
offers a reliable scientific prediction about when the sea will open
rationales: He urges firmness, not adaptability of purpose.
The speech insists on determination as the answer.
Victor figuratively makes steadfast will seem able to outlast the ice.
The claim is exhortation rather than measured forecasting.

questions.stem: Walton’s description of Victor’s voice and eye most clearly indicates
choices: his belief that the sailors have misunderstood the words
his attraction to the speech’s heroic appearance and his understanding of its power over the listeners
his suspicion that Victor has rehearsed a deliberate deception
his rejection of emotional appeal as an improper form of leadership
rationales: He reports their response but does not attribute it to misunderstanding.
He presents the modulation and heroic appearance as reasons the men are moved.
No such suspicion is voiced.
He admires the appeal and hopes their courage will return.

questions.stem: Victor’s collapse after the speech creates a contrast between
choices: the crew’s physical weakness and his restored health
the simplicity of his argument and his inability to express it
Walton’s fear of mutiny and the sailors’ immediate violence
the force of his exhortation and his bodily condition
rationales: The described weakness is Victor’s, not a recovery.
He has delivered a forceful extended speech, not failed to speak.
The crew retires; no immediate violence occurs.
Momentary vigor gives way to near lifelessness after he urges extraordinary endurance.

questions.stem: Walton’s promise not to lead the men farther north if they insist is qualified by
choices: his demand that they apologize before the ship turns south
his certainty that the ice will prevent any decision
his continuing wish that the men will interpret their reluctance as a failure of courage and reconsider
his announcement that Victor will replace him as captain
rationales: No apology is made a condition.
He still considers what will happen if the ship is freed.
He agrees conditionally while expressing a wish that their courage return.
No transfer of command is proposed.

questions.stem: The September 7 entry suggests that Walton’s decision to return
choices: changes his course more clearly than his values
resolves the conflict by adopting the crew’s account of courage
brings an immediate sense of gratitude toward the crew
follows his discovery that the expedition had no possible utility
rationales: He consents but continues to call the result cowardice, blasted hopes, and injustice.
He still describes the outcome through cowardice and indecision.
His language is resentful rather than grateful.
He mourns the loss of his hopes rather than declaring them worthless.

questions.stem: Darcy’s initial silence and agitated movement chiefly prepare the reader for
choices: a calm negotiation whose terms Elizabeth already knows
an emotionally charged declaration that breaks through his unsuccessful effort to keep his feelings under control
a report about Lady Catherine that Elizabeth has requested
an apology that he has carefully rehearsed with Elizabeth
rationales: Elizabeth is astonished by the proposal and does not share an established plan.
He rises, walks, and begins abruptly after struggling with his feelings.
He opens with his own feelings, not requested news of his aunt.
No joint rehearsal or intended apology is described.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s silence is important because Darcy
choices: uses it as evidence that she knows his earlier misconduct
abandons his intention to explain the strength of his feelings
correctly understands that she has already accepted him
takes surprise as permission to continue
rationales: The silence is not interpreted in that way.
He continues at length after reading the silence as encouragement.
Her eventual refusal shows that he misreads the silence.
The narrator says he considers her silence sufficient encouragement despite her astonishment.

questions.stem: The statement that Darcy is “not more eloquent on the subject of tenderness than of pride” chiefly
choices: suggests that he conceals his social objections with unusual skill
praises his ability to place Elizabeth’s feelings before his own
places sincere affection beside a prideful explanation that makes the declaration injurious to its listener
distinguishes the narrator’s certainty from Elizabeth’s inability to hear
rationales: The objections are conspicuous and injurious, not successfully concealed.
The speech’s emphasis on pride undermines its reception.
His declaration dwells on her inferiority as well as his love.
Elizabeth hears and reacts; the issue is not physical or interpretive incapacity.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s movement from compassion to resentment is caused chiefly by
choices: the manner in which Darcy describes overcoming her inferiority
her suspicion that his visit is intended to amuse Lady Catherine
her discovery that Darcy has already proposed to another woman
a realization that his financial circumstances are worse than expected
rationales: His account wounds her as he explains the obstacles he believes he has conquered.
No such purpose is established.
No other proposal is disclosed here.
His finances are not revised in the passage.

questions.stem: The contrast between Darcy’s spoken anxiety and his apparent certainty reveals
choices: a shared understanding that Elizabeth will delay rather than refuse
the narrator’s decision to conceal Darcy’s proposal from the reader
Elizabeth’s inability to distinguish speech from physical action
a discrepancy between the uncertainty Darcy expresses and the acceptance Elizabeth believes his manner confidently anticipates
rationales: She intends refusal, not a mutually planned delay.
The proposal is directly reported.
She explicitly compares the two sources of evidence.
Elizabeth sees little doubt of success in his manner despite his language.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s opening reference to the conventional expression of gratitude allows her to
choices: avoid expressing any judgment about Darcy’s conduct
acknowledge an expected response before refusing it
accept the proposal while criticizing Darcy’s timing
suggest that she has already thanked him on an earlier occasion
rationales: She proceeds to judge both his manner and his actions.
She names the usual obligation but explains that she cannot feel the gratitude it presumes.
Her reply rejects the proposal.
No earlier thanks are asserted.

questions.stem: Darcy’s question about being rejected “with so little endeavour at civility” shifts attention toward
choices: the apparent discourtesy of Elizabeth’s response before the reasons she considers sufficient to justify it
the practical arrangements needed to cancel their engagement
his admission that his own speech has been deliberately cruel
Elizabeth’s inability to understand the words of his proposal
rationales: He asks why her response lacks courtesy, prompting her to recall his own insulting declaration.
There has been no accepted engagement.
He does not make that admission here.
Her answer demonstrates that she understands and objects to them.

questions.stem: Elizabeth’s question about his professing love “against your will, against your reason, and even against your character” chiefly
choices: asks him to repeat a point she failed to hear clearly
separates his social pride from the content of the proposal
turns his account of resistance into an indictment of his manner
concedes that her acceptance would damage his reputation
rationales: The question is confrontational and interpretive, not a request for repetition.
It exposes how that pride shapes the declaration itself.
She repeats the logic of his struggle to show why gratitude is unreasonable.
She challenges the insulting framing rather than accepting its judgment.

questions.stem: The accusation concerning Jane and Bingley expands the dispute from
choices: uncertain attraction to an agreed plan for family reconciliation
the offense Elizabeth experiences herself to an intervention she believes has damaged her sister’s happiness
social inequality to a disagreement about inheritance law
private resentment to a confession of Elizabeth’s own deceit
rationales: No reconciliation plan emerges.
Elizabeth moves from how Darcy addressed her to what she believes he did to her sister.
Inheritance law is not the focus of the accusation.
She accuses Darcy rather than confessing deceit herself.

questions.stem: Darcy’s admission that he separated Bingley from Jane most clearly
choices: reveals that Elizabeth has confused him with another person
accepts Elizabeth’s account of the action as wholly unjust
withdraws the proposal in order to protect his friend
confirms the action while defending its justification
rationales: He identifies himself as the person who acted.
His stated pride in the result resists that judgment.
He acknowledges the action but does not explicitly withdraw the proposal at this point.
He does not deny the separation and says he was kinder to Bingley than to himself.

questions.stem: Victor’s distinction between former “burning hatred” and present justification chiefly attempts to
choices: present the creature’s destruction as a duty now justified by reason rather than the earlier force of revenge
admit that the creature’s violence was morally justified
show that he has forgotten the deaths of his friends
withdraw his request that Walton pursue the creature
rationales: He still desires the creature’s death but claims a changed moral basis for it.
He continues to condemn the creature’s actions.
He recalls their destruction as part of his justification.
He explicitly renews the request before later qualifying what he can ask.

questions.stem: The acknowledgment that he was “bound” to assure the creature’s well-being introduces
choices: a duty he says he has fulfilled without exception
a promise the creature made before receiving life
an obligation his later argument seeks to subordinate
a legal contract Walton is required to enforce
rationales: The passage does not establish complete fulfillment; he explains competing claims.
The obligation belongs to Victor as creator, not to a prior promise by the creature.
He recognizes a creator’s duty but claims a greater duty toward humanity.
The speech makes a moral argument, not a legal demand.

questions.stem: Victor’s defense of refusing a companion relies chiefly on
choices: his admission that no creator has duties toward a created being
his ranking of duties according to the greater amount of happiness or misery he associates with humanity
his certainty that the creature has ceased to want companionship
the belief that creation is technically impossible to repeat
rationales: He explicitly acknowledges such duties before ranking them.
He says the greater proportion of happiness or misery gives his own species stronger claims.
He does not make that claim.
Technical inability is not his stated justification.

questions.stem: The contrast between “selfish and vicious motives” and “reason and virtue” is best understood as
choices: a settled judgment the creature has already accepted
a difference between Walton’s past conduct and the crew’s present behavior
the narrator’s independent verification of Victor’s moral progress
Victor’s interpretation of his changing motives
rationales: The creature is not present to accept this account.
The contrast concerns Victor’s earlier and current request.
Walton records the speech; the claim is Victor’s self-assessment.
He presents the distinction while explaining why he renews the same request.

questions.stem: The sentence beginning “Yet I cannot ask you to renounce your country and friends” chiefly
choices: reproaches Walton for having no attachments outside the expedition
announces that Walton has agreed to remain in the Arctic
qualifies the renewed request by acknowledging attachments that Victor cannot reasonably require Walton to sacrifice
proves that Victor now considers the creature harmless
rationales: Victor explicitly recognizes his country and friends.
Walton is returning to England.
He acknowledges obligations that make imposing the pursuit on Walton problematic.
He continues to worry about the creature as an instrument of mischief.

questions.stem: The admission “I may still be misled by passion” complicates Victor’s speech by
choices: questioning his claim to act from reason alone
establishing that every event in his narrative was invented
withdrawing his belief that the creature has harmed anyone
transferring responsibility for his past actions to Walton
rationales: The possibility of passion unsettles the moral certainty asserted earlier.
Doubt about judgment does not establish wholesale fabrication.
He does not deny the harms he has named.
The statement qualifies his request rather than assigning his history to Walton.

questions.stem: Victor’s anticipation of joining “the beloved dead” makes death appear to him as
choices: punishment that he accepts as deserved repayment
proof that his earlier recollections were physically present visions
a new opportunity to achieve public scientific fame
an anticipated release from suffering through reunion with the people whose deaths he has continued to mourn
rationales: He presents comfort rather than an explicit acceptance of punishment.
The speech offers an expectation at death, not verification of literal appearances.
The image concerns personal loss and reunion, not fame.
He calls the hour happy and pictures hastening into their arms.

questions.stem: The phrase “even if it be only the apparently innocent one” broadens the warning against ambition by
choices: excluding intellectual work from the dangers he describes
including the pursuit of scientific distinction
identifying Walton’s voyage as a purely commercial enterprise
making personal happiness dependent on exceptional achievement
rationales: The phrase expressly includes that work.
Victor extends the warning to an aspiration that might seem harmless.
The warning concerns science and discovery, not a commercial classification.
He advises tranquillity and avoidance of ambition at this point.

questions.stem: The final question “Yet why do I say this?” introduces
choices: a self-questioning qualification that leaves success available as a possibility despite the preceding warning
a firm resolution to abandon every hope associated with discovery
a request that Walton explain a word he has misunderstood
an accusation that the crew has prevented his scientific work
rationales: Victor immediately allows that another person may succeed where he failed.
The following possibility of success preserves some attraction to the ideal.
The question is self-directed rather than a vocabulary request.
The crew is not the question’s stated subject.

questions.stem: The final speech as a whole presents Victor as
choices: unable to formulate any account of duty or responsibility
wholly detached from the desires that organized his life
self-critical yet still drawn to the values he questions
confident that Walton will complete an obligation he has fully defined
rationales: He offers an elaborate account, though it is unstable and self-qualified.
His renewed pursuit request and final qualification contradict complete detachment.
He acknowledges disturbed judgment and warns against ambition while retaining justification and possible success.
He leaves judgment to Walton and recognizes practical and moral limits on the request.

projects.title: A cabinet of contested objects
projects.brief: Construct a small fictional collection whose objects tell a story that its curator only partly understands. Use the opening of “The Yellow Wallpaper” to study how an apparently appreciative description can also reveal restriction. Your cabinet must develop its own situation and tension; it is not a model of the narrator’s room.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the descriptions
stages.instructions: Read the supplied opening. Choose six details from at least three different paragraphs. For each, record literal meaning, a possible implication, and one limit on that implication. Form a claim about how attractive surroundings coexist with unease.
stages.submit: Six-entry evidence ledger and a provisional claim.

stages.title: Invent the collection
stages.instructions: Choose a topic and invent a curator, an intended visitor, and an unstated conflict. Write five object labels of 100–140 words each. Each label must contain one exact physical detail and one qualification that complicates the curator’s confident account. Add a 150-word private note that changes, without completely overturning, how a visitor reads the labels.
stages.submit: Five labels and the private note, clearly marked as original fiction.

stages.title: Arrange a visual argument
stages.instructions: Draw or digitally compose the cabinet on one or two pages. Placement, scale, borders, and connections must imply relationships among the objects. Attach a key explaining three design decisions; provide a plain-text description so the arrangement remains accessible.
stages.submit: Cabinet plate, design key, and text description.

stages.title: Argue from source and artifact
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how description can make care and constraint difficult to separate in Gilman’s opening. Use at least four short source details and address one competing interpretation. Then write a 250–350-word self-analysis quoting two labels and explaining how diction, placement, and audience create your cabinet’s effect.
stages.submit: Literary argument and self-analysis with source references.

stages.title: Test what the objects imply
stages.instructions: Give a reader the labels before the private note. Ask for a claim about the curator and two supporting words. Then reveal the note and ask what changes. If working alone, reread after a day and write two competing readings. Revise at least one label and one visual relationship in response.
stages.submit: Feedback, before-and-after excerpts, and a 150-word revision rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on inference
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify one implication you could support and one you had to abandon. Explain how the difference changes your reading of a fresh passage. Credit the Gutenberg edition and any visual sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The correspondence bureau
projects.brief: Create an exchange in which several writers act on the same incomplete information. The opening of Pride and Prejudice provides a model for separating what a person knows from what a person hopes. Your task is to make readers infer priorities without giving them an all-knowing explanation.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Establish the limits of knowledge
stages.instructions: Read the Bennet conversation. Build a table of eight claims labeled stated fact, reported information, warranted inference, or unsupported assumption. Identify the speaker or narrator responsible for each. Explain any classification that could reasonably be disputed.
stages.submit: Knowledge table with textual references.

stages.title: Write the dossier
stages.instructions: Invent one event known incompletely by three correspondents. Write six dated letters or messages totaling 750–1,000 words. Each writer must know one fact the others lack and mistake one inference for certainty. Supply a private 150-word factual record for assessment, kept separate from the letters.
stages.submit: Six-message dossier and factual record.

stages.title: Map information visually
stages.instructions: Design a dated information map showing who knows each fact and when. Use line styles as well as color; distinguish fact, rumor, and inference. The reader must be able to test the map against exact sentences in the letters.
stages.submit: Information map and a text equivalent.

stages.title: Defend the reading
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Austen exposes the difference between desire and knowledge. Use four details, including one from the narrator and one from the dialogue. In a 250-word self-analysis, explain how two correspondents attempt to persuade their recipients and how readers can detect a gap in their reasoning.
stages.submit: Literary argument and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Run a certainty audit
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to list five things the dossier proves and five it merely suggests before seeing the factual record. Compare the list with your intentions. Revise two messages to repair either accidental confusion or over-obvious disclosure. A solo alternative is a delayed audit from two readers’ imagined positions, explicitly labeled as your own work.
stages.submit: Audit record, two revisions, and explanation of the changed evidence.

stages.title: Reflect on restraint
stages.instructions: Write 200–250 words about a conclusion that seemed plausible but exceeded the evidence. Explain how you would qualify it in an AP-style response. Provide credits and identify invented material.
stages.submit: Reflection and attribution note.

projects.title: The disputed exhibition label
projects.brief: Curate two defensible readings of one passage without pretending that they are equally supported at every point. stages.title: Collect and rank evidence

stages.submit: Evidence matrix and a 150-word ranking rationale.

stages.title: Compose the exhibition

stages.title: Design the encounter

stages.title: Make a judgment
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word argument defending the reading you find better supported while giving the other its strongest evidence. Use at least five source details and explain their relative weight. Add 250 words analyzing how your label wording and layout could steer a visitor unfairly, and what you did about that risk.
stages.submit: Comparative literary argument and curatorial self-analysis.

stages.title: Invite an adversarial reading

stages.title: Reflect on sufficiency

projects.title: Two encounters, one stranger

stages.title: Analyze a layered portrait

stages.title: Compose two encounters

stages.title: Create a double portrait

stages.title: Explain the construction

stages.title: Test the person behind the viewpoints

stages.submit: Response record, revised passages, and a rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on judgment

projects.title: A decision heard in three movements
projects.brief: Compose a sequence in which a person approaches, resists, and partly acts on a desire they cannot yet name. stages.title: Trace the pressure

stages.title: Write three connected poems
stages.instructions: Create three poems of 16–24 lines each: anticipation, resistance, and an incomplete decision. Keep one recurring sensory image, but change its function in each poem. Use at least one meaningful syntactic interruption and one action that leaves the motive partly unresolved.
stages.submit: Three-poem sequence, 48–72 lines total.

stages.title: Score the changing desire

stages.title: Argue the complexity
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Chopin makes awareness both attractive and disturbing. Use four details, including the paradoxical light and the sea. Add 300 words analyzing how your recurring image, interruptions, and intended reader shape the sequence’s mixed response.
stages.submit: Source argument and craft self-analysis.

stages.title: Listen for premature resolution

stages.submit: Reading notes, marked revisions, and a 150-word rationale.

projects.title: The unspoken negotiation
projects.brief: Write a short scene in which two people appear to discuss an ordinary object while negotiating a deeper disagreement. Use the opening of A Doll’s House to study how gestures, affection, and material exchanges can carry conflict. The scene must work for a reader without requiring actors or a public performance.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Track the exchange
stages.instructions: Build a beat sheet for six moments in Nora and Torvald’s conversation. For each, record the spoken topic, an action or prop, an implied desire, and who temporarily controls the exchange. Include the money gift without assuming it settles everything.
stages.submit: Six-beat analytical sheet.

stages.title: Compose the scene
stages.instructions: Write a 6–8-minute scene, approximately 850–1,100 spoken words, for two characters and one consequential object. Include at least eight purposeful stage directions, a temporary change in control, and an ending that alters the immediate situation while preserving a deeper tension.
stages.submit: Script with speaker names and playable directions.

stages.title: Block the disagreement
stages.instructions: Create a six-frame blocking storyboard keyed to the beats. Show distance, gesture, object possession, and a sightline in each frame. Supply a text description of the movement; artistic realism is not required.
stages.submit: Blocking storyboard and movement description.

stages.title: Defend the dramatic choices
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about the relationship between affection and authority in Ibsen’s opening. Add 300 words analyzing two moments when your stage directions change the meaning of spoken lines. Explain the intended audience response without claiming every reader must respond identically.
stages.submit: Literary argument and dramatic self-analysis.

stages.title: Conduct a table read
stages.instructions: Read both roles aloud or invite a partner. Mark places where a line explains what an action could show and where an action is unplayable. Revise one exchange and two directions. Record how these changes affect the balance of control.
stages.submit: Read-through notes and revised script passages.

stages.title: Reflect on resolution
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish the scene’s immediate settlement from its remaining conflict. Explain how that distinction could sharpen an essay about a different play. Credit the translation and any other sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The defense that reveals too much
projects.brief: Construct a narrator who wants to justify a questionable decision and inadvertently reveals a competing story. Use “The Tell-Tale Heart” to study the gap between a voice’s intended argument and its effect. Choose a nonviolent situation if preferred; intensity should come from language and reasoning, not sensational events.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate the roles
stages.instructions: Create three columns: what Poe composes, what the narrator claims, and what the addressed listener is asked to believe. Enter six moments from the supplied opening. Mark two places where the narrator’s proof may undermine the intended conclusion.
stages.submit: Six-moment role chart.

stages.title: Write the defense
stages.instructions: Invent a disputed decision and a narrator addressing a specific but unnamed listener. Write a 750–950-word defense containing three self-justifying claims, two revealing digressions, and one detail the narrator dismisses too quickly. Keep a separate 150-word author’s design note; do not insert it into the fictional voice.
stages.submit: Fictional defense and separate design note.

stages.title: Design a critical edition
stages.instructions: Lay out two pages of the defense with five numbered marginal notes written by an invented editor. The notes must distinguish quotation, inference, and uncertainty, rather than simply call the narrator a liar. Provide the notes in reading order as plain text.
stages.submit: Two-page annotated edition and linear notes.

stages.title: Analyze persuasion and composition
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Poe makes self-justification reveal more than its speaker intends. Add 300 words analyzing the narrator, imagined listener, and actual reader in your own artifact. Quote two rhetorical choices and explain their competing effects.
stages.submit: Literary argument and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the unintended disclosure
stages.instructions: Give a reader the defense without the notes. Ask what the narrator wants believed and what the reader instead suspects, with evidence for both. Revise a clue that is either invisible or too obvious. If alone, perform the same task after a delayed rereading and label it a solo test.
stages.submit: Response record, a revised passage, and an explanatory note.

stages.title: Reflect on attribution
stages.instructions: Write 200–250 words explaining why a narrator’s claim is not an author’s endorsement. Use a choice from your artifact and a source detail. Credit sources and identify the fictional editor.
stages.submit: Reflection and attribution statement.

projects.title: A remembered afternoon
projects.brief: Write a story in which an older narrator recalls an event that the younger self understood differently. Jane Eyre offers a model for preserving childhood perception while marking later knowledge. Your narrator may gain understanding without becoming completely certain about everyone else’s motives.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Locate the two selves
stages.instructions: Identify six moments in Jane’s opening that belong mainly to immediate perception, later interpretation, or both. Explain one borderline example. List two things the narration cannot directly know about another character.
stages.submit: Perspective ledger and knowledge limits.

stages.title: Compose the memory
stages.instructions: Write a 900–1,150-word retrospective story of one afternoon. Include three brief signals of later understanding, two passages limited to the younger self’s sensory attention, and one unresolved judgment. Do not introduce an omniscient account of another person’s unspoken thoughts.
stages.submit: Original story and a marked copy identifying the required features.

stages.title: Draw the knowledge layers
stages.instructions: Create a two-track timeline: what the younger self perceives and what the older self adds. Anchor eight entries to exact sentences and use a third line for what remains unknown. Provide a text version with the same entries.
stages.submit: Knowledge timeline and text equivalent.

stages.title: Argue the perspective’s effect
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Brontë’s retrospective perspective shapes the opening’s treatment of exclusion and imaginative refuge. Add 300 words analyzing how your narrator’s intended audience affects the balance of explanation and restraint.
stages.submit: Source argument and self-analysis.

stages.title: Audit accidental omniscience
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to mark any sentence that seems to know another character’s private thoughts without a source. Revise those sentences into observation, attributed speech, or explicitly qualified inference. Also revise one hindsight comment that overexplains the child’s experience.
stages.submit: Audit, before-and-after sentences, and a revision rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on memory
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one insight gained through hindsight and one uncertainty hindsight could not resolve. State how this distinction affects your reading of a first-person account. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A story with an argumentative margin
projects.brief: Create a short fiction about a person absorbing someone else’s judgment, then build an analytical margin that demonstrates how a paragraph develops a claim. Use Pip’s changing view of his hands as a source model. The margin should explain the work’s choices without simply announcing what the author intended.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Build a source paragraph
stages.instructions: Write a 200–250-word paragraph on how Estella’s contempt changes Pip’s self-perception. Use three details that do different work: establish a starting point, explain a change, and complicate its result. Label the function of each sentence in a separate copy.
stages.submit: Analytical paragraph and sentence-function map.

stages.title: Write the fiction
stages.instructions: Compose a 650–850-word story in which an ordinary object acquires a humiliating or aspirational meaning during an encounter. Include a before-and-after perception, a figurative comparison that helps enact the change, and an ending with mixed feeling.
stages.submit: Original microfiction.

stages.title: Build the folio
stages.instructions: Design a two-page folio with the story on one side and three analytical annotations on the other. Connect each annotation to exact wording; vary line style to show claim, evidence, and commentary. Include a plain-text sequence of the annotations.
stages.submit: Annotated folio and accessible notes.

stages.title: Develop the full argument
stages.instructions: Expand the source paragraph into a 650–850-word argument about humiliation and attraction in Dickens’s scene. Give each paragraph a distinct role in the line of reasoning. Add 250–350 words analyzing how your story’s object, comparison, and ending create effects that your margin can actually demonstrate.
stages.submit: Literary argument, paragraph-role outline, and self-analysis.

stages.title: Run a commentary test
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to underline sentences that merely paraphrase evidence. For each, add or revise reasoning about a relationship, contrast, or change. Test whether any paragraph can be moved unchanged to another position; if so, strengthen its connection or explain why that order is defensible.
stages.submit: Reader or delayed solo audit and two revised paragraphs.

stages.title: Reflect on development
stages.instructions: Write 200–250 words comparing your earliest and final commentary. Identify one sentence that now explains an effect instead of labeling a device. Credit the source and any design materials.
stages.submit: Reflection with before-and-after quotation and credits.

projects.title: Three voices at the same performance
projects.brief: Create a literary listening room in which an observer, a performer, and another audience member respond differently to the same event. Study the limits of the observer’s knowledge in “The Harlem Dancer.” Your original voices must have their own situation; do not claim to supply the actual dancer’s unrecorded thoughts.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the observer
stages.instructions: Annotate six details in McKay’s poem: two descriptions of the crowd, two of the dancer, and two markers of the speaker’s perspective. Write a 200-word account of what the observer can see and what the observer infers.
stages.submit: Annotated poem and knowledge account.

stages.title: Compose the voices
stages.instructions: Invent a performance or public demonstration. Write three 20–28-line poems spoken by the observer, performer, and a second spectator. Retain three shared facts, but give each voice a different purpose and a distinct pattern of attention. No voice may conclusively explain the other two.
stages.submit: Three poems, 60–84 lines total, with a shared-fact list.

stages.title: Stage the listening room
stages.instructions: Create a three-station exhibition plan showing the order in which visitors encounter the voices. Supply a 90–120-word placard for each station, a 4–6-minute read-aloud script or optional recording, and a text description of the layout. Use placement to make comparison possible without ranking one voice as automatically true.
stages.submit: Exhibition plan, placards, and script or recording with transcript.

stages.title: Argue about recognition
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about the speaker’s attempt to recognize an inward self in McKay’s poem. Address the limitation of “I knew.” Add 300 words analyzing how your voices use diction, address, and omission to influence their listeners.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the boundaries of knowledge
stages.instructions: Ask a reader or listener to assign each claim to observation, inference, or uncertainty. A solo alternative is a delayed rereading in a different voice order. Revise one overconfident claim and one distinction between the voices; document how the changes affect interpretation.
stages.submit: Test record, revised passages, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on representation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one ethical or interpretive limit you chose to preserve when inventing another person’s voice. Distinguish your fiction from claims about McKay’s dancer. Credit sources and any audio or visual materials.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Questions for an absent listener
projects.brief: Make a small chapbook in which a speaker’s questions create a relationship with an addressee who cannot answer in an ordinary conversation. Use “The Lamb” to examine how questions, explanation, and blessing change the speaking situation. Your chapbook must develop a different relationship and cannot simply replace the lamb with another animal.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Map the encounter
stages.instructions: Read “The Lamb” and trace the pronouns, questions, promised answer, shared name, and blessing. For six moments, identify the speaker’s role and the addressee’s implied position. Explain whether the questions request unknown information.
stages.submit: Six-moment situation map and 150-word explanation.

stages.title: Write the exchange
stages.instructions: Choose an absent person, place, object, or abstraction as the addressee. Compose a 24–32-line address and a 24–32-line imagined response. The response must challenge one assumption in the address without explaining every uncertainty. Include a 150-word note defining the circumstances of speaking.
stages.submit: Two poems and a situation note.

stages.title: Design the chapbook
stages.instructions: Arrange the poems in an eight-page folded-book plan. Use page turns, blank space, and a recurring border element to distinguish question, attempted answer, and revised relation. Add a reading-order transcript and annotations on three consequential design choices.
stages.submit: Chapbook plan, transcript, and design annotations.

stages.title: Defend the relationship
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Blake’s questions become an affirmation of kinship. Add 250–350 words analyzing how the audience, pronouns, and address in your own work change between poems. Quote the words that create the change.
stages.submit: Source argument and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Read for a changing situation
stages.instructions: Have a reader identify where the relationship changes and cite a verbal or visual cue. If alone, read aloud after a break and mark the same points. Revise one question, one response, and one page turn so each has a distinct function.
stages.submit: Reading notes and three documented revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on address
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what became possible because the listener was absent or unable to answer conventionally. Identify one risk of making that listener too convenient for the speaker. Cite the displayed Blake edition and other sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A lexicon of divided attachment
projects.brief: Build a lexicon for something a speaker both values and resists, then use it to compose a poem whose language preserves that division. “America” models how nourishment and injury can occupy the same phrase. Your lexicon should investigate contextual meaning rather than offer interchangeable synonyms.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the word fields
stages.instructions: In “America,” collect twelve words or short phrases into overlapping fields of injury, strength, value, and decline. Explain three placements that belong in more than one field and one tempting association the poem does not support.
stages.submit: Annotated semantic map and explanations.

stages.title: Write the lexicon and poem
stages.instructions: Invent eight lexicon entries of 60–90 words each. Give each word a plain definition, a context that makes it attractive, a context that makes it troubling, and an original illustrative sentence. Then compose a 24–36-line lyric using at least five entries to develop one divided attachment.
stages.submit: Eight-entry lexicon and original lyric.

stages.title: Make connotation visible
stages.instructions: Design a two-page typographic map connecting the eight entries. Use weight, spacing, and connecting lines to show shared or conflicting associations. Include labels and a text description; do not rely only on red/green or positive/negative categories.
stages.submit: Semantic plate and accessible explanation.

stages.title: Argue for exact words
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how McKay’s diction sustains attachment within resistance. Examine at least four phrases in context. Add 300 words comparing three actual words in your poem with plausible replacements and explaining what each replacement would lose.
stages.submit: Literary argument and substitution-based self-analysis.

stages.title: Test a substitution
stages.instructions: Give a reader two versions of six lines, changing three key words in one version. Ask for different interpretations with evidence; do not identify the preferred version first. If alone, evaluate both after a day. Revise the poem and one lexicon entry based on the comparison.
stages.submit: Two test versions, response notes, and revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on precision
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify a word that became more complex through context rather than more obscure. Explain how the exercise changes your use of a thesaurus. Credit all borrowed definitions or write definitions independently and label them editorial.
stages.submit: Reflection and attribution note.

projects.title: The suitcase of remembered places
projects.brief: Create a folio in which a present object opens a remembered place that cannot simply be recovered. Study the fruit display in “The Tropics in New York” as a movement from sensation to memory to bodily response. Your work may be wholly fictional; personal disclosure is not required.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Follow the sensory movement
stages.instructions: Mark the present display, the remembered landscape, and the final bodily response in McKay’s poem. Choose six sensory details and explain how each changes the object’s significance rather than merely naming a sense.
stages.submit: Six-detail commentary and a three-part movement diagram.

stages.title: Compose the folio
stages.instructions: Invent one carried object and write a 450–600-word prose scene in which it triggers memory. Add a 20–28-line poem that revisits the same object through a different sense. The prose and poem must disagree in one meaningful emphasis without contradicting the basic facts.
stages.submit: Prose scene, companion poem, and a shared-fact note.

stages.title: Unpack the visual sequence
stages.instructions: Create a four-panel suitcase or drawer folio: present object, sensory association, remembered space, and altered present. Use drawing, collage, or labeled shapes. Add 60–90 words of captioning per panel and a continuous text description.
stages.submit: Four-panel folio with captions and text equivalent.

stages.title: Argue the object’s transformation
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how sensory abundance intensifies absence in McKay’s poem. Add 300 words analyzing how your prose, poem, and panels direct attention differently. Explain one rhetorical choice made for the folio’s intended viewer.
stages.submit: Literary argument and cross-form self-analysis.

stages.title: Test what is evoked
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the moment the object becomes more than an object, citing an image. Check whether the remembered place feels specific rather than generic. Revise two sensory details and one panel transition. A delayed solo read is an alternative.
stages.submit: Feedback or solo notes, revised details, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on sensory evidence
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why one image carries the feeling more effectively than an abstract emotion label. Identify a detail you removed because it was vivid but irrelevant. Credit text and images.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A field guide for a newcomer
projects.brief: Write a field guide that helps a newcomer understand an unfamiliar place through comparisons with a familiar one. Then make the guide acknowledge where those comparisons fail. “To One Coming North” supplies a model of initial enchantment, discomfort, and revised attachment.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Audit the source comparisons
stages.instructions: For the snow, water, shared homesickness, and final North/South comparison, identify what is compared, what quality transfers, and what should not transfer. Explain the sequence’s changing emotional work.
stages.submit: Four-entry comparison audit and a 200-word sequence account.

stages.title: Compose the guide
stages.instructions: Invent a newcomer with a specific familiar world. Write six field-guide entries of 100–140 words about an unfamiliar setting. Each must use a different consequential simile and include one limit on the comparison. Add a 20–24-line poem in which the newcomer revises two entries after living there.
stages.submit: Six entries and a revision poem.

stages.title: Draw the comparison plates
stages.instructions: Create three paired plates showing a subject beside its comparison image. Annotate the shared feature and one mismatch on each. Use labels, textures, or simple diagrams; include plain-text descriptions.
stages.submit: Three comparison plates with limits clearly marked.

stages.title: Argue for a changing analogy
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how McKay’s comparisons shape the newcomer’s anticipated response. Add 300 words explaining how your guide’s audience affects its vehicles and how the poem exposes the guide’s limits.
stages.submit: Literary argument and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Test transfer and overreach
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to use two entries to predict details of the new place, then identify which predictions your comparisons unintentionally invited. Revise two similes or their framing. A solo alternative is to list every plausible transferred property before choosing the intended ones.
stages.submit: Transfer test and revised entries with rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on usefulness
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain when a comparison clarifies and when it distorts. Use one successful and one revised example, and describe a transfer to reading an unfamiliar poem. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Three clocks for one life
projects.brief: Represent one changing condition through three different systems of time. Study how Sonnet 73 moves from a season to twilight to a fire, then turns that sequence toward love. Your triptych must develop a new argument rather than merely substitute three objects into Shakespeare’s pattern.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Explain the source sequence
stages.instructions: Create a chart for the seasonal, daily, and fire metaphors. Identify what each retains, what declines, and what the next metaphor adds. Write a 200-word account of the final couplet’s dependence on the sequence.
stages.submit: Three-part chart and couplet analysis.

stages.title: Compose the triptych
stages.instructions: Choose a condition and three materially different time systems, such as growth, erosion, or repeated use. Write three linked poems of 14–20 lines each and a 6–10-line coda addressed to someone affected by the change. Each poem must add an implication the others cannot supply.
stages.submit: Three poems and an addressed coda, 48–70 lines total.

stages.title: Make time visible
stages.instructions: Design a three-panel clock or calendar plate whose scales differ. Anchor each panel to three exact phrases in your poems. Explain in labels why the scales cannot simply be converted into one another, and provide a text description.
stages.submit: Triptych plate with nine anchors and a reading key.

stages.title: Defend the sequence
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Shakespeare’s metaphors make mortality consequential for love. Add 300 words explaining the order of your metaphors and the coda’s address, including a limit on one comparison.
stages.submit: Literary argument and structural self-analysis.

stages.title: Try another order
stages.instructions: Give a reader the poems in two orders, withholding the coda until the end. Ask which argument each order suggests. If alone, write two accounts after rearranging the pieces. Revise one transition and one image so the final order has a defensible purpose.
stages.submit: Order comparison, revised lines, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on analogy
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain which metaphor generated an idea you had not planned. Identify where extending it further would have distorted the subject. Credit sources and images.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A city heard twice
projects.brief: Compose two versions of a walk through the same invented city, changing the speaker’s attitude while preserving the observed events. Use “London” to study how an observing voice can become an accusing voice. Sound can be represented through written notation; no recording equipment or public excursion is required.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Track the source attitude
stages.instructions: Follow Blake’s movement from faces to cries, institutions, and intimate life. Choose eight details and explain how each contributes to lament, accusation, or both. Distinguish the speaker’s attitude from a reader’s emotional response.
stages.submit: Eight-detail tone ledger.

stages.title: Write the two walks
stages.instructions: Invent five stops and four events that remain unchanged. Write two 24–32-line poems, one from a voice inclined to accept the city’s order and one from a voice that questions its costs. Do not simply replace approving adjectives with disapproving ones; change selection, syntax, and emphasis.
stages.submit: Two poems and a list of preserved facts.

stages.title: Map the listening
stages.instructions: Draw one route with two layers of sound notation. At each stop, connect a heard sound to a line from each version. Use symbols and labels rather than color alone, and write a 200-word accessible walkthrough.
stages.submit: Five-stop sound map and text walkthrough.

stages.title: Argue the tonal development
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Blake joins sorrow with institutional indictment. Add 300 words comparing three choices across your two versions and explaining how they guide the intended audience’s judgment.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative self-analysis.

stages.title: Read without labels
stages.instructions: Give a reader the two poems without their intended tone labels. Ask for two precise tone descriptions and the evidence for them. If alone, read each aloud after a break and mark emphasis. Revise one syntax pattern and one sound image in response.
stages.submit: Tone test, revised passages, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on complexity
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify a moment when the apparently approving version becomes uneasy or the critical version retains affection. Explain why this complication makes the voice more specific. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A fable with a fork
projects.brief: Create a verse fable whose first decision can lead to two different patterns of development. Study how “A Poison Tree” organizes concealed anger into cultivation, attraction, and consequence. Your fable should make sequence matter without merely rewarding a virtuous choice and punishing a bad one.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Name the stanza functions
stages.instructions: Give each stanza in Blake’s poem an action-based label and explain how it prepares the next. Identify the alternative introduced in the opening and distinguish the final implication from events the poem does not explicitly narrate.
stages.submit: Four-stage structural account, 250–300 words.

stages.title: Compose the branching fable
stages.instructions: Write a shared opening of two quatrains, then two routes of four quatrains each. Both routes must grow from the same initial conflict and contain a cost as well as a gain. Repeat one image in both routes but change its function. End each with an implication that a reader must interpret.
stages.submit: Ten-quatrain fable, 40 lines total, with two reading routes.

stages.title: Build the branch diagram

stages.submit: Branch diagram, six causal annotations, and two transcripts.

stages.title: Defend the organization
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Blake’s stanza sequence makes the ending consequential. Add 300 words explaining your formal regularity, branch point, and withheld implications; identify the audience judgment each route invites.
stages.submit: Literary argument and structural self-analysis.

stages.title: Test a missing stanza

projects.brief: Make a poem whose turn changes how a reader values the opening without erasing what the opening says. Sonnet 29 provides a model of inward revaluation rather than a magical change in circumstances. Your final artifact will use a hinged or folded page to make the relation between before and after visible.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the revaluation
stages.instructions: Annotate the opening condition, comparisons, connective, trigger, rising image, and final exchange in Sonnet 29. Write a 200-word explanation of what changes and what the poem does not establish as changed.
stages.submit: Six-part turn map and limits statement.

stages.title: Draft two possible turns
stages.instructions: Write an original 14-line poem with a clear initial condition and a turn after line 8 or 10. Draft a second ending of the same length that changes the speaker’s valuation in a different direction. Keep the opening identical. Write a 200-word letter from the speaker to the addressee clarifying what remains unresolved.
stages.submit: One shared opening, two endings, and a fictional letter.

stages.title: Design the hinge
stages.instructions: Create a two-flap page plan that lets readers encounter either ending after the shared opening. Use one repeated visual element whose meaning changes across the hinge. Number the reading order and supply both complete poems as plain text.
stages.submit: Hinged-page design and two linear poem transcripts.

stages.title: Argue for the turn
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Shakespeare’s turn revalues the speaker’s “state.” Add 300 words comparing your endings’ syntax, images, and address, then defend the ending you would retain for a single-version publication.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative craft argument.

stages.title: Test what actually changes
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to describe the before/after relation in each version and to identify any unexplained external change. If alone, write these descriptions after a delayed reread. Revise the chosen ending so its shift is earned by the opening.
stages.submit: Two-version test and a revised final poem.

stages.title: Reflect on the hinge
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why the turn is more than the word “yet” or “but.” Identify a detail whose meaning changes retrospectively and explain how that skill transfers to reading a new sonnet. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A program for a contested reading
projects.artifact: Original poem and critical performance booklet
projects.brief: Prepare a reading program in which an original poem and two competing interpretations invite an audience to think carefully about courage under constraint. projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Build an interpretive claim

stages.submit: Six-detail ledger and two qualified theses.

stages.title: Compose a new appeal
stages.instructions: Write a 28–40-line poem addressed to a group facing an invented nonviolent dilemma. The speaker must seek a particular response, acknowledge a real cost, and avoid guaranteeing success. Add a 250–350-word scene establishing the occasion without explaining the poem’s meaning.
stages.submit: Original poem and framing scene.

stages.title: Design the program
stages.instructions: Create a four-page program with the poem, a visual score of three changes in intensity, and two 150–200-word interpretive notes written from different reader positions. stages.submit: Program, visual score, interpretive notes, and transcript.

stages.title: Write the sustained analysis
stages.instructions: Write a 750–950-word essay on how McKay connects dignity, collective action, and mortal risk. Use a line of reasoning that develops across the poem rather than listing devices. Add 300 words analyzing your own appeal’s audience, concessions, and ending through exact quotations.
stages.submit: Literary essay and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Hold a small reading test

stages.submit: Test notes, revised poem, and a 150-word rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on a defensible disagreement
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify which difference between the two program notes remains defensible after revision and which claim the text cannot support. Explain how this distinction would shape an AP-style essay. Credit all sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The consequence machine
projects.brief: Build a sequence in which one coerced promise changes the choices available later. Use Pip’s churchyard promise to distinguish practical conditions, motives, threats, and consequences. Your sequence must remain a literary story with people and competing desires, rather than a diagram illustrated by interchangeable characters.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate the causes
stages.instructions: Read “A coerced promise.” Identify six links in the encounter and classify each as enabling condition, motive, coercive pressure, or consequence. Explain how the stranger’s story about a hidden young man differs from an independently established fact.
stages.submit: Six-link causal ledger and a 150-word distinction.

stages.title: Write the linked fiction
stages.instructions: Compose five connected scenes of 150–200 words each. Begin with a promise made under pressure; each later scene must alter an available choice. Include one consequence no character intends and one attempted repair that creates a new difficulty.
stages.submit: Five-scene story, 750–1,000 words.

stages.title: Draw the mechanism
stages.instructions: Create a causal diagram with separate symbols for events, beliefs, and material conditions. Label every arrow with a specific relation such as enables, misleads, constrains, or intensifies. Include a linear explanation of the five-scene chain.
stages.submit: Labeled causal diagram and accessible account.

stages.title: Argue about responsibility
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Dickens makes Pip’s promise a product of interacting pressures. Add 300 words explaining where your characters’ intentions differ from the consequences and how the narrative lets readers see that difference.
stages.submit: Literary argument and causal self-analysis.

stages.title: Run a counterfactual
stages.instructions: Remove one condition without changing the characters’ desires. Write a 250–350-word alternate scene and ask a reader whether the later chain still follows. If alone, audit each arrow against the alternate version. Revise one weak causal link in the original.
stages.submit: Counterfactual scene, test notes, and revised link.

stages.title: Reflect on explanation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why a consequence in your story is neither random nor fully intended. Connect that distinction to one source detail and credit borrowed materials.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Two editions of the same secret
projects.brief: Write a story that can be arranged to give readers either privileged knowledge or delayed discovery. stages.title: Map disclosure

stages.title: Write modular scenes

stages.title: Design the editions

stages.title: Defend the placement

stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative structural analysis.

stages.title: Test two reading experiences

stages.submit: Reading records and a justified final ordering decision.

stages.title: Reflect on withholding
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain the difference between withholding from a character and withholding from a reader. Identify a case where earlier disclosure creates more interest than secrecy. Credit sources.

projects.title: The hour after success
projects.brief: Write the hour after a character achieves something long desired and discovers that success has created a new uncertainty. stages.title: Read the failed refuges

stages.submit: Refuge sequence and three inference notes.

stages.title: Compose the hour

stages.submit: Original suspense scene with a one-sentence premise.

stages.title: Score duration and attention

stages.title: Argue the uncertainty

stages.title: Test the suspense

projects.title: A choice with a price
projects.brief: Design a short paper-based narrative in which every available choice has a cost, yet the character’s decisions still matter. Jane’s resistance offers a model for separating agency from unrestricted power. The game must communicate its hierarchy through scenes and consequences; it cannot simply announce that all choices lead to the same ending.

stages.title: Identify available action

stages.title: Write the playable narrative

stages.submit: Complete paper narrative, approximately 1,400–1,900 words, with numbered routes.

stages.title: Make the constraints visible

stages.title: Argue the limits of choice

projects.title: Letters to a former certainty
projects.brief: Create a character whose developing judgment changes how earlier letters are read. Use Elizabeth’s reassessment to examine the difference between receiving new information and recognizing the bias that organized old information. Your character should retain at least one important trait while revising a belief.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the mechanism of change
stages.instructions: In Elizabeth’s selection, identify four old details that receive new interpretations, two admissions about the self, and one sign that the emotional consequences remain unsettled. Explain the mechanism connecting them.

stages.title: Write the letters
stages.instructions: Compose four letters of 250–350 words from one character at separated moments: confidence, disturbance, recognition, and attempted action. projects.title: The price of an ordinary day
projects.brief: Create a shop catalogue that reveals a social world through what it sells, who can enter, and what customers must give up to buy. projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the material world

stages.title: Compose the catalogue

stages.title: Design access

stages.title: Argue the purchase’s meaning

stages.submit: Literary argument and rhetorical/visual self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the judgment

projects.title: The mediation that changes its terms
projects.brief: Write a mediation in which the parties disagree about the meaning of a word they initially seem to share. Study Nora and Torvald’s competing uses of love, happiness, and education. projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the speech acts

stages.title: Write the hearing

stages.title: Argue the reframing

stages.submit: Literary argument and dialogue self-analysis.

stages.title: Read the unresolved terms

projects.title: The silent half of a scene
projects.brief: Write one short dialogue that supports two contrasting but defensible stagings, then make the nonverbal action carry the difference. stages.title: Write the fixed dialogue

projects.title: The charter of a made world

projects.title: The apprentice’s five tasks
projects.brief: Reveal an apprentice through the way five apparently practical tasks are performed, recorded, and judged. Use the assembly scene in Pride and Prejudice to study how conduct produces social interpretations. The task book should let readers infer a character without supplying a list of personality adjectives.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read behavior and verdict
stages.instructions: Choose six actions or remarks from “Two guests at the assembly.” Separate what happens from the judgment attached to it, and identify who makes that judgment. Include one response by an observer that reveals the observer’s own priorities.
stages.submit: Six-entry conduct/verdict chart.

stages.title: Write the task book
stages.instructions: Invent an apprenticeship in a craft, institution, or fantastical occupation. Write five task entries of 150–200 words, each combining an instruction, a scene of performance, and a brief supervisor’s note. The apprentice must reveal a strength, a limitation, and a quality the supervisor misreads. Avoid trait labels in the scenes.
stages.submit: Five-entry narrative and a 150-word factual background note.

stages.title: Display the evidence
stages.instructions: Create a portfolio plate with five objects or traces left by the tasks. Annotate each with one quotation from the narrative and two possible inferences. Use simple drawings or labeled shapes and provide a text description.

projects.title: Two guides to the same estate
projects.brief: Write two guides to one invented estate, campus, garden, or public building. Each guide must reveal its writer through the same route and objects, and each must expose something the other overlooks. Study Bingley and Darcy as a contrast enacted through shared social opportunities rather than as a list of opposites.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Establish the shared conditions
stages.instructions: Make a comparison table for the men’s opportunities, actions, speech, and social reception at the assembly. Include two shared qualities or judgments so the contrast does not become absolute. Explain how their friendship makes the difference consequential.
stages.submit: Comparison table and a 200-word interpretation.

stages.title: Compose the guides
stages.instructions: Invent one route with five stops. Write two guidebook voices, each supplying a 90–120-word entry for every stop. Give the guides different intended visitors and values, but preserve the same physical facts. Add a 250-word encounter in which the guides must lead a visitor together.
stages.submit: Ten guide entries and a joint-guidance scene.

stages.title: Map selective attention
stages.instructions: Draw one route map with two annotation layers. At every stop, show what each guide emphasizes and one feature neither initially values. Provide a text route and explain three design decisions that invite comparison.
stages.submit: Layered map, text route, and design note.

stages.title: Argue the foil’s function
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Austen’s contrast develops social openness and exclusiveness. Add 300 words explaining how your guides illuminate each other, including a moment that resists a simple good-guide/bad-guide division.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the comparison
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to describe each guide using the same two stops and to identify a blind spot in both. Revise one entry per guide and the joint scene so the interaction changes what readers notice. A delayed solo comparison is an alternative.
stages.submit: Comparison test and three revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on shared ground
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why the guides needed a shared setting to function as foils. Identify a difference that proved superficial and one that changed the interpretation. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Terms of an alliance
projects.brief: Create an alliance whose public statement of mutual benefit conceals unequal expectations. Use Nora and Torvald’s reckoning to examine how attachment can coexist with a relationship one participant finds diminishing. Your alliance may involve friends, collaborators, siblings, or invented beings; it need not reproduce a marriage.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Map the relationship
stages.instructions: Read “A marriage reconsidered” and identify six terms the participants understand differently. Explain two genuine attachments or pleasures and two limits that those attachments do not resolve.
stages.submit: Relationship map and a 200-word account of coexistence.

stages.title: Write the agreement and its margins
stages.instructions: Compose a 400–500-word public agreement with six clauses. Add private annotations of 250–350 words from each participant, revealing different expectations about three clauses. Then write a 500–650-word scene in which one clause is tested and the alliance must change.
stages.submit: Agreement, two annotation voices, and testing scene.

stages.title: Design the shared document
stages.instructions: Make a facing-page document that distinguishes public language, each private voice, and the scene’s evidence without using color alone. Draw a relationship diagram showing exchanges of labor, recognition, and decision-making, with a text equivalent.
stages.submit: Annotated agreement layout and relationship diagram.

stages.title: Argue attachment and imbalance
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Ibsen makes pleasantness and kindness coexist with Nora’s critique. Add 300 words analyzing how your public wording persuades an outside audience while the margins expose divergent assumptions.
stages.submit: Literary argument and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Test a proposed repair
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to propose one changed clause that would address the actual imbalance. If alone, propose repairs from both participants’ positions. Revise the scene so a repair is tested rather than merely promised; it need not succeed.
stages.submit: Repair proposals, revised scene, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on reciprocity
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why affection or shared purpose alone does not settle the alliance’s problem. Identify what remains worth preserving and what must change, with source credits.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.
