projects.title: Within the lantern’s reach
projects.brief: Write a story whose viewpoint character can perceive only a defined portion of a larger event. The limited field should create both intimacy and uncertainty. Use the wallpaper selection to distinguish sincere experience from externally verified explanation; your character need not be deceptive or mentally unwell.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Classify the available knowledge
stages.instructions: In “Reading the pattern,” identify eight details as observation, interpretation, reported speech, or acknowledged uncertainty. Explain why neither the narrator’s conviction nor John’s authority independently settles every claim.
stages.submit: Eight-detail knowledge table and a 200-word explanation.

stages.title: Write within a boundary
stages.instructions: Invent a room, vehicle, garden wall, communication channel, or other defined limit. Write an 850–1,100-word story from one character’s perspective. Include four accurate observations, two plausible mistaken inferences, and one unresolved inference. Keep a private 200-word account of what occurred beyond the boundary.
stages.submit: Bounded story and separate factual account.

stages.title: Map access
stages.instructions: Create a lantern or sightline map showing what can be seen, heard, inferred, or not known at five moments. Use distinct symbols and cite the story’s wording. Provide a linear description that preserves the same knowledge limits.
stages.submit: Five-moment access map and text equivalent.

stages.title: Argue the restriction’s effect
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Gilman’s limited perspective makes private distress available without independently verifying every perception. Add 300 words explaining what your restriction permits and prevents a reader from concluding.
stages.submit: Literary argument and perspective self-analysis.

stages.title: Test warranted inference
stages.instructions: Give a reader the story before the factual account. Ask for three conclusions and confidence levels with evidence. Compare these with the private account. Revise one clue that is unfairly absent and one explanation that removes useful uncertainty. A delayed solo audit is acceptable.
stages.submit: Inference test, revised passages, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on sincerity
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how a sincere account can still be limited. Identify a claim in your story that should be qualified rather than accepted or rejected wholesale. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The supper no one understands
projects.brief: Narrate one meal with access to several minds, while making the reader’s wider knowledge purposeful and selective. Austen’s scene shows how a narrator can reveal intention, ignorance, and self-presentation in different people. Your narrator must use that range to develop an interpretation, not merely report everyone’s thoughts in turn.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Audit narrative access
stages.instructions: Identify six moments in “A visit disclosed” when narration supplies information beyond spoken words. State whose knowledge or intention is revealed and how that access changes the reader’s position.
stages.submit: Six-moment access audit.

stages.title: Compose the supper
stages.instructions: Write a 1,000–1,250-word scene with four characters, one shared dish or object, and one fact known to only two participants. Enter at least three minds, but withhold one relevant thought until late in the scene. Include a narratorial comment that adds a perspective no participant fully holds.
stages.submit: Original scene and a note identifying the withheld thought.

stages.title: Design the table of knowledge
stages.instructions: Draw the seating plan with a second layer showing what each person knows at the beginning, midpoint, and end. Add a reader track to show what the narration discloses. Use labels and a text table rather than color alone.
stages.submit: Seating/knowledge diagram and accessible table.

stages.title: Defend the narrator’s choices
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Austen’s selective mental access produces irony. Add 300 words explaining why your narrator enters particular minds at particular moments and how the narratorial comment shapes audience judgment.
stages.submit: Literary argument and narratorial self-analysis.

stages.title: Try a restricted version
stages.instructions: Rewrite 250–350 words of the scene through only one participant’s knowledge. Ask a reader, or perform a delayed solo comparison, to identify what irony or sympathy changes. Use the result to revise one disclosure in the omniscient version.
stages.submit: Restricted rewrite, comparison, and revised disclosure.

stages.title: Reflect on selection
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why knowing more does not require telling everything. Identify one piece of information you could have revealed but deliberately withheld, with its effect and source credits.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A sentence with two owners
projects.brief: Compose a scene in which third-person narration moves close to a character’s language without consistently marking the boundary. Use Mrs. Sommers’s shopping experience to study the blend of reported thought, immediate evaluation, and narratorial context. The aim is controlled ambiguity of voice, not grammatical confusion.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Locate the blend
stages.instructions: Choose six sentences or short passages from “An unexpected purchase.” Place them on a continuum from external report to character-colored immediacy, and justify two uncertain placements. Distinguish explicit thought report from free indirect phrasing.
stages.submit: Voice continuum and six annotations.

stages.title: Write three approaches
stages.instructions: Invent a consequential ordinary decision. Write a 180–220-word version as external observation and another as direct interior monologue. Then compose a 750–950-word third-person scene using free indirect discourse at at least five consequential moments. Preserve the event’s basic facts across versions.
stages.submit: Two short studies and one developed blended-voice scene.

stages.title: Make the voice plate
stages.instructions: Lay out a page from the final scene with five marginal notes explaining possible ownership of phrases. Use underlining, brackets, or line styles to represent degrees of certainty rather than forcing every word into one category. Supply a linear annotation list.
stages.submit: Annotated voice plate and accessible notes.

stages.title: Argue the proximity
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Chopin’s shifting proximity complicates the reader’s judgment of Mrs. Sommers. Add 300 words comparing one moment across your three versions and explaining its effect on intimacy and irony.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative self-analysis.

stages.title: Test attribution
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to mark where the narration seems closest to the character and where a phrase may carry two perspectives. If alone, read aloud with different emphases after a break. Revise two transitions so the blend is perceptible without being mechanically signposted.
stages.submit: Attribution test and two revised transitions.

stages.title: Reflect on ambiguity

projects.title: The collector’s account
projects.brief: Write a collector’s account of how an object was acquired, then let supporting records expose limits in the collector’s self-justification. Study “The Tell-Tale Heart” to distinguish careful method from adequate reasoning. The collector may report many facts accurately while interpreting ownership, merit, or fairness in a self-serving way.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Test the source’s proofs
stages.instructions: Identify five claims the narrator offers about motive or rationality and the evidence offered for each. Explain why at least two pieces of evidence do not establish the conclusion drawn from them. Avoid a clinical diagnosis.
stages.submit: Five-claim reasoning audit.

stages.title: Compose the provenance
stages.instructions: Invent an object and write a 700–900-word first-person acquisition account addressed to potential visitors or buyers. Add three fictional supporting records of 100–150 words each. Include at least two facts the collector reports accurately, one omission, and one disproportionate moral conclusion.
stages.submit: Collector’s account and three clearly fictional records.

stages.title: Design the catalogue entry
stages.instructions: Create a two-page illustrated catalogue entry with an object diagram, provenance timeline, and footnotes connecting records to claims. Label established fact, interpretation, and unresolved issue using words as well as symbols. Provide an accessible reading order.
stages.submit: Catalogue spread, timeline, and text equivalent.

stages.title: Argue the limits of trust
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Poe’s narrator attempts to make method prove rationality. Add 300 words explaining the difference between your collector’s factual candor and ethical self-justification, including the audience the account tries to persuade.
stages.submit: Literary argument and reliability self-analysis.

stages.title: Run an evidence hearing
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify one trustworthy report, one unsupported conclusion, and one unresolved matter. If alone, write a short case for and against the collector after a break. Revise one record and one claim to make scrutiny possible without making every sentence false.
stages.submit: Evidence test and two documented revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on partial trust
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why “unreliable” should not mean “ignore everything.” Identify how a reader can use even a self-serving account as evidence. Credit sources and label all invented documents.

projects.title: The primer, thirty years later
projects.artifact: Fictional childhood primer with adult margins
projects.brief: Create a child’s small guide to understanding the world, then annotate it from the perspective of the same person decades later. Study the older Pip’s treatment of his childhood inferences. The adult voice should neither endorse every childish conclusion nor dismiss the younger self as foolish.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the double perspective
stages.instructions: Choose six moments in “Pip in the churchyard” where immediate perception and retrospective understanding interact. Explain how one comic detail also preserves vulnerability.
stages.submit: Six-moment distance ledger and a 200-word explanation.

stages.title: Write the primer and margins
stages.instructions: Invent a child’s primer with eight rules of 60–90 words each about a household, neighborhood, or institution. Each rule must arise from a concrete observation, but at least three must misinterpret it. Add adult marginal responses totaling 500–700 words, including correction, uncertainty, affection, and one recognition that the child noticed something adults missed.
stages.submit: Eight-rule primer and adult marginal commentary.

stages.title: Illustrate two distances
stages.instructions: Create four paired illustrations: the child’s inferred world and the adult’s revised account. Tie each pair to a rule and a margin note. Provide descriptions that distinguish what is observed from what is imagined in each image.
stages.submit: Four illustration pairs and accessible descriptions.

stages.title: Argue humor and sympathy
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Dickens creates distance without extinguishing sympathy for Pip. Add 300 words explaining how your adult diction, corrections, and visual framing position readers toward the child.
stages.submit: Literary argument and retrospective self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the adult voice
stages.instructions: Ask a reader where the margins become condescending, sentimental, or usefully reflective, with exact evidence. If alone, read the child’s primer separately before returning to the margins. Revise two adult notes and one illustration to preserve a more precise relation.
stages.submit: Voice test and three revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on hindsight
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one thing the adult can understand better and one thing the adult cannot recover with certainty. Connect the distinction to retrospective narration and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The timetable of a return
projects.brief: Write a return journey in which the order of telling changes the meaning of an earlier promise. Use Walton’s letter to study how present sensation, remembered preparation, and imagined future can justify an undertaking. The journey may be entirely invented and requires no travel or historical research beyond the supplied source.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate time systems
stages.instructions: Make a chronological list of Walton’s experiences and a second list of the order in which the letter presents them. Mark projections that are not yet events. Explain one effect of the space given to an imagined future compared with years of preparation.
stages.submit: Dual timeline and 200-word duration analysis.

stages.title: Write the journey
stages.instructions: Compose a 1,000–1,250-word story in seven labeled sections. Include a present return journey, two flashbacks, one imagined future, and one moment narrated in unusually slow detail. Preserve enough temporal cues for a reader to reconstruct what actually happened.
stages.submit: Seven-section story and a separate factual chronology.

stages.title: Create the timetable
stages.instructions: Design a fictional railway or route timetable with columns for clock time, remembered time, and anticipated time. Anchor every entry to a passage and label imagined events clearly. Provide a linear text version and explain why one interval occupies more narrative space than another.
stages.submit: Narrative timetable, text version, and duration key.

stages.title: Defend the arrangement
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how Shelley’s arrangement of time shapes Walton’s self-presentation. Add 300 words explaining how your sequence changes the reader’s understanding of the promise and the returning character.
stages.submit: Literary argument and temporal self-analysis.

stages.title: Test reconstruction and effect
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to reconstruct the chronology and identify the most important delayed fact. If alone, shuffle the sections into chronology and compare the effect after a break. Revise one temporal cue and one allocation of narrative space.
stages.submit: Reconstruction test, revisions, and rationale.

stages.title: Reflect on prediction
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish a character’s projected future from the story’s confirmed outcome. Explain why preserving that difference matters to the interpretation of ambition. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A house that answers back
projects.brief: Write an architectural folktale in which a building narrates a visitor’s arrival, then give the visitor a brief counteraccount. Study Poe’s opening to examine how description and an interpreting mind shape each other. Your invented building can speak within the fiction, but your source analysis must not assume that Poe’s house literally possesses the same power.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Build the source argument
stages.instructions: Outline the opening of “The Fall of the House of Usher” in five functional stages. Select one detail from each and explain how it connects the building with the narrator’s attempt to understand it. Draft a thesis that accounts for the failed reflection experiment.
stages.submit: Five-stage evidence outline and provisional thesis.

stages.title: Compose the folktale
stages.instructions: Write an 850–1,100-word story narrated by an invented building as a visitor arrives. Give the building a desire, a limit on what it can know, and a mistaken interpretation of the visitor. Add a 250–350-word human counteraccount that revises one inference without resolving every uncertainty.
stages.submit: Architectural tale and human counteraccount.

stages.title: Draw the interpretive section
stages.instructions: Create a cutaway or elevation with five annotated features. Pair each feature with the building’s description and the visitor’s interpretation. Provide a plain-text walkthrough and distinguish literal architecture from figurative associations.
stages.submit: Five-feature architectural plate and accessible walkthrough.

stages.title: Write the sustained analysis
stages.instructions: Develop a 750–950-word essay explaining how Poe’s setting and self-conscious narration jointly produce disturbance. Add 300 words analyzing how your personified building, sensory selection, and counteraccount guide or resist reader sympathy.
stages.submit: Literary essay and cross-perspective self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the line of reasoning
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to name the main claim of each essay paragraph and explain its connection to the next. Separately ask which story inference the counteraccount changes. Revise one analytical transition and one fictional detail. A delayed solo reverse outline is acceptable.
stages.submit: Reverse outline, reading response, and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on interpretation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how writing the building changed your understanding of personification without authorizing you to treat every figurative source detail literally. Identify one strengthened commentary sentence and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A covenant with an impossible promise
projects.brief: Invent a promise whose meaning changes as its conditions become clearer. Study the grammar of Sonnet 116, then compose a poetic covenant between two fictional parties. Its clauses should reveal the tension between an attractive ideal and the pressures that test it; it is a literary artifact, not a real contract.
topics: Memory and the right to revise
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the conditions
stages.instructions: Map the complete sentences of Sonnet 116. Mark main assertions, relative clauses, concessions, and the final conditional. Write five annotations explaining what a dependent clause changes about a claim.
stages.submit: Sentence map and five effect annotations.

stages.title: Draft the covenant
stages.instructions: Write a 30–42-line poem defining a promise through three exclusions, two concessions, and one final conditional with a surprising consequence. Give each fictional party something to gain and something to fear. Add a 250-word prose scene showing the moment when the covenant is offered; do not explain every implication in that scene.
stages.submit: Poetic covenant and offering scene.

stages.title: Illuminate the clauses
stages.instructions: Create a two-page manuscript spread. Use branching stems, brackets, or connecting lines to show which clauses depend on which assertions. Make the central promise readable in a continuous text version and include a key explaining three visual decisions.
stages.submit: Annotated manuscript spread, text version, and design key.

stages.title: Argue the definition
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Shakespeare defines love through exclusion and concession. Explain the force and limit of the final wager. Add 250–350 words analyzing how the syntax of your covenant positions its imagined reader to accept, question, or resist the promise.
stages.submit: Literary argument and syntactic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test a clause
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to paraphrase the promise and identify its most consequential qualification. If alone, paraphrase it after a day without consulting the diagram. Remove one concession in a trial version, compare the resulting meaning, and revise two clauses in the final version.
stages.submit: Paraphrase test, trial deletion, and two justified revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on commitment
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish a strong assertion from an adequately supported one. Identify one condition you made clearer and one uncertainty the poem intentionally retains. Credit the source and label the covenant as fiction.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A poem at the fold
projects.brief: Create a foldout poem about crossing a boundary. The unfolding page should let readers experience temporary meanings that the next line revises. McKay’s “The White City” supplies a study in delayed grammar and entangled feeling; your poem should develop its own situation and conflict.
topics: A journey toward an unwelcome home
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Track suspended grammar
stages.instructions: Mark five places in “The White City” where a line ends before its grammatical unit is complete. For each, record the temporary emphasis and the meaning supplied by the continuation. Explain why the final catalogue needs its last predicate.
stages.submit: Five continuation notes and a 200-word account of the ending.

stages.title: Compose the crossing
stages.instructions: Write a 180–240-word prose paragraph about a fictional crossing, then use exactly those words in a 24–36-line poem. Create a second lineation of the same words that changes at least six endings. Choose one version and revise its wording into a final 24–36-line poem with at least four purposeful enjambments.
stages.submit: Prose base, two controlled lineations, and final poem.

stages.title: Build the foldout
stages.instructions: Make a paper mock-up or digital accordion with four panels. Place two important continuations across folds and explain what each concealment briefly encourages a reader to infer. Include the entire poem in a plain linear view so unfolding is optional.
stages.submit: Four-panel foldout, linear version, and two design annotations.

stages.title: Defend the delays
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word argument about how McKay’s syntax and lineation develop the speaker’s relation to the city. Add 300 words comparing three of your alternate endings and explaining the audience effect of the final page arrangement.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comparative self-analysis.

stages.title: Read without staging
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to mark natural pauses before showing the foldout. If alone, record two readings after a break, one following syntax and one emphasizing line endings. Revise any fold that creates accidental confusion, and document one retained productive suspension.
stages.submit: Pause test and documented design revision.

stages.title: Reflect on the line
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how a line ending can matter without being a mandatory pause. Identify a meaning that comes from syntax and a different emphasis created by the page. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The interrupted toast
projects.brief: Write a ceremonial toast whose pauses reveal that the speaker’s praise is more complicated than the occasion permits. Sonnet 130 models how affection can coexist with correction. Your speaker should have a reason to speak publicly and a reason to qualify what is said.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Listen to the turns
stages.instructions: Annotate six internal or terminal pauses in Sonnet 130. Explain the relation between the thoughts on either side of each pause. Compare the internal “yet” with the final “And yet,” attending to what each preserves.
stages.submit: Six pause annotations and a comparative note.

stages.title: Write the occasion
stages.instructions: Invent a fictional ceremony and give a 150-word account of speaker, audience, and occasion. Write a 28–40-line toast containing four meaningful internal pauses, four end-stopped lines, and two enjambed passages. Let one apparently unflattering admission become part of a more precise affirmation.
stages.submit: Occasion note and verse toast.

stages.title: Score two performances
stages.instructions: Prepare two marked scores of the same toast: one formally courteous, one more candid. Use a consistent key for short pause, long pause, emphasis, and continuation. Record both if convenient, or supply detailed reading directions; a recording is not required.
stages.submit: Two performance scores, key, and transcript or reading directions.

stages.title: Argue truthful praise
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of the relation between pause, concession, and affection in Sonnet 130. Add 300 words explaining how three performance decisions in your toast affect the audience’s judgment of the speaker’s sincerity.
stages.submit: Literary argument and performance self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the admission
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the moment at which the toast’s praise becomes more credible or more doubtful. If alone, compare the two scores after a break. Revise one internal pause and one ending, preserving the words initially; then decide whether a wording change is also needed.
stages.submit: Audience response, controlled pause revision, and final decision.

stages.title: Reflect on performance
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify a defensible difference between the two readings and an interpretation neither reading can support. Explain the evidence that sets that limit and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

levels.label: Accomplished
levels.description: Six annotations explain the relationships articulated by pauses and compare the poem’s two concessive turns.

projects.title: Two clocks for one day
projects.brief: Give one fictional day two different felt durations. Write a metrical poem and a freer companion in which attention changes the experience of time. Use Sonnet 18 to study how a recurring pattern can support an assurance while syntax supplies its conditions.
topics: A brief encounter remembered for years
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Establish a base pulse
stages.instructions: Read Sonnet 18 aloud and mark a plausible five-beat pattern in four lines, including line 13. Identify two places where natural emphasis or punctuation complicates a mechanical reading. Explain how the final repeated opening supports the argument.
stages.submit: Four scansions, two qualifications, and a 200-word closing analysis.

stages.title: Write the diptych
stages.instructions: Invent a day with one consequential encounter. Compose a 20–28-line poem using an iambic-pentameter base, with three deliberate variations that you can explain. Write a 20–28-line free-verse companion about the same event from a later perspective. Preserve three shared images but change their significance.
stages.submit: Two poems and a brief record of the three intended variations.

stages.title: Make the time score
stages.instructions: Design a paired timeline showing clock time, space devoted to each event, and stress or pause patterns in six selected lines. Provide a text table. An optional reading may accompany it, but the score must communicate without audio.
stages.submit: Paired temporal score and accessible table.

stages.title: Defend measured assurance
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Shakespeare’s pattern, parallel phrasing, and condition develop the claim for verse. Add 300 words explaining how your two rhythmic approaches alter the encounter’s felt duration and retrospective importance.
stages.submit: Literary argument and rhythmic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test natural speech
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to mark stresses in six lines without your scansion. If alone, record a natural reading and compare it with the intended pattern. Revise two lines that require distorted pronunciation; retain one purposeful variation and explain its effect.
stages.submit: Stress comparison, two revisions, and one justified variation.

stages.title: Reflect on regularity
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish a metrical framework from a compulsory performance. Explain one effect you can support from language and one subjective response you cannot require of every reader. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A foundry of questions
projects.brief: Imagine a maker confronting something powerful that they have brought into existence. Compose a poem built from questions, then design a small sound installation on paper. Blake’s repeated address and changing final question provide a source for studying how sonic return can intensify uncertainty.
topics: Beauty with a capacity for harm
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Hear the inquiry
stages.instructions: Annotate six sound relationships in “The Tiger”: repeated words, paired endings, concentrated stresses, or consonant patterns. Explain what ideas each brings together. Compare “Could” and “Dare” and avoid calling visually similar endings exact rhymes without testing pronunciation.
stages.submit: Six sound annotations and a refrain comparison.

stages.title: Compose the making
stages.instructions: Write a 28–40-line question-poem addressed to an invented creation. Include a returning two-line address, at least four meaningful rhyme pairs, two alliterative clusters, and a changed modal verb in the final return. Add a 250-word fictional maker’s note that offers one explanation the poem itself leaves uncertain.
stages.submit: Question-poem and maker’s note.

stages.title: Plan the listening space
stages.instructions: Draw a plan for a three-station installation: the making, the encounter, and the return. Assign lines, pauses, and optional nonverbal sounds to each station. Explain how visitors would move through the argument. Provide transcripts and descriptions so the plan works without sound equipment.
stages.submit: Installation plan, three station scores, and accessible transcript.

stages.title: Argue unresolved force
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Blake’s sound and question patterns sustain awe or unease without identifying the maker. Add 300 words evaluating how your refrain, sound pairs, and station order direct a listener’s response.
stages.submit: Literary argument and sonic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the return
stages.instructions: Read the first and final refrains to a listener, or compare recordings made after a break. Ask what changed beyond the single word. Revise one rhyme that distorts meaning and one station transition; explain why the final question remains open.
stages.submit: Listening test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on resonance
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain a sound pattern whose effect depends on its words rather than on a universal sound-emotion rule. Distinguish your fictional maker’s account from the poem’s established evidence and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: An appointment with Tomorrow
projects.brief: Stage an appointment between a human character and a personified force. The force must have recognizable manners and a limit on its own knowledge or power. Dickinson’s carriage poem shows how a familiar social encounter can make an unfamiliar process imaginable without making it fully reassuring.
topics: Rest and the fear of stopping
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read agency and courtesy
stages.instructions: Make a four-column table for the carriage poem: action, actor, social implication, unresolved question. Include at least six entries and distinguish Death, Immortality, the speaker, and the gazing grain. Use the twenty-line edition displayed here.
stages.submit: Six-entry agency table and an edition note.

stages.title: Write the appointment
stages.instructions: Compose a 900–1,200-word one-act scene between a fictional person and an abstraction such as Tomorrow, Reputation, Silence, or Habit. Give the abstraction a profession, a courteous ritual, and one limit it cannot overcome. End with a change in the human character’s understanding, without explaining the entire allegory.
stages.submit: One-act script with stage directions.

stages.title: Design the visiting card
stages.instructions: Create the abstraction’s visiting card and a stage plan with five meaningful objects. Annotate what each object makes familiar and what it leaves unsettling. Include a linear set description and avoid relying on color alone.
stages.submit: Visiting card, annotated set plan, and accessible description.

stages.title: Argue the social figure
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Dickinson’s personification connects civility, relinquishment, and an enlarged sense of time. Add 300 words analyzing how your abstraction’s manners and limit shape an audience’s judgment of the encounter.
stages.submit: Literary argument and dramatic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the human role
stages.instructions: Have a reader identify the abstraction from the scene with its name temporarily hidden. If alone, replace the abstraction with an ordinary professional and examine what meaning is lost. Revise two actions so the personification does interpretive work beyond its label.
stages.submit: Identification or substitution test and two action revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on the limit
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one aspect of the abstraction the scene makes graspable and one it cannot adequately represent. Relate that limit to the source poem’s unresolved destination and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The conservatory of forbidden growth
projects.artifact: Garden fable and annotated seed catalogue
projects.brief: Invent a garden whose rules change the meaning of what grows there. Pair a symbolic fable with a seed catalogue written by someone invested in those rules. stages.title: Test two gardens

stages.title: Write the fable and catalogue
stages.instructions: Compose an 800–1,050-word fable about an invented conservatory with one rule, one forbidden plant, and one apparently beneficial intervention that causes harm. Add five seed-catalogue entries of 60–90 words each in the voice of the garden’s keeper. Let at least two entries conflict with what the fable reveals.
stages.submit: Garden fable and five fictional catalogue entries.

stages.title: Draw the changing bed
stages.instructions: Make before-and-after planting plans with six labeled features. Connect changes in placement, access, or growth to exact passages in your fable. Include a text walkthrough that distinguishes literal design from symbolic interpretation.
stages.submit: Two plans, six annotations, and accessible walkthrough.

stages.title: Argue the pattern
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word comparative argument about how the two Blake poems associate life or joy with damaging forces. Add 300 words analyzing how your fable and catalogue create a symbolic pattern without assigning every object a fixed one-word code.
stages.submit: Comparative literary argument and symbolic self-analysis.

stages.title: Invite a counterreading

stages.title: Reflect on limits

stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Marginal constellations
projects.artifact: Allusive journey poem and reader’s apparatus
projects.brief: Write a poem whose speaker borrows figures from other stories to imagine leaving an immediate difficulty. Build a small reader’s apparatus that supplies necessary context without deciding the poem’s meaning. Keats’s “Ode to a Nightingale” provides a model for testing both the reach and the failure of imaginative departure.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Follow the borrowed figures
stages.instructions: Use the reading notes and the full poem to trace Lethe, the Dryad, Hippocrene, Bacchus, and Ruth. For each, explain what the reference contributes locally and how it participates in the poem’s movement. Distinguish supplied background from an inference about effect.
stages.submit: Five-reference function chart.

stages.title: Compose an imagined journey
stages.instructions: Write a 40–56-line poem about a speaker who seeks relief through an imagined journey and returns with an altered question. Incorporate three allusions from public-domain stories or myths, including one already glossed here. Supply short source excerpts or reliable links for the other two; no reader should need unexplained prior knowledge.
stages.submit: Journey poem, three source records, and a 150-word account of the immediate situation.

stages.title: Build the marginal map
stages.instructions: Design a page with the poem at the center and three connected marginal panels. Each panel should give a concise factual gloss, a relevant source detail, and a question rather than a prescribed interpretation. Provide the panels in linear reading order as well.
stages.submit: Annotated page, three panels, and accessible linear version.

stages.title: Argue imaginative reach
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how Keats’s allusions enlarge the song’s reach and prepare the return to the solitary self. Add 300 words explaining what each of your references changes about the speaker’s wish and where the borrowed stories resist that wish.
stages.submit: Literary argument and allusive self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the apparatus

stages.title: Reflect on borrowing

projects.title: An atlas of impossible measures
projects.brief: Measure an inward experience with instruments that cannot literally contain it. Create an atlas whose impossible measurements make emotional or intellectual relations more precise. Dickinson’s comparisons of brain, sky, sea, and divinity and her account of a scarless hurt provide studies in productive difficulty.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Locate the apparent contradictions
stages.instructions: Read “The Brain” and “A Certain Slant of Light.” Identify three apparent contradictions or category crossings in each. For each, explain the literal problem and a defensible figurative relation, then mark one uncertainty the language preserves.
stages.submit: Six-entry paradox ledger with interpretive limits.

stages.title: Write the atlas
stages.instructions: Compose five prose poems of 150–200 words each, measuring one chosen inward experience through length, weight, volume, temperature, and duration. Give each an ordinary instrument and one impossible result. Across the sequence, revise the reader’s understanding of the experience rather than repeating the same paradox five times.
stages.submit: Five-poem atlas and a 150-word sequence note.

stages.title: Draw the instruments
stages.instructions: Design five labeled instrument plates with scales or legends. Each must correspond to an exact phrase and show where literal measurement breaks down. Provide descriptions and a text table of readings; do not present the invented measurements as scientific findings.
stages.submit: Five plates, descriptions, and measurement table.

stages.title: Defend productive difficulty
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word comparison of how Dickinson’s two poems make difficult inward relations intelligible without fully resolving them. Add 300 words explaining two of your strongest paradoxes and one ambiguity you deliberately clarified.
stages.submit: Comparative argument and interpretive self-analysis.

stages.title: Test intelligibility
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to paraphrase two entries and identify what remains uncertain. If alone, attempt plain-language paraphrases after a break. Revise one entry whose contradiction is merely confusing and one visual scale that implies a false precision.
stages.submit: Paraphrase test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on precision
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how an impossible statement can still be more precise than a vague one. Identify the textual evidence that limits one of your atlas entries and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A petition in fourteen lines
projects.brief: Write a sonnet that petitions an imagined force for an exception to its rule. Then rearrange the same argument to test what the sonnet’s divisions contribute. Sonnet 60 develops several accounts of time’s damage before offering a hopeful counterclaim; your petition should earn its turn through what precedes it.
topics: A plea for one more moment
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Map the pressure
stages.instructions: Divide Sonnet 60 into three quatrains and a couplet. Explain the work of each section, select one verb that intensifies pressure, and analyze how “And yet” and “in hope” shape the final claim.
stages.submit: Four-part structural map and a 200-word qualification analysis.

stages.title: Write the petition
stages.instructions: Compose a fourteen-line sonnet with a deliberate rhyme pattern and three developing grounds for the petition. In the couplet, introduce a counterclaim or qualified hope that the earlier sections make difficult. Add a 300-word fictional reply from the addressed force that challenges one premise without simply rejecting every part.
stages.submit: Sonnet, declared rhyme pattern, and fictional reply.

stages.title: Make the rival arrangement
stages.instructions: Set the sonnet as a decorated chapter opening, with an adjacent diagram linking each section to its argumentative role. Then arrange exactly the same words as a single prose paragraph and as seven couplets. Provide all three as selectable or separately labeled text, with a plain reading order.
stages.submit: Designed opening, structural diagram, and two controlled rearrangements.

stages.title: Argue the earned turn
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Sonnet 60’s developing images make its final hope consequential. Add 300 words comparing your three arrangements and explaining how the original division controls emphasis, expectation, and closure.
stages.submit: Literary argument and formal self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the petition
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the strongest premise and whether the ending feels earned. If alone, write the strongest objection to the petition after reading the fictional reply. Revise one quatrain and the couplet together so the turn responds to an established pressure.
stages.submit: Objection test and coordinated revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on form
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one effect produced by the fourteen-line arrangement and one effect carried by the wording regardless of arrangement. State what the petition still cannot promise and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: An almanac with a missing season
projects.brief: Invent a community that repeats an annual ritual while refusing to acknowledge a change. Build a narrative in four dated entries whose returning objects acquire different meanings. Dickens’s stopped room offers a source for studying how recurrence can preserve an unresolved past without explaining it directly.
topics: A celebration that no longer fits its purpose
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Inventory the pattern
stages.instructions: Group eight details from “The stopped room” under time, clothing, light, and performance. Explain the order in which Pip notices them and identify one detail that complicates a simple claim that nothing changes.
stages.submit: Eight-detail pattern table and a 200-word sequence analysis.

stages.title: Write the almanac
stages.instructions: Compose four dated entries of 250–325 words each, spanning at least three years. Repeat one object, one action, and one phrase in every entry, but change the context of each return. Omit one expected annual entry and make its absence interpretable through the surrounding entries.
stages.submit: Four-entry narrative with a deliberately missing date.

stages.title: Design the recurring page
stages.instructions: Create an almanac spread showing the ritual’s calendar and three visual variations of the repeated object. Tie each alteration to a sentence, and mark the missing entry without inventing an explanatory event the story does not establish. Provide a text table.
stages.submit: Calendar spread, three object studies, and accessible table.

stages.title: Argue repetition and change
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Dickens arranges recurring conditions in the room to shape Pip’s experience. Add 300 words explaining how two returns and the missing entry in your narrative change the reader’s interpretation of the ritual.
stages.submit: Literary argument and structural self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the missing year
stages.instructions: Ask a reader what the omitted entry permits them to infer and what remains unknown. If alone, draft the missing entry privately, then compare the published sequence without it. Revise one recurrence so it develops rather than merely repeats the same meaning.
stages.submit: Inference test, private trial if used, and documented recurrence revision.

stages.title: Reflect on preservation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what the ritual preserves and what it distorts. Distinguish an intentional gap from an accidental continuity error and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A letter carried by three voices
projects.artifact: Nested tale with an editor’s record
projects.brief: Transmit one fictional event through a witness, a listener, and an editor. The resulting account should preserve useful evidence while making its route visible. Walton’s record of Victor shows that admiration, corroboration, and revision can coexist within the same frame.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the source record
stages.instructions: Diagram the route from Victor’s experience through oral narration, Walton’s notes, Victor’s revisions, and the letter to Margaret. Identify two reasons Walton believes the story and two ways his response may shape its presentation.
stages.submit: Transmission diagram and four evidence notes.

stages.title: Compose the nested account
stages.instructions: Write a 500–650-word witness’s account of an invented event, embed it in a 400–500-word listener’s letter, and add a 250–350-word editor’s note. Give each voice a distinct audience and interest. Include one corroborating object, one explicitly revised phrase, and one disagreement that the final frame cannot settle.
stages.submit: Three-layer tale and a private list of established event facts.

stages.title: Create the editorial plate
stages.instructions: Lay out a facsimile page with the revised phrase visible, source labels for the three voices, and a diagram of the corroborating object. Supply an uninterrupted text version and a record explaining who authorized each alteration within the fiction.
stages.submit: Facsimile, linear version, and fictional revision record.

stages.title: Argue mediated credibility
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of Walton’s mixture of evidentiary checking and admiration. Add 300 words explaining how your frames change confidence in specific claims without making the entire account unusable.
stages.submit: Literary argument and framing self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the chain
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the original witness for three claims and rank their confidence with reasons. If alone, remove the outer frame and compare which judgments change. Revise one attribution and one interested comment so mediation is visible without becoming a puzzle of basic identity.
stages.submit: Attribution test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on the record
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish corroborating an event from endorsing its teller’s moral explanation. Identify what your editor cannot know and credit the source.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Two errands before midnight
projects.brief: Write two small quests that initially seem unrelated but make each other harder to interpret. One character should seek something materially valuable; another should pursue something that appears trivial but carries a different kind of worth. Hamlet’s comparison with the army provides a source for examining the relation between the scale of action and the value of its goal.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Examine the comparison
stages.instructions: Read Hamlet’s speech and the preceding exchange with the captain. Make a table of goal, cost, available knowledge, and claimed value for Hamlet and the expedition. Identify two phrases that complicate treating the army as an uncomplicated model.
stages.submit: Parallel-action table and two qualified interpretations.

stages.title: Write the errands
stages.instructions: Compose eight scenes of 150–200 words each, alternating between two protagonists until their actions intersect in scene seven. Give each a goal, obstacle, mistaken assumption, and consequential choice. The final scene must revise the apparent value of one goal without making the other story irrelevant.
stages.submit: Eight-scene dramatic sequence and separate chronologies for both plots.

stages.title: Prepare the double playbill
stages.instructions: Design a two-column playbill with a route for each plot, three points of comparison, and the moment of intersection. Use crossing lines with labels, not color alone. Include a linear scene synopsis that preserves the same relations.
stages.submit: Double playbill and accessible synopsis.

stages.title: Argue the parallel
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how the expedition presses Hamlet toward action while complicating its own value as an example. Add 300 words explaining how your two plots alter judgments of cost, motive, or worth at three points.
stages.submit: Literary argument and subplot self-analysis.

stages.title: Test removal
stages.instructions: Give a reader only the primary plot, then the complete version, or conduct the same comparison after a break. Record which interpretation changes when the secondary plot returns. Revise one scene so the subplot contributes more than delay or decorative variety.
stages.submit: Removal test and a consequential scene revision.

stages.title: Reflect on scale
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why a small object need not produce a small conflict and why great effort need not prove a worthy purpose. Connect the distinction to one choice in each plot and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The warning under the table
projects.brief: Build a scene around a visible sign that one character reads incorrectly. Let the audience know something that changes the significance of that reading. The task is to control the timing of information, as the prayer scene does, without making a character foolish simply to force the plot.
topics: A promise heard without its condition
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Chart who knows
stages.instructions: Divide the prayer scene into Claudius’s confession, Hamlet’s observation, and Claudius’s final words. Record the audience’s knowledge, each character’s knowledge, and the inference that drives the decision. Explain one limit on what the audience can conclude.
stages.submit: Three-stage knowledge chart and a 200-word limit statement.

stages.title: Write the scene modules
stages.instructions: Compose three dramatic modules totaling 1,000–1,250 words: private preparation, a consequential encounter, and a private aftermath. Use two characters and one object whose visible meaning differs from its known history. Give the mistaken reader a plausible reason for the inference.
stages.submit: Three-module script and a list of what each character knows.

stages.title: Stage the information
stages.instructions: Arrange the same modules in three orders: preparation first, preparation last, and preparation divided around the encounter. Create a storyboard of six frames for your preferred order, labeling exactly when the audience learns each key fact. Supply text descriptions.
stages.submit: Three sequence plans and a six-frame accessible storyboard.

stages.title: Defend the audience’s position
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Shakespeare’s speech order creates irony in the prayer scene. Add 300 words comparing the effects of your three orders, distinguishing suspense during a choice from surprise after it.
stages.submit: Literary argument and sequence self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the inference
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to stop before the decision and state what they expect and why. If alone, write predictions for a reader with only the information available at that point. Revise one cue that makes the mistake implausible or gives away more than the chosen order should reveal.
stages.submit: Prediction test and cue revision.

stages.title: Reflect on knowing more
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why greater audience knowledge does not guarantee knowledge of the best alternative action. Identify one consequence your story confirms and one it leaves hypothetical. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: An irreversible cut
projects.brief: Write a short tragedy in which an attempt to remove an obstacle destroys something the protagonist does not fully understand. The loss may concern trust, an archive, a friendship, or a public promise; physical violence is not required. Study Hamlet’s action behind the curtain to examine how uncertainty, pressure, and later explanation interact.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Reconstruct the decision
stages.instructions: Make an exact sequence of the arras scene from Polonius’s concealment through Hamlet’s return to confronting Gertrude. Mark what is known before the act and what is learned afterward. Analyze two phrases through which responsibility is assigned.
stages.submit: Decision sequence and two responsibility annotations.

stages.title: Write the shadow play
stages.instructions: Compose a 900–1,200-word script in six scenes for three characters. Establish an uncertain sign, an available but costly opportunity to verify it, a choice to act, and an irreversible loss. Give the protagonist a post-event explanation that is partly illuminating and partly self-protective.
stages.submit: Six-scene script and a 150-word account of the unchosen verification.

stages.title: Design the silhouettes
stages.instructions: Create five paper or digital silhouette designs and a stage plan using visibility and concealment to support the decision. Annotate what the audience can see that the protagonist cannot. Supply descriptions and a nonvisual staging alternative.
stages.submit: Five designs, stage plan, and accessible staging notes.

stages.title: Argue agency under pressure
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how the arras scene joins incomplete knowledge with action and retrospective blame. Add 300 words explaining how your verification cost preserves both constraint and responsibility.
stages.submit: Literary argument and tragic-choice self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the alternative
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the last credible opportunity for a different choice. If alone, write a 250-word alternate scene using that opportunity. Revise the original so the alternative is available but carries an established cost; do not claim the alternate outcome is certain.
stages.submit: Alternative test, optional scene, and causal revision.

stages.title: Reflect on explanation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish understanding a decision from excusing it. Explain which part of the protagonist’s final account the play supports and which part the staging puts under pressure. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The committee for preventing surprises
projects.brief: Invent a committee whose elaborate effort to prevent an unwanted event accidentally makes it possible. The comedy should arise from conflicting aims and misread conduct, not from mocking a vulnerable character. Austen’s engaged lovers show how a formerly obstructive intervention can acquire a comic meaning after its consequences are understood.
topics: Order that produces its own disruption
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the source reversal
stages.instructions: Map the intention, action, transmitted information, and result of Lady Catherine’s intervention as Darcy describes it. Analyze three exchanges in which teasing or revised interpretation turns former difficulty into shared understanding.
stages.submit: Reversal map and three dialogue annotations.

stages.title: Write the festival
stages.instructions: Compose a five-scene comedy of 1,000–1,300 words with a committee of three and one outsider. Give each committee member a different reason to prevent the same event. Let three precautions contribute causally to its occurrence, and leave one cost visible after the comic resolution.
stages.submit: Five-scene script and a three-precaution causal key.

stages.title: Make the public poster
stages.instructions: Design the committee’s official festival poster and an annotated version produced after the event. Alter no more than twelve words between versions; use those changes to expose the reversal. Supply both as plain text and explain the hierarchy of notices.
stages.submit: Two poster states, text versions, and design explanation.

stages.title: Argue comic consequence
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Austen uses playful dialogue and unintended consequence to develop the relationship. Add 300 words explaining how your precautions earn the outcome and how the remaining cost qualifies the comedy.
stages.submit: Literary argument and comic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test causality and tone
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to trace one precaution to its unexpected result and identify the target of the humor. If alone, remove one precaution and examine whether the ending still follows. Revise a coincidence into a causal link and reconsider any joke that replaces characterization with ridicule.
stages.submit: Causality/tone test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on resolution
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what the ending repairs and what it cannot repair. Distinguish a satisfying reversal from the claim that every problem has vanished, and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Between the door and the bell
projects.artifact: Private speech with a public counterpart
projects.brief: Place a character outside a room where a difficult announcement must be made. Compose the private reasoning before the entrance, a brief aside during the encounter, and the public statement itself. Study Hamlet’s self-exhortation to see how a speech can try to create resolve rather than merely report a settled inner state.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Outline the thinking
stages.instructions: Divide Hamlet’s response to Fortinbras into five movements. For each, name the mental action—questioning, distinguishing, accusing, comparing, or resolving—and cite a phrase that performs it. Identify one uncertainty the final command does not settle.
stages.submit: Five-movement reasoning outline.

stages.title: Compose the threshold sequence
stages.instructions: Write a 45–60-line soliloquy outside an invented room, a 6–10-line aside during the encounter, and a 300–400-word public exchange. The soliloquy must consider two explanations of the character’s hesitation and reject one imperfectly. Let the public words differ from the private resolution in a consequential way.
stages.submit: Three-part dramatic sequence with clear hearing conventions.

stages.title: Score the threshold
stages.instructions: Create a stage diagram showing the door, bell or signal, audience position, and who can hear each passage. Mark six shifts in pace or address in a performance score. Supply a linear description of every movement and hearing boundary.
stages.submit: Stage diagram, six-mark score, and accessible description.

stages.title: Argue self-persuasion
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of Hamlet’s movement from self-accusation toward a resolution. Add 300 words explaining how your private speech, aside, and public exchange distribute knowledge and reveal a limit in the character’s self-understanding.
stages.submit: Literary argument and dramatic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the private voice
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to distinguish what the character believes, what the character wants to believe, and what the scene confirms. If alone, annotate those categories after a break. Revise one line that simply announces a trait into language that performs a thought process.
stages.submit: Belief test and a process-focused revision.

stages.title: Reflect on sincerity
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why a private utterance can be sincere yet incomplete or self-serving. Identify one claim the subsequent exchange tests, and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Passages through the borrowed house
projects.brief: Invent a household in which access to rooms, objects, or knowledge depends on a set of permissions. Tell a story in which one resident discovers that an apparently protective rule serves another person’s interest. Nora’s disputes over law and duty provide a source for examining how authority names an obligation and controls the means of fulfilling it.
topics: The right to ask a serious question
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Compare two authorities
stages.instructions: Read “The disputed signature” and “Duties under dispute.” Identify six claims about what Nora may or must do, the authority invoked for each, and her response. Distinguish Krogstad’s legal assertions from independently established law; analyze them as dramatic speech.
stages.submit: Six-claim authority table.

stages.title: Write the permissions story
stages.instructions: Compose a 1,000–1,250-word story set in an invented household with four residents and six explicit access rules. Include one rule that protects, one that controls, and one that does both. Let a character challenge a rule by acting on an obligation the rule makes difficult to fulfill.
stages.submit: Original story and six-rule household register.

stages.title: Map access
stages.instructions: Create a floor plan and four permission cards showing who may enter, use, speak about, or alter each important space or object. Mark one change after the conflict. Provide a text matrix and explain how the design distinguishes formal permission from practical power.
stages.submit: Plan, four cards, and accessible permission matrix.

stages.title: Argue the contested duty
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word argument about how the two Ibsen exchanges connect duty, knowledge, and authority. Add 300 words analyzing how your household’s rules and narrative perspective shape a reader’s judgment of protection and control.
stages.submit: Literary argument and institutional self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the rule
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to argue for the most defensible rule and against the most troubling one. If alone, write both cases. Revise one rule or scene so the conflict cannot be solved merely by labeling one resident good and another bad.
stages.submit: Two-sided rule test and a substantive revision.

stages.title: Reflect on inquiry
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how asking who may judge can change a conflict before any material rule changes. Identify one dependency the story leaves unresolved and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The inn at low tide
projects.artifact: Tidal story and changing landscape model
projects.brief: Set a story in an invented inn reached by a causeway that the tide periodically covers. The same place should invite different choices at different moments. Jane’s red-room provides a study in how a material restriction can interact with memory, perception, and unequal social relations.
topics: A familiar place seen under pressure
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate place and perception
stages.instructions: Identify eight details in the red-room selection. Classify each as a physical condition, a remembered association, an imaginative comparison, or a combination. Explain how the locked door and mirror produce different kinds of evidence about Jane’s situation.
stages.submit: Eight-detail table and a 200-word comparison.

stages.title: Write three tides
stages.instructions: Compose three linked scenes of 350–450 words each at low tide, rising tide, and high tide. Give two guests incompatible reasons to leave or remain. Repeat three landscape details, changing their significance through perspective and available action. Establish the tide’s limits before they become decisive.
stages.submit: Three-scene story and a factual timeline of the tide.

stages.title: Model changing access
stages.instructions: Create three cross-sections or maps showing the causeway and inn at each stage. Annotate physical access separately from each guest’s interpretation. Include a plain-text route description and do not use color as the sole distinction.
stages.submit: Three-stage landscape model and accessible route notes.

stages.title: Argue confinement
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Brontë joins material enclosure with Jane’s social and imaginative experience. Add 300 words explaining how your tide changes both possible actions and the meanings of three repeated details.
stages.submit: Literary argument and environmental self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the setting’s necessity
stages.instructions: Ask a reader how the conflict would change in an inn on an ordinary street. If alone, rewrite 200 words in that alternative setting. Revise one environmental detail so it affects a choice instead of serving only as atmosphere.
stages.submit: Setting-substitution test and a consequential revision.

stages.title: Reflect on projection
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish something the environment actually prevents from something a character merely fears or imagines. Explain how keeping the distinction visible strengthens the story and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The hearing of a created thing
projects.artifact: Literary tribunal with a reasoned judgment
projects.brief: Invent a created being or object capable of addressing its maker, then stage a hearing about an obligation neither party defines in the same way. Use the confrontation in Frankenstein to practice moving from evidence to an interpretation of responsibility. The final judgment must reason through the evidence rather than merely choose the more sympathetic speaker.
topics: Suffering as explanation and as excuse
The right to be heard before judgment
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Build the source chain
stages.instructions: Select six details from the creature’s confrontation with Victor. For each, write an observation, an inference, and a sentence explaining its contribution to a larger claim. Include one detail that complicates sympathy for each speaker.
stages.submit: Six evidence-to-reasoning chains and a provisional thesis.

stages.title: Write the hearing
stages.instructions: Compose two fictional testimonies of 350–450 words each, one from a maker and one from a made being or speaking object. Add a 250–350-word exchange in which each questions a premise of the other’s account. Establish three agreed facts and two contested interpretations.
stages.submit: Two testimonies, cross-questioning, and a fact/interpretation register.

stages.title: Design the evidence bench
stages.instructions: Create a hearing display with three illustrated exhibits and a reasoning map connecting each to competing claims. Use labeled arrows for support, qualification, and contradiction. Supply a linear account of the same relations.
stages.submit: Three-exhibit display, reasoning map, and accessible account.

stages.title: Write two connected arguments
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word literary essay on how Shelley develops responsibility through the demand to be heard. Then write a 450–600-word judgment for your fictional hearing, including a qualified conclusion and commentary on all three exhibits. Add 250 words explaining how you shaped the two testimonial voices for their audiences.
stages.submit: Source essay, fictional judgment, and rhetorical self-analysis.

stages.title: Reverse-outline the reasoning
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to label each paragraph’s distinct contribution and identify a leap between evidence and conclusion. If alone, reverse-outline after a day. Revise one paragraph that repeats rather than advances the claim, and one commentary sentence that overstates what an exhibit proves.
stages.submit: Reverse outline and two documented reasoning revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on judgment
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how hearing an account can change an obligation without requiring acceptance of every claim. Identify a conclusion you qualified because of evidence, and credit sources while labeling all invented testimony.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Instructions for the perfect patron
projects.artifact: Satirical handbook with a resistant reader
projects.brief: Invent a handbook that claims to teach generosity while revealing its writer’s appetite for recognition. Add responses from a reader who notices different problems than the writer anticipates. Austen’s letter scene offers a study in how praise of duty can expose dependence, vanity, and the interests of those receiving it.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Identify the satirical distance
stages.instructions: Select six moments from Collins’s letter and the family’s responses. For each, distinguish the apparent claim, the implied evaluation, and the target. Include one detail that allows a charitable reading without canceling the satire.
stages.submit: Six-entry irony table and one qualified counterreading.

stages.title: Write the handbook
stages.instructions: Compose eight fictional handbook entries of 80–110 words each, addressed by a self-important patron to apprentices in benevolence. Give the writer two sincere values as well as a blind spot. Add four reader’s marginal replies of 70–100 words each, with one reply that misreads the handbook in a revealing way.
stages.submit: Eight-entry handbook and four marginal responses.

stages.title: Design the exemplary page
stages.instructions: Create a title page, a mock seal, and one annotated spread. Make three design choices that advance the patron’s self-presentation rather than merely making the page ornate. Provide a plain-text reading order and descriptions of the seal’s claims.
stages.submit: Three designed elements and accessible reading version.

stages.title: Argue the target
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Austen makes the act of writing and reading the letter satirical. Add 300 words explaining the gap between your handbook’s professed instruction and the judgment its wording invites. Identify the target precisely.
stages.submit: Literary argument and satirical self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the double meaning
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the writer’s sincere value, blind spot, and the misleading marginal reply. If alone, write a literal paraphrase of three entries and compare it with the implied evaluation. Revise one passage whose irony depends only on a sneering tone.
stages.submit: Double-meaning test and a substantive revision.

stages.title: Reflect on criticism
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how the satire criticizes a practice without making every person associated with it identical. Identify a limit on the resistant reader’s judgment and credit sources.

projects.title: The journal between visits
projects.brief: Write a journal whose conditions of production affect what can be recorded. Its gaps must be visible enough to invite inference and limited enough to resist arbitrary invention. Use a wholly fictional situation; personal disclosure is neither needed nor evaluated. Gilman’s interrupted entries offer a source for distinguishing external restriction from the writer’s own changing capacity.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the breaks
stages.instructions: Annotate six transitions in “Writing interrupted”: stops, resumptions, corrections, or changes of topic. Identify the stated cause where one is supplied, and distinguish an inference from an unknown. Explain how fatigue and prohibition can coexist.
stages.submit: Six-transition record and a 200-word causal distinction.

stages.title: Compose the journal
stages.instructions: Write seven dated entries totaling 1,000–1,250 words across a fictional month. Establish two different causes of interruption, three explicit gaps, and one topic that returns in altered language. Keep a private chronology of ten events, including three that the journal does not directly narrate.
stages.submit: Seven-entry journal and private chronology labeled as author planning.

stages.title: Make the interrupted page
stages.instructions: Create three facsimile entry pages using spacing, unfinished lines, or a clearly labeled blank interval to indicate different kinds of absence. Do not rely on illegible handwriting or hidden text. Supply a complete transcript with each gap described but not filled.
stages.submit: Three facsimiles and accessible transcript.

stages.title: Argue the conditions of telling
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Gilman makes the act of writing part of the narrator’s constraint. Add 300 words explaining what your journal allows readers to infer about two gaps and why the third must remain less determinate.
stages.submit: Literary argument and omission self-analysis.

stages.title: Test inference limits
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to mark three inferences with confidence levels and cite evidence. If alone, make the same list after a break without consulting the private chronology. Revise one gap that is unintelligible and one clue that overexplains its absence.
stages.submit: Inference audit and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on the unwritten
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish what the writer cannot say, chooses not to say, and does not know. Identify one interpretation your private planning does not entitle a reader to claim from the published journal. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The first successful attempt
projects.artifact: Graphic narrative of a limited discovery
projects.brief: Create a graphic narrative about someone learning a physical or artistic skill and mistaking the first success for a larger kind of mastery. The discovery should be meaningful without being complete. No real attempt at a dangerous activity is required; the action is fictional and can involve something ordinary such as dancing, drawing, or balancing a model.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the recognition
stages.instructions: Divide Edna’s swim into prior dependence, success, expansion, fear, return, and others’ judgment. Select one detail for each stage and distinguish the narrator’s qualification from Edna’s immediate feeling.
stages.submit: Six-stage recognition chart.

stages.title: Write the sequence
stages.instructions: Script a twelve-panel narrative with 600–800 words of captions and dialogue. Give the learner an earlier difficulty, a first success, an expansive inference, a limit, and an aftermath. Add a 300-word scene from one observer’s perspective that interprets the departure or silence differently.
stages.submit: Twelve-panel script and observer’s scene.

stages.title: Draw changes of scale
stages.instructions: Storyboard the twelve panels using simple drawings, collage, or labeled shapes. Change framing or scale at three turning points to distinguish actual distance or capacity from perceived possibility. Supply panel descriptions and a linear transcript.
stages.submit: Twelve-panel storyboard and accessible transcript.

stages.title: Argue partial insight
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Chopin develops discovery and its limit in the swim. Add 300 words explaining how your visual scale, narration, and observer’s scene prevent either total triumph or total failure from exhausting the event.
stages.submit: Literary argument and visual-narrative self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the change
stages.instructions: Ask a reader what the learner now knows, what the learner wrongly assumes, and what the observer misses. If alone, answer from only the finished sequence after a break. Revise one panel and one sentence so the recognition has a specific, bounded content.
stages.submit: Recognition test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on aftermath
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what later evidence would be needed to claim a lasting transformation. Identify a change the sequence establishes and a future it cannot promise. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.
