projects.title: The last page and the unprinted future
projects.artifact: Short story with a designed stopping point
projects.brief: Write a story that completes one action while leaving a consequential future unconfirmed. Then design its last page so the ending’s material form participates in the stopping point. Ibsen’s final objects, exit, question, and sound show how an ending can be definite about the present without promising a sequel.
topics: Leaving without knowing where to go
A repaired object and an unrepaired relationship
A promise whose conditions remain unmet
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate kinds of closure
stages.instructions: List six details from Nora’s final departure. For each, state what it closes, what it leaves open, and whose belief or hope it presents. Distinguish the final sound from a prediction of future events.
stages.submit: Six-detail closure table.

stages.title: Compose the story and trials
stages.instructions: Write an 850–1,100-word story ending with a completed action and an unresolved relational question. Draft two alternative final paragraphs of 150–200 words each: one that overexplains the future and one that withholds too much basic information. Use the trials to choose and revise the original ending.
stages.submit: Story, two trial endings, and final selected version.

stages.title: Design the final leaf
stages.instructions: Create a last-page layout with one visual element, such as a returned object, interrupted pattern, or blank interval. Explain its relation to the final sentence without using decoration as a substitute for an ending. Provide a plain-text version and a description of the visual choice.
stages.submit: Designed final leaf and accessible alternative.

stages.title: Argue the stopping point
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Ibsen combines decisive separation with an unconfirmed possibility. Add 300 words comparing your three endings and explaining why the chosen stopping point gives enough information for a defensible interpretation.
stages.submit: Literary argument and closure self-analysis.

stages.title: Test predictions
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to propose two plausible futures and identify evidence limiting each. If alone, perform the same test after a break. Revise a detail that accidentally guarantees a future you intended to leave conditional, or supplies too little basis for any inference.
stages.submit: Two-future test and a calibrated revision.

stages.title: Reflect on completion
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why an unresolved future does not make the story incomplete. Identify the completed action and the interpretive work the final page leaves to the reader. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The travelling stain
projects.brief: Invent a recurring mark that moves through an ordinary community and changes meaning with each appearance. It may be a stain, a sound, a phrase, or a small repair. The repetitions must develop a pattern of attention and response rather than merely announce that the object is important.
topics: A sign of damage becoming a badge
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Track the source motif
stages.instructions: Choose six returns or transformations of the wallpaper in “The pattern in changing light.” Include visual change, stillness, surveillance, and smell. Explain how at least two returns alter the relation between observer and observed.
stages.submit: Six-entry motif-development ledger.

stages.title: Write the installments
stages.instructions: Compose five installments of 220–280 words each. Return the same mark in every installment through a different observer or sensory context. Give the mark one material cause, but allow at least three meanings to develop around it. The fifth installment must revise an earlier association without erasing the cause.
stages.submit: Five-part serial tale and a material-cause note.

stages.title: Print the recurring ornament
stages.instructions: Design a small opening ornament for each installment. Preserve two visual features across all five and alter a third to reflect changing interpretation. Add five concise captions tied to exact sentences and provide descriptions independent of color.
stages.submit: Five related ornaments, captions, and accessible descriptions.

stages.title: Argue development through return
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Gilman develops the wallpaper through changing perception and repeated acts of watching. Add 300 words explaining how your five appearances form a developing argument rather than a repeated code.
stages.submit: Literary argument and motif self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the sequence
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to order the five appearances by their changing meaning, or shuffle the installments and perform the test after a break. Revise one return that adds no new relation, and check that the final revision of meaning has earlier support.
stages.submit: Sequence test and a meaningful recurrence revision.

stages.title: Reflect on cause and meaning
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish the mark’s material origin from what people make it signify. Explain a symbolic association the story supports and one it does not. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Postcards from within reach
projects.brief: Create postcards written from one physically limited place toward several imagined destinations. Each card should reveal both the desired elsewhere and the present that makes it desirable. Jane’s outward view and inward tale provide a source for examining how actual and imagined spaces can offer different forms of movement.
topics: A wider life imagined from routine
Privacy as both refuge and limit
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Map actual and imagined reach
stages.instructions: Identify six spatial details in Jane’s horizon passage. Distinguish actual movement, visible distance, imagined experience, and social restriction. Explain how the corridor permits something the roof cannot provide.
stages.submit: Six-detail spatial table and a comparative paragraph.

stages.title: Write the cards
stages.instructions: Compose six postcards, each containing a 12–16-line poem on the imagined destination and a 100–140-word note about the writer’s actual surroundings. Keep one fictional sender and one location throughout. Let the final card revise a desire from the first without simply renouncing it.
stages.submit: Six paired poetic and prose postcards.

stages.title: Design fronts and backs
stages.instructions: Design three complete cards with a front image and a reverse layout. Make the front/back relation complicate rather than merely illustrate the same claim. Supply image descriptions and a continuous reading version of all six cards.
stages.submit: Three designed cards and accessible sequence.

stages.title: Argue range and opportunity
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Brontë relates physical range, imagination, and the desire for experience. Add 300 words explaining three contrasts between your cards’ imagined destinations and their present-tense notes.
stages.submit: Literary argument and spatial self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the sender
stages.instructions: Ask a reader what the sender values nearby and what remains unavailable. If alone, read only the prose notes, then only the poems, and compare the character each creates. Revise one pair that makes the present wholly worthless or the elsewhere automatically liberating.
stages.submit: Split-reading test and a qualified pair revision.

stages.title: Reflect on elsewhere
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one movement the imagination enables and one practical limit it does not remove. Identify how the final card changes the opening desire and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The house of guaranteed safety
projects.brief: Invent a residence advertised as completely secure from one ordinary human difficulty. Let its protective design produce an unexpected form of unease. Poe’s abbey provides a source for examining how an enclosure’s promise can be challenged by features already inside it; the project need not use violence or graphic horror.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the refuge
stages.instructions: Annotate six details in the Masque opening that promise security or disturb it. Include the sealed gates, restricted sight, exceptional chamber, and clock. Explain one feature that serves both protection and constraint.

stages.title: Write promise and experience
stages.instructions: Compose a 400–500-word fictional prospectus for the residence and an 800–1,000-word visitor’s tale set during one evening there. Give the house four advertised protections and one recurring ordinary sound. Let the sound challenge a promise without requiring a confirmed supernatural explanation.
stages.submit: Prospectus, visitor’s tale, and a four-promise correspondence key.

stages.title: Design the reassuring plan
stages.instructions: Create an eight-space floor plan with controlled routes and sight lines. Add the prospectus’s reassuring captions and the visitor’s later annotations. Provide a text walkthrough that identifies both physical constraints and perceived threats.
stages.submit: Annotated plan and accessible walkthrough.

stages.title: Argue the ordinary made strange
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Poe’s architecture and clock unsettle the courtiers’ assurance. Add 300 words explaining how your ordinary sound, spatial design, and contrasting documents produce unease without relying only on dark decoration.
stages.submit: Literary argument and Gothic self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the promise
stages.instructions: Ask a reader which advertised protection becomes troubling and where the text first prepares that change. If alone, remove all overtly frightening adjectives and reread. Revise one structural or sensory detail so unease survives without those adjectives.
stages.submit: Promise test and a structural revision.

stages.title: Reflect on uncertainty
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish what the visitor observes from what the visitor attributes to the house. Explain why the unresolved explanation matters and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: An obituary and an answering voice
projects.brief: Write a public memorial for an invented person whose life helped some people and harmed others. Pair it with an answering voice that complicates the account without becoming automatically authoritative. Frankenstein’s final encounter offers a source for holding sympathy, confession, loyalty, and responsibility in the same interpretive field.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Audit the allocation of sympathy
stages.instructions: Identify six moments in the final creature exchange that invite sympathy, limit it, assign blame, or question an account. Include Walton’s loyalty and the creature’s admission concerning innocent victims. State whose experience is not directly heard.
stages.submit: Six-moment ethical ledger and a 150-word account of absent perspectives.

stages.title: Write the memorial and response
stages.instructions: Invent a person and establish a private chronology of eight events. Write a 600–750-word obituary by an admiring acquaintance and a 500–650-word response by someone differently affected. Let each voice report at least two accurate facts and omit one consequential fact; the response must also have a limit in perspective.
stages.submit: Two fictional texts and a clearly labeled author’s fact register.

stages.title: Design the memorial spread
stages.instructions: Create a two-page spread with one image, a timeline, and an explicit reading order that prevents the response from becoming an unreadable footnote. Label what the image can and cannot establish. Supply a linear accessible version.
stages.submit: Memorial spread, image caption, and accessible texts.

stages.title: Argue understanding without acquittal
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how Shelley makes suffering relevant without allowing it to settle responsibility. Add 300 words explaining how your two voices distribute credibility and attention, including the person or group neither fully represents.
stages.submit: Literary argument and ethical self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the missing cost
stages.instructions: Ask a reader which facts they trust in each account and whose experience they still cannot reconstruct. If alone, make a claim-by-claim confidence table after a break. Revise one emotionally persuasive sentence that outruns its evidence and one omission that makes the second voice too easily authoritative.
stages.submit: Credibility test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on remembrance
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how a reader can understand a person without approving every act. Identify a limit on your own fictional memorial and label all invented people and events. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The disputed final panel
projects.brief: Create a short comic whose final action supports two serious readings of a character’s situation. The alternatives must arise from shared evidence, not from withholding a basic fact that would make one interpretation impossible. Gilman’s ending provides a source for examining how resistance and continuing constraint can remain entangled.
topics: A victory that preserves a dependency
A welcome that may also be a boundary
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Build two strong readings
stages.instructions: For the wallpaper ending, write two 180–220-word interpretations with three details each. Give the strongest case for resistance and the strongest case for continued constraint, then identify a detail both must explain. Avoid inventing a future beyond the ending.
stages.submit: Two evidence-based readings and a shared difficulty.

stages.title: Script the comic
stages.instructions: Write an eight-panel comic with 500–700 words of captions and dialogue. End with one definite action that can be interpreted in two consequential ways. Supply enough prior information to make both readings plausible. Add a 250-word scene from earlier in the same fictional world that clarifies stakes without resolving the ending.
stages.submit: Eight-panel script and prior-stakes scene.

stages.title: Draw the final sequence
stages.instructions: Storyboard all eight panels and produce a more finished version of the last two. Use framing, repeated objects, or the relation between caption and image to sustain the alternatives. Include panel-by-panel descriptions that preserve the ambiguity.
stages.submit: Storyboard, two finished panels, and accessible description sequence.

stages.title: Defend and compare
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Gilman’s ending supports a qualified account of escape. Add two 200–250-word critical notes on your comic, each defending one reading, followed by a 150-word judgment of their relative strengths and limits.
stages.submit: Literary argument, competing notes, and evaluative self-analysis.

stages.title: Test fairness
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to defend the reading you consider weaker using the comic alone. If alone, do so after a break. Revise one detail that makes an alternative a straw argument or lets it ignore a consequential fact. Do not resolve the ambiguity merely to simplify the test.
stages.submit: Alternative-reading test and a fairness revision.

stages.title: Reflect on scope
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain whether the readings compete, overlap, or operate at different levels. Name a third interpretation the comic does not support and explain why. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Two poems from a farewell
projects.brief: Make two poems from the problem of a farewell: one composed from a carefully credited selection of Dickens’s words, and one newly written from another perspective. Then explain how selection changes the account a reader receives. The aim is to make the difference between vivid evidence and sufficient evidence tangible through composition.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Assign evidence roles
stages.instructions: Choose eight details from Joe’s departure and give each a role: distance, affection, self-qualification, change, or unresolved consequence. Draft a claim supported by three details that perform different roles, then identify a fourth that limits it.
stages.submit: Eight-detail evidence table and a qualified claim.

stages.title: Compose the two poems
stages.instructions: Create a 16–24-line found poem using only words from the displayed Dickens selection, preserving their order within each borrowed phrase and marking any rearrangement in a source key. Then write an original 28–40-line lyric from the perspective of a fictional person receiving an awkward farewell. Use at least three concrete details that complicate the speaker’s preferred explanation.
stages.submit: Credited found poem, original lyric, and exact source key.

stages.title: Make the selection folio
stages.instructions: Design a three-page folio showing source phrases, the found poem, and the original lyric. Connect five selected phrases to what their removal from context changes. Supply a plain-text sequence and avoid erasing the original source in the only available view.
stages.submit: Three-page folio, five context annotations, and accessible version.

stages.title: Argue what the evidence permits
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how Dickens develops affection under social pressure, using evidence with distinct functions. Add 300 words comparing what your found poem emphasizes or suppresses with what the original lyric can invent, and explain the audience effect of each selection.
stages.submit: Literary argument and selection self-analysis.

stages.title: Test sufficiency
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to infer the relationship from the found poem, then read the full source and revise that inference. If alone, compare the two after a break. Restore or annotate one omitted complication and revise one original line whose claim exceeds the scene’s evidence.
stages.submit: Context-restoration test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on transformation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish creative transformation from a faithful critical account. Explain why a found poem may narrow a source deliberately while an analytical essay must acknowledge relevant counterevidence. Credit Dickens, the edition, and all visual sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and full attribution.

projects.title: The account that will not close
projects.brief: Write a sequence in which a speaker repeatedly tries to settle an emotional account. Let each sonnet change what counts as loss, repayment, or restoration. Sonnet 30 offers a study in how an accumulated burden can meet a compact but qualified counterforce.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the reckoning
stages.instructions: Map Sonnet 30’s quatrains and couplet. Annotate six words from its legal or financial field and explain how the syntax renews rather than closes grief. Identify the condition governing the final restoration.
stages.submit: Formal map and six metaphor annotations.

stages.title: Compose the sequence
stages.instructions: Write three fourteen-line sonnets spoken by one fictional person at different moments. Use a declared rhyme pattern in each, with at least one poem organized as three quatrains and a couplet. Reuse one line in a changed context across all three. Let the last poem revise what the first considers a settled account.
stages.submit: Three sonnets and a 200-word account of their speaking occasions.

stages.title: Bind the ledger
stages.instructions: Design a three-spread booklet in which columns, ruled lines, or marginal balances make the account visible. Annotate the reused line each time without reducing the feeling to an actual monetary sum. Supply the poems in uninterrupted reading order.
stages.submit: Ledger booklet, three annotations, and accessible sequence.

stages.title: Argue the turn
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Sonnet 30’s accumulation and couplet develop consolation. Add 350 words explaining the turn in each of your sonnets and the changing function of the repeated line.
stages.submit: Literary argument and sequence self-analysis.

stages.title: Test each closure
stages.instructions: Ask a reader what each couplet or final section resolves and what remains. If alone, remove each ending and write the expectation created by the preceding lines. Revise one ending that merely repeats the poem and one transition between sonnets.
stages.submit: Closure test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on restoration
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish a changed relation to loss from the reversal of the loss itself. Identify what your final sonnet can and cannot restore, and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Praise and remembrance of one place
projects.artifact: Ode–elegy diptych with a memorial leaf
projects.brief: Choose an invented public place and write about it first as a living presence and later as an absence. The ode and elegy should share particulars but perform different work. Keats and Gray provide sources for distinguishing sustained appreciation from remembrance without excluding transience from praise.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Compare the modes
stages.instructions: Read “To Autumn” and the opening of Gray’s “Elegy.” Select three details from each that show how attention moves. Explain the difference between autumn’s own music and the familiar sounds that can no longer rouse the buried villagers.
stages.submit: Six-detail comparison and two movement outlines.

stages.title: Write the diptych
stages.instructions: Invent a public place with five concrete features and a history of ordinary use. Write a 30–42-line ode attending to it while it exists and a 30–42-line elegy after its disappearance. Repeat three details with changed functions. The elegy may offer, qualify, or refuse consolation, but must make that movement perceptible.
stages.submit: Two poems and a 200-word fictional place history.

stages.title: Design the memorial leaf
stages.instructions: Create one page from a local commemorative volume with an image of the place, an empty or altered version, and three captions connecting repeated details. Include descriptions and distinguish invented history from any real visual source used.
stages.submit: Memorial leaf and accessible descriptions.

stages.title: Argue value and absence
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word comparison of how Keats and Gray make ordinary life or seasonal experience worthy of attention. Add 300 words explaining how your two poems differ in address, movement, and treatment of consolation.
stages.submit: Comparative argument and genre self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the difference
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify what each poem does beyond being happy or sad. If alone, exchange the titles and see whether the internal movement still distinguishes the forms. Revise one repeated image whose function has not changed enough.
stages.submit: Genre test and an image-function revision.

stages.title: Reflect on remembrance
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what the elegy remembers that the ode overlooked, and what the ode preserves that mourning risks simplifying. Credit the source poems and edition.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The parcel no one claims
projects.brief: Tell a community’s story through a disputed unclaimed parcel. A returning refrain should mean something different after each new piece of testimony. Wordsworth’s child and adult provide a source for examining how a narrative frame can judge another voice while leaving that voice room to resist.
topics: A community’s rules for counting someone as present
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate the voices
stages.instructions: Map the adult frame and the child’s embedded account in “We Are Seven.” Annotate five returns of the number or related counting language. Explain how the child’s ordinary activities near the graves affect the adult’s interpretation.
stages.submit: Voice map and five recurrence annotations.

stages.title: Compose the ballad
stages.instructions: Write a 12–16-stanza narrative poem using four-line stanzas and a declared recurring rhyme pattern. Include three speakers, a disputed parcel, and a one- or two-line refrain that returns at least four times. Let the final stanza change the frame narrator’s relation to the evidence without requiring every speaker to agree.
stages.submit: Ballad and a 150-word key identifying the speakers.

stages.title: Make the broadside
stages.instructions: Design a single-sheet broadside with three small scene images and a clear reading order. Mark changes of speaker through labels or typographic conventions, and provide a plain transcript. Add a 300-word prose account by one minor speaker that challenges a framing assumption.
stages.submit: Broadside, accessible transcript, and counteraccount.

stages.title: Argue the contested count
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Wordsworth’s framing and the child’s narrative sustain the disagreement. Add 300 words explaining how your refrain changes across four appearances and what the counteraccount reveals about the narrator.
stages.submit: Literary argument and ballad self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the refrain
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to paraphrase the refrain after its first and final appearances. If alone, read the refrain separately and then restore its contexts. Revise one stanza so the changed meaning comes from an event or detail rather than a new explanatory label.
stages.submit: Context test and a narrative revision.

stages.title: Reflect on telling
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain which speaker gets the last word and whether that placement makes the speaker wholly authoritative. Identify one unresolved but bounded disagreement and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The curator conducts a tour
projects.brief: Invent a curator who displays a collection while trying to secure a new patron. The tour should reveal the curator’s values through what is praised, dismissed, controlled, and left unexplained. Browning’s duke provides a source for studying how a speaker can manage a listener yet disclose more than intended.
topics: Taste as a claim to authority
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Infer the listener
stages.instructions: Identify six cues in “My Last Duchess” that establish the listener’s role or direct the encounter. Explain the difference between what the duke explicitly reports and what the compressed commands suggest. Do not invent a precise unseen event as fact.
stages.submit: Six-cue audience chart and a 200-word inference limit.

stages.title: Write the tour
stages.instructions: Compose a 60–80-line dramatic monologue by a fictional curator to a silent potential patron. Include three displayed objects, two courteous commands, one disclaimer of skill contradicted by the performance, and one consequential omission. Reveal the listener’s practical stake only in the final third.
stages.submit: Original monologue and a private note on the omitted event.

stages.title: Prepare the guide
stages.instructions: Create a three-object exhibition guide with labels in the curator’s voice and unobtrusive factual notes that complicate them. Draw or diagram the route through the display and show where the listener is asked to pause. Supply object descriptions and a linear tour.
stages.submit: Guide, route, and accessible text.

stages.title: Argue unintended disclosure
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how Browning makes the duke’s explanation disclose his expectations of relationships. Add 300 words analyzing three moments where your curator’s wording reveals a value the curator does not directly confess.
stages.submit: Literary argument and monologue self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the inference
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the listener’s stake and distinguish a supported implication from a guess about the omission. If alone, make that distinction after a break. Revise one cue that explains too much and one whose ambiguity has no evidentiary basis.
stages.submit: Inference test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on control
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how the curator controls the tour and where the reader can resist that control. Identify a limit on the factual notes’ authority and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A conversation with a silent monument
projects.artifact: Address poem and response-bearing sculpture plan
projects.brief: Address an invented monument that cannot answer, then make the poem reveal how much of the conversation the speaker supplies. Keats’s urn offers a source for examining praise, questioning, consolation, and attributed speech directed toward a silent object. The project can use a paper model or diagram; no permanent installation is required.
topics: Public memory that cannot explain itself
An object asked to console the living
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Follow the addresses
stages.instructions: Chart six changes of addressee or speaking action in the urn poem. Include a question, a command, a consolation, and an attributed reply. Distinguish depicted details from the imagined town and its consequences.
stages.submit: Six-moment address chart.

stages.title: Compose the encounter
stages.instructions: Invent a monument with three visible features and an uncertain purpose. Write a 45–60-line poem that addresses the object, one represented figure, and an absent place or person. Include five unanswered questions and a brief response the speaker attributes to the monument, whose authority the surrounding poem complicates.
stages.submit: Address poem and a 200-word account of visible features.

stages.title: Model silence
stages.instructions: Draw three views or make a simple paper model of the monument. Place short excerpts at three viewing positions and explain what can be seen from each. Provide descriptions and a linear text version so physical movement is optional.
stages.submit: Three-view model, excerpt placements, and accessible route.

stages.title: Argue the supplied voice
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how Keats’s changing addresses develop permanence as both attraction and deprivation. Add 300 words explaining what your speaker supplies beyond the monument’s visible evidence and how the attributed response remains open to scrutiny.
stages.submit: Literary argument and address self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the object
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to separate visible facts from the speaker’s projections. If alone, compare the poem with the three-view description after a break. Revise one projection that is accidentally presented as verified history and one question that adds no interpretive pressure.
stages.submit: Projection audit and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on answering
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what changes when a speaker imagines an object answering. Identify one claim the monument cannot independently verify and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A banquet made of time
projects.brief: Invent a banquet whose courses are portions of an intangible experience. Develop one coherent comparison through appetite, preparation, service, and leaving the table. Dickinson’s natural intoxication provides a source for examining how a familiar image field can expand beyond its ordinary limits.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Map the figure
stages.instructions: Trace six linked drinking terms in Dickinson’s poem. Identify what each contributes to the experience of nature and where the figure changes scale. Explain why the landlords and heavenly spectators matter beyond decorative novelty.
stages.submit: Six-part metaphor map and a scale note.

stages.title: Write the banquet
stages.instructions: Choose one intangible experience and compare it consistently with a meal. Write a five-course fictional menu with 70–100 words per course, then a 36–48-line lyric by a guest moving through it. Include one course that resists consumption and one point where the comparison deliberately strains.
stages.submit: Five-course menu, lyric, and a 150-word statement of the central comparison.

stages.title: Design the service
stages.instructions: Create a place setting and sequence diagram with five labeled elements. Tie each to an exact phrase and identify one element whose significance changes between menu and poem. Provide a text table and descriptions of all symbolic objects.
stages.submit: Place-setting design, sequence, and accessible key.

stages.title: Argue extension
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how Dickinson extends the drinking metaphor through limits, companions, and spectators. Add 300 words explaining what three extensions and one strain contribute to your lyric’s treatment of the chosen experience.
stages.submit: Literary argument and metaphor self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the mapping
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to explain the central comparison and identify a detail that does not fit neatly. If alone, make a literal paraphrase after a break. Revise one accidental inconsistency while retaining and defending the deliberate strain.
stages.submit: Mapping test and a justified distinction between revision and retention.

stages.title: Reflect on appetite
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what the banquet model makes understandable and what it risks simplifying. Identify one feature of the experience that cannot be fully reduced to consumption. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A city in six returns
projects.artifact: Urban lyric sequence and recurring image strip
projects.brief: Build a lyric sequence around an ordinary detail that passes through several people’s lives in an invented city. The pattern should widen the speaker’s attention without reducing those people to symbols. McKay’s repeated feet provide a source for examining the relation between concrete bodies, social conditions, and a speaker’s identification.
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the changing detail
stages.instructions: Annotate six references or associations around feet in “Harlem Shadows.” Track diction, time, sensory exposure, and the speaker’s changing address. Explain the difference between expressing solidarity and claiming direct access to another person’s thoughts.
stages.submit: Six-entry pattern chart and a 200-word perspective limit.

stages.title: Compose the returns
stages.instructions: Write six linked poems of 12–18 lines each around one recurring urban detail. Use at least three distinct human situations and change the speaker’s relation to the detail across the sequence. Give each represented person a concrete action or desire beyond the symbolic pattern.
stages.submit: Six-poem sequence and a brief record of the three situations.

stages.title: Make the image strip
stages.instructions: Create six small prints, drawings, or labeled collages with one recurring visual element. Alter context, scale, or placement in each. Add captions tied to specific lines and descriptions that preserve the people’s particular actions.
stages.submit: Six-image strip, captions, and accessible descriptions.

stages.title: Argue pattern and person
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how McKay’s recurrences connect bodily experience with social pressure and identification. Add 350 words explaining how your pattern develops while preserving differences among the people represented.
stages.submit: Literary argument and representational self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the individuals
stages.instructions: Ask a reader what distinguishes the people besides their relation to the recurring object. If alone, remove the motif temporarily and reread their actions. Revise two lines or captions that turn a person into a generic illustration of suffering or hope.
stages.submit: Particularity test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on identification
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what the speaker can observe, what the speaker infers, and what remains another person’s unspoken experience. Credit sources and label the city and people as invented.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: A fixed pattern with an unsettled ending
projects.artifact: Constrained poem and deliberately loosened version
projects.brief: Place an unresolved experience inside a strict pattern, then test what happens when the pattern changes. The point is not to assume that constraint means oppression or looseness means freedom. McKay’s “Outcast” shows how a formally completed utterance can leave the represented condition unfulfilled.
topics: An obligation without a clear endpoint
A wish organized but not granted
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Locate the tension
stages.instructions: Map the rhyme and argument of “Outcast.” Identify three wishes, three constraints, and the work of the final causal couplet. Explain what formal closure achieves without claiming that it resolves the speaker’s estrangement.
stages.submit: Form/modality map and a closure distinction.

stages.title: Write under a rule
stages.instructions: Compose a 28-line poem in seven quatrains. Use an ABAB rhyme pattern in each quatrain, repeat one complete line in stanzas 1, 4, and 7, and keep a consistent base rhythm. Let the final stanza complete the pattern while leaving a particular obligation or wish unresolved. Then create a free-verse version using the same images and at least two-thirds of the original words.
stages.submit: Constrained poem, free-verse version, and a word-retention record.

stages.title: Make the constraint visible
stages.instructions: Design facing pages that show the recurring line and rhyme relations through a restrained border or connecting pattern. Add a separate diagram of the emotional or argumentative movement so form and meaning are not collapsed into one image. Provide a text key.
stages.submit: Facing-page layout, movement diagram, and accessible key.

stages.title: Argue relation rather than code
stages.instructions: Write a 650–850-word analysis of how McKay’s formal ending relates to continuing estrangement. Add 350 words comparing three moments in your two versions, including one where loosened form does not produce the effect you expected.
stages.submit: Literary argument and controlled formal self-analysis.

stages.title: Test expectation
stages.instructions: Ask a reader where each version seems to promise closure and whether the ending fulfills that promise. If alone, read each aloud after a break. Revise one forced rhyme and one unresolved detail that lacks enough prior development.
stages.submit: Expectation test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on constraint
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain one productive pressure of the rule and one limitation you chose to accept or alter. Distinguish the poem’s completed pattern from its character’s unresolved situation and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: Two songs for the same household
projects.artifact: Paired voice poems and comparative edition
projects.brief: Write two poems about one invented household routine, each with a different relation to the comfort it offers. The second poem should change how the first can be read without merely announcing that its speaker is wrong. Blake’s paired chimney-sweeper poems provide a source for comparing the reality of consolation with the uses made of it by authority.
topics: Comfort used as evidence of fairness
A tradition that means different things to participants
Happiness that coexists with a cost
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Build parallel evidence
stages.instructions: Make a comparison table with six rows: speaker, listener, clothing, song, comfort, and ending. Supply one exact detail from each Blake poem in every row and explain the functional difference. Draft a claim that requires both poems.
stages.submit: Six-row comparison and a relational thesis.

stages.title: Compose the paired songs
stages.instructions: Invent a household routine with a real benefit and an unequal cost. Write two poems of 28–40 lines each from distinct participants’ perspectives. Repeat four images but alter their functions. Give both speakers something accurately perceived and something their position makes difficult to see.
stages.submit: Two poems and a 200-word factual account of the shared routine.

stages.title: Edit the facing pages
stages.instructions: Design a comparative edition with paired margins for the four recurring images. Connect corresponding lines without forcing them to mean the same thing. Include a linear edition and concise descriptions of any imagery.
stages.submit: Facing-page edition, four comparative notes, and accessible version.

stages.title: Write the comparison
stages.instructions: Write a 750–950-word essay comparing how Blake’s two poems relate consolation to continuing injury. Organize paragraphs around shared questions rather than one whole poem at a time. Add 300 words explaining how your second poem revises but does not simply cancel the first.
stages.submit: Comparative literary essay and paired-voice self-analysis.

stages.title: Test fairness to both
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to defend each speaker using the poems alone. If alone, write two short defenses after a break. Revise one image that has the same function in both poems and one sentence that makes a speaker only a mouthpiece for your conclusion.
stages.submit: Two-voice test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on comparison
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify a claim that becomes possible only through reading the poems together. Explain what remains distinct and cannot be merged into a single voice. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The last reliable sensation
projects.artifact: Sensory lyric and annotated uncertainty record
projects.brief: Write a poem about a moment when a speaker expects a decisive sign but receives something harder to interpret. The moment can concern an announcement, a reunion, a performance, or an ordinary discovery; death is not required. The poem should offer enough evidence for a clear claim while establishing a boundary beyond which certainty would be invented.
topics: Expectation interrupted by an ordinary detail
A sign whose meaning remains conditional
The difference between perception and explanation
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Mark the source’s limits
stages.instructions: In Dickinson’s fly poem, identify five observations, three inferences a reader might make, and two claims the ending does not establish. Explain how the anticipated king and the final failed sight differ in explicitness.
stages.submit: Observation/inference/limit record.

stages.title: Compose the uncertain moment
stages.instructions: Write a 32–44-line lyric with a specific speaker, occasion, and anticipated sign. Include four concrete sensory details, an ordinary interruption, and an ending that limits perception without erasing the event. Add a 250–350-word prose account by a different observer whose information overlaps but does not settle every question.
stages.submit: Lyric and partial counteraccount.

stages.title: Design the perception plate
stages.instructions: Create an annotated page using three clearly labeled categories: observed, inferred, and unknown. Apply them to six moments across the poem and counteraccount. Do not annotate every ambiguity away; provide a separate linear list of the evidence and its limits.
stages.submit: Perception plate and accessible evidence list.

stages.title: Argue with a boundary
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how Dickinson develops expectation and interruption, ending with a precise qualification. Add 300 words explaining how your lyric and counteraccount support one strong interpretation and resist one overclaim.
stages.submit: Literary argument and qualification self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the overclaim
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to write the strongest claim they can defend and one tempting claim they cannot. If alone, perform the test after a break. Revise one vague phrase into specific evidence and one categorical statement into a warranted limit; keep the central interpretation clear.
stages.submit: Claim test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on certainty
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why qualification strengthens rather than empties your interpretation. Identify the exact detail that sets its boundary and credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The education of a mistaken ambition
projects.artifact: Branching story with a development atlas
projects.brief: Create a fictional apprenticeship in which a desired status depends on someone the protagonist initially undervalues. The branches should expose different costs of learning rather than offer a simple good ending and bad ending. Read Pip’s recognition across the novel as a model of development that takes time and action.
topics: An education that changes the meaning of achievement
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace a formation
stages.instructions: Read the two Pip selections and locate two intervening episodes in Great Expectations. Build a four-moment record of what Pip knows, values, and does. Distinguish the older narrator’s understanding from the younger character’s response.
stages.submit: Four-episode evidence record with chapter references.

stages.title: Write the branches
stages.instructions: Write 1,400–1,800 words of original fiction in six linked scenes. Begin with a mistaken ambition, introduce a revelation about its source, and offer two consequential decisions leading to three possible endings. Each ending must preserve one cost that knowledge cannot erase. Give the supporting character an aim beyond educating the protagonist.
stages.submit: Six-scene branching story and a list of its decision points.

stages.title: Map the education
stages.instructions: Draw an atlas of the branches using different paths for changes in knowledge, conduct, and status. Annotate four places where these do not change together. Provide a numbered reading route and text description of every connection.
stages.submit: Development atlas and accessible route.

stages.title: Argue the change
stages.instructions: Write a 750–950-word argument about how Pip’s changing judgment contributes to the novel’s treatment of gentility. Add 300 words comparing two of your endings and explaining why recognition does or does not produce changed conduct.
stages.submit: Whole-work argument and branch self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the choices
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to choose a route and explain the protagonist’s reason at each decision. If alone, revisit the routes after a day without your planning notes. Revise one choice whose consequence feels arbitrary and one supporting-character action that exists only to teach a lesson.
stages.submit: Route record and two substantive revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on formation
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, identify a value the protagonist revises and a limitation the story leaves intact. Explain how an ending can show growth without rewarding every desire. Credit the novel and any visual sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The catalogue of an impossible refuge
projects.artifact: Genre-changing story in three catalogue entries
projects.brief: Invent a refuge whose official catalogue promises safety. Tell one continuous story through entries that begin as Gothic warning, become domestic observation, and end in a form you deliberately choose. Let the shift change the reader’s judgment of an unfamiliar inhabitant without excusing every action.
topics: Care discovered in an alarming place
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Identify the expectation
stages.instructions: Read the cottage selection and the earlier creation scene in Frankenstein. Annotate three details that invite fear and three that complicate it. Explain how access to the creature’s account changes the grounds of judgment.
stages.submit: Six-detail genre analysis with two source locations.

stages.title: Compose the catalogue
stages.instructions: Write three linked entries of 450–600 words each for an invented refuge: its entrance, a shared room, and a forbidden object. Use the first to establish a threatening expectation, the second to reveal a routine of care, and the third to test both accounts through a consequential action. Include a cataloguer whose assumptions become visible.
stages.submit: Three-entry story and a 150-word declared genre plan.

stages.title: Design the cabinet
stages.instructions: Create three illustrated catalogue leaves with an object number, image or diagram, and a caption whose wording reveals the cataloguer’s judgment. Add a fourth leaf that corrects one classification without replacing it with an equally simplistic label. Supply text descriptions.
stages.submit: Four catalogue leaves and accessible descriptions.

stages.title: Defend the change
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word argument about how Shelley complicates the relation between appearance and moral judgment. Add 300 words explaining the expectations established and revised by each entry in your catalogue.
stages.submit: Literary argument and genre self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the expectation
stages.instructions: Give a reader the first entry before the others and record a prediction. If alone, write three plausible predictions before rereading the ending. Revise one later detail so the change is prepared by evidence rather than a concealed fact introduced only at the end.
stages.submit: Prediction record and a foreshadowing revision.

stages.title: Reflect on classification
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what your final genre makes visible and what it still obscures. Identify an action that remains open to moral judgment despite the changed expectation. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: The reader’s recovered library
projects.artifact: Original story with three fictional source fragments
projects.brief: Invent a reader who finds three incompatible accounts of how a person should live. Create the fragments as well as the story of their use. The reader must borrow, misunderstand, and revise something from each, making intertextuality an action within the narrative.
topics: A story mistaken for an instruction
Self-knowledge shaped by an unsuitable model
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Follow the borrowed models
stages.instructions: Chart the creature’s response to Werter, Plutarch, and Paradise Lost. For each, identify an attraction, a limit of understanding, and an effect on his self-description. Explain one comparison that changes when its differences become apparent.
stages.submit: Three-book chart with six quotations or precise references.

stages.title: Build the recovered texts
stages.instructions: Write three original fragments of 180–250 words: a civic biography, an intimate letter, and a creation tale. Then write a 1,000–1,300-word story in which one reader encounters all three. Repeat one phrase from each fragment in the story with a changed meaning, and let one misreading produce a material consequence.
stages.submit: Three fictional sources and an original story.

stages.title: Annotate the library
stages.instructions: Design six facing-page spreads or a six-panel digital equivalent. Place fragments beside the reader’s marginal notes at two different moments. Use a clear key to distinguish source, first response, and later revision; provide a linear transcript.
stages.submit: Annotated library and accessible transcript.

stages.title: Argue the transformation
stages.instructions: Write a 700–900-word analysis of how the creature’s reading develops his relation to his creator and to human society. Add 350 words tracing your three repeated phrases and explaining the consequential misreading.
stages.submit: Source argument and intertextual self-analysis.

stages.title: Test attribution

stages.submit: Attribution audit and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on influence
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why a text can shape a person without being fully understood or faithfully followed. State what your fictional fragments cannot establish about any real tradition and credit Shelley’s edition.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

projects.title: An afternoon entered in the household book
projects.brief: Create a fictional household whose social calendar depends on labor its official records barely acknowledge. A missed appointment should expose competing understandings of duty. Research one bounded historical custom, then use invention to explore its pressures without presenting the invented household as typical of an entire period.
topics: Respectability maintained through other people’s time
A private preference treated as a public failure
projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Separate text and context
stages.instructions: Read the Tuesday-reception passage. Record six details about time, clothing, cards, money, and work. Verify one contextual claim using the linked Kate Chopin International Society account and one additional reputable source you identify. Keep publication date, setting, and fictional events separate.
stages.submit: Evidence chart and two-source context note with links and access dates.

stages.title: Write the afternoon
stages.instructions: Write a 12–15-minute original one-room drama with four speaking roles: host, visitor, household worker, and someone whose appointment is displaced. Include a missed call, a written record, and one disagreement about whose time counts. Give each role a defensible immediate aim; avoid making any person merely a representative of a social category.
stages.submit: Script with stage directions and a 200-word historical/invented boundary note.

stages.title: Assemble the household book
stages.instructions: Design a calendar page, three calling cards, and a labor ledger for the same afternoon. Let two documents disagree about what happened or what mattered. Include readable transcripts and captions distinguishing researched convention from invented detail.
stages.submit: Five-document dossier with accessible text.

stages.title: Argue the social arrangement
stages.instructions: Write a 750–950-word analysis of how Chopin connects domestic routine with social and economic expectations. Add 300 words explaining how your drama and documents expose unequal demands without claiming universal historical experience.
stages.submit: Contextual argument and creative self-analysis.

projects.brief: Stage the same short speech for two different kinds of audience. projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the performance theory

stages.title: Score two versions

stages.title: Draw the rooms

stages.title: Defend the interpretation

projects.title: The room under three descriptions

projects.brief: Write one event three times through narrators attentive to different kinds of evidence. Keep the event’s factual sequence constant while changing what is noticed and explained. topics: Ownership and the right to leave

projects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Ask competing questions
stages.instructions: Read Jane’s exchange with Rochester. Form one question about resources and dependence, one about gender and bodily freedom, and one about the narrator’s retrospective construction. Answer each with two details and identify a resistant detail for each initial answer.

stages.title: Write the triptych

stages.title: Design the viewing guide

stages.title: Argue the interaction

stages.title: Test the facts

stages.submit: Continuity test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on lenses
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why no single account exhausts the event without claiming that all accounts are equally supported. Name the evidence that limits one narrator’s interpretation and credit sources.

stages.title: Write the continuation

stages.title: Make the whole-work case

projects.title: The council before the return
projects.artifact: Deliberation drama with competing decision records
projects.brief: Invent a group deciding whether to continue an ambitious undertaking after an unexpected cost. Write arguments strong enough that a responsible reader could initially favor either course. Separate the decision reached from the values that remain unresolved after it.

stages.title: Build both readings

stages.title: Write the council

stages.title: Make the decision table

stages.title: Argue with the alternative

stages.title: Test fairness

stages.title: Read the changing response

stages.submit: Six annotations and an initial analytical draft.

stages.title: Compose and revise the scene

stages.title: Build the critical edition

stages.submit: Four-spread edition, eight notes, and accessible final texts.

stages.title: Explain the decisions

stages.title: Test the new reading

stages.submit: Version comparison and a documented final decision.

projects.title: The testament with an unfinished wish

projects.brief: Invent a person who warns a successor against a consuming desire while leaving something that keeps the desire alive. topics: A legacy that contradicts its instructions
Care expressed through a dangerous inheritance

stages.title: Trace the qualifications

stages.title: Write the testament

Include a warning, an acknowledgment of harm, a justified obligation, and an object or instruction that preserves the warned-against desire. stages.title: Design the inheritance

stages.title: Sustain the tension

stages.title: Test the complexity

stages.title: Reflect on limits

classicalProjects.brief: Read Pride and Prejudice in full, then build a fictional correspondence in which invitations distribute opportunity, embarrassment, and influence. Family loyalty in conflict with social ambition

stages.title: Read the network

stages.title: Compose the correspondence
stages.instructions: Invent a community of five people linked by a contested invitation. Write seven letters of 180–250 words in at least three distinct voices. End with a 250-word scene that tests the correspondence against action.

stages.title: Draw the atlas

stages.title: Argue the pattern
stages.instructions: Write an 850–1,100-word argument about how encounters and revised judgments shape the novel’s treatment of social value. Use at least four source episodes and address one case where judgment does not improve. Add 350 words analyzing three voice choices in your letters.

stages.title: Test the information

classicalProjects.title: The archive of a disputed creation
classicalProjects.artifact: Nested fictional archive with an accountability hearing
classicalProjects.brief: Read the complete novel, including Walton’s letters. Construct an archive in which a maker, a made being, and a recorder disagree about responsibility. The central problem is who can describe an obligation and who has power to make that description count.
topics: Care after an act of creation
A testimony preserved by an interested editor
Ambition that transfers risk to others
classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Audit the frames
stages.instructions: Choose six moments distributed among Walton, Victor, and the creature. Record who speaks, who records the speech, what the speaker wants, and what another account complicates. Include the crew’s demand and Victor’s final advice.
stages.submit: Six-entry frame and responsibility chart.

stages.title: Write the archive
stages.instructions: Invent a nonhuman creation in an original setting. Write a 450-word maker’s statement, a 650-word created being’s narrative, a 350-word recorder’s letter, and a 500-word hearing transcript where their claims meet. Give each voice a legitimate concern and an omission; avoid reproducing Shelley’s plot under new names.
stages.submit: Four-document fictional archive.

stages.title: Design the provenance
stages.instructions: Create an archive box or six-screen equivalent showing how documents were received, edited, and arranged. Mark three interventions by the recorder and supply both an edited sequence and a readable account of what was changed.
stages.submit: Archive design, provenance labels, and accessible text.

stages.title: Argue responsibility
stages.instructions: Write a 900–1,150-word argument about how narrative framing complicates the novel’s assignment of responsibility. Use evidence from all three narrative levels. Add 350 words explaining how your recorder changes the force of two other voices.
stages.submit: Whole-novel argument and editorial self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the hearing
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to identify the strongest obligation each speaker acknowledges and one each evades. If alone, make the three cases separately after a break. Revise one overly convenient omission and one voice whose position is weaker than its evidence permits.
stages.submit: Three-position test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on custody
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain the difference between preserving a voice and giving it authority. Identify an unresolved duty in your archive and credit the 1831-form source edition and any research.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

classicalProjects.title: A house with rooms the narrator cannot enter
classicalProjects.artifact: Architectural novella and a boundary commentary
classicalProjects.brief: Read Jane Eyre in full. Design an original house whose rooms regulate work, intimacy, knowledge, and freedom, then tell a story through three visits to it. Examine the retrospective narrator’s authority as carefully as the restrictions imposed by the house.
topics: A place remembered differently after departure
Privacy protected for one person and denied to another
classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the thresholds
stages.instructions: Trace six rooms or thresholds across Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Moor House, and Ferndean. Record access, authority, and Jane’s retrospective language. Include a passage that limits what Jane can know about another person; do not convert her account into that person’s complete interior life.
stages.submit: Six-space evidence chart and a 200-word narrative-limit note.

stages.title: Compose three visits
stages.instructions: Write a 1,600–2,000-word original story in three sections: entry, return, and departure. One narrator revisits an invented house at three life stages. Repeat two rooms and one sound with changed meanings. Give a person with restricted access a consequential action while preserving uncertainty about what the narrator cannot know.
stages.submit: Three-part architectural story.

stages.title: Build the house book
stages.instructions: Draw three floor plans or paper cross-sections corresponding to the visits. Mark permitted and forbidden routes, annotate six changes, and include one blank area explicitly labeled as unknown rather than filled with invented certainty. Provide text routes.
stages.submit: House book with six annotations and accessible descriptions.

stages.title: Argue the boundary
stages.instructions: Write a 900–1,150-word argument about how spaces and retrospective narration develop the novel’s treatment of autonomy. Address a limit or exclusion in that account. Add 350 words analyzing your repeated rooms, sound, and unknown area.
stages.submit: Whole-novel argument and spatial self-analysis.

stages.title: Test perspective
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to distinguish observed fact, inference, and admitted ignorance in the story. If alone, mark these after a day. Revise a passage that accidentally grants the narrator impossible knowledge and a repeated detail whose function remains unchanged.
stages.submit: Perspective audit and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on dwelling
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what the final departure makes possible and what it leaves unresolved. Discuss why representing another person’s exclusion does not authorize inventing that person’s entire experience. Credit sources.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

classicalProjects.title: The museum of borrowed distinctions
classicalProjects.artifact: Object biography, illustrated catalogue, and a restitution scene
classicalProjects.brief: Read Great Expectations in full. Create a fictional museum of objects whose prestige conceals the labor or sacrifice that produced them. The collection’s labels must change as its curator learns where the objects came from.
topics: Status built from another person’s work
Shame attached to a useful object
Gratitude that cannot restore lost time
classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Follow material histories
stages.instructions: Choose five objects or material details from different stages of Pip’s life. Trace possession, value, and a changed judgment. Include evidence involving Joe and Magwitch, and distinguish Pip’s earlier feelings from the older narrator’s account.
stages.submit: Five-object source dossier with at least eight chapter references.

stages.title: Write the biographies
stages.instructions: Invent five objects belonging to one fictional collector. Write a 200-word official label and a 200-word recovered history for each. Then write a 600–800-word scene in which the collector attempts restitution and encounters a limit that money or apology cannot remove.
stages.submit: Ten object texts and a restitution scene.

stages.title: Curate the display
stages.instructions: Design a five-case exhibition with the official and recovered accounts readable in a deliberate order. Use placement, scale, or material contrast to make one discrepancy visible in each case. Supply object descriptions and a linear catalogue.
stages.submit: Exhibition plan and accessible catalogue.

stages.title: Argue value
stages.instructions: Write a 900–1,150-word argument about how the novel revises the relation among gentility, labor, and gratitude. Use at least four episodes, including a later response that complicates earlier shame. Add 350 words explaining how the exhibition changes the value of two objects.
stages.submit: Whole-novel essay and curatorial self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the recovery

stages.submit: Display test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on repair
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, distinguish acknowledgment, repayment, and repair. Explain which your collector achieves and which remains incomplete. Credit the source edition and any borrowed visual materials.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

classicalProjects.title: The score of an interrupted day
classicalProjects.brief: Read The Awakening in full, distinguishing it from the additional stories in this volume. Invent a day whose desired freedom depends on other people’s schedules and labor. Use recurring sounds to connect private awareness with a social world that continues beyond the central character.
topics: Solitude made possible by someone else’s work
Desire that alters the meaning of familiar sounds
Freedom imagined differently by connected people
classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace recurring sound
stages.instructions: Select six moments involving music, voices, silence, or the sea across the novel. Explain their changing relation to Edna’s awareness and obligations. Include two scenes where another person’s needs complicate an account centered only on her wishes.
stages.submit: Six-moment sound and obligation chart.

stages.title: Compose the daybook
stages.instructions: Write eight time-stamped entries totaling 1,500–1,900 words across one fictional day. Use three voices with distinct aims, repeat two sounds at least three times, and let an interruption change the day’s outcome. Give every voice an action that affects another person rather than serving only as commentary.
stages.submit: Polyphonic daybook and a voice key.

stages.title: Score the day
stages.instructions: Create a visual sound score with time, location, and voice tracks. Annotate six recurrences or silences and identify whose labor sustains each apparently private moment. An audio version is optional; provide a transcript and non-audio description.
stages.submit: Sound score and accessible reading version.

stages.title: Argue the relation
stages.instructions: Write an 850–1,100-word argument about how recurrent sound and social relations complicate the novel’s treatment of selfhood. Address its ending without reducing it to a single universal lesson. Add 350 words explaining your voice distribution and two transformed sounds.
stages.submit: Whole-novel interpretation and compositional self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the voices
stages.instructions: Ask a reader to state each voice’s aim and track a sound’s changing function. If alone, separate the entries by voice after a day. Revise one voice that exists only to support the protagonist and one recurrence that is decorative.
stages.submit: Voice-and-sound test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on autonomy
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain how the daybook makes dependence visible without denying a desire for autonomy. Identify a perspective it cannot fully represent. Credit the novel, contextual research, and any recordings.
stages.submit: Reflection and credits.

stages.title: Write two registers

stages.title: Design the changing surface

classicalProjects.artifact: Three linked tales and a disputed curator’s catalogue
classicalProjects.brief: Read “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” and “The Fall of the House of Usher” in full. Create three short tales linked by one museum object, each with a narrator whose attempt to explain events creates a different problem of trust.

stages.title: Distinguish unreliability
stages.instructions: For each story, select three details establishing the narrator’s purpose, knowledge, and limits. Explain a different source of uncertainty in each; do not assume every narrator is unreliable in the same way or invent a clinical diagnosis.

stages.title: Write the linked tales
stages.instructions: Invent one object and write three 550–700-word tales about its successive owners. Use confession, recollection, and eyewitness report as different forms. stages.submit: Three tales and a curator’s introduction.

stages.title: Assemble the cabinet
stages.instructions: Design an object display with three labels, a provenance trail, and a sealed or missing item whose absence has a specific evidentiary effect. Provide an image description and a chronological list of established facts separate from claims.
stages.submit: Cabinet design and accessible evidence inventory.

stages.title: Argue narrative pressure
stages.instructions: Write an 850–1,100-word comparison of how the three Poe stories make explanation itself disclose limitations. Use two details from each story. Add 350 words distinguishing the reliability problem in each original tale.
stages.submit: Comparative argument and narrative self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the shared facts

stages.submit: Reliability test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on confidence
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain why confidence, detail, or eloquence does not independently establish truth in your cabinet. Identify a fact that remains stable despite disagreement and credit each source story.

classicalProjects.title: The court watches itself
classicalProjects.artifact: Surveillance play, cue book, and audience diagram
classicalProjects.brief: Read Hamlet in full. Invent a court, workplace, or household in which people stage encounters to discover what others know. topics: A test that changes the evidence it seeks

classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Trace the watchers

stages.title: Write the play
stages.instructions: Write a 15–18-minute original play with four or five roles and two arranged encounters. One character must know they are watched in the first encounter but misjudge the observer in the second. Include a short performance within the play and an ending in which a decision exceeds the available certainty.
stages.submit: Original script with complete stage directions.

stages.title: Prepare the cue book

stages.title: Argue the test

stages.submit: Whole-play argument and theatrical self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the audience

stages.submit: Knowledge test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on certainty
stages.instructions: In 200–250 words, explain what your final decision resolves and what it cannot establish. Identify a cost of making another person the object of a test and credit the edition and production sources.

classicalProjects.title: The household’s unwritten agreement

classicalProjects.brief: Read all three acts of A Doll’s House in the linked translation. Invent a household whose members believe they have agreed on its obligations but discover that their definitions differ. Education required before a relationship can be freely chosen

stages.title: Read the terms

stages.title: Write the rupture

stages.title: Make the manuals

stages.title: Argue the relationship

stages.submit: Ending test and two revisions.

stages.title: Reflect on consent

classicalProjects.title: Two songs for one institution
classicalProjects.artifact: Paired illuminated poems and a reader’s counterpage
classicalProjects.brief: Read “The Lamb,” “The Tiger,” both “Chimney-Sweeper” poems, “London,” and “The Garden of Love.” Create paired songs about an invented institution whose promises and effects can be understood differently by two speakers. topics: A comforting explanation that conceals a cost
Innocence as insight as well as vulnerability
classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read the paired voices
stages.instructions: Compare the two chimney-sweeper poems, then connect their differences to four details from the other assigned poems. stages.submit: Comparison chart with eight textual details and an edition note.

stages.title: Compose the songs

Repeat a refrain with changed implications, use a declared stanza and rhyme pattern, and let each speaker perceive something the other misses. Add a 16–24-line third poem that questions a shared assumption without settling every dispute.
stages.submit: Three original poems and speaking-situation notes.

stages.title: Illuminate the disagreement

stages.submit: Three illuminated pages and accessible texts.

stages.title: Argue the relation

stages.submit: Comparative argument and illuminated-poetry self-analysis.

stages.title: Test the voices

stages.title: Reflect on pairing

A boundary between knowing and imagining
Consolation interrupted by a small perception

stages.title: Compose the fascicle

stages.submit: Six-poem collection and two controlled variants.

stages.title: Bind the pocket book

stages.title: Argue the uncertainty

stages.title: Test the variants

stages.title: Reflect on editing

classicalProjects.title: A lyric atlas of divided belonging
classicalProjects.brief: Read “The Harlem Dancer,” “Harlem Shadows,” “The Tropics in New York,” “America,” “Outcast,” “If We Must Die,” and “The White City.” Create a poetry cycle about belonging to a place that both sustains and excludes a fictional speaker. Use specific imagined circumstances rather than borrowing an identity as a costume.
topics: Attachment to a place that imposes a cost
Public visibility and an inward life withheld from spectators
classicalProjects.time: Five to eight work sessions, plus reading

stages.title: Read divided attachment
stages.instructions: Choose six details across at least five assigned poems that complicate a single emotional label. Trace address, form, and perspective, distinguishing speaker from author and introductory commentary from the poems. Include a detail where observation does not grant access to another person’s inner life.
stages.submit: Six-detail comparative map with poem titles and line references.

stages.title: Compose the cycle
stages.instructions: Invent a speaker with a specific relation to an imagined town or district. Write five poems totaling 100–140 lines: one sonnet, one address, one object-centered lyric, one street scene, and one departure or return. Give the speaker a stake beyond a general desire to belong and let one poem correct an assumption made in another.
stages.submit: Five-poem cycle and a 200-word speaking-position note.

stages.title: Draw the counter-map
stages.instructions: Create a map with five locations corresponding to the poems. Overlay remembered, permitted, and desired routes using labels as well as visual distinctions. Add a six-line caption at each location and provide a text itinerary.
stages.submit: Lyric atlas and accessible route descriptions.

stages.title: Argue the doubleness
stages.instructions: Write an 850–1,100-word comparison of how McKay’s formal choices and images sustain divided attachment in three poems. Add 350 words explaining your cycle’s correction, its formal variety, and the limits of its speaker’s knowledge.
stages.submit: Comparative argument and lyric self-analysis.
